n.1: Six months of meetings shows effort, but the clues next to succinct describe how short the report was, not how it was researched.
n.2: This matches a nearby word, "clarity," which describes a separate quality the board praised. The clues tied to succinct are about length.
n.3: Nothing describes the tone of the recommendations; the passage focuses on the report's length.

Craft & Structure.q:
Charge nurse Angela Morris is writing an annual review for Kayla Brooks, a nurse on her unit. When a patient's pain medication is late or a test result is missing, Kayla calls the pharmacy or the lab again and again until the problem is solved. Angela wants the review to praise this habit. She drafts the sentence, "Kayla is ______ when she advocates for her patients."

Which word best completes the sentence in a way that matches Angela's purpose?
o: obstinate
nagging
pushy
tenacious
Craft & Structure.w: All four words describe someone who keeps pressing, so their denotations overlap. Only "tenacious" carries a positive connotation (admirably determined), which fits a sentence meant to praise.

n.0: "Obstinate" suggests unreasonable stubbornness, a negative connotation that would criticize rather than praise.
n.1: "Nagging" suggests annoying, repeated complaining, which is negative.
n.2: "Pushy" describes the same behavior with a negative connotation of being rude or overbearing.

Craft & Structure.q:
I still remember Sunday mornings in my grandmother's kitchen: the radio playing gospel music, the smell of biscuits and coffee, and the yellow curtains she sewed herself. My cousins and I would crowd around the table while she told stories about growing up in Georgia. Grandma is ninety now and lives in a bright apartment near my parents, but whenever I smell fresh biscuits, I am eight years old again, waiting for the first one to cool.

Which word best describes the tone of the passage?
o: mournful
indifferent
humorous
nostalgic
Craft & Structure.w: The author recalls a cherished past with warm sensory details and a longing to return to it ("I am eight years old again"). A fond, wistful attitude toward the past is a nostalgic tone.

n.0: "Mournful" suggests grief over a loss. The grandmother is alive and well, and the memories are warm rather than sad.
n.1: "Indifferent" means not caring, but the vivid, affectionate details show the author cares deeply.
n.2: The passage is warm, not joking; no detail is meant to make the reader laugh.

Craft & Structure.q:
The Westside Free Clinic runs on a modest budget. Its two exam rooms share a single blood pressure machine, and most of the staff are volunteers who give one evening a week. Even so, the clinic saw more than 2,000 patients last year, and its director, Dr. Samuel Price, hopes to add a dental chair next spring if a local foundation approves his grant request.

The author describes the clinic's budget as "modest" rather than "meager." What is the effect of this word choice?
o: It suggests that the budget is too small to run the clinic.
It presents the small budget in a respectful light.
It suggests that the budget has grown since last year.
It makes the dollar amount of the budget more precise.
Craft & Structure.w: Both words mean small (similar denotation). "Modest" has a neutral-to-positive connotation of simple and unpretentious, while "meager" suggests a pitiful shortage. The choice frames the clinic with respect, which fits the author's admiring account of what it achieves.

n.0: That is the connotation of "meager," the word the author avoided; the passage stresses what the clinic accomplishes despite its size.
n.2: Neither word refers to change over time; the passage gives no information about last year's budget.
n.3: Neither word states an amount; the choice affects the feeling of the description, not its precision.

Craft & Structure.q:
Council member Ray Delgado has served the Third Ward for twelve years. Supporters call him resourceful, pointing to the new library he funded by combining three small state grants. His critics see a crafty politician who trades favors behind closed doors. Both sides agree that he is experienced and practical, and few people expect anyone to challenge him in the next election.

Which word from the passage carries a negative connotation?
o: resourceful
crafty
practical
experienced
Craft & Structure.w: "Crafty" means clever, but it suggests cunning or sneaky behavior. The critics use it alongside "trades favors behind closed doors," which confirms the negative connotation.

n.0: "Resourceful" also means clever at solving problems, but it carries a positive connotation; supporters use it as praise.
n.2: "Practical" is neutral to positive, suggesting sensible, realistic choices.
n.3: "Experienced" is neutral to positive; both sides use it as a fair description.

Craft & Structure.q:
The company claims its new wristband can detect dehydration before the wearer feels thirsty. Perhaps it can. But the company has not released any test data, and the two reviewers who wore the device during the same workout got readings that differed by 30 percent. Until an independent lab checks these claims, I would hold off on spending $199 for one. I'll believe it when I see the numbers.

Which word best describes the author's tone?
o: hostile
cynical
pessimistic
skeptical
Craft & Structure.w: The author doubts the claim but stays open to evidence ("Perhaps it can," "I'll believe it when I see the numbers"). Doubt that waits for proof is a skeptical tone.

n.0: "Hostile" suggests anger or attack; the author's language is measured and practical.
n.1: A cynical writer distrusts people's motives and assumes the worst. This author does not accuse the company of lying and allows that the device might work.
n.2: "Pessimistic" means expecting a bad outcome. The author withholds judgment until data arrive instead of predicting failure.

Craft & Structure.q:
After 34 years at Riverside Hospital, Nurse Paulette Greene retired last Friday. Former students lined the hallway to thank her. Many said they still hear her voice when they check an IV line. She was famous for her candid feedback: if a student's technique was wrong, she said so plainly, then stayed until the student got it right. "She told me the truth when I needed it most," one former student said.

Which word could replace candid without changing the author's admiring tone?
o: tactless
honest
brutal
blunt
Craft & Structure.w: "Honest" keeps both the meaning (saying things plainly and truthfully) and the positive connotation that fits an admiring tribute.

n.0: "Tactless" means insensitive to others' feelings, a clearly negative connotation that clashes with the praise.
n.2: "Brutal" suggests harshness or cruelty, which contradicts the patient teacher who stayed until students succeeded.
n.3: "Blunt" shares the meaning of speaking plainly, but it suggests abruptness or lack of tact, which would add a critical edge to the tribute.

Craft & Structure.q:
Ever since the new neighbor moved in, Mrs. Abbott has watched him from behind her curtains. "He's a scrawny young man," she told her sister, "and nosy, too. He asked me how long I'd lived here." Her sister laughed. "He sounds curious and friendly to me. And didn't you say he was lean and fit, out jogging every morning?" Mrs. Abbott frowned. "He rides that bicycle like a reckless child." Her sister shrugged. "Or like an adventurous one."

Which words from the passage carry a negative connotation? Select all that apply.
o: adventurous
curious
lean
reckless
scrawny
nosy
Craft & Structure.w: Mrs. Abbott chooses words with negative connotations: "scrawny" (unhealthily thin), "nosy" (intrusive) and "reckless" (dangerously careless). Her sister describes the same traits with positive words.

n.0: "Adventurous" describes the same willingness to take risks as "reckless" but suggests an appealing love of excitement, a positive connotation.
n.1: "Curious" names the same interest in others as "nosy" but with a positive connotation of healthy interest.
n.2: "Lean" describes the same thin build as "scrawny" but suggests fitness, a positive connotation.

Craft & Structure.q:
Last month, Lakeside Medical Center raised its parking fee for visitors to $28 a day. Families sitting at the bedsides of seriously ill loved ones, many of whom visit every day for weeks, now pay more than $800 a month simply to be present. The hospital made the change without a single public notice. This is an outrage, and the board owes these families an explanation and a refund.

Which word best describes the author's tone toward the hospital's decision?
o: resigned
indignant
sympathetic
sarcastic
Craft & Structure.w: "An outrage" and the demand for an explanation and a refund express anger at something the author considers unjust. Angry protest at an unfair act is an indignant tone.

n.0: "Resigned" means accepting something unwelcome as unavoidable, but the author demands that the board act.
n.2: The author does show sympathy, but toward the families. The question asks about the tone toward the hospital's decision, which is angry, not sympathetic.
n.3: Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant; the author states the complaint directly.

Craft & Structure.q:
In a report on a hospital's new staffing model, the author writes: "Letting nurses design their own schedules through a shared online calendar is a bold experiment, and early results are encouraging. Overtime fell by 18 percent in the first quarter, and fewer nurses left the unit."

By calling the staffing model "a bold experiment," the author suggests that the model is
o: a daring new approach that deserves credit.
a careless gamble with nurses' schedules.
a proven method that other units already use.
a costly plan that the hospital should reconsider.
Craft & Structure.w: "Bold" carries a positive connotation of admirable daring, and "experiment" marks the model as new and untested. Together with "early results are encouraging," the word choice presents the model as a risk worth praising.

n.1: "Careless gamble" gives risk-taking a negative connotation. The author calls the results "encouraging," so the attitude is approving, not critical.
n.2: "Experiment" and "early results" show the model is new and still being tested, so it is not presented as proven or borrowed from other units.
n.3: The passage reports falling overtime and fewer nurses leaving and raises no cost concern, so nothing suggests the hospital should reconsider.

Craft & Structure.q:
Starting March 1, the county health department will require all restaurant employees who handle food to complete a two-hour safety course. The course is offered online and in person, costs $15 and covers handwashing, safe cooking temperatures and food storage.

Restaurant owners, do not wait. Classes are already filling up, and any employee without a certificate after March 1 will be barred from the kitchen. Sign your staff up today.

Which of the following best describes how the tone changes from the first paragraph to the second?
o: It moves from humorous to serious.
It moves from optimistic to pessimistic.
It moves from critical to celebratory.
It moves from objective to urgent.
Craft & Structure.w: The first paragraph reports the rule's details neutrally. The second uses commands ("do not wait," "sign your staff up today") and a warning about filling classes, which creates urgency.

n.0: The first paragraph contains no humor; it lists dates, costs and topics.
n.1: Neither paragraph expresses hope or gloom about the outcome; the second paragraph pushes for quick action rather than predicting a bad result.
n.2: Neither paragraph criticizes the rule or celebrates it; the shift is from reporting to pressing for action.

Craft & Structure.q:
A copywriter is preparing an advertisement for a discount pharmacy. Her first draft calls the store's generic vitamins "inexpensive." Her manager asks her to look for a word that means the same thing as inexpensive but that shoppers might read as an insult to the product's quality, so that she can be sure to avoid it in the final version.

Which word should the copywriter avoid?
o: shoddy
low-cost
cheap
affordable
Craft & Structure.w: "Cheap" shares the denotation of low price but often suggests poor quality, a negative connotation the manager wants to avoid.

n.0: "Shoddy" does insult the product's quality, but it means badly made, not low in price. It fails the manager's first test: it does not mean the same thing as inexpensive.
n.1: "Low-cost" states the low price in neutral terms and suggests nothing about quality.
n.3: "Affordable" means low in price with a positive connotation of good value, so it would not insult the product.

Craft & Structure.q:
To: Billing Department Staff
Subject: Forms (again)

As I have now explained at three separate meetings, completed insurance forms go in the blue tray, not the red one. I realize this may be a lot for some of you to keep track of, so I have taped a large, colorful sign above each tray with an arrow pointing to the right one. If anyone is still unsure, please feel free to stop by my office, and I will walk you through it slowly.

Which word best describes the tone of the memo?
o: lighthearted
accommodating
condescending
apologetic
Craft & Structure.w: Phrases such as "a lot for some of you to keep track of," the "large, colorful sign" and "walk you through it slowly" suggest the staff cannot handle a simple task. Talking down to the reader is a condescending tone.

n.0: The memo is not playful or trying to amuse; its mockery is aimed at the staff's abilities.
n.1: The offer of help looks accommodating on the surface, but "(again)," "three separate meetings" and "slowly" show irritation and talking down, not a genuine wish to help.
n.3: The writer apologizes for nothing; the memo places the blame on the staff.

Craft & Structure.q:
By 9 p.m. on Saturday, the emergency room was a beehive. Nurses moved quickly from bay to bay, phones rang at the front desk, and a steady line of patients waited to be checked in. Dr. Imani Carter, working her fourth night in a row, kept a list of every patient on a clipboard so that no one would be missed.

The phrase "the emergency room was a beehive" is an example of which of the following?
o: personification
simile
hyperbole
metaphor
Craft & Structure.w: The sentence says the room "was" a beehive, comparing the busy room to a hive directly, without "like" or "as." A direct comparison of this kind is a metaphor.

n.0: Personification gives human traits to something non-human. The room is compared to a hive; it is not given human actions or feelings.
n.1: A simile makes the comparison with "like" or "as" ("busy as a beehive"); this sentence has neither word.
n.2: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration. The comparison conveys the busy activity, which the details show is accurate rather than overstated.

Craft & Structure.q:
The research team had spent four months collecting blood samples from 200 volunteers. Then, during a power outage, the freezer that stored the samples failed overnight, and every sample was ruined. When the lead researcher, Dr. Kim, called the team together the next morning, she admitted that they were back to square one. Within a week, the team had begun recruiting new volunteers.

As used in the passage, the phrase "back to square one" means that the team was
o: returned to its original laboratory.
forced to start the work over.
waiting for the power to return.
blamed for losing the samples.
Craft & Structure.w: The idiom means having to start again from the beginning. The ruined samples and the team's decision to recruit new volunteers confirm that the work had to restart.

n.0: This reads the idiom literally as a place; the passage never mentions the team moving anywhere.
n.2: The outage had already happened; the idiom describes the loss of progress, not a wait for power.
n.3: No one is blamed; the freezer failed during a power outage.

Craft & Structure.q:
On the third day after surgery, the nurse removed Mr. Osei's bandage and checked the incision. The edges had closed, the surrounding skin was only slightly pink, and there was no discharge on the gauze. She recorded that the wound was healing well and told him that the stitches could come out at his follow-up visit.

As used in the passage, the word discharge most nearly means
o: a gap between the edges of a cut.
official release from the hospital.
redness of the skin around a wound.
fluid released from a wound.
Craft & Structure.w: The nurse is examining the gauze over an incision, so the word refers to fluid such as pus or blood coming from the wound. Its absence is a sign of healing.

n.0: The passage says separately that the edges had closed. A gap in the incision is not something that would appear on the gauze.
n.1: Release from the hospital is the most common meaning in a hospital setting, but the word here describes something that would appear on gauze.
n.2: The passage describes the skin's color separately ("only slightly pink"); discharge is something found on the gauze, not a color of the skin.

Craft & Structure.q:
The night shift on 6 North began quietly. A cold rain streaked the windows, and the hallway lights hummed overhead. At the nurses' station, an old coffee maker grumbled its way through one more pot. By midnight, the call lights were blinking at a steady pace, and Nurse Diaz had already walked what felt like ten miles.

Which phrase from the passage is an example of personification?
o: the hallway lights hummed overhead
walked what felt like ten miles
grumbled its way through one more pot
the call lights were blinking at a steady pace
Craft & Structure.w: To grumble is a human action (complaining in a low, irritated voice). Giving the coffee maker this human behavior is personification.

n.0: Lights and machines literally hum; this describes a real sound, not a human action.
n.1: This is hyperbole, an exaggeration of how far she walked, not a human trait given to an object.
n.3: Call lights really do blink; this is a literal description of the signals, not a human trait given to an object.

Craft & Structure.q:
Journal entry, week one of clinical rotations: By the end of my first twelve-hour shift, my feet weighed a thousand pounds. I had taken vital signs on eleven patients, helped turn a man who had just come out of surgery, and answered more call lights than I could count. I sat in my car in the parking garage for twenty minutes before I had the energy to drive home.

The author most likely writes that her feet "weighed a thousand pounds" in order to
o: show that she worked longer than planned.
emphasize how exhausted she felt.
compare nursing with heavy lifting work.
describe swelling caused by an injury.
Craft & Structure.w: The statement is hyperbole, a deliberate exaggeration. Together with sitting in the car for twenty minutes before she could drive, it emphasizes extreme tiredness.

n.0: The shift is described as twelve hours with no sign that it ran over; the phrase is about how she felt, not about the schedule.
n.2: She does turn a patient, but the phrase describes her own fatigue rather than comparing nursing to another job.
n.3: This reads the exaggeration literally; nothing in the entry describes an injury.

Craft & Structure.q:
The storm had knocked out the power for the third time that afternoon. Water was dripping from a crack in the kitchen ceiling into a row of mixing bowls, the basement was flooding, and the phone battery was at four percent. Marcus looked around the dark, damp room, sighed, and said to his sister, "Well, this is turning out to be a relaxing weekend."

Marcus's statement is an example of which of the following?
o: hyperbole
verbal irony
personification
situational irony
Craft & Structure.w: Marcus says the weekend is "relaxing" when he means the opposite. Saying one thing while meaning its opposite is verbal irony.

n.0: Hyperbole exaggerates the truth; Marcus reverses the truth rather than overstating it.
n.2: Marcus gives no human traits to an object; he comments on his own weekend.
n.3: Situational irony is an outcome that is the opposite of what is expected. The storm is unfortunate, but the irony here lies in Marcus's words, not in an unexpected outcome.

Craft & Structure.q:
In October, a regional pharmacy chain launched a campaign urging customers to get their flu shots early. The company hired a well-known local news anchor to appear in its ads, which showed her smiling as she rolled up her sleeve. On the day the campaign was set to launch, the anchor was unable to attend the kickoff event. She was home in bed with the flu.

Which of the following best describes the final two sentences of the passage?
o: They foreshadow a later event by hinting at what will happen to the campaign.
They create dramatic irony, because the reader knows something the anchor does not.
They create situational irony, because the outcome contradicts expectations.
They create verbal irony, because the anchor says the opposite of what she means.
Craft & Structure.w: The face of a campaign to prevent flu catches the flu on launch day. An outcome that contradicts what the situation leads us to expect is situational irony.

n.0: The passage ends with the outcome; it hints at no future event, so this is not foreshadowing.
n.1: Dramatic irony requires the reader to know something a character does not; here the reader learns about the flu at the same moment as the outcome is revealed.
n.3: The anchor says nothing in the passage, so there are no words that could mean the opposite of their literal sense.

Craft & Structure.q:
Ms. Patel came to the clinic with a sore throat and a fever of 101.8 degrees. The nurse practitioner swabbed the back of her throat and explained that the lab would culture the sample to see whether strep bacteria were present. Results would be ready in about 48 hours, and Ms. Patel was asked to rest at home until then.

As used in the passage, the word culture most nearly means
o: study the customs of a group.
grow microorganisms for testing.
kill germs on equipment and surfaces.
improve through education.
Craft & Structure.w: The lab is checking whether bacteria are present in a throat sample, and results take 48 hours. In this context, to culture means to grow microorganisms from a sample so they can be identified.

n.0: This is the most common meaning of culture (the customs and arts of a people), but it does not fit a lab testing a throat swab.
n.2: Killing germs is the opposite of what the lab needs; it wants any bacteria in the sample to grow so they can be identified.
n.3: "Cultured" can describe a person refined by education, a meaning unrelated to a lab sample.

Craft & Structure.q:
Monday mornings in the hospital admissions office are organized chaos. The phones ring nonstop, and the line at the front desk stretches like a ribbon to the main doors. Clerks wade through a sea of paperwork while the old printer in the corner coughs out one form after another. Somehow, every patient is registered by noon.

Which phrase from the passage is an oxymoron?
o: organized chaos
a sea of paperwork
stretches like a ribbon
coughs out one form
Craft & Structure.w: An oxymoron joins two words with opposite meanings. "Organized" and "chaos" contradict each other, and together they capture an office that is busy and messy yet still gets the job done.

n.1: This is a metaphor: it calls a large amount of paperwork a sea without using "like" or "as."
n.2: This is a simile: it compares the line to a ribbon using "like."
n.3: This is personification: coughing is a human action given to a printer.

Craft & Structure.q:
The hospital spent $2 million on new records software last year, and nurses were promised faster access to patient information. Instead, finding a single lab result now takes six clicks and two passwords, and the system logs users out after five minutes. For the nurses on the night shift, the new software has become a locked door between them and their patients.

In the final sentence, the author's description of the software as "a locked door" suggests that the software
o: keeps patient records more secure than before.
is closed to nurses who work the night shift.
blocks nurses from the information they need.
physically separates the nurses' station from rooms.
Craft & Structure.w: The details before the metaphor (six clicks, two passwords, frequent logouts) show nurses struggling to reach patient information. The "locked door" stands for that barrier.

n.0: Locks can suggest security, but the passage criticizes the software for slowing nurses down; it never praises its protection of records.
n.1: Night-shift nurses are mentioned as the group most affected, but they can still use the system; the passage describes difficulty, not a ban.
n.3: This reads the metaphor literally; the software is not a physical barrier between rooms.

Craft & Structure.q:
Read the sentences from a short story set in a pediatric clinic.

Her laugh rang out like a bell across the waiting room. By noon, the waiting room was an oven. The toddler was as restless as a puppy in a bathtub. Parents who would like a blanket for their child can ask at the desk. The old radiator groaned and complained all morning. The receptionist moved through the crowd like a seasoned conductor.

Which of the following sentences contain a simile? Select all that apply.
o: The toddler was as restless as a puppy in a bathtub.
Parents who would like a blanket for their child can ask at the desk.
The old radiator groaned and complained all morning.
By noon, the waiting room was an oven.
Her laugh rang out like a bell across the waiting room.
The receptionist moved through the crowd like a seasoned conductor.
Craft & Structure.w: A simile compares two unlike things using "like" or "as." The laugh is compared to a bell, the toddler to a puppy, and the receptionist to a conductor.

n.1: "Would like" means "want"; the word "like" here makes no comparison.
n.2: Groaning and complaining are human actions given to a radiator, which is personification.
n.3: This compares the room to an oven directly, without "like" or "as," so it is a metaphor.

Craft & Structure.q:
Hurricane Delia tore across Port Ellis last weekend with winds of 120 miles per hour. It ripped the roofs from more than half of the town's homes, flooded the only bridge to the mainland and left 9,000 residents without power. At a press conference on Monday, Mayor Teresa Ruiz looked at the crowd of reporters and said, "We've had a bit of a rough week."

The mayor's statement is an example of which of the following?
o: understatement
allusion
hyperbole
personification
Craft & Structure.w: Calling a devastating hurricane "a bit of a rough week" makes the situation sound far less serious than it is. Deliberately downplaying something is understatement.

n.1: An allusion refers to a well-known person, place, event or work; the mayor refers to none.
n.2: Hyperbole is the opposite: exaggerating to make something seem bigger. The mayor makes the disaster sound smaller.
n.3: Personification gives human traits to a non-human thing; the mayor describes the town's week without giving any object human qualities.

Craft & Structure.q:
To the Bellmont City Council:

Every school morning, about 300 students cross Route 6 to reach Lincoln Elementary. The road has no crosswalk within half a mile of the school, and cars there travel at an average of 41 miles per hour, according to the county's own traffic study. Last year, police recorded four collisions involving pedestrians on that stretch. A marked crosswalk with flashing lights would cost about $60,000, less than the city spent repaving the parking lot at City Hall. I urge you to fund it at your next meeting.

What is the author's primary purpose in this letter?
o: to describe the morning walk that students take to school
to persuade the council to install a crosswalk near the school
to inform readers about the county's traffic study on Route 6
to criticize the council for repaving the City Hall parking lot
Craft & Structure.w: The letter closes with a direct request ("I urge you to fund it"), and each fact is chosen to support that request. Facts that serve a claim make the purpose persuasive, not informative.

n.0: The students' crossing is mentioned to show the danger, not described in detail.
n.2: The traffic study is used as evidence for the request; the letter does not explain the study for its own sake.
n.3: The parking lot comparison is a single supporting point used to show the crosswalk is affordable; it is not the main aim of the letter.

Craft & Structure.q:
Most vaccines must be kept between 36 and 46 degrees Fahrenheit from the moment they leave the factory until they are given to a patient. This unbroken chain of refrigeration is called the cold chain. Vaccines travel in insulated containers with temperature monitors, and clinics store them in refrigerators that record the temperature every few minutes. If a reading falls outside the safe range, staff label the vaccines "do not use" and contact the state health department, which decides whether the doses can still be given.

What is the primary purpose of the passage?
o: to persuade readers to receive recommended vaccines
to explain how vaccines are kept safely cold
to criticize clinics that store vaccines incorrectly
to describe the history of vaccine refrigeration
Craft & Structure.w: The passage defines the cold chain and walks through how vaccines are shipped, stored, monitored and handled when a problem occurs. Its neutral, step-by-step explanation shows an informative purpose.

n.0: The topic is vaccines, but the passage never urges anyone to be vaccinated. Confusing the topic with the purpose leads to this choice.
n.2: The passage describes what staff do when temperatures go out of range; it does not fault any clinic.
n.3: No dates or past developments are given; the passage describes current practice.

Craft & Structure.q:
Our beagle, Biscuit, has never once come when called. But on Thanksgiving, as my uncle set the turkey on the counter and turned to find the carving knife, Biscuit materialized like a furry magician. By the time my uncle turned back, the turkey was gone, and so was the dog. We found them both under my parents' bed twenty minutes later: Biscuit asleep with his paws around a drumstick, looking prouder than any dog has a right to look. We had pizza for dinner. Biscuit had nothing to eat for the rest of the day, and he did not seem to mind.

What is the author's primary purpose in this passage?
o: to explain how to prepare a holiday meal for a large family
to entertain readers with a funny story about a family dog
to persuade readers to keep food out of a dog's reach
to inform readers about why beagles are hard to train
Craft & Structure.w: The passage tells a story with comic details (the "furry magician," the proud dog hugging a drumstick, pizza for Thanksgiving dinner) and makes no argument or lesson. Its purpose is to entertain.

n.0: The holiday meal is the setting of the story, not a set of instructions.
n.2: A reader might draw this lesson, but the author never urges it; the story is told for amusement.
n.3: The author mentions that Biscuit never comes when called, but offers no information about beagles as a breed or about training.

Craft & Structure.q:
When Rosa Jimenez, 58, felt a sudden ache in her jaw while gardening, she assumed she had pulled a muscle. Two hours later, she was in a cardiac unit. Rosa's experience is common. Women having a heart attack often notice symptoms other than chest pain, such as jaw or back pain, nausea, shortness of breath or unusual fatigue. Because these symptoms are less familiar, women often wait longer than men before seeking care. Doctors advise anyone with these symptoms to call 911 rather than drive to the hospital.

Why does the author most likely begin the passage with Rosa Jimenez's experience?
o: to show that jaw pain is the most common symptom in women
to entertain readers with a dramatic story
to draw readers in with a real example of the problem
to argue that gardening is risky for older adults
Craft & Structure.w: The anecdote puts a human face on the problem the passage goes on to explain: women's heart attack symptoms are often missed. An opening story in an informational text usually serves to engage the reader and introduce the topic.

n.0: Jaw pain is listed as one of several possible symptoms; the passage does not rank it as the most common.
n.1: The story is dramatic, but it introduces factual health information; the passage as a whole informs rather than entertains.
n.3: Gardening is simply what Rosa was doing; the passage never suggests that gardening caused her heart attack.

Craft & Structure.q:
(1) Mercy Valley Hospital should turn the empty lot behind its east wing into a community garden. Patients could see green space from their windows, staff could take breaks outdoors, and the hospital's nutrition program could teach classes using fresh vegetables.

(2) Some board members argue that the lot should be saved for a future parking garage. However, the hospital's own ten-year plan places new parking on the west side of campus, and a garden could be moved in a single season if plans ever changed.

(3) A garden would cost less than $20,000 to build. The board should approve it this spring.

What is the main purpose of paragraph 2?
o: to answer an objection to the author's proposal
to provide evidence that gardens improve patient health
to describe the location of the empty lot on the hospital campus
to summarize the costs and benefits of the garden
Craft & Structure.w: Paragraph 2 states an opposing view (save the lot for parking) and then rebuts it with the hospital's own plan and the garden's flexibility. Raising and answering an objection is a common purpose of a paragraph in a persuasive text.

n.1: Benefits to patients appear in paragraph 1, and no health evidence is offered anywhere in the passage.
n.2: The lot's location is given in paragraph 1; paragraph 2 mentions campus locations only to rebut the parking argument.
n.3: Cost appears only in paragraph 3, and paragraph 2 does not weigh costs against benefits.

Craft & Structure.q:
I was twenty-three when I lost my first patient. Mr. Alvarez had told me about his grandchildren every morning for two weeks, and I had promised to see the photos his daughter was bringing on Friday. He died on Thursday night. I followed every step I had been taught: I called the physician, notified the family and prepared the body with care. Then I sat in the supply room and cried. Twenty years later, I still think of him whenever a patient starts to tell me about the people they love.

What is the author's primary purpose in this passage?
o: to persuade hospitals to offer grief counseling to nurses
to express the author's feelings about a past experience
to inform new nurses about the steps to follow after a death
to entertain readers with a suspenseful hospital story
Craft & Structure.w: The first-person reflection, the detail about the photos and the admission that the author cried and still remembers the patient all show a writer sharing personal feelings. Expressing emotion about an experience is the purpose.

n.0: The passage never mentions counseling or asks hospitals to do anything.
n.2: The steps after a death are mentioned in a single sentence as part of the memory; they are not explained in a way meant to teach.
n.3: The story is moving rather than suspenseful, and it is told to share feelings rather than to amuse or thrill.

Craft & Structure.q:
Many parents worry that their toddlers are not eating enough vegetables. Children's appetites can change from day to day, and refusing a new food is a normal stage of development. "It can take ten or more tries before a child accepts a new vegetable," says Dr. Maya Thompson, a pediatrician who has studied children's eating habits for fifteen years. Parents can help by serving small portions of new foods next to familiar favorites and by eating the same foods themselves.

Why does the author most likely include the quotation from Dr. Thompson?
o: to support the advice with an expert's credibility
to tell a personal story that appeals to parents' emotions
to introduce a view that the author goes on to argue against
to change the subject from toddlers to older children
Craft & Structure.w: Dr. Thompson's credentials (a pediatrician with fifteen years of research) lend authority to the claim that repeated tries are normal. Using an expert's standing to support a point is an appeal to credibility, or ethos.

n.1: The quotation states a research-based fact rather than a personal story, and its appeal rests on expertise, not emotion.
n.2: The author agrees with Dr. Thompson; the advice that follows builds on her statement.
n.3: The passage stays focused on toddlers; the quotation is about children accepting new vegetables, the same subject.

Craft & Structure.q:
Our county's public pools close every year on Labor Day, even though September temperatures here average 88 degrees. According to the county parks report, pool attendance on the last two weekends of August averaged 1,400 swimmers a day. A splash pad, a ground-level area of water jets with no standing water, costs far less to staff than a pool. It is shameful that families with no air conditioning are left with nowhere to cool off. The county must keep at least one pool open through September. Call your commissioner today.

Which features of the passage indicate that its primary purpose is to persuade rather than to inform? Select all that apply.
o: the average September temperature
the instruction to call a commissioner today
the emotionally charged word "shameful"
the demand that the county keep a pool open
the attendance figures from the county parks report
the definition of a splash pad
Craft & Structure.w: Loaded language ("shameful"), a direct claim about what the county must do and a call to action are features that mark persuasive writing. They show the facts in the passage are being used to push readers toward an action.

n.0: A temperature figure is a neutral fact that could appear in any kind of text.
n.4: Statistics appear in informative and persuasive texts alike; the figures alone do not show the author's purpose.
n.5: Defining a term is a typical feature of informative writing, so the definition does not mark the passage as persuasive.

Craft & Structure.q:
The blue light from phones and tablets signals the brain to stay awake, and a 2023 survey found that children who used screens in the hour before bed slept 40 minutes less on school nights than children who did not. Tired children struggle to pay attention in class and are more likely to be irritable. Parents, it is time to act. Set a family rule that all screens go into a basket in the kitchen one hour before bedtime, and follow the rule yourselves.

Which of the following best states the author's purpose?
o: to discuss the topic of children's sleep and electronic devices
to report the results of a 2023 survey about children's screen use
to describe a typical bedtime routine in an American family
to convince parents to limit children's screen use before bed
Craft & Structure.w: The passage builds to direct commands ("Parents, it is time to act. Set a family rule..."), so its purpose is to convince parents to take a specific action.

n.0: This names the topic, not the purpose. It leaves out the author's clear push for a particular action.
n.1: The survey is one piece of supporting evidence; the passage does not report its methods or full results.
n.2: The basket in the kitchen is a recommendation, not a description of what families already do.

Craft & Structure.q:
Hospitals today spend millions of dollars on hand-hygiene programs, yet studies still find that health care workers clean their hands less than half as often as they should. The idea itself is not new. In 1847, a Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis required doctors at a Vienna maternity clinic to wash their hands in a chlorine solution before examining patients, and deaths among new mothers in his ward fell sharply. The challenge today is not knowledge but habit: busy staff forget, skip steps or assume gloves are enough.

The author mentions Ignaz Semmelweis mainly to
o: show that the value of handwashing has been known for a long time.
entertain readers with a story about a famous European doctor.
explain how chlorine solutions kill the germs that cause infection.
persuade readers that modern doctors should study medical history.
Craft & Structure.w: The sentence just before the example says "The idea itself is not new," and the Semmelweis example from 1847 supports that point. The detail sets up the author's argument that today's problem is habit, not lack of knowledge.

n.1: The example is brief and factual; it serves the author's point about habit rather than amusing the reader.
n.2: The passage says Semmelweis used chlorine but never explains how it works on germs.
n.3: The author never suggests that doctors study history; the example supports a point about hand hygiene.

Craft & Structure.q:
The Clearwater City Council will vote on June 9 on a plan to place 30 bike-share stations downtown. Riders would pay $2 for a 30-minute trip or $90 for a yearly pass. Supporters, including the downtown business association, say the program would reduce traffic and bring shoppers to Main Street. Opponents, including several residents of the Elm Park neighborhood, worry that the stations would take up 60 parking spaces. A similar program in nearby Fairview has averaged 410 rides a day since it opened in 2022.

What is the primary purpose of the passage?
o: to report on a proposal and the views on both sides
to criticize residents who oppose the bike-share stations
to compare Clearwater's traffic problems with Fairview's
to persuade readers to support the bike-share plan
Craft & Structure.w: The passage gives the vote date, the prices and the Fairview figures, and it reports both supporters' and opponents' views without taking a side. Balanced reporting of a proposal is an informative purpose.

n.1: Opponents' concerns are presented in neutral terms, with no criticism from the author.
n.2: Fairview appears once as background; the passage says nothing about traffic problems in either city.
n.3: Supporters' arguments are reported, but so are opponents' concerns, and the author never urges a vote either way.

Craft & Structure.q:
A Nutrition Facts label lists the serving size at the top, followed by the number of calories in one serving. Below that, the label shows nutrients such as fat, sodium and added sugars, along with a Percent Daily Value for each. A Percent Daily Value of 5 percent or less means a food is low in that nutrient, and 20 percent or more means it is high. All of these numbers apply to one serving, so a person who eats two servings must double them.

Which sentence, if added to the end of the passage, would best fit the author's purpose?
o: Percent Daily Values are based on a 2,000-calorie diet for a typical adult.
Food companies make labels confusing so that shoppers will buy more.
I still remember how confused I was the first time I tried to read a label.
Every family should stop buying snacks with more than 10 grams of added sugar.
Craft & Structure.w: The passage explains, in a neutral way, how to read the parts of a label, so its purpose is to inform. A sentence adding another factual detail about the label (the 2,000-calorie basis of Percent Daily Values) continues that purpose.

n.1: This accuses companies of a motive without evidence, adding a biased claim that does not match the neutral explanation.
n.2: A personal memory would add an expressive, first-person note to an impersonal explanation.
n.3: This tells families what they should do, which would shift the passage from informing to persuading.

Craft & Structure.q:
Grayson County Hospital began in 1912 as a six-bed clinic above a hardware store. In 1925, after a fire destroyed the store, the town raised money for a two-story brick building on Elm Street. During the 1950s, the hospital added a maternity ward and its first X-ray machine. A new emergency department opened in 1978, and in 2004 the hospital joined the regional Lakeshore Health network. Today, Grayson County Hospital has 140 beds and employs more than 900 people.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: compare and contrast
cause and effect
problem and solution
chronological order
Craft & Structure.w: The passage moves through the hospital's history date by date, from 1912 to today. Ordering events by time is chronological structure.

n.0: The passage traces one hospital over time; it does not set two subjects side by side.
n.1: One causal link appears (the fire led to a new building), but the passage as a whole is organized by dates, not by causes and their results.
n.2: No central problem is identified and solved; the passage lists milestones in order.

Craft & Structure.q:
Oral and tympanic thermometers are both common in clinics. An oral thermometer is placed under the tongue and takes about 10 to 40 seconds to give a reading, depending on the model. A tympanic thermometer, by contrast, reads the temperature inside the ear in one to two seconds. Both give reliable results when used correctly. However, oral readings can be thrown off if a patient has just had a hot or cold drink, whereas tympanic readings can be affected by earwax or a poorly placed probe.

Which organizational structure does the author use?
o: chronological order
description
classification into types
compare and contrast
Craft & Structure.w: The passage sets two thermometers side by side, noting similarities ("both") and differences ("by contrast," "however," "whereas"). That is compare-and-contrast structure.

n.0: Times appear (seconds per reading), but the passage does not narrate events or steps in order.
n.1: Each thermometer is described, but the descriptions are arranged to show how the two are alike and different, which makes the structure comparative.
n.2: Classification sorts many items into categories; this passage weighs two specific devices against each other.

Craft & Structure.q:
Last year, patients at Northgate Hospital's emergency department waited an average of 74 minutes before seeing a provider, and nearly one in ten left before being seen. To address this, the hospital made three changes in January. A nurse now assesses each patient at the front door, patients with minor injuries go to a separate fast-track area, and lab tests can be ordered before a patient reaches a room. Since the changes, the average wait has dropped to 31 minutes.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: order of importance
problem and solution
description
compare and contrast
Craft & Structure.w: The passage opens with a problem (long waits and patients leaving), explains the steps taken "to address this," and reports the result. That is problem-and-solution structure.

n.0: The three changes are listed as equal parts of one plan; none is ranked as most or least important.
n.2: The changes are explained as a response to a problem rather than as features described for their own sake.
n.3: The before-and-after wait times show results, but the passage is built around fixing a problem, not around comparing two subjects.

Craft & Structure.q:
Using Your Metered-Dose Inhaler

1. Remove the cap and shake the inhaler well for five seconds.
2. Breathe out fully, away from the inhaler.
3. Place the mouthpiece between your teeth and close your lips around it.
4. Press down on the canister once while breathing in slowly and deeply.
5. Hold your breath for 10 seconds, then breathe out slowly.
6. If a second puff is prescribed, wait one minute, shake the inhaler again and repeat steps 2 through 5.
7. If your inhaler contains a steroid, rinse your mouth with water after each use.

Which feature of this text most clearly marks it as technical writing rather than expository writing?
o: It numbers each action the reader must take, in order.
It uses a title that names the subject of the text.
It leaves out opinions and emotional language.
It presents accurate information about a medical device.
Craft & Structure.w: Technical (procedural) texts give exact, ordered directions for doing a task or using equipment. The numbered commands ("Remove," "Breathe out," "Hold your breath") set this text apart from an expository text, which explains a topic without walking the reader through actions step by step.

n.1: Expository articles also have titles naming their subject, so a title does not identify a text as technical.
n.2: Expository writing is also neutral and free of opinion, so this feature is shared by both types rather than distinguishing them.
n.3: Expository texts also present accurate information, so accuracy does not separate the two types.

Craft & Structure.q:
Why do so many water mains break in January? Water expands by about 9 percent when it freezes. When the ground around a buried pipe freezes, it shifts and pushes against the pipe, placing stress on joints and older sections. Cold water inside the pipe also makes metal and plastic more brittle. As a result, a pipe that has handled years of normal pressure can crack during a hard freeze. Older cast-iron mains are especially likely to fail because decades of corrosion have already thinned their walls.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: problem and solution
chronological order
classification
cause and effect
Craft & Structure.w: The passage opens with a "why" question and answers it with causes (freezing, shifting ground, brittleness, corrosion) and their effect (cracked pipes). Signal words such as "as a result" and "because" confirm a cause-and-effect structure.

n.0: The passage explains the breaks but proposes no fix, so it lacks the solution half of this structure.
n.1: The passage explains why something happens, not a series of events in time order.
n.2: Cast-iron mains are singled out once, but the passage does not sort pipes into categories.

Craft & Structure.q:
Why should healthy adults get a flu shot every fall? Above all, the vaccine lowers your risk of serious illness, hospitalization and death from influenza. It also protects the people around you, including infants and older adults, who are more likely to become seriously ill. In addition, a flu shot can reduce the number of workdays and school days you miss. Finally, and least important for most people, vaccination can spare you a week of feeling miserable on the couch.

How does the author organize the reasons in the passage?
o: in chronological order, from the first event to the last
from the most important reason to the least important
by classifying adults into groups at different risk
by comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated adults
Craft & Structure.w: "Above all" introduces the strongest reason, and "least important for most people" marks the weakest at the end. Ranking reasons from most to least important is order-of-importance structure.

n.0: "Finally" can signal time order, but here it introduces the last reason in a ranked list, not the last event in a sequence.
n.2: Infants and older adults are mentioned as people who benefit, but the passage does not sort adults into risk categories.
n.3: The passage lists benefits of vaccination; it never describes unvaccinated adults for comparison.

Craft & Structure.q:
Burns are grouped into types according to how deeply they damage the skin. A superficial burn, often called first-degree, affects only the outer layer of skin and causes redness and pain. A partial-thickness burn, or second-degree burn, reaches into the layer below and usually forms blisters. A full-thickness burn, or third-degree burn, destroys both layers and may look white, brown or leathery. Because nerve endings can be destroyed, a full-thickness burn may cause less pain than a smaller, shallower one.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: classification
chronological order
spatial order
cause and effect
Craft & Structure.w: The opening sentence says burns are "grouped into types," and the rest of the passage defines each type by its depth. Sorting a subject into categories is classification.

n.1: The types are listed by depth, not in time order; no events unfold.
n.2: Skin layers are mentioned, but the passage is not a description of where things are located in space; it defines categories.
n.3: The last sentence explains one cause and effect (destroyed nerves, less pain), but that detail sits inside the larger classification.

Craft & Structure.q:
Welcome to the Oakridge Family Clinic. As you enter through the main doors, the check-in desk is directly in front of you. The waiting area lies to your right, with a children's play corner along its far wall. To the left of the check-in desk, a short hallway leads to exam rooms 1 through 6. The lab is at the end of that hallway, across from the restrooms. The pharmacy window is just outside the main doors, to the left of the entrance.

Which organizational structure does the author use?
o: chronological order
order of importance
spatial order
classification
Craft & Structure.w: The passage locates each area by its position relative to the visitor ("directly in front of you," "to your right," "at the end of that hallway"). Organizing details by location is spatial order.

n.0: "As you enter" sets a starting point, but the passage maps where things are rather than narrating events in time.
n.1: No area is ranked as more or less important; each is placed by location.
n.3: The areas are not sorted into types or categories; they are positioned on a mental map.

Craft & Structure.q:
Many older adults in Lakeview County miss medical appointments because they no longer drive and the nearest bus stop is more than a mile from the clinic. To fix this, the county launched a ride program last spring. First, a patient calls the clinic at least two days before the visit. Next, a dispatcher schedules a volunteer driver. Then the driver picks the patient up at home and waits during the appointment. In its first six months, the program provided 1,800 rides, and missed appointments fell by a third.

Which of the following best describes the overall organization of the passage?
o: cause and effect, because it explains why patients miss visits
compare and contrast, because it gives results before and after
chronological order, because it lists the steps a patient follows
problem and solution, because it presents a need and a response
Craft & Structure.w: The passage opens with a problem (missed appointments due to lack of transportation), describes the county's ride program as the fix, and reports its results. The ordered steps and the opening cause are parts of that larger problem-and-solution structure.

n.0: "Because" explains the problem in the first sentence, but most of the passage describes the program created to solve it.
n.1: A drop in missed appointments shows the solution worked; the passage does not set two subjects side by side.
n.2: "First," "next" and "then" order the steps of the solution, but they cover one section, not the passage as a whole.

Craft & Structure.q:
When a child has a high fever or a deep cut on a Saturday night, parents in Millbrook have two choices. Urgent care centers treat minor injuries and illnesses, such as sprains, ear infections and cuts that need stitches. Visits typically cost less, and waits are often under an hour. Emergency rooms, on the other hand, are equipped for life-threatening problems such as trouble breathing, seizures or severe bleeding. They are open around the clock but usually cost more and can involve longer waits for less serious cases.

The author most likely uses a compare-and-contrast structure in order to
o: show how emergency rooms have changed over the years.
argue that urgent care centers should replace emergency rooms.
help parents decide which place fits a child's needs.
explain what causes most childhood injuries on weekends.
Craft & Structure.w: Setting the two options side by side (what each treats, cost, wait times, hours) gives parents the information they need to choose between them. The structure serves that practical purpose.

n.0: The passage describes both places as they are now; it gives no history.
n.1: The passage presents emergency rooms as necessary for life-threatening problems, so it does not argue for replacing them.
n.3: Injuries are named as examples of what each place treats; their causes are never discussed.

Craft & Structure.q:
In 2019, the town of Ridgeway closed its only grocery store. As a result, many residents began buying most of their food at gas stations and dollar stores. Because of the distance to the nearest supermarket, 12 miles away, families without cars ate fewer fresh fruits and vegetables. For example, a survey by the county health department found that produce purchases fell by half. Meanwhile, rates of diabetes in the town continued to rise. In contrast, a neighboring town that kept its grocery store saw little change. The store's closing led to a new effort to start a weekly farmers market.

Which phrases from the passage signal a cause-and-effect relationship? Select all that apply.
o: Meanwhile
In contrast
Because of
led to
For example
As a result
Craft & Structure.w: "As a result" introduces an effect of the closing, "Because of" introduces a cause of the change in eating habits, and "led to" links the closing to the farmers market effort. All three signal cause and effect.

n.0: "Meanwhile" signals that two things happened at the same time, a time relationship rather than a causal one.
n.1: "In contrast" signals a difference between two towns, which is a compare-and-contrast signal.
n.4: "For example" introduces supporting evidence (the survey), not a cause or effect.

Craft & Structure.q:
We reached the trailhead at dawn, our breath fogging in the cold. By noon we had climbed above 11,000 feet, and my sister Leah said she felt dizzy and had a pounding headache. I remembered from our guidebook that altitude sickness often appears above 8,000 feet and that the safest treatment is to go back down. We turned around without reaching the summit. By the time we reached the lake at 9,500 feet, Leah's headache had eased, and we ate our sandwiches on a rock, watching the clouds drift over the peak we had left behind.

Which type of text is this passage?
o: narrative
technical
expository
persuasive
Craft & Structure.w: The passage tells a first-person story with characters, a setting and events in order (the climb, Leah's symptoms, the decision to turn back). That makes it a narrative.

n.1: No step-by-step instructions are given; the guidebook detail is remembered, not presented as directions.
n.2: The passage includes a fact about altitude sickness, but that fact is part of the story; the text as a whole recounts an experience rather than explaining a topic.
n.3: The narrator never argues for a position or urges the reader to act.

Craft & Structure.q:
The night before my first clinical shift, I laid out my scrubs, packed my stethoscope and set three alarms. When I walked onto the unit at 6:45 a.m., the charge nurse looked up from her computer. "You must be the new student," she said. "You'll be with Marcus today. Stick close to him, ask questions, and don't touch any pumps unless he says so." I nodded and tried to look calmer than I felt. My hands were shaking as I followed Marcus down the hall.

From which point of view is the passage narrated?
o: third person omniscient
third person limited
first person
second person
Craft & Structure.w: The narrator takes part in the events and refers to herself as "I" and "my" throughout. That is first-person narration.

n.0: An omniscient narrator reports every character's thoughts; this narrator reports only her own feelings and what others say aloud.
n.1: A third-person narrator stands outside the story and uses "he" or "she" for the main character; this narrator is the main character.
n.3: "You" appears only inside the charge nurse's dialogue. Pronouns in quoted speech do not set the narrator's point of view.

Craft & Structure.q:
Dr. Nadia Hassan studied the X-ray for a long moment. She was almost sure the fracture would need surgery, but she wanted the orthopedic team to confirm it before she said anything to the family. In the waiting room, Mr. Brooks paced between the vending machine and the window, checking his phone every few seconds. His daughter sat with her arm in a sling, staring at the floor. When Dr. Hassan finally walked in, she smiled and said, "Let's talk about next steps."

Which point of view does the author use in the passage?
o: first person
third person omniscient
third person limited
third person objective
Craft & Structure.w: The narrator uses "she" and reports Dr. Hassan's private thoughts (she was almost sure about surgery, she wanted confirmation). Mr. Brooks and his daughter are shown only through their actions. Access to one character's mind is third person limited.

n.0: The narrator never says "I"; the only first-person words would be in dialogue, and there are none.
n.1: An omniscient narrator would reveal what Mr. Brooks and his daughter were thinking. Here we see only their actions.
n.3: An objective narrator reports only actions and speech, but this narrator tells us Dr. Hassan's thoughts.

Craft & Structure.q:
Coach Rivera paced the sideline, certain that his team had one more good play left in them. On the bench, Tyler rubbed his sore ankle and hoped the coach would not notice, because he wanted desperately to finish the game. In the stands, Tyler's mother gripped her program and wondered whether she should have let him play at all. And the referee, who had made a questionable call in the first half, quietly promised himself that he would get the next one right.

Which point of view does the author use?
o: third person objective
first person, told by an observer
third person limited
third person omniscient
Craft & Structure.w: The narrator stands outside the story and reveals the private thoughts of four different people: the coach, Tyler, his mother and the referee. Knowing the minds of many characters is third person omniscient.

n.0: An objective narrator reports only what can be seen and heard, but this narrator tells us what each person hopes, wonders and promises privately.
n.1: No narrator refers to himself or herself as "I," not even an onlooker; every character is described from outside.
n.2: A limited narrator reveals one character's thoughts; this one moves freely among several.

Craft & Structure.q:
As a pharmacist for twenty years, I have watched patients struggle to open childproof medicine caps. Those caps have saved countless children from accidental poisonings, and I would never want them removed from homes with young children. But many of my older customers have arthritis, and some of them leave their bottles open on the counter because they cannot reopen them. Federal rules already allow patients to request easy-open caps. Pharmacies should make that choice clear to every customer over sixty-five who lives without children.

Which of the following best describes the author's point of view on childproof caps?
o: They should be removed from all prescription bottles.
They are useful but should be optional for some patients.
They are a federal requirement that pharmacies cannot change.
They have failed to prevent accidental poisonings in children.
Craft & Structure.w: The author praises the caps for protecting children yet argues that older adults without children at home should be clearly offered easy-open caps. The view is balanced: keep the caps, but make the alternative known.

n.0: The author says the caps should not be removed from homes with young children, so this goes too far.
n.2: The author notes that federal rules already allow patients to request easy-open caps, so the caps are not an unchangeable requirement.
n.3: The author says the opposite: the caps "have saved countless children."

Craft & Structure.q:
Opponents of the city's plan to put calorie counts on restaurant menus argue that diners do not read them and that the signs will only raise costs for small businesses. It is true that calorie labels alone will not solve obesity. But a 2018 study of a large restaurant chain found that customers ordered about 4 percent fewer calories after labels appeared, and many restaurants quietly made their dishes lighter. Those small changes add up across millions of meals. The council should pass the measure.

With which statement would the author most likely agree?
o: Calorie labels offer small benefits that add up over time.
Most diners do not read calorie counts printed on menus.
Calorie labels are not worth the cost to small businesses.
Calorie labels by themselves can solve the problem of obesity.
Craft & Structure.w: The author argues that a 4 percent reduction and lighter recipes "add up across millions of meals" and urges the council to pass the measure. Small but meaningful benefits sum up the author's view.

n.1: This is the opponents' claim, which the author reports in order to rebut it. A view the author reports is not necessarily the author's own.
n.2: This is also the opponents' argument; the author supports the measure despite the cost concern.
n.3: The author concedes that labels "alone will not solve obesity," so the author would reject this claim.

Craft & Structure.q:
The so-called wellness program at Harmon Industries is a disaster. Fewer than 22 percent of employees signed up last year, and the company paid a consulting firm $180,000 to run it. Workers were bombarded with nagging emails about step counts, and the heavily promoted health screenings drew only 140 people out of 2,300. Anyone who thinks this program is helping employees has not been paying attention.

Which of the following best describes the passage?
o: It is objective, because it is written in the third person.
It is subjective, because it is written from the employees' view.
It is objective, because its claims are based on numbers.
It is subjective, because its word choice shows a clear slant.
Craft & Structure.w: The statistics are factual, but "so-called," "disaster," "bombarded" and "nagging" reveal the author's negative judgment. Slanted word choice makes a text subjective even when it includes numbers.

n.0: Third-person writing can be subjective; this passage uses third person yet clearly argues a judgment.
n.1: The passage is subjective, but not because of whose view it reflects; the author never says employees share this view. The slanted wording is what makes it subjective.
n.2: Statistics do not make a text neutral. The author selects and frames the numbers with loaded language to support a strong opinion.

Craft & Structure.q:
Since the new staffing rules took effect, each nurse on our unit has cared for no more than five patients per shift, down from seven. I finally have time to explain a new medication properly, to notice when a patient's breathing changes, and to eat lunch sitting down. Management keeps talking about the cost of hiring more staff. They are not the ones running between rooms at 3 a.m. when two call lights go off at once.

The author of the passage is most likely
o: a reporter writing a news story about staffing rules.
a hospital administrator reviewing the cost of new staff.
a patient who was recently treated on the unit.
a nurse who works shifts on the unit.
Craft & Structure.w: The author refers to "our unit," describes caring for patients and explaining medications, and contrasts the writer's own night-shift experience with management's view. These details point to a staff nurse's perspective.

n.0: A news reporter would write in a neutral voice, but this author writes from personal, first-hand experience.
n.1: The author criticizes management for focusing on cost, which is the opposite of an administrator's perspective.
n.2: The author describes caring for several patients at once, which a patient would not do.

Craft & Structure.q:
You wake at 4:30 a.m., before the alarm, because your body has learned the schedule. You pull on scrubs in the dark so you will not wake anyone, grab the lunch you packed last night and drive through empty streets to the hospital. By 6:45 you are taking report from the night nurse, and by 7:15 you have already answered three call lights. Your feet ache by noon. Still, when a patient squeezes your hand and thanks you, you remember why you chose this work.

From which point of view is the passage written?
o: first person
third person limited
third person objective
second person
Craft & Structure.w: The narration addresses the reader directly as "you" and places the reader in the role of the nurse. That is second-person point of view.

n.0: The passage reads like a personal memory, but no "I" or "we" appears; every action is assigned to "you."
n.1: Third-person limited would describe a character as "he" or "she" and reveal that character's thoughts.
n.2: Third-person objective would describe characters from outside using "he" or "she," reporting only actions and speech.

Craft & Structure.q:
The bus pulled up to the clinic at 8:02. A woman in a red coat stepped off first, holding a toddler on her hip. She walked to the front desk and set down a folder. "We have a nine o'clock with Dr. Lee," she said. The receptionist glanced at the clock, then at the folder. "You're early," she said. "Have a seat." The woman sat down by the window. The toddler pressed his hand against the glass and watched the bus pull away.

Which point of view does the author use?
o: third person limited
first person
third person omniscient
third person objective
Craft & Structure.w: The narrator reports only what could be seen and heard (arrivals, movements and dialogue) and never reveals any character's thoughts or feelings. That is third-person objective.

n.0: A limited narrator would reveal one character's thoughts, such as why the woman came early; none are given.
n.1: "We" and "you" appear only inside the dialogue. The narrator never speaks as "I."
n.2: An omniscient narrator would reveal several characters' thoughts; this narrator reveals none.

Craft & Structure.q:
Our school district's plan to give every high school student a free tablet has real promise. Students without computers at home would finally be able to complete online assignments, and teachers could share lessons more easily. Still, I have questions. The district has not explained who will repair broken devices, and it has budgeted no money for training teachers to use them well. If those gaps are filled before the fall, I will be among the plan's strongest supporters.

Which of the following best describes the author's attitude toward the tablet plan?
o: opposed, with a few exceptions
supportive, with reservations
enthusiastic, with no concerns
neutral, with no stated view
Craft & Structure.w: The author praises the plan's "real promise" but raises questions about repairs and training, and promises full support only if those gaps are filled. Support with conditions is a qualified, or cautiously supportive, attitude.

n.0: The author's main stance is favorable; the concerns are conditions for full support, not reasons to oppose the plan.
n.2: The author raises two specific concerns, so the support is not unqualified.
n.3: The author clearly expresses a view ("real promise," "I have questions"), so the passage is not neutral.

Craft & Structure.q:
The county's proposal to close the Pine Street library branch, which opened in 1964, has drawn strong reactions. The county manager calls the branch "an expensive relic in the age of e-books." Several council members argue that the money would be better spent on road repairs. But the branch is the only place in the neighborhood with free internet access, and I see seniors there every day filling out benefit forms they cannot complete at home. Closing it would cut off people who have no other option. The county should find savings elsewhere.

Which statements from the passage express the author's own point of view? Select all that apply.
o: The Pine Street branch opened in 1964.
The proposal to close the branch has drawn strong reactions.
The money would be better spent on road repairs.
Closing it would cut off people who have no other option.
The branch is an expensive relic in the age of e-books.
The county should find savings elsewhere.
Craft & Structure.w: In the author's own sentences, the author judges that closing the branch would harm people with no alternative and concludes that the county should find savings elsewhere. These two statements express the author's position in favor of keeping the branch.

n.0: The opening date is a checkable background fact; it expresses no judgment about the proposal.
n.1: This is a neutral report that people have reacted strongly; it takes no side and does not state the author's own position.
n.2: This is the argument of several council members, which the author reports but does not share.
n.4: These are the county manager's words, quoted by the author in order to argue against them.

Craft & Structure.q:
The Brookside Health Fair drew about 600 visitors to the community center on Saturday. Nurses from three local clinics offered free blood pressure checks, and a dentist handed out toothbrushes to children. Organizers called the event "our best fair yet" and plan to hold it again next spring. Sadly, the fair's single diabetes screening table could not keep up with the line. Dozens of people left without being tested, some after waiting more than an hour.

Which sentence from the passage most clearly reveals the author's perspective?
o: Nurses from three local clinics offered free blood pressure checks.
Organizers called the event "our best fair yet" and plan to hold it again next spring.
Dozens of people left without being tested, some after waiting more than an hour.
Sadly, the fair's single diabetes screening table could not keep up with the line.
Craft & Structure.w: "Sadly" is the author's own reaction, and it shows concern that the fair fell short in an important area. The other sentences report events or quote someone else without the author adding a judgment.

n.0: This neutrally reports a service that was offered.
n.1: "Our best fair yet" is a judgment, but it is the organizers' view, which the author quotes. A view the author reports is not the author's own perspective.
n.2: This sentence supports the author's concern, but it reports a checkable outcome without any judgment word; it does not state the author's attitude as clearly as "Sadly" does.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q:
Mara checked the supply cart twice before her shift began, then a third time after report. When the charge nurse asked why, Mara pointed to a note taped inside the top drawer. The reminder, written in her own handwriting, dated from the night a missing suction catheter had cost the team four minutes during an emergency. "I'd rather lose thirty seconds now," she said. The charge nurse nodded slowly. The following week, a cart check appeared on the start-of-shift list for every nurse on the unit.

Which conclusion about Mara is best supported by the passage?
o: She does not trust the other nurses on the unit to stock the supply cart correctly.
She was the nurse responsible for the missing catheter on the night of the emergency.
She was asked by the charge nurse to train the other nurses to check their carts.
A past delay she witnessed shapes the way she prepares for each of her shifts.
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: The note recalls the night a missing catheter cost four minutes, and Mara says she would rather lose thirty seconds now. Her repeated checks are explained by that earlier delay.

n.0: Nothing in the passage blames other nurses; her checks are tied to one past event, not to distrust of coworkers.
n.1: The note is in her handwriting, but the passage never says who left the catheter out; this is an assumption.
n.2: The charge nurse added a cart check to the shift list; the passage never says Mara was asked to train anyone.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q:
Westbrook Clinic offered walk-in flu shots this fall for the first time, in addition to scheduled appointments. The table shows the percentage of the clinic's patients in each age group who received a flu shot at the clinic.
Age group | Last year | This year
18 to 34 | 22% | 35%
35 to 64 | 41% | 47%
65 and older | 68% | 69%
The clinic manager plans to keep walk-in hours next year.

Which conclusions are supported by the passage and table? Select all that apply.
o: More patients aged 35 to 64 got a shot this year than patients aged 65 and older.
The youngest age group showed the largest increase in its vaccination rate.
Walk-in hours caused the rise in vaccination among patients aged 18 to 34.
Older patients used the walk-in hours more often than younger patients did.
Patients 65 and older had the highest vaccination rate of the three groups this year.
The percentage of patients who got a flu shot rose in each age group this year.
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Every group rose (22 to 35, 41 to 47, 68 to 69). The 18 to 34 group gained 13 points, more than 6 or 1. At 69%, patients 65 and older had the highest rate this year.

n.0: The table gives percentages, not numbers of patients; without group sizes the counts cannot be compared.
n.2: Walk-in hours began the same year, but the table shows only rates, not why they changed; causation is not established.
n.3: The table does not separate walk-in shots from scheduled ones, so use of walk-in hours by age is unknown.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q:
A school district surveyed 1,200 high school students about sleep. Students who used their phones in bed after 10 p.m. reported sleeping about 50 minutes less on school nights than students who did not, even though both groups reported going to bed at similar times. The district then launched a campaign urging families to charge phones outside the bedroom. Early results from 80 families who joined a trial of the campaign show that the students fell asleep about 20 minutes sooner on average.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Students who use phones in bed go to bed later than students who do not use them.
Students who join the campaign can expect to gain about 50 minutes of sleep on school nights.
Phone use in bed may delay sleep even when students go to bed at the same time as their peers.
Most high school students in the district probably use their phones in bed after 10 p.m.
Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.w: Both groups went to bed at similar times, yet phone users slept about 50 minutes less, and removing phones helped trial students fall asleep sooner. Together these details support the idea that phone use delays falling asleep.

n.0: This contradicts the passage, which says both groups reported going to bed at similar times.
n.1: This over-extends the data: 50 minutes was the survey gap, but the trial showed students falling asleep about 20 minutes sooner.
n.3: The passage gives no share of students who use phones in bed, so a majority cannot be concluded.

Integration of Knowledge & Ideas.q:
To cut absences from stomach illness, Lincoln Elementary placed handwashing posters above every sink in October. The school nurse also taught a five-minute handwashing lesson in each classroom. From October through March, absences linked to stomach illness fell by 30 percent compared with the same months the year before.
