Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A: sum 110, mean 22, median 22, range 30 - 14 = 16. B: sum 110, mean 22, median 22, range 36 - 8 = 28. Same center, but B is more spread out.

n.1: Both medians are 22 (the 3rd value of 5), and the ranges are 16 and 28, not equal.
n.2: A's evenly spaced values span only 30 - 14 = 16, while B's span 36 - 8 = 28.
n.3: B's values also sum to 110, so both means are 22; only the ranges differ (16 and 28).

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A nurse researcher studies whether patients' fasting blood glucose levels are affected by the number of steps they walk each day. Every patient wears the same model of step counter for 30 days, and glucose is always checked at 7 a.m. Which is the dependent variable?
o: Fasting blood glucose level
Number of steps walked each day
Time of day glucose is checked
Model of step counter worn
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The dependent variable is the measured outcome that may respond to the change. The study asks whether glucose is affected by daily steps, so fasting glucose level depends on the number of steps walked.

n.1: Daily steps is the independent variable: it is the factor whose effect on glucose is being tested, even though it is named second.
n.2: Checking glucose at 7 a.m. for every patient holds this factor constant, which makes it a controlled variable.
n.3: Every patient wears the same model, so it is held constant: a controlled variable, not the measured outcome.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A taxi company sets the cost of a ride, C, based on the number of miles driven, m. Which statement correctly identifies the variables in this relationship?
o: C is independent, because it is the amount the rider pays
m is independent, and C depends on m
m is dependent, because it is measured during the ride
Both are dependent, because each changes with the other
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The cost is calculated from the miles, so miles (m) is the input, or independent variable, and cost (C) is the output, or dependent variable.

n.0: The amount paid is the result of the miles driven, which makes C dependent.
n.2: Being measured does not make a variable dependent; m is the input that sets the cost.
n.3: One variable is the input and the other the output; C changes because m changes, not the reverse.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A study asks whether a person's resting heart rate is affected by the number of cups of coffee the person drinks per day. What is the independent variable in this study?
o: Time of day heart rate is measured
Resting heart rate
Cups of coffee per day
The people in the study
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The study tests the effect of coffee intake on heart rate. Coffee intake is the possible cause (independent); heart rate is the response (dependent).

n.0: Measurement time should be held the same, which makes it a controlled variable.
n.1: Heart rate is named first, but it is the outcome being affected, so it is dependent.
n.3: The participants are the sample, not a variable.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A researcher graphs how the dose of a pain reliever, in milligrams, affects the time until a patient reports relief, in minutes. How should the axes of the graph be labeled?
o: Dose on the y-axis, because the dose is what the researcher controls
Time until relief on the x-axis, because time is the independent variable
Either variable on either axis, since the graph shows a correlation
Dose on the x-axis and time until relief on the y-axis
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The independent variable (dose, which the researcher sets) goes on the x-axis, and the dependent variable (time until relief, which responds) goes on the y-axis.

n.0: The variable the researcher controls is independent and belongs on the x-axis, not the y-axis.
n.1: Time is often independent, but here the time until relief is the response to the dose, so it is dependent.
n.2: Convention places the independent variable on the x-axis so the graph shows how y responds to x.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: Students test how water temperature affects the time it takes 5 grams of sugar to dissolve. They use the same cup, the same volume of water, and the same stirring speed in every trial. What is the stirring speed in this investigation?
o: The dependent variable
The independent variable
A controlled variable
The control group
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Stirring speed is kept the same in every trial so it cannot affect the results. A factor held constant is a controlled variable.

n.0: The dependent variable is the outcome measured: time to dissolve.
n.1: The independent variable is the factor deliberately changed: water temperature.
n.3: A control group is a set of trials used for comparison, not a factor held constant.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A table lists the number of hours since a medication was given and the amount of the medication remaining in the bloodstream, in milligrams. Which statement correctly describes the variables?
o: The amount remaining depends on the hours since the dose
The hours since the dose depend on the amount remaining
The amount remaining is independent, since it is the value measured
Both are independent, since neither is set by the nurse
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Time passes on its own, and the amount remaining changes as time passes. Time is independent and the amount remaining is dependent.

n.1: This reverses the relationship; elapsed time does not change because of the amount in the blood.
n.2: A measured outcome is the dependent variable, not the independent one.
n.3: A variable can be independent without anyone setting it; elapsed time is the input here.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A gym's total membership cost, y, in dollars, after x months is given by y = 12x + 30. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the variables?
o: x is independent; each increase of 1 in x raises y by 12
x is independent; each increase of 1 in x raises y by 30
y is independent; each increase of 1 in y raises x by 12
x is dependent, because it is multiplied by 12
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The cost is calculated from the number of months, so x is independent and y is dependent. The coefficient 12 is the change in y for each 1-unit increase in x ($12 per month); 30 is the starting fee.

n.1: 30 is the starting value (the y-intercept), not the change per month.
n.2: This swaps the roles of the variables; y is calculated from x.
n.3: Having a coefficient does not make a variable dependent; x is the input.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A graph has 'Outdoor temperature (°F)' labeled on the x-axis and 'Heat-related emergency room visits' labeled on the y-axis. Which question is the graph designed to investigate?
o: How does outdoor temperature affect emergency room visits?
How do emergency room visits change from month to month?
How do emergency room visits affect outdoor temperature?
How many patients visit the emergency room each day?
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The x-axis holds the independent variable and the y-axis the dependent variable, so the graph shows how ER visits respond to temperature.

n.1: Change over months would need time on the x-axis, but the x-axis shows temperature.
n.2: This reverses the variables; the y-axis variable is the one that responds.
n.3: A daily count needs no temperature axis; this graph relates two variables.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A dietitian studies whether daily sodium intake affects blood pressure. All participants are 40 to 50 years old, follow the same exercise routine, and take no blood pressure medication. Which are controlled variables in this study? Select all that apply.
o: Blood pressure
Exercise routine
Daily sodium intake
Age range of participants
Medication use
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Controlled variables are factors held the same for everyone so they cannot explain differences in the outcome: the age range, the exercise routine, and medication use.

n.0: Blood pressure is the outcome measured, so it is the dependent variable.
n.2: Sodium intake is the factor being tested, so it is the independent variable.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A table shows the number of workers assigned to a job (x) and the days needed to finish it (y): 2 workers, 12 days; 4 workers, 6 days; 6 workers, 4 days; 8 workers, 3 days. Which statement correctly describes the variables?
o: Workers depends on days needed; as days decrease, workers decrease
Days needed depends on workers; as workers increase, days increase
Days needed depends on workers; as workers increase, days decrease
Neither depends on the other, since y falls as x rises
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The number of workers is the input (independent) and the days needed is the output (dependent). From 2 to 8 workers, the days fall from 12 to 3.

n.0: This reverses the roles, and in the table fewer days go with more workers, not fewer.
n.1: The roles are right, but the days fall as workers increase.
n.3: A falling y as x rises is still a relationship (an inverse one), not a lack of one.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A student writes each pair of variables in the form (independent variable, dependent variable). Which pair is written in the correct order?
o: (Hours worked at $18 per hour, weekly paycheck)
(Weekly grocery bill, number of people in the household)
(Distance traveled, hours driven at a steady speed)
(Crop yield, inches of rainfall)
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The paycheck is calculated from the hours worked, so hours worked is independent and the paycheck is dependent; the pair is in the correct order.

n.1: The grocery bill depends on household size, so the order is reversed.
n.2: At a steady speed, distance depends on the hours driven, so the order is reversed.
n.3: Crop yield depends on rainfall, so the order is reversed.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A child's dose of a liquid medicine, M, in milliliters, is calculated from the child's weight, W, in kilograms, using the formula M = 0.4W. Which statement is correct?
o: M is independent, because the dose is what the nurse controls
M is independent, and W rises by 2 kg when M rises by 5 mL
W is independent, and M rises by 12.5 mL when W rises by 5 kg
W is independent, and M rises by 2 mL when W rises by 5 kg
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The dose is calculated from the weight, so W is independent and M is dependent. An increase of 5 kg changes M by 0.4 x 5 = 2 mL.

n.0: The dose is the output of the formula; the weight is the input.
n.1: This swaps the variables; the dose is calculated from the weight.
n.2: 5 / 0.4 = 12.5 divides by the rate instead of multiplying: 0.4 x 5 = 2 mL.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A math teacher lists four everyday situations involving two related quantities. Which situation is an example of direct variation?
o: The balance on a $500 gift card after spending $25 per week
The time needed to drive 100 miles at different speeds
Total pay at $22 per hour, with no other pay
A taxi fare of $3 for pickup plus $2.50 per mile
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Direct variation has the form y = kx: zero hours gives zero pay, and doubling the hours doubles the pay (pay = 22h).

n.0: Balance = 500 - 25w is a decreasing linear relationship, not y = kx.
n.1: Time = 100 / speed is inverse variation: doubling the speed halves the time.
n.3: Fare = 2.50m + 3 is linear, but the $3 starting fee means it does not pass through the origin, so it is not direct variation.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: Four tables each use the x-values 1, 2, 3, 4. Which set of y-values shows a linear relationship between x and y?
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A relationship is linear when equal steps in x give equal differences in y. Here y rises by 3 each time (5, 8, 11, 14).

n.0: The differences are 2, 4, 6, which are not constant.
n.1: These are the squares of x; the differences are 3, 5, 7.
n.3: Each y doubles (a constant ratio), which is exponential; the differences are 2, 4, 8.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A home health agency charges C dollars for a visit lasting h hours, where C = 45h + 30. In this equation, what does the 30 represent?
o: The number of hours covered by the base fee
The total cost of a 1-hour visit
The cost for each hour of the visit
A flat $30 fee on top of the hourly charge
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: In C = 45h + 30, the constant 30 is the y-intercept: the cost when h = 0. It is a fixed fee added to the $45 per hour.

n.0: 30 is in dollars, not hours, and the equation includes no free hours.
n.1: A 1-hour visit costs 45(1) + 30 = $75.
n.2: The cost per hour is the slope, 45.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A table shows the x-values 2, 5, and 8 paired with the y-values 7, 17.5, and 28. Which equation models the relationship shown in the table?
o: y = x + 5

n.0: This fits (2, 7) but gives 16, not 17.5, when x = 5.
n.2: This fits (2, 7) but gives 10, not 17.5, when x = 5.
n.3: This fits (2, 7) but gives 2.8 when x = 5; y increases as x increases, so it is not inverse.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: It takes 6 nurses 8 hours to complete a set of patient assessments. Working at the same rate, how many hours would it take 4 nurses to complete the same set of assessments?
o: 10 hours
12 hours
About 5.3 hours
6 hours
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Fewer workers need more time: an inverse relationship with a constant product. 6 x 8 = 48 nurse-hours. 48 / 4 = 12 hours.

n.0: Adding 1 hour per missing nurse is not supported; the total work, 48 nurse-hours, must be shared.
n.2: 8 x 4 / 6 = 5.3 treats the relationship as direct, as if fewer nurses would finish sooner.
n.3: Fewer nurses cannot finish sooner; subtracting 2 hours reverses the relationship.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A table shows the x-values 2, 4, 5, and 10 paired with the y-values 25, 12.5, 10, and 5. Which describes the relationship between x and y?
o: Linear: y = -6.25x + 37.5
Direct variation: y = 12.5x
Inverse variation: y = 25/x
Inverse variation: y = 50/x
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Each product xy is 50 (2 x 25, 4 x 12.5, 5 x 10, 10 x 5), so y varies inversely with x: y = 50/x.

n.0: This line fits the first two points but gives 6.25, not 10, when x = 5.
n.1: y = 12.5x fits (2, 25) but gives 50 when x = 4; also y falls as x rises.
n.2: 25 is the first y-value, not the constant; 25 / 4 = 6.25, not 12.5.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A table shows the volume remaining in a patient's IV bag: 0 minutes, 1,000 mL; 30 minutes, 940 mL; 60 minutes, 880 mL; 90 minutes, 820 mL. If this constant rate continues, how many minutes after the start will the bag hold 400 mL?

tr.200: 400 / 2, the time to empty the last 400 mL
tr.210: the time after the 90-minute reading (420 / 2), not after the start
tr.500: 1,000 / 2, the time to empty the full bag

Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Rate of change = (940 - 1,000) / 30 = -2 mL per minute. To fall from 1,000 to 400 mL is 600 mL, which takes 600 / 2 = 300 minutes.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: The dose of a medicine varies directly with a patient's body weight. A patient who weighs 60 kg receives 150 mg. What dose, in milligrams, should a patient who weighs 84 kg receive?

tr.107.1: treating it as inverse variation (150 x 60 / 84)
tr.2.5: the constant of variation, not the dose

Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Direct variation: dose = k x weight. k = 150 / 60 = 2.5 mg per kg. Dose = 2.5 x 84 = 210 mg.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A gym charges a one-time sign-up fee plus a fixed monthly fee. A 3-month membership costs $135 in total, and an 8-month membership costs $285 in total. What is the sign-up fee?

n.0: 135 / 3 - 30 = 15 spreads the sign-up fee across the 3 months before subtracting.
n.2: 135 - 30 = 105 removes one month's fee instead of three.
n.3: $30 is the monthly fee (the slope), not the starting fee.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: The number of doses, D, remaining in a multi-dose vial after t days of use is given by D = 40 - 3t. Which statement describes this relationship?
o: The vial starts with 40 doses and loses 3 doses per day
The vial starts with 3 doses and loses 40 doses per day
The vial starts with 40 doses and gains 3 doses per day
The vial starts with 37 doses and loses 3 doses per day
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: At t = 0, D = 40, the starting amount (y-intercept). The slope is -3, so D decreases by 3 for each day.

n.1: This swaps the intercept and the rate.
n.2: The coefficient of t is -3, a decrease, not a gain.
n.3: 37 is the amount left after 1 day; at t = 0 the vial holds 40.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: Four tables each list three (x, y) pairs. In which table does y vary directly with x?
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Direct variation needs the same ratio y / x for every pair: 6 / 4 = 1.5, 9 / 6 = 1.5, 15 / 10 = 1.5. So y = 1.5x.

n.0: Each product xy is 36, which is inverse variation.
n.1: The ratio is 1.5 for the first two pairs but 9 / 8 = 1.125 for the third.
n.2: y rises 2 per unit of x, but y = 2x + 5 has a starting value of 5, so the ratios (7, 4.5, 3.25) differ.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A solution is warmed at a constant rate. Its temperature is 26°C after 4 minutes and 44°C after 10 minutes. What was the temperature of the solution at 0 minutes?
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Rate = (44 - 26) / (10 - 4) = 18 / 6 = 3°C per minute. Going back 4 minutes from 26°C: 26 - 4(3) = 14°C.

n.0: 26 - 18 = 8 subtracts the whole 6-minute change instead of 4 minutes' worth.
n.2: 3°C is the rate of change per minute, not the starting temperature.
n.3: 26 / 4 = 6.5 assumes direct variation (starting at 0°C), but the solution did not start at 0°C.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A nurse wants to display how a patient's body weight changed over 12 weekly clinic visits so that the trend is easy to see. Which type of display is most appropriate?
o: Line graph
Circle graph
Histogram
Stem-and-leaf plot
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A line graph shows how one quantity changes over time; connecting the weekly points makes the trend visible.

n.1: A circle graph shows parts of a whole, and the weekly weights are not parts of a total.
n.2: A histogram groups values into intervals and loses the order in time.
n.3: A stem-and-leaf plot shows the spread of values but not their order over the 12 weeks.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A bar graph compares patient satisfaction at two clinics: Clinic A 84% and Clinic B 88%. The vertical axis starts at 82%, so Clinic B's bar appears three times as tall as Clinic A's. Which statement most accurately describes the data?
o: B's rating is about 200% higher than A's
B's rating is about 3 times A's, as the bar heights show
The difference cannot be found, since the axis does not start at 0
B's rating is 4 percentage points higher than A's
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Read the values, not the bar heights: 88% - 84% = 4 percentage points. The axis starting at 82% makes the bars 2 and 6 units tall, which exaggerates the gap.

n.0: Bar heights of 2 and 6 would suggest a 200% increase, but the actual values differ by 4 points (about 4.8%).
n.1: The bars look 3 times as tall only because the axis is truncated; 88% is not 3 times 84%.
n.2: The values can still be read from the scale; a truncated axis distorts the picture, not the numbers.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A pie chart in a hospital newsletter shows how staff members answered a survey question: Yes 45%, No 38%, Unsure 27%. What is the main problem with this chart?
o: The sectors must be ordered from largest to smallest first
Three categories are too few, so a histogram is needed instead
The Unsure sector should be drawn smaller as a non-answer
The sectors total 110%, so they cannot form a single whole
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: The sectors of a pie chart must total 100% of one whole. 45 + 38 + 27 = 110%, so the chart cannot be correct; respondents may have been allowed more than one answer.

n.0: Ordering sectors can help readability, but it does not fix percents that total 110%.
n.1: A pie chart can show three categories, and a histogram is for numeric intervals, not answer categories.
n.2: Each sector's size must match its percent; shrinking one would distort the data further.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A health department wants to show the distribution of cholesterol levels for 200 adults, grouped into intervals of 20 mg/dL, so that readers can see where most levels fall. Which display is most appropriate?
o: Line graph
Circle graph
Scatterplot
Histogram
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A histogram shows the distribution of one numeric variable grouped into intervals, with bar heights giving the frequency in each interval.

n.0: A line graph shows change over time, and these data have no time order.
n.1: A circle graph shows parts of a whole and makes the shape of a distribution hard to see.
n.2: A scatterplot needs two numeric variables, but only cholesterol level is given.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: An advertisement compares a clinic's flu vaccination rate in 2020 and 2025. The rate doubled, so the artist drew the 2025 syringe picture twice as tall and twice as wide as the 2020 picture. Why is the graphic misleading?
o: The 2025 picture is twice as wide, so it understates the increase
The 2025 picture has 2 times the area, which shows the doubling accurately
The 2025 picture has 8 times the area, suggesting an eightfold increase
The 2025 picture has 4 times the area, so the increase looks larger than double
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Scaling both dimensions by 2 multiplies the area by 2 x 2 = 4. Readers judge pictures by area, so a doubling looks like a fourfold increase.

n.0: The extra width makes the increase look larger, not smaller.
n.1: Doubling the height and the width multiplies the area by 4, not 2.
n.2: A factor of 8 (2 x 2 x 2) applies to volume; a flat picture scales its area by 4.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A bar graph of hospital admissions has a vertical axis that starts at 900. The 2024 bar shows 950 admissions and the 2025 bar shows 1,100 admissions, so the 2025 bar looks 4 times as tall. By what percent did admissions actually increase from 2024 to 2025? Round to the nearest tenth and enter the number only.

tr.150: the number of extra admissions, not the percent
tr.300: the visual increase in bar height (50 to 200)

Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Percent increase = (new - original) / original x 100 = (1,100 - 950) / 950 x 100 = 150 / 950 x 100 = 15.79%, about 15.8%. The truncated axis makes the bars 50 and 200 units tall, which suggests a 300% increase.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A researcher has recorded each of 40 adults' average daily calorie intake and their change in weight over one month. Which display best shows whether the two variables are related?
o: Line graph
Scatterplot
Double bar graph
Circle graph
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A scatterplot plots one point per adult using two numeric variables, which shows whether they tend to rise or fall together.

n.0: A line graph tracks change over time, but these data pair two measurements for each person.
n.2: A double bar graph compares two series across categories, and 40 individual adults are not categories to compare.
n.3: A circle graph shows parts of a whole, not a relationship between two variables.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A news article claims 'Emergency room waits have soared' and shows a line graph covering only March and April, when the mean wait rose from 42 to 51 minutes. Over the full year, monthly mean waits ranged from 42 to 60 minutes and averaged 52 minutes. What is the best criticism of the graph?
o: The two-month window hides that April was below the yearly average
The increase from 42 to 51 minutes is a 9% rise, not a large one
The yearly average of 52 minutes proves that waits are falling
A line graph cannot show monthly changes, so a pie chart was needed
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Choosing a short time window (cherry-picking) can make an ordinary change look dramatic. April's 51 minutes was below the yearly average of 52 and well under the 60-minute high.

n.1: The rise is 9 minutes, which is 9 / 42 = 21.4%, not 9%.
n.2: An average does not show a direction of change, so it cannot prove waits are falling.
n.3: A line graph is the right display for change over time; the problem is the window chosen.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A news graph titled 'ER Visits Explode' shows yearly visits at one hospital. The vertical axis runs from 4,000 to 4,600, and the years 2019, 2021, and 2024 are spaced equally along the horizontal axis. Which features make the graph misleading? Select all that apply.
o: The vertical axis begins at 4,000 instead of 0
The title states a conclusion the data may not support
The years are evenly spaced despite unequal gaps
The vertical axis is labeled with the number of visits
A line is used to show change over time
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A truncated vertical axis exaggerates changes, equal spacing for unequal gaps (2 years, then 3 years) distorts the rate of change, and a loaded title pushes a conclusion before the reader checks the scale.

n.3: Labeling the axis with what is counted is good practice and helps readers.
n.4: A line graph is the appropriate display for change over time.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A hospital wants to show what percent of its $2.4 million annual budget goes to each of its five departments. Which display is most appropriate?
o: Histogram
Scatterplot
Circle graph
Line graph
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: A circle (pie) graph shows how a whole, here the total budget, is divided into parts, with each sector's size matching its percent.

n.0: A histogram shows the distribution of a numeric variable in intervals, not shares of a total.
n.1: A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numeric variables.
n.3: A line graph shows change over time, and the budget split is for one year.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: Two bar graphs are placed side by side. Hospital X's graph has a vertical axis from 0 to 50 and shows 40 infections. Hospital Y's graph has a vertical axis from 0 to 500 and shows 400 infections. Both bars reach 80% of the way up their axes. Which conclusion is correct?
o: Hospital Y had 10 times as many infections as Hospital X
The hospitals had about the same number of infections
Hospital X had 10 times as many infections as Hospital Y
Hospital Y had 80% more infections than Hospital X
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: Read each bar against its own scale: X = 40 and Y = 400. 400 / 40 = 10, so Y had 10 times as many, even though the bars look equal.

n.1: The bars look equal only because the two graphs use different scales.
n.2: This reverses the comparison; Y's value, 400, is the larger one.
n.3: 80% is how far each bar reaches up its own axis, not a comparison between the hospitals.

Data, Statistics & Variables.q: A graph of the total (cumulative) number of flu cases at a college shows 120 cases by the end of week 1, 210 by week 2, 270 by week 3, and 300 by week 4. A student says the graph shows the outbreak getting worse each week. Which statement about new cases per week is correct?
o: New cases fell each week, from 120 to 30
New cases stayed steady at about 75 per week
New cases rose each week, from 120 to 300
New cases peaked in week 4 at 300 cases
Data, Statistics & Variables.w: New cases each week are the differences between totals: 120, 210 - 120 = 90, 270 - 210 = 60, 300 - 270 = 30. A cumulative graph keeps rising even as new cases fall.

n.1: 300 / 4 = 75 is the mean per week; the actual weekly counts fell from 120 to 30.
n.2: 120 to 300 are running totals, not new cases each week.
n.3: 300 is the total after 4 weeks; only 30 of those cases were new in week 4.

A&P: Body Organization.q: The stomach wall has a lining that secretes mucus, layers that contract to churn food, nerves that coordinate the contractions, and a layer that binds these together. Which statement explains why the stomach is classified at the organ level?
o: It works with the esophagus and intestines to digest food
Its wall combines two or more tissue types working together
It contains several cell types, all within its mucus lining
Its lining cells are specialized to secrete mucus and acid
A&P: Body Organization.w: The mucus-secreting lining is epithelial tissue, the contracting layers are muscle tissue, the nerves are nervous tissue and the binding layer is connective tissue. Two or more tissue types working together make an organ, and the stomach has all four.

n.0: Cooperating with other organs is what places the stomach in an organ system (the digestive system); it does not explain why the stomach itself is an organ.
n.2: Several cell types within one layer can still be a single tissue, as in blood. An organ needs two or more tissue types.
n.3: Specialized cells describe the cellular or tissue level. Specialization alone does not make a structure an organ.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Place the levels of structural organization in order from the simplest to the most complex, starting with the simplest.
o: Cellular
Chemical
Organism
Organ system
Organ
Tissue
A&P: Body Organization.w: Atoms and molecules (chemical level) build cells (cellular level). Similar cells form tissues, two or more tissue types form an organ, organs that cooperate form an organ system, and all the organ systems together make up the organism.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A biology quiz pairs four structures with levels of organization. Which pairing correctly matches the structure with the level of organization it represents?
o: A single neuron with the tissue level
Cardiac muscle tissue with the organ level
A kidney with the organ system level
A glucose molecule with the chemical level
A&P: Body Organization.w: Atoms and molecules such as glucose make up the chemical level, the simplest level of organization.

n.0: A single neuron is one cell, so it belongs at the cellular level. Nervous tissue is the tissue-level structure.
n.1: Cardiac muscle is a tissue. The heart, which contains cardiac muscle plus other tissues, is the organ.
n.2: A kidney is one organ. The kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra together form the urinary system.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A tutor asks a student to sort structures by level of organization. Which of the following belong at the organ level? Select all that apply.
o: Hyaline cartilage
Femur (thigh bone)
Skin
Urinary bladder
Blood
Neuron
A&P: Body Organization.w: A whole bone such as the femur combines bone tissue, cartilage, marrow, blood vessels and nerves, so it is an organ. The skin (epithelial epidermis plus connective dermis) and the urinary bladder (transitional epithelium, smooth muscle, connective tissue) are also organs.

n.0: Hyaline cartilage is one connective tissue (it covers bone ends within joints), so it belongs at the tissue level.
n.4: Blood is a connective tissue with a fluid matrix (plasma), so it belongs at the tissue level.
n.5: A neuron is a single nerve cell, so it belongs at the cellular level.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A patient education leaflet groups the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra together because they work as a unit to remove wastes in urine. Which level of organization does this grouping represent?
o: Tissue, because the structures are lined by similar epithelial cells
Organ, because each structure contains two or more tissue types
Organ system, because several organs cooperate in one function
Organism, because removing wastes keeps the whole body alive
A&P: Body Organization.w: Each structure listed is an organ. A group of organs that cooperate to carry out one major function is an organ system, here the urinary system.

n.0: A shared epithelial lining is one tissue within each organ. The leaflet groups whole organs, not a tissue.
n.1: That reasoning describes each structure on its own. The question asks about the group, and a group of cooperating organs is an organ system.
n.3: The organism level is the whole person made of all organ systems together, not a single system.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A medication works by binding to a receptor protein on the surface of liver cells. At which level of organization does the receptor protein itself belong?
o: Chemical, because a protein is a large molecule built from atoms
Cellular, because it sits on the plasma membrane of a cell
Tissue, because liver cells form a group with a shared function
Organ, because its effects change how the whole liver functions
A&P: Body Organization.w: A protein is a molecule, and atoms and molecules make up the chemical level. Its location on a cell does not change its own level.

n.1: The receptor is part of a cell, but a part of a cell is not a cell. The protein is a molecule at the chemical level.
n.2: The liver cells together form a tissue, but the receptor protein on one cell is a molecule.
n.3: The drug's effect reaches the organ, but the receptor protein itself is a molecule at the chemical level.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A student argues that a single cardiac muscle cell taken from the heart should be classified at the tissue level. Which statement best explains why this classification is incorrect?
o: A muscle cell belongs at the chemical level because it is made of proteins
A tissue is a group of similar cells working together, and this is a single cell
A tissue requires an extracellular matrix of fibers, which one muscle cell lacks
A tissue must be supplied by blood vessels, and a single muscle cell has none
A&P: Body Organization.w: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together. One cell on its own, even a highly specialized one, is classified at the cellular level.

n.0: Proteins are at the chemical level, but a whole living cell built from them is at the cellular level.
n.2: An abundant extracellular matrix is a feature of connective tissue. Epithelial and muscle tissues have very little matrix between their cells, yet they are still tissues.
n.3: Epithelium is a tissue but is avascular, so blood vessels are not what makes something a tissue.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Which sequence names a structure at each of three successive levels of organization, listed from the lowest of the three levels to the highest?
o: Stomach, digestive system, small intestine
Epithelial cell, epithelial tissue, stomach
Protein, epithelial tissue, epithelial cell
Muscle cell, the heart, cardiac muscle tissue
A&P: Body Organization.w: An epithelial cell is the cellular level, epithelial tissue is the tissue level, and the stomach (built from four tissue types) is the organ level: three successive levels in rising order.

n.0: This runs organ, organ system, organ. The small intestine is another organ, so the sequence drops back a level.
n.2: This runs chemical, tissue, cellular. The cell must come before the tissue.
n.3: This runs cell, organ, tissue. The tissue level must come before the organ level.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A tissue sample viewed under a microscope shows cells packed tightly together in a sheet, resting on a basement membrane, with no blood vessels between the cells. Which tissue type is this?
o: Epithelial tissue
Connective tissue
Nervous tissue
Smooth muscle tissue
A&P: Body Organization.w: Epithelial tissue is made of tightly packed cells that sit on a basement membrane and are avascular, receiving nutrients by diffusion from the tissue beneath.

n.1: Connective tissue has cells scattered in an extracellular matrix, and most connective tissue is vascular.
n.2: Nervous tissue is made of neurons and supporting neuroglia, not a sheet of cells on a basement membrane.
n.3: Smooth muscle is vascular, with capillaries running between its bundles of spindle-shaped cells, and its cells contract rather than forming a covering sheet.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A histology student is comparing the four basic tissue types. Which feature distinguishes connective tissue from epithelial, muscle and nervous tissue?
o: Cells that generate and conduct electrical impulses
Cells scattered within an extracellular matrix of fibers
Cells joined tightly together with an exposed free surface
Cells that shorten when stimulated to produce movement
A&P: Body Organization.w: Connective tissue cells are scattered within an extracellular matrix made of ground substance and fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular). In blood, the matrix is fluid plasma.

n.0: Generating and conducting impulses describes the neurons of nervous tissue.
n.2: Tightly joined cells with a free (apical) surface describe epithelial tissue.
n.3: Contractility describes muscle tissue.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A classmate claims that epithelial tissue and every kind of connective tissue are supplied directly by blood vessels. Which correction is accurate?
o: Bone and blood are avascular and are nourished by diffusion
Cartilage is vascular, but epithelium is nourished by diffusion
Epithelium and cartilage are both avascular and fed by diffusion
Epithelium is vascular, but cartilage is nourished by diffusion
A&P: Body Organization.w: Epithelial tissue is avascular and is fed by diffusion from underlying connective tissue. Most connective tissue is vascular, but cartilage is an avascular exception.

n.0: Bone is a vascular connective tissue, and blood flows inside vessels as the fluid connective tissue.
n.1: Cartilage is the avascular connective tissue; this option reverses the facts for both tissues.
n.3: Epithelium has no blood vessels between its cells; it relies on diffusion from the tissue below.

A&P: Body Organization.q: On an anatomy quiz, a student must classify blood among the four basic tissue types and give the reason. Which answer is correct?
o: An organ, because it holds red cells, white cells and platelets
Epithelial tissue, because its cells line the inside of each vessel
Connective tissue, because its cells are scattered in a fluid matrix
Nervous tissue, because it carries chemical signals such as hormones
A&P: Body Organization.w: Blood is a connective tissue. Like other connective tissues, its cells are scattered in an extracellular matrix; in blood the matrix is the fluid plasma.

n.0: An organ combines two or more tissue types. Several cell types within one tissue still make a tissue.
n.1: The cells lining vessels form an epithelial layer of the vessel wall. Blood is the fluid inside the vessel.
n.3: Carrying hormones does not make blood nervous tissue. Nervous tissue is made of neurons and neuroglia that conduct impulses.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A slide of tissue from a gland duct shows a single layer of cells that are about as tall as they are wide, each resting on the basement membrane. Which name fits this tissue?
o: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Simple cuboidal epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
Stratified cuboidal epithelium
A&P: Body Organization.w: Epithelium is named by layers and cell shape. One layer is "simple," and cells about as tall as they are wide are "cuboidal," giving simple cuboidal epithelium.

n.0: Pseudostratified epithelium has tall cells with nuclei at different heights that look layered; these cells are cube-shaped.
n.2: Columnar cells are taller than they are wide; these cells are about equal in height and width.
n.3: "Stratified" means two or more layers; the sample has one layer.

A&P: Body Organization.q: The lining of the urinary bladder must stretch as the bladder fills and then return to its resting shape as it empties. Which tissue lines the bladder?
o: Transitional epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
Simple columnar epithelium
Dense regular connective tissue
A&P: Body Organization.w: Transitional epithelium is a stretchable epithelium whose cells change shape as the organ fills and empties. It lines the urinary bladder.

n.1: Stratified squamous epithelium is layered and protective (as in the epidermis) but is not the stretchable bladder lining.
n.2: Simple columnar epithelium is a single layer of tall cells, as in the lining of the GI tract; it does not stretch like the bladder lining.
n.3: Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments; it is not a lining tissue.

A&P: Body Organization.q: In a tissue lining an airway, the nuclei sit at several different heights so the tissue looks layered, yet every cell touches the basement membrane. How should this tissue be classified?
o: Stratified, because the nuclei form two or more rows
Transitional, because its cells vary in height and shape
Pseudostratified, a single layer that only looks layered
Simple cuboidal, because each cell rests on the membrane
A&P: Body Organization.w: Pseudostratified epithelium is one layer of cells (every cell touches the basement membrane) whose nuclei sit at different heights, so it looks stratified.

n.0: Stratified epithelium has two or more true layers, with upper cells that do not touch the basement membrane.
n.1: Transitional epithelium is the stretchable lining of the bladder; uneven nuclei in one layer describe pseudostratified tissue.
n.3: Simple cuboidal cells are cube-shaped with nuclei in one row; nuclei at different heights point to pseudostratified epithelium.

A&P: Body Organization.q: The pancreas releases digestive enzymes through a duct into the small intestine and also releases insulin directly into the bloodstream. Which classification of the pancreas is correct?
o: An endocrine gland, because its enzymes act as hormones in the blood
Both an exocrine and an endocrine gland, with ducted and ductless parts
An exocrine gland, because insulin also leaves the gland through a duct
An endocrine gland, because a gland making any hormone is endocrine
A&P: Body Organization.w: Exocrine glands secrete through ducts onto a surface (the pancreatic enzymes), and endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood (insulin). The pancreas does both.

n.0: Digestive enzymes travel through a duct to the small intestine; they are exocrine secretions, not hormones.
n.2: Insulin is a hormone released directly into the blood without a duct, which is an endocrine function.
n.3: Making a hormone shows endocrine function, but the pancreas also secretes enzymes through a duct, so it is exocrine as well.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A nursing student is reviewing epithelial tissue before an exam. Which statements about epithelial tissue are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It is the most abundant tissue type in the body
It rests on a basement membrane
Capillaries run between its tightly packed cells
It is nourished by diffusion from underlying tissue
Its cells regenerate rapidly after injury
Its cells are scattered in an extracellular matrix
A&P: Body Organization.w: Epithelium sits on a basement membrane, is avascular (fed by diffusion from the connective tissue beneath) and has a high capacity for regeneration.

n.0: Connective tissue is the most abundant and widespread tissue type.
n.2: Epithelium is avascular; its capillaries lie in the underlying connective tissue.
n.5: Cells scattered in an extracellular matrix describe connective tissue; epithelial cells are tightly packed.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Tendons attach skeletal muscles to bones and must resist strong pulling forces in one direction. Which tissue forms tendons?
o: Dense irregular connective tissue
Loose areolar connective tissue
Dense regular connective tissue
Skeletal muscle tissue
A&P: Body Organization.w: Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue: tightly packed collagen fibers run parallel to one another, resisting strong pull in one direction.

n.0: Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen fibers running in many directions, suited to pull from several directions (as in the dermis), not the parallel fibers of a tendon.
n.1: Areolar tissue is loose connective tissue with a loose, open arrangement of fibers; it does not withstand strong one-direction pull.
n.3: Skeletal muscle generates the pull; the tendon that transmits it to bone is connective tissue.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Nervous tissue contains two main categories of cells: neurons and neuroglia. Which statement correctly describes the role of neuroglia?
o: They relay impulses between sensory and motor neurons in the CNS
They carry impulses from receptors toward the brain and spinal cord
They support, insulate and protect neurons but do not conduct impulses
They carry commands from the CNS out to muscles and glands
A&P: Body Organization.w: Neuroglia (glial cells) such as astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells support, nourish, insulate (myelin) and protect neurons. Conducting impulses is the job of the neurons themselves.

n.0: Relaying impulses between sensory and motor neurons is the role of interneurons, which are neurons.
n.1: Carrying impulses toward the CNS is the role of sensory (afferent) neurons.
n.3: Carrying commands from the CNS to effectors is the role of motor (efferent) neurons.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A patient has equal-sized scrapes to the outer layer of the skin and to the cartilage of the outer ear. Which prediction about healing is best supported?
o: Both heal at the same rate, because both tissues lack blood vessels
The cartilage heals first, because its matrix is supplied by capillaries
The skin heals first, because epithelium regenerates and cartilage is avascular
The cartilage heals first, because connective tissue is the most abundant tissue
A&P: Body Organization.w: Two facts combine. Epithelium (the outer layer of skin) has a high capacity for regeneration. Cartilage is an avascular connective tissue, so nutrients reach it slowly by diffusion and repair is slow. The skin heals first.

n.0: Both are avascular, but epithelium regenerates quickly while cartilage does not, so the rates differ.
n.1: Cartilage is avascular; its matrix has no capillaries, which is why it heals slowly.
n.3: How abundant a tissue type is in the body does not determine how fast a small injury heals.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Directional terms in anatomy are defined relative to anatomical position. Which description matches anatomical position?
o: Lying face up, arms at the sides, palms facing up, feet pointing forward
Standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward
Standing upright, facing forward, arms raised, palms facing forward
Standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing the thighs
A&P: Body Organization.w: In anatomical position the body is upright and facing forward, feet flat and pointing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward (anterior) with the thumbs pointing away from the body.

n.0: Lying face up is the supine position. Anatomical position is upright.
n.2: The arms hang at the sides in anatomical position; they are not raised.
n.3: Palms facing the thighs is a relaxed standing posture. In anatomical position the palms face forward.

A&P: Body Organization.q: The radius and ulna are the two bones of the forearm. In anatomical position, which term describes the location of the radius relative to the ulna?
o: Posterior
Lateral
Proximal
Medial
A&P: Body Organization.w: In anatomical position the palms face forward, so the radius (on the thumb side) lies farther from the midline than the ulna. The radius is lateral to the ulna.

n.0: With the palms facing forward, the two bones lie side by side, not one behind the other.
n.2: Proximal and distal compare distance from the limb's attachment. The radius and ulna lie side by side along the same length of forearm.
n.3: The ulna (little-finger side) is the medial bone; the radius is lateral to it.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A charting guide lists four example sentences that use proximal or distal. Which sentence uses one of these terms correctly?
o: The fingers are proximal to the palm
The knee is proximal to the ankle
The wrist is proximal to the elbow
The heart is distal to the stomach
A&P: Body Organization.w: Proximal means closer to where a limb attaches to the trunk. The knee is closer to the hip than the ankle is, so the knee is proximal to the ankle.

n.0: The fingers are farther from the limb's attachment than the palm, so they are distal to the palm.
n.2: The wrist is farther from the shoulder than the elbow is, so the wrist is distal to the elbow.
n.3: Proximal and distal describe limbs and branching structures. Organs of the trunk are compared with superior/inferior or anterior/posterior.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A radiology report describes a mass on the ventral surface of the liver. In human anatomy, which term means the same as ventral?
o: Posterior
Caudal
Inferior
Anterior
A&P: Body Organization.w: In humans, ventral means anterior (the front, belly side) and dorsal means posterior.

n.0: Posterior is the back, which is the meaning of dorsal, the opposite of ventral.
n.1: Caudal means toward the feet (tail end), a synonym of inferior, not of ventral.
n.2: Inferior means toward the feet. Ventral refers to the front of the body, not to a lower position.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A patient is lying face down on an exam table, and a nurse notes a bruise on the back of the right thigh, the surface facing the ceiling. Which term correctly describes the bruised surface of the thigh?
o: Lateral, because that surface faces away from the exam table
Superior, because the bruise faces upward while the patient lies prone
Anterior, because the bruise is on the surface farthest from the table
Posterior, because terms are based on anatomical position
A&P: Body Organization.w: Directional terms are defined by anatomical position no matter how the patient is lying. The back of the thigh is posterior.

n.0: Lateral means away from the midline of the body, not away from a table. The back of the thigh is its posterior surface.
n.1: Superior means toward the head in anatomical position, not toward the ceiling in the patient's current position.
n.2: Anterior is the front of the body. The back of the thigh stays posterior when the patient lies face down.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A nurse gives an intramuscular injection into the deltoid muscle of the upper arm. Which statement about the layers at the injection site uses superficial or deep correctly?
o: The hypodermis is superficial to the dermis
The epidermis is deep to the dermis
The deltoid muscle is deep to the hypodermis
The deltoid muscle is superficial to the dermis
A&P: Body Organization.w: From the surface inward the needle passes the epidermis, the dermis, the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) and then the muscle. Deep means farther from the body surface, so the deltoid is deep to the hypodermis.

n.0: The hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) lies beneath the dermis, so it is deep to the dermis.
n.1: The epidermis is the outermost layer, so it is superficial to the dermis.
n.3: The deltoid lies beneath both the dermis and the hypodermis, so it is deep to the dermis.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Using the abdominal quadrants, which term describes the position of the sigmoid colon relative to the spleen?
o: Ipsilateral
Bilateral
Superior
Contralateral
A&P: Body Organization.w: The spleen is in the left upper quadrant and the sigmoid colon is in the left lower quadrant. Both lie on the patient's left side, and ipsilateral means on the same side of the body.

n.1: Bilateral describes paired structures found on both sides, such as the kidneys; it does not compare two unpaired organs.
n.2: The sigmoid colon is in a lower quadrant and the spleen in an upper one, so the sigmoid colon is inferior to the spleen.
n.3: Contralateral means on opposite sides. It would fit only if the spleen or the sigmoid colon were on the right, a common quadrant mistake.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Place these regions of the upper limb in order from most proximal to most distal, starting with the most proximal.
o: Palmar
Digital
Carpal
Brachial
Antecubital
A&P: Body Organization.w: Proximal means closer to where the limb attaches to the trunk. Brachial is the upper arm, antecubital the front of the elbow, carpal the wrist, palmar the palm and digital the fingers, so the digital region is the most distal.

A&P: Body Organization.q: The diaphragm forms the floor of the thoracic cavity. Which statement correctly describes its position in anatomical position?
o: It is superior to the lungs and inferior to the stomach
It is inferior to the heart and superior to the liver
It is inferior to the stomach and superior to the bladder
It is superior to the heart and inferior to the trachea
A&P: Body Organization.w: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity (heart, lungs) from the abdominopelvic cavity (liver, stomach). It lies below the heart and above the liver.

n.0: The lungs sit above the diaphragm and the stomach below it, so the diaphragm is inferior to the lungs and superior to the stomach.
n.2: The stomach lies below the diaphragm in the abdominal cavity, so the diaphragm is superior to the stomach.
n.3: The heart rests on the diaphragm, so the diaphragm is inferior to the heart.

A&P: Body Organization.q: For a person standing in anatomical position, which of the following statements are correct? Select all that apply.
o: The thumb is lateral to the little finger
The elbow is distal to the wrist
The vertebral column is anterior to the sternum
The sternum is anterior to the heart
The ears are lateral to the eyes
The ulna is lateral to the radius
A&P: Body Organization.w: With the palms facing forward, the thumb is farther from the midline than the little finger. The ears are farther from the midline than the eyes. The sternum lies in front of the heart.

n.1: The elbow is closer to the shoulder than the wrist is, so the elbow is proximal to the wrist.
n.2: The vertebral column is at the back of the body, so it is posterior to the sternum.
n.5: The radius (thumb side) is lateral; the ulna is medial to it.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A cut lies on the forearm, midway between the elbow and the wrist, on the thumb side. Using anatomical position, which description of the cut is accurate?
o: Proximal to the wrist, on the medial side of the forearm
Proximal to the wrist, on the lateral side of the forearm
Distal to the elbow, on the medial side of the forearm
Distal to the wrist, on the lateral side of the forearm
A&P: Body Organization.w: Two judgments are needed. The cut is closer to the shoulder than the wrist is, so it is proximal to the wrist. With palms facing forward, the thumb side is lateral.

n.0: Proximal to the wrist is right, but in anatomical position the thumb side is lateral, not medial.
n.2: Distal to the elbow is right, but the thumb side is lateral, not medial.
n.3: The cut is between the elbow and the wrist, so it is proximal to the wrist, not distal.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A post-surgical note states that a patient's incision lies caudal to the umbilicus, on the patient's right side. Which organ lies in the same abdominal quadrant as the incision?
o: The gallbladder
The appendix
The spleen
The sigmoid colon
A&P: Body Organization.w: Caudal is a synonym of inferior (toward the feet), so the incision is below the navel on the patient's right: the right lower quadrant, which contains the appendix and cecum.

n.0: The gallbladder is in the right upper quadrant. Choosing it treats caudal as if it meant cranial (toward the head).
n.2: The spleen is in the left upper quadrant, which is cranial to the navel and on the patient's left.
n.3: The sigmoid colon is below the navel but in the left lower quadrant, on the patient's left side.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A CT scan image shows a horizontal slice through the abdomen, dividing the body into an upper portion and a lower portion. Which plane does this image represent?
o: Transverse plane
Parasagittal plane
Frontal plane
Midsagittal plane
A&P: Body Organization.w: The transverse (horizontal, cross-sectional) plane divides the body into superior and inferior portions, which is the view in a CT cross-section.

n.1: The parasagittal plane is vertical and divides the body into unequal left and right portions.
n.2: The frontal (coronal) plane is vertical and divides the body into anterior and posterior portions.
n.3: The midsagittal plane is vertical and divides the body into equal left and right halves.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A model of the human body is cut along a vertical plane that separates the face and chest from the back of the head and the back. Which plane was used?
o: Frontal (coronal) plane
Transverse (horizontal) plane
Midsagittal (median) plane
Parasagittal plane
A&P: Body Organization.w: The frontal (coronal) plane is vertical and divides the body into anterior (front) and posterior (back) portions.

n.1: The transverse plane is horizontal and divides superior from inferior.
n.2: The midsagittal plane divides the body into left and right halves, not front and back.
n.3: A parasagittal plane divides the body into unequal left and right parts.

A&P: Body Organization.q: The ventral body cavity is subdivided by a dome-shaped muscle that contracts during breathing. Which two cavities does the diaphragm separate?
o: The pleural and pericardial cavities
The abdominal and pelvic cavities
The cranial and vertebral (spinal) cavities
The thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities
A&P: Body Organization.w: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity (lungs, heart) above from the abdominopelvic cavity below.

n.0: The pleural and pericardial cavities both lie within the thoracic cavity above the diaphragm.
n.1: The abdominal and pelvic cavities are continuous, both within the abdominopelvic cavity below the diaphragm.
n.2: The cranial and vertebral cavities form the dorsal cavity; the diaphragm is part of the ventral cavity.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A diagram shows a patient facing the viewer, and an instructor points to the lower abdominal quadrant on the viewer's left side. Which organ is located in that quadrant?
o: The spleen
The appendix
The gallbladder
The sigmoid colon
A&P: Body Organization.w: Two steps: a patient facing the viewer has their right side on the viewer's left, so the instructor is pointing to the patient's right lower quadrant (RLQ), which contains the appendix and cecum.

n.0: The spleen is in the left upper quadrant, not a lower quadrant.
n.2: The gallbladder is in the right upper quadrant, under the liver, not a lower quadrant.
n.3: The sigmoid colon is in the left lower quadrant. That is the patient's left, which appears on the viewer's right.

A&P: Body Organization.q: The mediastinum is the central region of the thoracic cavity between the two lungs. Which structure is found in the mediastinum?
o: The spinal cord
The left lung
The esophagus
The right pleural cavity
A&P: Body Organization.w: The mediastinum contains the heart within its pericardial cavity, the trachea, the esophagus, the thymus and the great vessels.

n.0: The spinal cord is in the vertebral cavity, part of the dorsal cavity, not the ventral thoracic cavity.
n.1: Each lung lies in its own pleural cavity on either side of the mediastinum.
n.3: The pleural cavities flank the mediastinum; they surround the lungs.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Serous membranes reduce friction around organs in the ventral cavity. Which layer adheres directly to the outer surface of each lung?
o: Visceral pleura
Parietal peritoneum
Parietal pleura
Visceral pericardium
A&P: Body Organization.w: Serous membranes have a parietal layer lining the cavity wall and a visceral layer covering the organ. The pleura surrounds the lungs, so the layer on the lung surface is the visceral pleura.

n.1: The parietal peritoneum lines the wall of the abdominopelvic cavity.
n.2: The parietal pleura lines the wall of the thoracic cavity, not the lung surface.
n.3: The visceral pericardium covers the heart, not the lungs.

A&P: Body Organization.q: During a lumbar puncture, a needle is inserted between two lumbar vertebrae into the fluid-filled space of the vertebral canal. Which body cavity, and its larger division, does this space belong to?
o: The cranial cavity, part of the ventral cavity
The mediastinum, part of the thoracic cavity
The pelvic cavity, part of the ventral cavity
The vertebral cavity, part of the dorsal cavity
A&P: Body Organization.w: The spinal cord lies in the vertebral (spinal) cavity. Together with the cranial cavity, it forms the dorsal body cavity, protected by bone and meninges.

n.0: The cranial cavity holds the brain, and it belongs to the dorsal cavity, not the ventral cavity.
n.1: The mediastinum is in the ventral thoracic cavity and holds the heart, trachea and esophagus, not the spinal cord.
n.2: The pelvic cavity holds the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs; the spinal cord lies in the dorsal cavity.

A&P: Body Organization.q: In the nine-region scheme of the abdomen, three regions run down the midline. Which region lies directly inferior to the umbilical region?
o: Right lumbar region
Hypogastric (pubic) region
Epigastric region
Left iliac (inguinal) region
A&P: Body Organization.w: The middle column of the nine regions runs epigastric (top), umbilical (middle), hypogastric or pubic (bottom). The hypogastric region lies directly below the umbilical region.

n.0: The right lumbar region lies lateral to the umbilical region, in the middle row.
n.2: The epigastric region lies directly superior to the umbilical region, not inferior to it.
n.3: The left iliac (inguinal) region is in the bottom row but lateral, not directly below the umbilical region.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A patient points to an area of the abdomen directly beside the navel on their own right side. Using the nine-region scheme, which region is this?
o: Left lumbar region
Right iliac (inguinal) region
Right lumbar region
Right hypochondriac region
A&P: Body Organization.w: The middle row of the nine regions runs right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar. The area beside the navel on the patient's own right is the right lumbar region.

n.0: Regions are named for the patient's own sides, so the patient's right side is the right lumbar region.
n.1: The right iliac (inguinal) region is in the bottom row, below the right lumbar region.
n.3: The right hypochondriac region is in the top row, beneath the lower ribs, above the right lumbar region.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Place the following in order from the most superior to the most inferior in a person standing in anatomical position, starting with the most superior.
o: Diaphragm
Cranial cavity
Thoracic cavity
Abdominal cavity
Pelvic cavity
A&P: Body Organization.w: The cranial cavity (brain) is highest. Below the neck is the thoracic cavity, whose floor is the diaphragm. Below the diaphragm lies the abdominopelvic cavity: the abdominal cavity above and the pelvic cavity below.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A student is labeling a diagram of the ventral body cavity. Which organs lie in the abdominopelvic cavity? Select all that apply.
o: Lower lobe of the right lung
Lower spinal cord
Rectum
Thymus
Spleen
Gallbladder
A&P: Body Organization.w: The abdominal cavity holds the stomach, liver, gallbladder, intestines and spleen; the pelvic cavity holds the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs. Both lie in the abdominopelvic cavity below the diaphragm.

n.0: The lower lobe of the lung sits on top of the diaphragm in its pleural cavity, so it is in the thoracic cavity even though it is level with the upper abdomen.
n.1: The spinal cord lies in the vertebral cavity, part of the dorsal cavity, not the ventral abdominopelvic cavity.
n.3: The thymus is in the mediastinum of the thoracic cavity, above the diaphragm.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A patient's chart notes a rash in the popliteal region and on the plantar surface of the same leg. Which two areas are affected?
o: The front of the thigh and the sole of the foot
The front of the knee and the sole of the foot
The back of the knee and the sole of the foot
The back of the knee and the top of the foot
A&P: Body Organization.w: Two regional terms: popliteal means the back of the knee, and plantar means the sole of the foot.

n.0: The front of the thigh is part of the femoral region; popliteal is the back of the knee.
n.1: The front of the knee is the patellar region; popliteal is the back of the knee.
n.3: Popliteal is right, but plantar is the sole, not the top of the foot.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A physiology instructor asks the class to define homeostasis in a single sentence. Which statement best defines homeostasis?
o: Keeping each internal variable fixed at one exact, unchanging value
Adjusting the internal environment to match conditions outside the body
Maintaining a relatively stable internal environment as conditions change
Amplifying a change in the body until a specific end event is reached
A&P: Body Organization.w: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment. Variables fluctuate within a narrow range around a set point rather than staying fixed.

n.0: Homeostasis is dynamic: variables such as body temperature move within a narrow range around a set point rather than holding one exact value.
n.1: Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable despite outside changes; it does not make it match the outside.
n.3: Amplifying a change until an end event describes positive feedback, which is one mechanism, not the definition of homeostasis.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A feedback loop has three main components. Which component receives information about a change and compares it with the set point before directing a response?
o: Effector
Stimulus
Sensory receptor
Control center
A&P: Body Organization.w: The receptor (sensor) detects the change, the control center (often the brain, such as the hypothalamus) compares it with the set point, and the effector (a muscle or gland) produces the response.

n.0: The effector, a muscle or gland, carries out the response that the control center directs.
n.1: The stimulus is the change itself, not a component that processes information.
n.2: The receptor detects the change and sends the information on; it does not compare it with the set point.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Most homeostatic mechanisms use negative feedback, but a few use positive feedback. Which of the following is an example of positive feedback?
o: Oxytocin release that strengthens uterine contractions in labor
A slower heart rate that lowers a sudden rise in blood pressure
Insulin release that lowers blood glucose after a meal
Shivering that raises body temperature when it falls
A&P: Body Organization.w: During childbirth, pressure on the cervix triggers oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions, which triggers more oxytocin. The change is amplified until the baby is delivered.

n.1: The baroreceptor reflex reverses a rise in blood pressure, which is negative feedback.
n.2: Insulin reverses a rise in blood glucose, which is negative feedback.
n.3: Shivering reverses a fall in body temperature, which is negative feedback.

A&P: Body Organization.q: During a long run on a hot day, a runner's sweat glands release sweat, and its evaporation cools the skin. In this feedback loop, which role do the sweat glands play?
o: Control center
Receptor
Effector
Set point
A&P: Body Organization.w: An effector is the muscle or gland that produces the response. The sweat glands carry out the cooling response directed by the control center (the hypothalamus).

n.0: The control center for body temperature is the hypothalamus in the brain, which directs the sweat glands.
n.1: Receptors are the temperature sensors that detect the rise; the sweat glands respond to the change.
n.3: The set point is the target value (normal body temperature), not a structure.

A&P: Body Organization.q: Place the events of a negative feedback response to overheating in order, starting with the first event.
o: Sweat glands increase sweat secretion
Body temperature falls back toward the set point
The hypothalamus compares the input with the set point
Temperature receptors detect the rise
Body temperature rises above the set point
A&P: Body Organization.w: The stimulus (rising temperature) is detected by receptors, which signal the control center (hypothalamus). The control center compares the input with the set point and activates the effectors (sweat glands). The response reverses the change, returning temperature toward the set point.

A&P: Body Organization.q: After a large meal, blood glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, and blood glucose falls back to normal. Why is this classified as negative feedback?
o: The response lowers a variable, and any decrease counts as negative feedback
The response amplifies the rise until all of the glucose has been stored
The control center is a gland rather than the brain, which defines negative feedback
The response reverses the original change, bringing glucose back toward normal
A&P: Body Organization.w: Negative feedback means the response opposes (reverses) the original change. A rise in glucose leads to a response that lowers it back toward the set point.

n.0: "Negative" refers to opposing the change, not to lowering a value. Releasing glucagon to raise low blood glucose is also negative feedback.
n.1: Amplifying a change describes positive feedback. Insulin opposes the rise in glucose.
n.2: Feedback type depends on whether the response opposes or amplifies the change, not on which structure acts as the control center.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A student says that positive feedback is named "positive" because it benefits the body, while negative feedback harms it. Which correction is accurate?
o: "Positive" means the effector is a muscle rather than a gland in that feedback loop
"Positive" means the response amplifies the original change toward an end event
"Positive" means the response adds a hormone to the blood and raises its level
"Positive" means the response returns the variable to its set point after a change
A&P: Body Organization.w: Positive feedback amplifies the original change until an end event occurs, such as delivery of a baby or formation of a clot. The term describes direction, not whether the outcome is good.

n.0: Effectors in both kinds of loops can be muscles or glands; feedback type does not depend on the effector.
n.2: Negative feedback loops also release hormones (insulin, glucagon). What makes feedback positive is that the response amplifies the change.
n.3: Returning a variable to its set point is what negative feedback does.

A&P: Body Organization.q: When blood pressure suddenly rises, stretch receptors in large arteries signal the brain, which then slows the heart rate. Which statement correctly identifies the type of feedback and the heart's role?
o: Positive feedback; the heart acts as the effector
Negative feedback; the heart acts as the receptor
Negative feedback; the heart acts as the effector
Positive feedback; the heart acts as the control center
A&P: Body Organization.w: Two steps. Slowing the heart reverses the rise in pressure, so this is negative feedback (the baroreceptor reflex). The heart carries out the response directed by the brain, so it is the effector.

n.0: The heart is the effector, but the response opposes the rise in blood pressure, which is negative feedback.
n.1: This is negative feedback, but the receptors are the stretch receptors in the arteries; the heart produces the response.
n.3: The response opposes the change (negative feedback), and the control center is the brain, not the heart.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A study guide lists six body processes. Which of these processes are regulated mainly by negative feedback? Select all that apply.
o: Uterine contractions during childbirth
Blood glucose level
Body temperature
Blood clotting after an injury
Milk ejection during breastfeeding
Blood calcium level
A&P: Body Organization.w: Body temperature, blood glucose and blood calcium are kept near their set points by responses that reverse any change, which is negative feedback.

n.0: Labor contractions are driven by positive feedback through oxytocin until delivery.
n.3: Blood clotting is a positive feedback cascade: each step accelerates the next until a clot forms.
n.4: Milk ejection is a positive feedback loop: suckling triggers oxytocin release, which continues while the infant feeds.

A&P: Body Organization.q: When a vessel is cut, platelets that stick to the injury release chemicals that attract more platelets, and the process speeds up until the opening is sealed. Which statement best describes this process?
o: Negative feedback, because sealing the wound restores normal blood volume
Positive feedback, because each step intensifies the next until a clot forms
Positive feedback, because the outcome is helpful to the body's survival
Negative feedback, because platelet numbers return to their usual set point
A&P: Body Organization.w: Each platelet that sticks recruits more platelets, so the response amplifies the original change until an end event (the clot) stops it. Amplification toward an end event is positive feedback.

n.0: A helpful end result does not make a loop negative. The mechanism amplifies the change, which is positive feedback.
n.2: This is positive feedback, but because the response amplifies the change, not because the outcome is helpful.
n.3: The process builds up platelets at the injury site rather than reversing a change back to a set point.

A&P: Body Organization.q: A swimmer's core temperature falls to 35 degrees C (95 degrees F) in cold water, and her skeletal muscles begin shivering. Which statement best describes the shivering?
o: A receptor response that detects the drop in core temperature
A positive feedback response that amplifies the temperature drop
A control center response that lowers the body's temperature set point
An effector response in negative feedback that generates heat
A&P: Body Organization.w: Skeletal muscles are effectors. Shivering produces heat that reverses the fall in temperature, so it is a negative feedback response.

n.0: Temperature receptors detect the drop; the shivering muscles produce the response.
n.1: Shivering opposes the drop by generating heat, so it does not amplify the change.
n.2: The control center (hypothalamus) directs shivering to restore the set point, not to lower it.

A&P: Body Organization.q: In an experiment, the receptors that monitor blood pressure in an animal are prevented from sending signals to the brain. Which outcome is most likely?
o: Blood pressure would stay at its set point, because no corrections occur
The effectors would amplify each change until an end event occurred
Changes would go undetected, so blood pressure would vary more widely
The control center would switch the loop over to positive feedback
A&P: Body Organization.w: Without receptor input, the control center cannot detect changes from the set point, so it cannot trigger corrective responses. Blood pressure would drift more widely than normal.

n.0: Corrections are what hold a variable near its set point; without them the variable drifts.
n.1: Amplification is a feature of positive feedback loops; losing receptors removes the signal that starts any correction.
n.3: Loss of receptor input does not turn a negative feedback loop into a positive one; the loop simply stops correcting.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: The trachea is held open by rings of hyaline cartilage that are incomplete on the posterior side. What is the main advantage of leaving the back of each ring open?
o: The open ends anchor the vocal cords inside the trachea
The esophagus behind it can expand as a swallowed bolus passes
The trachea can collapse completely during each quiet expiration
Gases can diffuse through the thin posterior wall into the blood
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The C-shaped rings keep the trachea open for airflow, while the open back faces the esophagus so the esophagus can bulge forward as food passes down.

n.0: The vocal cords are in the larynx, above the trachea, not attached to tracheal rings.
n.2: The rings exist to stop the trachea from collapsing; it stays open in both inspiration and expiration.
n.3: No gas exchange occurs in the trachea; it is part of the conducting zone (anatomical dead space).

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Years of smoking destroy many of the cilia that line a patient's bronchi. Which normal airway function is most directly impaired?
o: Sweeping mucus and trapped particles up toward the pharynx
Producing mucus from goblet cells to trap inhaled dust
Warming and humidifying air as it passes over the conchae
Secreting surfactant to keep the alveoli from collapsing
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Cilia on the airway epithelium beat to move the mucus sheet, with its trapped particles, up toward the pharynx (the mucociliary escalator). Without cilia, mucus pools and is cleared by coughing.

n.1: Mucus is made by goblet cells, not cilia, so mucus is still produced; it is moving it that fails.
n.2: Warming and humidifying occur mainly in the nasal cavity, over the vascular mucosa of the conchae, not by bronchial cilia.
n.3: Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells, which have no cilia.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which type of epithelium lines most of the trachea and bronchi and carries the cilia of the mucociliary escalator?
o: Simple ciliated columnar epithelium
Ciliated simple cuboidal epithelium
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The conducting airways are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells: one layer of cells that looks layered, with cilia that sweep mucus upward.

n.0: Simple ciliated columnar epithelium is a true single layer of tall cells that lines the uterine tubes; the trachea and bronchi have the pseudostratified form, whose nuclei sit at different heights.
n.1: Cuboidal cells, some with cilia, line only the smallest bronchioles near the respiratory zone, not the trachea and bronchi.
n.3: Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium resists abrasion in the oropharynx, laryngopharynx and esophagus; it has no cilia and does not line the trachea.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: In an alveolus, which cell type secretes surfactant, and what does surfactant do?
o: Type II alveolar cells; it lowers surface tension so alveoli resist collapse
Type I alveolar cells; it lowers surface tension so alveoli resist collapse
Type II alveolar cells; it raises surface tension so alveoli recoil on expiration
Alveolar macrophages; it coats inhaled dust so the dust can be digested
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant, which lowers the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli so they do not collapse at the end of each breath.

n.1: The effect is right but the cell is wrong: type I cells are thin squamous cells specialized for gas exchange.
n.2: The cell is right but the effect is reversed: surfactant decreases surface tension.
n.3: Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) engulf particles; they do not make surfactant.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A baby born at 26 weeks has not yet produced enough of the substance secreted by type II alveolar cells. Which problem is this baby most likely to have?
o: Mucus builds up in the bronchi because the cilia cannot beat effectively
Alveoli overinflate during each breath because surface tension stays too low
Alveoli collapse at the end of each breath because surface tension stays high
Inhaled dust builds up in the alveoli because too few dust cells are made
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: type II alveolar cells make surfactant. Step 2: surfactant lowers surface tension; without enough of it, surface tension stays high and alveoli tend to collapse after each exhalation, making every breath hard work.
