n.0: Moving mucus is the job of ciliated airway cells in the bronchi, not type II alveolar cells.
n.1: This reverses the effect: surfactant lowers surface tension, so a shortage leaves surface tension too high, not too low.
n.3: Dust cells are alveolar macrophages, which engulf particles; type II cells secrete surfactant, so a shortage of it does not reduce dust clearance.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which statement correctly describes the pleural membranes and the fluid between them?
o: Parietal pleura covers each lung and visceral pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid lowers alveolar surface tension
Visceral pleura covers each lung and parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid lowers alveolar surface tension
Visceral pleura covers each lung and parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid reduces friction
Parietal pleura covers each lung and visceral pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid reduces friction
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Visceral pleura covers the lung surface and parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall. Pleural fluid between them reduces friction and holds the lungs against the chest wall so they expand with it.

n.0: Both parts are wrong: visceral pleura is the layer on the lung, and lowering alveolar surface tension is the role of surfactant, not pleural fluid.
n.1: The membranes are named correctly, but lowering alveolar surface tension is the job of surfactant inside the alveoli; pleural fluid lies outside the lung and reduces friction.
n.3: The layers are reversed: visceral means on the organ (the lung), parietal means on the cavity wall.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which structures are part of the conducting zone of the respiratory system? Select all that apply.
o: Segmental bronchus
Respiratory bronchiole
Trachea
Alveolar duct
Alveolus
Terminal bronchiole
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The conducting zone runs from the nose to the terminal bronchioles: it moves, warms and cleans air but does not exchange gas. The trachea, segmental (tertiary) bronchi and terminal bronchioles all belong to it.

n.1: Respiratory bronchioles have alveoli budding from their walls and are the first part of the respiratory zone.
n.3: Alveolar ducts belong to the respiratory zone and take part in gas exchange.
n.4: Alveoli are the main site of gas exchange and are the core of the respiratory zone.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Place the structures in the order inhaled air passes through them, starting with the first.
o: Laryngopharynx
Trachea
Secondary (lobar) bronchus
Larynx
Respiratory bronchiole
Nasopharynx
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Air passes from the nasal cavity into the nasopharynx, down through the oropharynx to the laryngopharynx, then into the larynx and trachea. The trachea divides into primary bronchi, then secondary (lobar) and tertiary bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles and finally respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A student rests a hand on her abdomen and feels it move outward during a normal, quiet inspiration. What is her diaphragm doing at that moment?
o: It relaxes and flattens, which lets the ribs fall and draws air in
It contracts, flattens and moves downward, enlarging the thoracic cavity
It contracts and domes upward, which pushes air into the lungs
It relaxes and domes upward, which enlarges the thoracic cavity
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: In inspiration the diaphragm contracts, flattens and moves down, increasing the vertical size of the thoracic cavity. The larger volume lowers pressure in the lungs, so air flows in.

n.0: A relaxed diaphragm domes upward rather than flattening, and falling ribs reduce thoracic volume.
n.2: A contracting diaphragm flattens and moves down; it does not dome upward or push air.
n.3: Relaxing and doming upward is what the diaphragm does in expiration, and it makes the thoracic cavity smaller.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: When the volume of the thoracic cavity increases during inspiration, what happens to the pressure inside the lungs, and which way does air move?
o: Pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, so air flows in
Pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in
Pressure stays equal to atmospheric pressure as air flows in
Pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows out
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related. Larger thoracic volume means lower intrapulmonary pressure; air flows from high (atmosphere) to low (lungs).

n.0: A larger volume lowers the pressure; higher pressure in the lungs would push air out.
n.2: Air moves only when a pressure gradient exists; equal pressures mean no airflow.
n.3: The pressure change is right, but air moves from high to low pressure, which is into the lungs.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which statement best describes quiet expiration in a healthy adult at rest?
o: It is passive: the inspiratory muscles relax and the lungs recoil elastically
It is passive: the abdominal muscles relax and the diaphragm flattens out
It is active: the internal intercostals contract and pull the ribs down
It is active: the diaphragm contracts and pushes upward against the lungs
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Quiet expiration is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, the elastic lungs and chest wall recoil, thoracic volume falls and pressure rises above atmospheric, so air flows out.

n.1: A flattening diaphragm enlarges the thorax, which belongs to inspiration, not expiration.
n.2: Internal intercostals are used in forced expiration (coughing, exercise), not quiet breathing.
n.3: The diaphragm relaxes during expiration; when it contracts it flattens downward.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A spinal cord injury high in the neck damages the nerve that supplies the main muscle of quiet breathing. Which nerve is it?
o: The vagus nerve
The accessory nerve
The intercostal nerves
The phrenic nerve
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The phrenic nerve, which arises from the cervical spinal cord, supplies the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing.

n.0: The vagus nerve (CN X) carries parasympathetic fibers to thoracic and abdominal organs; it does not drive the diaphragm.
n.1: The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies neck and shoulder muscles such as the trapezius.
n.2: Intercostal nerves supply the intercostal muscles, which assist breathing but are not the main muscle.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Vital capacity is the largest volume of air a person can exhale after taking the deepest possible breath. Which volumes add up to vital capacity?
o: Tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + residual volume
Inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume + residual volume
Tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume
Tidal volume + expiratory reserve volume + residual volume
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume: everything that can be moved in and out. Residual volume stays in the lungs and is excluded.

n.0: Residual volume cannot be exhaled, so it is not part of vital capacity; expiratory reserve volume is missing.
n.1: This leaves out tidal volume and wrongly includes residual volume.
n.3: This leaves out inspiratory reserve volume and wrongly includes residual volume.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A basic spirometer measures the air a person breathes in and out through a mouthpiece. Which lung volume cannot be measured directly with this device?
o: Inspiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
Vital capacity
Expiratory reserve volume
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Residual volume is the air that remains in the lungs after the most forceful exhalation; because it is never breathed out, a simple spirometer cannot record it.

n.0: Inspiratory reserve volume is extra air inhaled beyond a normal breath and is measured by spirometry.
n.2: Vital capacity is the total that can be exhaled after a maximal breath, so it is measured directly.
n.3: Expiratory reserve volume is the extra air forced out after a normal exhalation, so the spirometer records it.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A spirometry report lists a vital capacity of 4,800 mL and a residual volume of 1,200 mL. What is this person's total lung capacity?
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume = 4,800 + 1,200 = 6,000 mL.

n.0: 4,800 mL is the vital capacity; it leaves out the residual volume that is always in the lungs.
n.1: 5,300 mL adds a 500 mL tidal volume, which is already included in vital capacity.
n.2: 3,600 mL subtracts residual volume instead of adding it.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: During a hard cough or a forced exhalation, which muscles contract to push air out of the lungs?
o: The external intercostals and the diaphragm
The external intercostals and abdominal muscles
The diaphragm and the internal intercostals
The internal intercostals and abdominal muscles
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Forced expiration is active: the internal intercostals pull the ribs down and the abdominal muscles push the abdominal organs up against the relaxed diaphragm, shrinking the thorax.

n.0: The external intercostals and diaphragm are the muscles of inspiration.
n.1: The abdominal muscles help, but the external intercostals lift the ribs for inspiration.
n.2: The internal intercostals help, but the diaphragm relaxes during expiration; contraction would enlarge the thorax.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which pair of values is typical for a healthy adult breathing quietly at rest?
o: Tidal volume about 150 mL; 12 to 20 breaths per minute
Tidal volume about 1,200 mL; 12 to 20 breaths per minute
Tidal volume about 500 mL; 60 to 100 breaths per minute
Tidal volume about 500 mL; 12 to 20 breaths per minute
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: A normal resting breath moves about 500 mL (tidal volume), and a resting adult breathes about 12 to 20 times per minute.

n.0: About 150 mL is the anatomical dead space of the conducting zone, not the whole tidal volume.
n.1: About 1,200 mL is a typical residual volume, far larger than one quiet breath.
n.2: 60 to 100 per minute is the normal resting heart rate, not the breathing rate.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A healthy adult's spirometry shows a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 3,000 mL, an expiratory reserve volume of 1,100 mL and a residual volume of 1,200 mL. What is the vital capacity? Enter your answer in milliliters as a whole number.

tr.3500: Added only tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume (inspiratory capacity).
tr.5800: Added the residual volume as well; that gives total lung capacity.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume = 500 + 3,000 + 1,100 = 4,600 mL. Residual volume is not included because it cannot be exhaled.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which events occur during a normal, quiet inspiration? Select all that apply.
o: Thoracic volume decreases as the diaphragm domes
Lung pressure falls below atmospheric pressure
The internal intercostals pull the ribs downward
The external intercostals lift the ribs
The diaphragm contracts and moves downward
Elastic recoil of the lungs draws air inward
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Quiet inspiration is active: the diaphragm contracts and descends, the external intercostals lift the ribs, thoracic volume rises, and intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric so air flows in.

n.0: A doming diaphragm and shrinking thorax describe expiration.
n.2: Internal intercostals pull the ribs down in forced expiration.
n.5: Elastic recoil drives quiet expiration by pushing air out, not drawing it in.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Place the events of a quiet inspiration in order, starting with the first.
o: Air flows into the lungs until the pressures are equal
The phrenic nerve stimulates the diaphragm
Pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure
The diaphragm contracts and flattens
The volume of the thoracic cavity increases
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Nerve impulses in the phrenic nerve make the diaphragm contract and flatten. This enlarges the thoracic cavity; by Boyle's law the larger volume lowers intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in until the pressures equalize.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: By what process do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the respiratory membrane between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries?
o: Simple diffusion down their partial-pressure gradients
Osmosis driven by the solute concentration of plasma
Facilitated diffusion through protein gas channels
Active transport by carrier proteins that use ATP
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: O2 and CO2 are small, nonpolar gases that move across the thin respiratory membrane by simple diffusion, each from its higher partial pressure to its lower partial pressure. No energy is used.

n.1: Osmosis is the movement of water, not of dissolved gases.
n.2: Small nonpolar gases pass straight through the lipid bilayer without carrier or channel proteins.
n.3: Gas exchange needs no ATP; the gases move down their gradients, not against them.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: In a healthy adult, how is most of the oxygen in arterial blood carried to the tissues?
o: Bound to hemoglobin inside red blood cells
Bound to albumin and other plasma proteins
As bicarbonate ions carried in the plasma
Dissolved directly in the plasma around the cells
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: About 98.5% of oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells as oxyhemoglobin; only about 1.5% is dissolved in plasma.

n.1: Albumin maintains osmotic pressure and carries some drugs and hormones; it is not an oxygen carrier.
n.2: Bicarbonate is the main carrier form of carbon dioxide, not oxygen.
n.3: Oxygen dissolves poorly in plasma, so only about 1.5% is carried this way.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Carbon dioxide produced by working muscle must be carried to the lungs. In which form is most of this carbon dioxide transported in the blood?
o: Bound to hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin
Bound to the iron atoms of heme groups
Dissolved as carbon dioxide gas in plasma
As bicarbonate ions in the plasma
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: About 70% of CO2 is carried as bicarbonate (HCO3-), formed inside red blood cells by carbonic anhydrase and then moved into the plasma. About 20-23% rides on hemoglobin and 7-10% is dissolved.

n.0: Carbaminohemoglobin carries only about a fifth of the CO2, not most of it.
n.1: Iron in heme binds oxygen; CO2 that binds hemoglobin attaches to the globin protein, and it is still the minority route.
n.2: Only about 7-10% of CO2 is carried dissolved in plasma.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A stroke damages the region of the brain that generates the basic rhythm of breathing. Which region is damaged?
o: Hypothalamic nuclei
Pons
Cerebellar cortex
Medulla oblongata
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The respiratory centers in the medulla oblongata set the basic breathing rhythm; the pons helps smooth the pattern.

n.0: The hypothalamus regulates temperature, hunger and thirst; it does not generate the breathing rhythm.
n.1: The pons modifies and smooths the breathing pattern, but the basic rhythm is generated in the medulla.
n.2: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance; it is not a breathing center.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: In a healthy person at rest, which change in the blood is the strongest stimulus to increase the rate and depth of breathing?
o: A fall in oxygen, sensed by the central chemoreceptors
A fall in carbon dioxide, sensed as a rise in pH
A rise in oxygen, sensed by the carotid bodies
A rise in carbon dioxide, sensed as a fall in pH
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Rising CO2 is the main everyday drive to breathe. CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering the pH of cerebrospinal fluid, which central chemoreceptors in the medulla detect.

n.0: Low oxygen is a weaker, backup stimulus in healthy people, and it is sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors, not central ones.
n.1: Falling CO2 and rising pH slow breathing rather than speed it up.
n.2: A rise in oxygen would not drive breathing up; the carotid bodies respond to a fall in O2.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A hiker climbs to high altitude, where each breath holds less oxygen. Which receptors respond most directly to the drop in blood oxygen?
o: Central chemoreceptors on the surface of the medulla oblongata
Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies
Stretch receptors in the walls of the bronchioles
Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond to low O2 (and also to CO2 and H+), signaling the medulla to increase ventilation.

n.0: Central chemoreceptors respond to CO2 through the pH of cerebrospinal fluid, not to low oxygen.
n.2: Bronchiolar stretch receptors sense lung inflation, not blood oxygen.
n.3: Baroreceptors sense stretch from blood pressure, not oxygen levels.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A patient sedated after surgery breathes slowly and shallowly for over an hour. Which change in the patient's arterial blood is expected?
o: CO2 falls and pH rises (respiratory alkalosis)
CO2 rises and pH rises (respiratory alkalosis)
CO2 falls and pH falls (respiratory acidosis)
CO2 rises and pH falls (respiratory acidosis)
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: hypoventilation removes too little CO2, so CO2 builds up. Step 2: CO2 + H2O forms carbonic acid, which releases H+, so pH falls: respiratory acidosis.

n.0: Falling CO2 and rising pH follow hyperventilation, not slow shallow breathing.
n.1: CO2 does rise, but extra CO2 adds H+, which lowers pH rather than raising it.
n.2: Slow breathing retains CO2, so CO2 rises rather than falls.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: During a panic attack, a student breathes rapidly and deeply for several minutes. Using CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3-, what happens in her blood?
o: CO2 builds up, the reaction shifts right, H+ rises and pH falls
CO2 is blown off, the reaction shifts left, H+ falls and pH rises
CO2 is blown off, the reaction shifts right, H+ rises and pH falls
CO2 is blown off, the reaction shifts left, H+ falls and pH falls
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: hyperventilation removes CO2 faster than it is made. Step 2: with less CO2, the equilibrium shifts left, using up H+; fewer H+ ions means a higher pH (respiratory alkalosis).

n.0: CO2 builds up with slow, shallow breathing, not with rapid deep breathing.
n.2: Removing a reactant (CO2) shifts the equilibrium left, not right, so H+ falls.
n.3: The shift and the fall in H+ are right, but fewer H+ ions means pH rises.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Physiologists distinguish pulmonary ventilation, external respiration, internal respiration and cellular respiration. Which event is an example of internal respiration?
o: A mitochondrion uses oxygen to make ATP from glucose
Oxygen diffuses from an alveolus into a pulmonary capillary
Oxygen diffuses from a systemic capillary into a muscle cell
Air moves into the alveoli as the diaphragm contracts
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Internal respiration is gas exchange between systemic capillary blood and body cells: O2 diffuses into the cells and CO2 diffuses out into the blood.

n.0: Using O2 to make ATP is cellular respiration, a separate process inside the mitochondria.
n.1: Exchange between alveoli and pulmonary capillaries is external respiration.
n.3: Moving air into the lungs is pulmonary ventilation (breathing), not gas exchange.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Carbon dioxide entering the blood at the tissues is rapidly combined with water to form carbonic acid, which then releases bicarbonate. Where does the enzyme that speeds this reaction act?
o: Carbonic anhydrase inside red blood cells
Carbonic anhydrase dissolved in the plasma
Surfactant lining the alveolar walls
Hemoglobin inside the red blood cells
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Carbonic anhydrase inside red blood cells catalyzes CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3. Carbonic acid releases H+ and HCO3-, and most of the bicarbonate then moves out into the plasma for transport.

n.1: The bicarbonate ends up mostly in plasma, but the enzyme that makes it works inside red blood cells.
n.2: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and is not an enzyme for CO2 conversion.
n.3: Hemoglobin carries O2 and some CO2 and buffers H+, but it is not the enzyme that forms carbonic acid.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Why does carbon monoxide poisoning reduce oxygen delivery to the tissues even when a person is breathing air with a normal oxygen content?
o: CO thickens the respiratory membrane, slowing O2 diffusion into blood
CO dissolves in plasma and lowers the amount of O2 plasma can hold
CO binds hemoglobin far more strongly than O2, leaving fewer sites for O2
CO converts bicarbonate to carbonic acid, making the blood too acidic
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, so hemoglobin sites are occupied by CO and less O2 can be carried, although lung oxygen levels are normal.

n.0: CO does not thicken the respiratory membrane; diffusion into the blood is not the problem.
n.1: Plasma carries only about 1.5% of oxygen, so this could not explain the large fall in delivery.
n.3: CO does not act on the bicarbonate system; its effect is on hemoglobin binding.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which statements about the transport of respiratory gases in the blood are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: About 98% of O2 travels bound to hemoglobin
Most oxygen travels dissolved in the plasma
Most CO2 travels bound to hemoglobin
One hemoglobin carries up to four O2
Most CO2 travels as bicarbonate in plasma
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: About 98.5% of O2 rides on hemoglobin, and each hemoglobin carries up to 4 O2. About 70% of CO2 is carried as bicarbonate in plasma.

n.1: Only about 1.5% of oxygen is dissolved; most is bound to hemoglobin.
n.2: Only about 20-23% of CO2 is bound to hemoglobin; most travels as bicarbonate.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which heart chamber has the thickest myocardium, and what explains the difference in wall thickness?
o: The left ventricle, because it pumps blood through the whole systemic circuit
The right atrium, because its wall contains the heart's pacemaker tissue
The left atrium, because it receives oxygenated blood at high pressure
The right ventricle, because it receives blood returning from the entire body
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must generate enough pressure to push blood through the entire systemic circulation, a much longer, higher-resistance circuit than the lungs.

n.1: The SA node is in the right atrial wall, but pacemaker tissue does not make the wall thick.
n.2: Atria are thin-walled receiving chambers; the left atrium receives low-pressure blood from the pulmonary veins.
n.3: The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs at low pressure, so its wall is thinner; blood from the body returns to the right atrium.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which valve prevents blood from flowing back into the left atrium when the left ventricle contracts?
o: Aortic semilunar valve
Mitral (bicuspid) valve
Pulmonary semilunar valve
Tricuspid valve
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The mitral (bicuspid) valve is the left atrioventricular valve, between the left atrium and left ventricle. It closes during ventricular systole to stop backflow into the left atrium.

n.0: The aortic valve guards the exit from the left ventricle into the aorta and prevents backflow from the aorta.
n.2: The pulmonary valve guards the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.
n.3: The tricuspid valve is the right AV valve, between the right atrium and right ventricle.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A cardiologist describes damage to the layer of the heart wall that contracts to pump blood. Which choice names that layer and its tissue correctly?
o: Myocardium, a layer of cardiac muscle
Endocardium, a layer of cardiac muscle
Myocardium, a layer of smooth muscle
Epicardium, a layer of cardiac muscle
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The myocardium is the thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of cardiac muscle, and it contracts to pump blood; it is the layer damaged in a heart attack. The epicardium and endocardium are thin non-muscular coverings.

n.1: The endocardium is a thin lining of endothelium and connective tissue over the chambers and valves; it does not contract.
n.2: The layer is right, but the myocardium is cardiac muscle (striated, branched, with intercalated discs); smooth muscle lines vessels and hollow organs.
n.3: The epicardium (visceral pericardium) is a thin serous membrane on the heart surface; it contains no contractile muscle.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: What is the function of the chordae tendineae and the papillary muscles attached to them?
o: They anchor the AV valve cusps so the cusps do not evert as the ventricles contract
They anchor the semilunar cusps so blood does not flow back from the arteries
They carry impulses from the AV node down to the walls of the ventricles
They pull the AV valves open so the atria can push blood into the ventricles
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Chordae tendineae run from the cusps of the tricuspid and mitral valves to papillary muscles. When the ventricles contract, they hold the cusps so the valves do not turn inside out (evert) into the atria.

n.1: Semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves have no chordae tendineae; their cup-shaped cusps close on their own.
n.2: Impulses travel through the bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers, not the chordae.
n.3: AV valves open passively when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure; the chordae keep them from everting when closed.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which layer of the heart wall is also called the visceral layer of the serous pericardium?
o: Endocardium
Fibrous pericardium
Parietal pericardium
Epicardium
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The epicardium is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium: it lies directly on the heart's surface, with pericardial fluid between it and the parietal layer.

n.0: The endocardium lines the chambers and valves on the inside of the heart.
n.1: The fibrous pericardium is the tough outermost sac, not a serous layer on the heart.
n.2: The parietal pericardium lines the inside of the fibrous sac; visceral means on the organ itself.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: The first heart sound, S1 ("lub"), is produced by which event in the cardiac cycle?
o: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the start of diastole
Closure of the tricuspid and mitral valves as ventricular systole begins
Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves as the ventricles eject
Contraction of the atria at the end of ventricular filling
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: S1 ("lub") is the sound of the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) closing as the ventricles begin to contract. S2 ("dub") is the semilunar valves closing.

n.0: Closure of the semilunar valves at the start of diastole produces S2 ("dub"), not S1.
n.2: Normal heart sounds come from valves closing, not opening.
n.3: Atrial contraction tops up ventricular filling but is not the source of S1.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which pair of valves guards the exits from the ventricles into the great arteries?
o: Tricuspid and pulmonary valves
Mitral and aortic valves
Pulmonary and aortic valves
Tricuspid and mitral valves
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) sit where blood leaves the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk and the left ventricle into the aorta.

n.0: The pulmonary valve is a ventricular exit, but the tricuspid valve is an AV valve.
n.1: The aortic valve is a ventricular exit, but the mitral valve is an AV valve.
n.3: Tricuspid and mitral are the AV valves, between atria and ventricles.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which statement correctly describes the position of the heart in the thorax?
o: It lies in the left pleural cavity with its apex pointing up and to the left
It lies in the mediastinum with its apex pointing down and to the left
It lies in the mediastinum with its base resting downward on the diaphragm
It lies in the mediastinum with its apex pointing up and to the right
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The heart sits in the mediastinum between the lungs, enclosed in the pericardial cavity, with its apex pointing down, forward and to the left.

n.0: The pleural cavities surround the lungs; the heart is in the mediastinum, and its apex points down.
n.2: The broad base faces up and back toward the great vessels; the apex is the part that points down.
n.3: The apex points down and to the left, not up and to the right.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: The atrioventricular valve with three cusps opens, and blood moves from one chamber into another. Which chamber is receiving the blood?
o: Left ventricle
Right atrium
Pulmonary trunk
Right ventricle
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: the AV valve with three cusps is the tricuspid valve, on the right side. Step 2: AV valves let blood pass from atrium to ventricle, so the right ventricle is receiving blood from the right atrium.

n.0: The left ventricle receives blood through the mitral (bicuspid) valve, which has two cusps.
n.1: The right atrium is the chamber sending blood through the tricuspid valve, not receiving it.
n.2: The pulmonary trunk receives blood through the pulmonary semilunar valve, not an AV valve.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: An infant has a congenital opening that lets oxygenated blood pass from the left ventricle straight into the right ventricle. Which structure has the defect?
o: The interatrial septum
The tricuspid valve
The mitral (bicuspid) valve
The interventricular septum
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The interventricular septum is the muscular wall between the right and left ventricles; it normally keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart, so an opening in it (a ventricular septal defect) lets blood cross from the left ventricle to the right.

n.0: The interatrial septum separates the two atria; an opening there lets blood pass between the atria, not the ventricles.
n.1: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle; it does not connect the two ventricles.
n.2: The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle; a faulty mitral valve lets blood leak back into the left atrium, not into the right ventricle.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which statements about the valves of the heart are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The mitral valve is also called the bicuspid valve
The aortic valve lies between the left ventricle and the aorta
The mitral valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle
The pulmonary valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle
Chordae tendineae anchor the aortic and pulmonary valves
The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Tricuspid = right AV valve (RA to RV). Mitral = bicuspid = left AV valve (LA to LV). The aortic valve guards LV to aorta and the pulmonary valve guards RV to pulmonary trunk.

n.2: The mitral valve is on the left, between the left atrium and left ventricle.
n.3: The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk; the tricuspid lies between RA and RV.
n.4: Chordae tendineae anchor the AV valves (tricuspid and mitral), not the semilunar valves.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Place the layers and spaces in order from the outermost covering of the heart to the innermost lining of a chamber.
o: Myocardium
Fibrous pericardium
Parietal layer of the serous pericardium
Epicardium (visceral pericardium)
Pericardial cavity
Endocardium
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: From outside in: the tough fibrous pericardium, lined by the parietal serous layer; the pericardial cavity with its lubricating fluid; the epicardium (visceral layer) on the heart surface; the thick muscular myocardium; and the endocardium lining the chambers and valves.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which vessels carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs back to the heart?
o: Pulmonary arteries
Superior vena cava
Pulmonary veins
Pulmonary trunk
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The pulmonary veins carry freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart.

n.0: Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs.
n.1: The superior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the upper body to the right atrium.
n.3: The pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood out of the right ventricle toward the lungs.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A vessel carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Which statement about this vessel is correct?
o: It is an artery, and its blood is low in oxygen
It is a vein, and its blood is rich in oxygen
It is a vein, and its blood is low in oxygen
It is an artery, and its blood is rich in oxygen
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Arteries are defined by direction: they carry blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen content. The pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs before gas exchange, so they are arteries carrying oxygen-poor blood.

n.1: A vessel carrying blood away from the heart is an artery, and blood on its way to the lungs is oxygen-poor.
n.2: Low oxygen does not make a vessel a vein; vessels are named by direction, and this one carries blood away from the heart.
n.3: It is an artery, but blood leaving the right ventricle has returned from the body and has not yet picked up oxygen in the lungs.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: When the right ventricle contracts, blood leaves it through which valve and enters which vessel?
o: The pulmonary valve, into the pulmonary trunk
The aortic valve, into the aorta
The pulmonary valve, into the pulmonary veins
The tricuspid valve, into the pulmonary trunk
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary (semilunar) valve into the pulmonary trunk, which divides into the pulmonary arteries to the lungs.

n.1: The aortic valve and aorta are the exit route from the left ventricle.
n.2: Pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium; they do not connect to the right ventricle.
n.3: The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle, at the entrance to the ventricle, not its exit.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: The systemic circulation begins in which chamber of the heart, and to which chamber does it return blood?
o: It begins in the right ventricle and returns blood to the left atrium
It begins in the left ventricle and returns blood to the right atrium
It begins in the left atrium and returns blood to the right ventricle
It begins in the left ventricle and returns blood to the left atrium
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Systemic circulation: left ventricle to aorta, body tissues and venae cavae, ending in the right atrium. Pulmonary circulation runs from the right ventricle to the lungs and back to the left atrium.

n.0: Right ventricle to left atrium describes the pulmonary circulation.
n.2: Atria receive blood rather than pump it into a circuit; the systemic circuit starts at the left ventricle.
n.3: Systemic blood returns through the venae cavae to the right atrium, not the left.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: The coronary arteries supply oxygenated blood to the myocardium. From which vessel do they branch?
o: The coronary sinus, on the back of the heart
The superior vena cava, where it enters the right atrium
The base of the aorta, directly above the aortic valve
The pulmonary trunk, directly above the pulmonary valve
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The right and left coronary arteries branch from the base of the aorta directly above the aortic valve. They fill mainly during diastole.

n.0: The coronary sinus is a vein that collects blood from the heart muscle and drains it into the right atrium.
n.1: The superior vena cava carries deoxygenated blood into the right atrium.
n.3: The pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood, which could not supply the myocardium.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: After a meal, blood carrying absorbed nutrients from the small intestine travels first to which organ before returning to the heart?
o: The kidneys, through the renal veins
The liver, through the hepatic artery
The heart, through the inferior vena cava
The liver, through the hepatic portal vein
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Blood from the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas drains into the hepatic portal vein, which takes it to the liver for processing before it reaches the inferior vena cava and the heart.

n.0: Renal veins drain the kidneys, not the intestine.
n.1: The hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood from the aorta to the liver; it does not carry blood from the intestine.
n.2: Intestinal blood does not go straight to the vena cava; the hepatic portal system diverts it through the liver first.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: In a fetus, the umbilical vein carries blood from the placenta to the fetus. Based on how veins are defined, which statement is correct?
o: It carries deoxygenated blood toward the fetal heart
It carries oxygenated blood toward the fetal heart
It carries oxygenated blood away from the fetal heart
It carries deoxygenated blood away from the fetal heart
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: a vein carries blood toward the heart. Step 2: blood leaving the placenta has picked up oxygen, so the umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood toward the fetal heart (the umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood away).

n.0: Blood coming from the placenta has just been oxygenated there.
n.2: Carrying blood away from the heart would make it an artery.
n.3: This describes the umbilical arteries, which return deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A red blood cell leaves the left ventricle, travels to a capillary in the big toe and eventually returns to the left ventricle. Which capillary beds does it pass through, and in what order?
o: Two beds: the toe, then the pulmonary capillaries
Three beds: the toe, the coronary bed, then the lungs
Two beds: the pulmonary capillaries, then the toe
One bed: the systemic capillaries in the toe
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: from the left ventricle the cell goes through systemic arteries to the toe capillaries, then back by veins to the right atrium. Step 2: the right ventricle sends it to the pulmonary capillaries, and the pulmonary veins return it to the left atrium and left ventricle. Two beds, systemic first.

n.1: The coronary bed is a separate branch of the systemic circuit, not a stop on the route to and from the toe.
n.2: Leaving the left ventricle, it enters the systemic circuit first; the lungs come after the right ventricle.
n.3: To get back to the left ventricle it must also pass through the lungs, a second capillary bed.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A blood sample is drawn from a pulmonary artery and compared with a sample from a pulmonary vein. How does the pulmonary artery sample differ?
o: It has the same oxygen, since both vessels serve the lungs
It has higher oxygen and lower carbon dioxide
It has higher oxygen and higher carbon dioxide
It has lower oxygen and higher carbon dioxide
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: the pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, before gas exchange. Step 2: the pulmonary vein carries blood after exchange. So the arterial sample is lower in O2 and higher in CO2 (the classic exception to the oxygen rule).

n.0: Gas exchange in the lung capillaries lies between the two vessels, so their oxygen content differs.
n.1: This would be true of a systemic artery compared with a systemic vein, but the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.
n.2: Blood that is high in CO2 has not yet unloaded it in the lungs, so its O2 is low as well.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which vessels carry deoxygenated blood in a healthy adult? Select all that apply.
o: Superior vena cava
Coronary sinus
Pulmonary arteries
Aorta
Pulmonary veins
Coronary arteries
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs; the superior vena cava and coronary sinus return blood from the body and from the heart muscle to the right atrium. All three carry deoxygenated blood.

n.3: The aorta carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.
n.4: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
n.5: Coronary arteries branch from the aorta and carry oxygenated blood to the myocardium.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Place the structures in the order deoxygenated blood returning from the lower body passes through them, starting with the first.
o: Right ventricle
Pulmonary valve
Tricuspid valve
Pulmonary artery
Inferior vena cava
Right atrium
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Blood from the lower body returns in the inferior vena cava to the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, then leaves through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries to the lungs.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Place the structures in the order oxygenated blood passes through them after leaving the lungs, starting with the first.
o: Mitral valve
Aorta
Left atrium
Pulmonary vein
Left ventricle
Aortic valve
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, passes the mitral (bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle, and is pumped through the aortic valve into the aorta and the systemic circulation.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which structure in the wall of the heart normally acts as its natural pacemaker, setting a resting rate of about 60 to 100 impulses per minute?
o: Purkinje fibers
Sinoatrial (SA) node
Bundle of His (AV bundle)
Atrioventricular (AV) node
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The sinoatrial (SA) node, in the wall of the right atrium, fires fastest (about 60 to 100 impulses per minute), so it sets the pace for the whole heart.

n.0: Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the ventricles; their own intrinsic rate is about 20 to 40 per minute.
n.2: The bundle of His conducts the impulse from the AV node into the septum; it does not set the rate.
n.3: The AV node delays the impulse and can act as a backup pacemaker, but at a slower 40 to 60 per minute.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Why does the electrical impulse pause briefly at the atrioventricular (AV) node before passing to the ventricles?
o: To let the atria refill with blood before they contract again
To let the SA node reset before it fires the next impulse
To let the semilunar valves close before the atria contract
To let the ventricles fill with blood before they contract
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The AV node delay gives the atria time to finish contracting and push blood into the ventricles, so the ventricles are full before they contract.

n.0: The atria refill during ventricular systole and diastole; the AV delay serves ventricular filling.
n.1: The SA node's timing does not depend on the AV node delay; the delay is about ventricular filling.
n.2: The semilunar valves close at the end of ventricular systole, not before atrial contraction.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A nursing student is reading a normal electrocardiogram (ECG) tracing. Which electrical event does the P wave represent?
o: Atrial depolarization
Atrial repolarization
Ventricular depolarization
Ventricular repolarization
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The P wave is atrial depolarization, which triggers atrial contraction. The QRS complex is ventricular depolarization and the T wave is ventricular repolarization.

n.1: Atrial repolarization is hidden within the QRS complex and has no separate wave.
n.2: Ventricular depolarization is the QRS complex.
n.3: Ventricular repolarization is the T wave.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A client's heart rate rises from 70 to 90 beats per minute while stroke volume falls from 80 mL to 70 mL per beat. What happens to cardiac output?
o: It rises, from 5.6 to 7.2 L/min
It stays at 5.6 L/min, as the changes offset
It falls, from 5.6 to 4.9 L/min
It rises, from 5.6 to 6.3 L/min
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Before: 70 × 80 mL = 5,600 mL/min (5.6 L/min). After: 90 × 70 mL = 6,300 mL/min (6.3 L/min). Output rises.

n.0: 7.2 L/min is 90 × 80 mL: it applies the new heart rate but keeps the old stroke volume of 80 mL.
n.1: Cardiac output is a product, not a sum: the rise in rate (× 90/70) outweighs the fall in stroke volume (× 70/80).
n.2: 4.9 L/min is 70 × 70 mL: it applies the new stroke volume but keeps the old heart rate of 70.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Atrial repolarization does not appear as a separate wave on a normal ECG. Why?
o: It occurs during the QRS complex and is hidden by it
It occurs during the T wave and is hidden by it
It occurs after the T wave and is too small to record
It occurs during the P wave and is hidden by it
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The atria repolarize at about the same time the ventricles depolarize, so the small atrial repolarization signal is masked by the much larger QRS complex.

n.1: The T wave is ventricular repolarization, which happens later, while the atria are already at rest.
n.2: After the T wave the whole heart is at rest; the atria repolarized much earlier.
n.3: The P wave is atrial depolarization; repolarization cannot occur at the same moment.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Cardiac muscle is autorhythmic. Which statement best describes the role of the autonomic nervous system in heart rate?
o: It sets the rhythm: the medulla sends one impulse to the ventricles per beat
It adjusts the rate: sympathetic nerves speed it and the vagus nerve slows it
It adjusts the rate: the vagus nerve speeds it and sympathetic nerves slow it
It starts each beat: sympathetic nerves fire the SA node with each heartbeat
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The SA node generates each beat without nerve input. The autonomic nervous system only changes the rate: sympathetic stimulation speeds it up and parasympathetic (vagus) stimulation slows it.

n.0: The medulla's cardiac center adjusts autonomic output, but the impulse for each beat comes from the SA node.
n.2: The roles are reversed: the vagus (parasympathetic) slows the heart and sympathetic nerves speed it.
n.3: The SA node fires on its own (autorhythmicity); nerves modify the rate but do not trigger each beat.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: If the SA node stops firing and the AV node takes over as the pacemaker, which heart rate is most likely?
o: About 100 to 120 beats per minute
About 60 to 100 beats per minute
About 20 to 40 beats per minute
About 40 to 60 beats per minute
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Each part of the conduction system has its own intrinsic rate. The AV node fires at about 40 to 60 per minute, slower than the SA node's 60 to 100.

n.0: Backup pacemakers fire more slowly than the SA node, not faster.
n.1: 60 to 100 per minute is the SA node's normal rate, which is lost here.
n.2: 20 to 40 per minute is the intrinsic rate of the ventricular (Purkinje) tissue, used when the AV node also fails.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A clinic records an adult's blood pressure as 118/76 mmHg. What does the 76 represent?
o: Arterial pressure while the ventricles contract (systolic pressure)
Arterial pressure while the ventricles relax (diastolic pressure)
Arterial pressure while the atria contract at the end of filling
Venous pressure while the ventricles relax and fill with blood
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Blood pressure is written systolic/diastolic. The lower number (76) is the diastolic pressure in the arteries while the ventricles relax and fill.

n.0: Systolic pressure, during ventricular contraction, is the top number (118).
n.2: Diastolic pressure is the minimum arterial pressure during ventricular relaxation; it is not defined by atrial contraction.
n.3: A blood pressure cuff measures arterial pressure, not venous pressure.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Using the American Heart Association category for normal adult blood pressure (systolic below 120 and diastolic below 80 mmHg), which reading is normal?
o: 116/78 mmHg
120/80 mmHg
118/82 mmHg
124/76 mmHg
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Normal means both conditions are met: systolic < 120 and diastolic < 80. Only 116/78 satisfies both (116 < 120 and 78 < 80).

n.1: 120/80 is not below 120/80; both values sit at the cut-off, so it is not in the normal category.
n.2: The systolic value is fine, but a diastolic of 82 is not below 80.
n.3: The diastolic value is fine, but a systolic of 124 is not below 120.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: At rest, a client's heart rate is 80 beats per minute and the stroke volume is 65 mL per beat. What is the cardiac output? Enter your answer in liters per minute, rounded to the nearest tenth.

tr.145: Added heart rate and stroke volume instead of multiplying.
tr.5200: Gave the answer in milliliters per minute; divide by 1,000 to get liters.
tr.0.8: Divided stroke volume by heart rate instead of multiplying.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 80 × 65 = 5,200 mL/min. Convert to liters: 5,200 ÷ 1,000 = 5.2 L/min.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which statements about the conduction system of the heart are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The AV node normally fires faster than the SA node
Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the ventricular walls
The bundle branches run down the interventricular septum
The SA node lies in the wall of the right atrium
The bundle of His carries impulses from the ventricles up to the atria
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The SA node (right atrial wall) starts the impulse; the AV node delays it; the bundle of His and the right and left bundle branches carry it down the interventricular septum; Purkinje fibers spread it through the ventricles so they contract from the apex upward.

n.0: The AV node's intrinsic rate (about 40 to 60 per minute) is slower than the SA node's, which is why the SA node leads.
n.4: The bundle of His carries impulses downward from the AV node toward the ventricles, not back up to the atria.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Place the parts of the cardiac conduction system in the order a normal impulse travels through them, starting with the first.
o: Purkinje fibers
Atrioventricular (AV) node
Bundle of His (AV bundle)
Sinoatrial (SA) node
Right and left bundle branches
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: The SA node fires and the atria contract; the AV node delays the impulse; the bundle of His carries it into the septum; the right and left bundle branches carry it down the septum; the Purkinje fibers spread it through the ventricular walls.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Gases, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between blood and tissues in capillaries rather than in arteries or veins. Which feature of capillaries makes this possible?
o: Their wall has all three tunics, each thinned to one cell
Their wall is a single layer of endothelial cells
Their wall is a thin tunica media with no inner lining
Their wall is a single layer of cuboidal epithelial cells
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: A capillary wall is a single layer of endothelium (simple squamous epithelium), giving a very short diffusion distance. Blood also flows slowest in capillaries, allowing time for exchange.

n.0: Capillaries lack the tunica media and tunica externa; only the endothelial layer of the tunica intima remains.
n.2: Capillaries have no tunica media (smooth muscle); their wall is the endothelium of the tunica intima alone.
n.3: Capillary walls are one cell thick, but the cells are flat (simple squamous) endothelium; cuboidal cells would lengthen the diffusion distance.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Blood in the veins of the legs is under low pressure, yet it returns upward to the heart. Which features make this possible?
o: Narrow lumens that raise the pressure inside them
Elastic walls that recoil after each heartbeat
One-way valves aided by the skeletal muscle pump
Thick smooth-muscle walls that pump blood upward
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Veins have one-way valves, and contracting leg muscles squeeze the veins (the skeletal muscle pump), pushing blood toward the heart while the valves prevent backflow.

n.0: Veins have large lumens and low pressure; narrow lumens describe arterioles.
n.1: Elastic recoil after each beat is a feature of large arteries, not veins.
n.3: Veins have thinner walls with less smooth muscle than arteries, and they do not pump.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A lab technician examines a stained blood smear from a healthy adult. Which description fits a mature red blood cell?
o: Biconcave disc with no nucleus that lives about 12 days
Biconcave disc with a nucleus that lives about 120 days
Biconcave disc with no nucleus that lives about 120 days
Spherical cell with no nucleus that lives about 120 hours
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Mature red blood cells are biconcave discs, lose their nucleus so they can pack in more hemoglobin, and circulate for about 120 days before macrophages in the spleen and liver remove them.

n.0: The lifespan is about 120 days, ten times longer than 12 days.
n.1: Mature RBCs have no nucleus; they lose it during development.
n.3: RBCs are biconcave, not spherical, and they live about 120 days, not 120 hours.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which white blood cell is the most numerous in normal blood and is usually the first to arrive at a site of bacterial infection?
o: Neutrophil
Eosinophil
Monocyte
Lymphocyte
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Neutrophils make up about 50-70% of white blood cells and are the first phagocytes to reach a bacterial infection; dead neutrophils form pus.

n.1: Eosinophils target parasites and take part in allergic reactions; they are a small fraction of WBCs.
n.2: Monocytes are the largest WBCs and become macrophages, but they are far fewer and arrive later.
n.3: Lymphocytes are the second most numerous (about 20-40%) and drive the specific, slower adaptive response.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A 25-year-old woman needs red blood cells immediately, before her blood type can be tested. Which donor type is the safest choice?
o: O positive
AB positive
O negative
AB negative
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Type O negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh (D) antigens, so the recipient's antibodies have nothing to attack. O negative is the universal red-cell donor, and avoiding Rh exposure matters in a woman who may later become pregnant.

n.0: O positive cells carry the Rh (D) antigen, which could sensitize an Rh-negative woman.
n.1: AB positive is the universal recipient; its cells carry A, B and D antigens that most people's antibodies would attack.
n.3: AB negative cells carry A and B antigens, which would react with anti-A or anti-B in most recipients.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A patient with type A blood is mistakenly given type B red blood cells and has a transfusion reaction. What causes the reaction?
o: Her anti-B antibodies bind the B antigens on the donor red cells
Her plasma lacks antibodies, so the donor B antigens attack her cells
Her anti-A antibodies bind the A antigens on the donor red cells
Her A antigens bind directly to the B antigens on the donor red cells
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: type A blood has A antigens on the cells and anti-B antibodies in the plasma. Step 2: donor type B cells carry B antigens, so her anti-B antibodies bind them and destroy the donor cells.

n.1: Type A plasma does contain antibodies (anti-B), and antigens are markers, not attackers.
n.2: Type A blood does not contain anti-A antibodies (they would attack her own cells), and type B cells carry no A antigen.
n.3: Antigens do not bind one another; antibodies bind antigens.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A runner moves to a high-altitude city where the air holds less oxygen, and over several weeks her red blood cell count rises. Which organ releases the hormone responsible?
o: The liver, which releases erythropoietin
Red bone marrow, which releases erythropoietin
The spleen, which releases erythropoietin
The kidneys, which release erythropoietin
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: low blood oxygen is sensed by the kidneys. Step 2: the kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red bone marrow to make more red blood cells.

n.0: The liver makes plasma proteins such as albumin; in adults, EPO comes from the kidneys.
n.1: Red bone marrow responds to EPO by making RBCs; it does not secrete the hormone.
n.2: The spleen removes old red blood cells; it does not release EPO.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Which plasma protein is the most abundant and is chiefly responsible for maintaining the osmotic pressure of the blood?
o: Fibrinogen
Hemoglobin
Albumin
Globulin
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Albumin, made by the liver, is the most abundant plasma protein; it holds water in the blood vessels by osmotic pressure.

n.0: Fibrinogen is the clotting protein that becomes fibrin.
n.1: Hemoglobin is inside red blood cells, not a plasma protein.
n.3: Globulins include antibodies and transport proteins; they are less abundant than albumin.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Arterioles throughout the body constrict while cardiac output stays the same. What happens to blood pressure, and why?
o: It stays the same, because cardiac output is unchanged
It rises, because the stroke volume of the heart increases
It rises, because peripheral resistance increases
It falls, because less blood reaches the capillaries
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Step 1: blood pressure depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance. Step 2: arterioles control resistance, so narrowing them raises resistance; with cardiac output unchanged, blood pressure rises.

n.0: Pressure depends on resistance as well as cardiac output, so a rise in resistance raises it.
n.1: Stroke volume is unchanged here (cardiac output is the same); the rise comes from resistance.
n.3: Constriction raises arterial pressure even though capillary flow falls.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: A blood sample from a healthy adult is spun in a centrifuge and separates into layers. Which result is typical?
o: About 55% plasma on top and about 45% formed elements, mostly red cells, below
About 55% formed elements on top and about 45% plasma, mostly water, below
About 92% plasma on top and about 8% formed elements, mostly platelets, below
About 45% plasma on top and about 55% formed elements, mostly white cells, below
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Plasma (about 55%) rises to the top; the formed elements (about 45%, the hematocrit) settle below, and nearly all of them are red blood cells, with a thin buffy coat of WBCs and platelets.

n.1: Formed elements are denser than plasma, so they settle at the bottom, not the top.
n.2: About 92% is the water content of plasma, not the plasma share of whole blood.
n.3: The percentages are reversed, and red cells, not white cells, make up most of the formed elements.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Blood is allowed to clot in a tube, and the clear fluid above the clot (serum) is collected. Which component of plasma is missing from the serum?
o: Glucose
Fibrinogen
Antibodies
Albumin
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Serum is plasma without the clotting factors. Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin and used up in the clot, so it is absent from serum.

n.0: Glucose is a dissolved nutrient that stays in the serum.
n.2: Antibodies (globulins) are not used in clotting and remain in the serum.
n.3: Albumin does not take part in clotting, so it remains in the serum.

A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.q: Compared with veins, which features are typical of arteries? Select all that apply.
o: Higher internal pressure and a palpable pulse
Valves that prevent backflow in the limbs
Thicker walls with more smooth muscle and elastic tissue
A wall made of a single endothelial layer
A larger lumen that holds most of the blood at rest
A&P: Respiratory & Cardiovascular.w: Arteries have thick walls with more smooth muscle and elastic tissue to withstand and smooth the high pressure from the ventricles, which is felt as a pulse.

n.1: Valves are a feature of veins, especially in the legs.
n.3: A single endothelial layer describes capillaries.
n.4: Veins have the larger lumens and hold about 60-70% of blood volume at rest.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A patient has had most of the colon surgically removed because of disease. Which change in digestive function is most expected after the surgery?
o: Poorer uptake of vitamin B12 with intrinsic factor
Slower final breakdown of peptides by colon enzymes
Poorer absorption of glucose and amino acids
Looser stools from reduced water absorption
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The large intestine's main job is absorbing water and electrolytes and forming feces. Removing most of the colon leaves less surface to reclaim water, so stools become looser.

n.0: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed in the ileum of the small intestine, which is not part of the colon.
n.1: The large intestine has no digestive enzymes of its own; brush-border peptidases of the small intestine finish protein digestion.
n.2: Glucose and amino acids are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine; the colon has no villi and absorbs mainly water and electrolytes.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A patient's terminal ileum is removed because of disease, but the duodenum and jejunum are left in place. Absorption of which nutrient is most at risk after this surgery?
o: Glucose
Vitamin B12
Vitamin K
Dietary iron
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Vitamin B12, bound to intrinsic factor from the stomach, is absorbed in the ileum. Removing the ileum therefore threatens B12 absorption even though the rest of the small intestine remains.

n.0: Glucose is absorbed mainly in the jejunum, which is still present.
n.2: Vitamin K is made by bacteria in the large intestine, which is untouched.
n.3: Intrinsic factor and the ileum are linked to vitamin B12, not iron; confusing them is a classic trap.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: When the stomach is empty, its inner lining forms large folds that flatten out as a meal arrives. What are these folds called, and what is their main role?
o: Rugae, which allow the stomach to expand with food
Microvilli, which hold brush-border digestive enzymes
Circular folds, which slow chyme to aid absorption
Villi, which add surface area for absorbing nutrients
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Rugae are the folds of the stomach lining. They flatten as the stomach fills, letting it stretch to hold a meal.

n.1: Microvilli form the brush border of small intestine cells, not folds of the stomach lining.
n.2: Circular folds belong to the small intestine wall and do not flatten when the stomach fills.
n.3: Villi are finger-like projections of the small intestine, not stomach folds.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Material leaving the last segment of the small intestine must pass a one-way valve before entering the large intestine. Which structure controls this passage?
o: Pyloric sphincter
Lower esophageal sphincter
Ileocecal valve
Hepatopancreatic sphincter
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The ileum ends at the ileocecal valve, which opens into the cecum, the first part of the large intestine.

n.0: The pyloric sphincter controls emptying of the stomach into the duodenum.
n.1: The lower esophageal sphincter sits between the esophagus and stomach and limits reflux.
n.3: The hepatopancreatic sphincter (of Oddi) controls bile and pancreatic juice entering the duodenum.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Digestion includes both mechanical and chemical processes. Which pairing of a digestive process with its type of digestion is correct?
o: Segmentation mixing chyme in the small intestine: mechanical
Lactase splitting lactose at the brush border: mechanical
Churning of food by the stomach's muscle layers: chemical
Salivary amylase breaking starch into maltose: mechanical
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Mechanical digestion physically breaks up and mixes food: chewing, stomach churning and segmentation in the small intestine. Enzymes breaking chemical bonds is chemical digestion.

n.1: Lactase is an enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose, so this is chemical digestion.
n.2: Churning physically breaks up and mixes food without breaking chemical bonds, so it is mechanical digestion.
n.3: Salivary amylase is an enzyme that breaks chemical bonds in starch, so this is chemical digestion.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A patient leaflet explains the role of the large intestine. Which of the following are functions of the large intestine? Select all that apply.
o: Absorbing water and electrolytes
Absorbing most dietary amino acids through villi
Secreting brush-border enzymes such as lactase
Forming and storing feces
Absorbing vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor
Housing bacteria that make vitamin K
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes, forms and stores feces, and houses bacteria that make vitamin K and some B vitamins and ferment fiber. It has no villi and no digestive enzymes of its own.

n.1: Amino acids are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine; the large intestine has no villi.
n.2: Brush-border enzymes such as lactase are found on the microvilli of the small intestine.
n.4: Vitamin B12 with intrinsic factor is absorbed in the ileum of the small intestine.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Place the structures in the order food passes through them after it is swallowed, starting with the first.
o: Ileum
Esophagus
Duodenum
Stomach
Jejunum
Pharynx
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: After the mouth, food passes through the pharynx and down the esophagus to the stomach. Chyme then enters the small intestine in the order duodenum, jejunum, ileum before reaching the cecum.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Place the regions of the large intestine in the order that undigested material moves through them, starting with the first region after the ileocecal valve.
o: Rectum
Cecum
Descending colon
Ascending colon
Sigmoid colon
Transverse colon
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Material enters the cecum at the ileocecal valve, rises in the ascending colon, crosses in the transverse colon, falls in the descending colon, curves through the sigmoid colon and is stored in the rectum before the anal canal.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A clinic handout reviews the jobs of the digestive organs that food does not pass through. Which of the following functions is carried out by the liver?
o: Converting ammonia into urea
Storing and concentrating bile
Producing insulin and glucagon
Secreting trypsinogen into the duodenum
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The liver converts toxic ammonia from protein breakdown into urea, which the kidneys then excrete. It also makes bile, stores glycogen, detoxifies drugs and alcohol, and makes plasma proteins.

n.1: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile; the liver makes it.
n.2: Insulin and glucagon come from the islets of the pancreas, its endocrine part.
n.3: Trypsinogen is made by the acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A student chews a plain cracker for a full minute without swallowing and notices that it begins to taste slightly sweet. Which enzyme best explains this?
o: Salivary amylase
Pancreatic amylase
Lingual lipase
Brush-border maltase
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Salivary amylase starts the chemical digestion of starch in the mouth, breaking it into smaller sugars that taste sweet.

n.1: Pancreatic amylase digests starch in the duodenum, not in the mouth.
n.2: Lingual lipase is in saliva, but it acts on fats, not starch.
n.3: Maltase splits maltose into glucose, but it sits on the brush border of the small intestine, not in the mouth.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Which pairing of an accessory digestive organ with something it secretes into the digestive tract is correct?
o: Salivary glands: pepsinogen
Gallbladder: bile that it produces
Pancreas: bicarbonate and lipase
Liver: trypsin and chymotrypsin
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The exocrine pancreas releases pancreatic juice containing bicarbonate (to neutralize acid chyme) and enzymes such as lipase, amylase, trypsinogen and nucleases.

n.0: Pepsinogen is made by chief cells in the stomach; saliva contains amylase and lingual lipase.
n.1: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, but the liver produces it.
n.3: Trypsin and chymotrypsin are pancreatic enzymes; the liver makes bile, not digestive enzymes.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A patient asks how she will digest fat after her gallbladder is removed. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Her pancreas will take over storing bile
Her stomach digests most fat, so bile is less needed
Her liver still makes bile that reaches the duodenum
Her small intestine will make the lipase it once supplied
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The liver, not the gallbladder, makes bile. Without a gallbladder, bile from the liver still drains into the duodenum to emulsify fat; it is simply not stored and concentrated between meals.

n.0: The pancreas makes pancreatic juice and does not store bile.
n.1: Most fat digestion happens in the small intestine, not the stomach.
n.3: The gallbladder never supplied lipase; lipase comes from the pancreas.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Bile salts released into the duodenum are essential for normal fat digestion. Which statement correctly describes how bile salts act on dietary fat?
o: They convert inactive pepsinogen into pepsin
They carry fats into villus blood capillaries
They break large fat droplets into smaller ones
They hydrolyze triglycerides into fatty acids
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Bile is not an enzyme. Bile salts emulsify fat, breaking large droplets into many small ones so pancreatic lipase has more surface to act on.

n.0: Pepsinogen is activated by hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
n.1: Digested fats are absorbed into lacteals (lymph), not blood capillaries.
n.3: Splitting fats into fatty acids is chemical digestion by pancreatic lipase, not by bile.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Shortly after a meal high in fat, cells of the duodenum release a hormone that makes the gallbladder contract. Which hormone is this, and what other effect does it have?
o: Secretin; it also triggers pancreatic bicarbonate release
Glucagon; it also triggers glycogen breakdown
Gastrin; it also triggers gastric acid secretion
Cholecystokinin; it also triggers pancreatic enzyme release
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Cholecystokinin (CCK) from the duodenum makes the gallbladder contract to release bile and stimulates the pancreas to release its digestive enzymes.

n.0: Secretin does trigger bicarbonate release from the pancreas, but it is not the hormone that contracts the gallbladder.
n.1: Glucagon is a pancreatic islet hormone that raises blood glucose; it is not a duodenal hormone.
n.2: Gastrin comes from the stomach and stimulates acid secretion; it does not contract the gallbladder.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: When acidic chyme enters the duodenum, a hormone is released that signals the pancreas to secrete a fluid rich in bicarbonate. Which hormone sends this signal?
o: Secretin
Glucagon
Cholecystokinin
Gastrin
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Secretin from the duodenum causes the pancreas to release bicarbonate, which neutralizes acid chyme arriving from the stomach.

n.1: Glucagon is an islet hormone that raises blood glucose and does not control bicarbonate.
n.2: Cholecystokinin mainly triggers pancreatic enzyme release and gallbladder contraction.
n.3: Gastrin is a stomach hormone that increases acid secretion, the opposite of neutralizing it.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Blood leaving the capillaries of the small intestine carries newly absorbed sugars and amino acids. To which organ does this blood travel first for processing, and by which vessel?
o: The liver, by the hepatic artery
The heart, by the inferior vena cava
The liver, by the hepatic portal vein
The liver, by the hepatic veins
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Nutrient-rich blood from the intestines drains into the hepatic portal vein, which delivers it to the liver for processing before it reaches the general circulation.

n.0: The hepatic artery brings oxygen-rich blood from the aorta to the liver, not nutrient-rich blood from the intestines.
n.1: Blood from the intestines reaches the inferior vena cava only after it has passed through the liver.
n.3: The hepatic veins drain blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava; they do not bring intestinal blood to it.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A patient with severe liver failure has a low blood albumin level and bleeds easily from minor cuts. Which loss of liver function best explains both findings?
o: Reduced synthesis of plasma proteins
Reduced storage of glycogen
Reduced conversion of ammonia to urea
Reduced production of bile salts
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The liver makes plasma proteins, including albumin and clotting factors such as fibrinogen and prothrombin. Losing this function explains both the low albumin and the easy bleeding.

n.1: Glycogen storage affects blood glucose control, not albumin or clotting.
n.2: Failing urea production raises blood ammonia; it does not lower albumin or impair clotting.
n.3: Less bile could reduce fat-soluble vitamin absorption, but it would not explain the low albumin.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: The pancreas has an exocrine part and an endocrine part. Which of these products is released through ducts into the duodenum rather than into the blood?
o: Somatostatin made by delta cells
Insulin made by beta cells
Glucagon made by alpha cells
Trypsinogen made by acinar cells
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas make pancreatic juice, including trypsinogen, which travels through ducts to the duodenum. Islet hormones enter the blood.

n.0: Somatostatin is an islet hormone that acts on other islet cells; it is not part of pancreatic juice.
n.1: Insulin is an endocrine hormone from the islets and enters the blood, not a duct.
n.2: Glucagon is an islet hormone secreted into the blood to raise blood glucose.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A gallstone blocks the bile duct before it joins the pancreatic duct, so bile cannot reach the duodenum. Which digestive process in the small intestine is most directly impaired?
o: Splitting of maltose by brush-border maltase
Emulsification of dietary fat
Breakdown of protein by trypsin
Absorption of glucose into villus capillaries
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Bile salts emulsify fat. If bile cannot reach the duodenum, fat stays in large droplets, so fat digestion by lipase and its absorption suffer.

n.0: Maltase sits on the microvilli of the small intestine and splits maltose without any help from bile.
n.2: Trypsin comes from the pancreas; the block is above the pancreatic duct, so pancreatic juice still flows.
n.3: Glucose is absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi, a process that does not depend on bile.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A nursing student reviews the largest internal organ, which sits in the right upper quadrant. Which of the following are functions of the liver? Select all that apply.
o: Secreting bicarbonate into the duodenum
Storing glucose as glycogen
Secreting insulin into the blood
Producing bile
Storing and concentrating bile
Detoxifying drugs and alcohol
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The liver stores glycogen and helps regulate blood glucose, detoxifies drugs and alcohol, and makes bile. It also converts ammonia to urea and makes plasma proteins.

n.0: Bicarbonate in pancreatic juice comes from the pancreas.
n.2: Insulin is secreted by beta cells in the pancreatic islets.
n.4: The gallbladder, not the liver, stores and concentrates bile between meals.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A patient eats a lunch of grilled chicken, which is mostly protein. In which organ does chemical digestion of this protein begin, and which enzyme starts it?
o: The mouth, by salivary amylase
The duodenum, by trypsin
The mouth, by lingual lipase
The stomach, by pepsin
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Protein digestion begins in the stomach, where pepsin (activated from pepsinogen by hydrochloric acid) breaks proteins into shorter peptides. Carbohydrate digestion is the one that begins in the mouth.

n.0: Salivary amylase digests starch, not protein; protein digestion does not begin in the mouth.
n.1: Trypsin continues protein digestion in the small intestine after pepsin has started it in the stomach.
n.2: Lingual lipase acts on fats, and protein digestion does not begin in the mouth.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: After pancreatic lipase splits dietary fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides, intestinal cells repackage them for absorption. Into which vessels do these fats first pass, and in what form?
o: Villus blood capillaries, as free fatty acids
Lacteals in the villi, as monosaccharides
The hepatic portal vein, as triglycerides
Lacteals in the villi, as chylomicrons
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Absorptive cells package digested fats into chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries and enter the lacteals, the lymphatic capillaries of the villi.

n.0: Sugars and amino acids enter blood capillaries; fats enter the lymph through lacteals.
n.1: Lacteals are the right vessels, but monosaccharides are sugars and are absorbed into blood capillaries.
n.2: The hepatic portal vein carries absorbed sugars and amino acids to the liver, not chylomicrons.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Brush-border enzymes complete the chemical digestion of carbohydrates in the small intestine. Which set lists the end products that are absorbed into the blood?
o: Starch, glycogen and glucose
Glucose, fructose and galactose
Glycerol, fatty acids and glucose
Maltose, sucrose and lactose
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Carbohydrates are absorbed only as monosaccharides: glucose, fructose and galactose. Maltase, sucrase and lactase split the disaccharides to produce them.

n.0: Starch and glycogen are polysaccharides, far too large to be absorbed.
n.2: Glycerol and fatty acids come from fat digestion, not carbohydrate digestion.
n.3: Maltose, sucrose and lactose are disaccharides that brush-border enzymes still have to split before absorption.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A person who makes too little lactase has cramping and bloating after drinking milk. Where is lactase normally produced and active?
o: In gastric juice secreted by chief cells
