On the brush border of the small intestine
In saliva secreted by the parotid glands
In pancreatic juice from the acinar cells
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Lactase is a brush-border enzyme on the microvilli of the small intestine, along with maltase, sucrase and peptidases. It splits lactose into glucose and galactose.

n.0: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen for protein digestion.
n.2: Saliva contains salivary amylase and lingual lipase, not lactase.
n.3: Pancreatic juice contains amylase, lipase, proteases and nucleases, but lactase is a brush-border enzyme.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Parietal cells in the stomach lining secrete hydrochloric acid, which keeps gastric pH very low. Which of the following is a role of this acid?
o: Binding vitamin B12 for uptake in the ileum
Emulsifying fat droplets so lipase can act
Activating pancreatic trypsinogen into trypsin
Converting pepsinogen into active pepsin
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Hydrochloric acid activates pepsinogen into pepsin, which begins protein digestion, and it kills many swallowed microbes.

n.0: Binding vitamin B12 is the role of intrinsic factor, the other product of parietal cells, not the acid.
n.1: Emulsifying fat is the job of bile salts in the duodenum, not stomach acid.
n.2: Trypsinogen is activated in the duodenum by the brush-border enzyme enteropeptidase (and then by trypsin itself), not by stomach acid.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: An autoimmune disease destroys a patient's gastric parietal cells. Which pair of problems would be expected as a result?
o: Poor fat emulsification and poor vitamin K production
Poor trypsin activation and poor amino acid absorption
Poor pepsin activation and poor vitamin B12 absorption
Poor bicarbonate release and poor glucose absorption
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid, which activates pepsin, and intrinsic factor, which is needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the ileum. Losing them impairs both.

n.0: Fat emulsification depends on bile from the liver, and vitamin K is made by colon bacteria.
n.1: Trypsin is activated in the small intestine and comes from the pancreas; amino acid absorption continues there.
n.3: Bicarbonate comes from the pancreas, and glucose is absorbed in the small intestine.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Which enzyme is correctly matched with both the site where it acts and the nutrient it digests?
o: Pancreatic lipase: small intestine; starch
Salivary amylase: small intestine; starch
Pepsin: stomach; proteins
Trypsin: stomach; proteins
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Pepsin acts in the stomach on proteins. Each other option gets either the site or the nutrient wrong.

n.0: Pancreatic lipase does act in the small intestine, but it digests fats, not starch.
n.1: Salivary amylase digests starch, but it acts in the mouth; pancreatic amylase digests starch in the small intestine.
n.3: Trypsin digests proteins, but it acts in the small intestine, where pancreatic juice enters, not in the stomach.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A meal contains bread, lean turkey and butter. When the resulting chyme first enters the duodenum, which statement about the chemical digestion of this meal is accurate?
o: Protein digestion has begun; starch and fat digestion have not
Starch and protein digestion have begun; most fat digestion has not
Starch digestion has begun; protein and fat digestion have not
Fat and protein digestion have begun; starch digestion has not
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Step 1: starch digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase. Step 2: protein digestion begins in the stomach with pepsin. Fat digestion is mostly in the small intestine, after bile and pancreatic lipase act (lingual lipase does very little), so most fat digestion has not yet occurred.

n.0: Starch digestion began in the mouth with salivary amylase, before the stomach.
n.2: Protein digestion has already begun in the stomach by the time chyme reaches the duodenum.
n.3: Most fat digestion waits for bile and pancreatic lipase in the small intestine, while starch digestion began in the mouth.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Pancreatic juice contains enzymes for each major class of nutrient. Which enzyme in pancreatic juice breaks down the DNA and RNA found in food?
o: Chymotrypsin
Maltase
Peptidase
Nuclease
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Pancreatic nucleases digest nucleic acids into nucleotides, which are broken into sugars, bases and phosphate and absorbed into the blood.

n.0: Chymotrypsin is a pancreatic enzyme, but it digests proteins.
n.1: Maltase is a brush-border enzyme that splits the sugar maltose.
n.2: Peptidases are brush-border enzymes that finish protein digestion.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A poison control leaflet explains that a few substances can enter the blood directly through the stomach lining, before reaching the small intestine. Which substance is one of these?
o: Alcohol
Vitamin B12
Fatty acids
Amino acids
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The stomach absorbs very little, but some water, alcohol and aspirin can cross its lining. Nutrients are absorbed mainly in the small intestine.

n.1: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum with intrinsic factor, not across the stomach lining.
n.2: Fatty acids are absorbed in the small intestine and enter the lacteals as chylomicrons.
n.3: Amino acids are absorbed into blood capillaries of the small intestine villi.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A study group writes statements about chemical digestion on a whiteboard. Which of these statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Chief cells secrete pepsin in its active form
Protein digestion begins with enzymes in saliva
Most digested fats are absorbed into villus blood capillaries
Maltase and sucrase are brush-border enzymes
Carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth
Bile emulsifies fat but does not hydrolyze it
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Bile is not an enzyme; it emulsifies fat so lipase can digest it. Salivary amylase starts carbohydrate digestion in the mouth. Maltase, sucrase and lactase sit on the brush border of the small intestine.

n.0: Chief cells secrete inactive pepsinogen, which hydrochloric acid converts to pepsin.
n.1: Protein digestion begins in the stomach with pepsin; saliva starts carbohydrate digestion.
n.2: Most digested fats are packaged as chylomicrons and absorbed into lacteals (lymph), not blood capillaries.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Place the events of fat digestion and absorption in the order they occur, starting with the first.
o: Pancreatic lipase splits fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides
Chylomicrons enter the lacteals of the villi
Bile salts emulsify large fat droplets in the duodenum
Intestinal cells package the products into chylomicrons
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Bile first emulsifies fat into small droplets, giving lipase more surface. Lipase then produces fatty acids and monoglycerides, which intestinal cells absorb and package into chylomicrons. Chylomicrons are too large for blood capillaries, so they enter the lacteals (lymph).

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A patient's imaging report describes a small stone lodged partway along the tube that carries urine from the left kidney to the urinary bladder. In which structure is the stone located?
o: Ureter
Urethra
Collecting duct
Renal pelvis
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Each ureter carries urine from a kidney to the urinary bladder by peristalsis. The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the outside.

n.1: The urethra drains the bladder to the outside; mixing up ureter and urethra is a classic trap.
n.2: Collecting ducts lie inside the kidney medulla and carry urine toward the calyces.
n.3: The renal pelvis is the funnel inside the kidney that collects urine and leads into the ureter.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Each kidney contains about a million microscopic units, each able to filter blood and form urine on its own. What is this functional unit of the kidney called?
o: Renal corpuscle
Nephron
Renal pyramid
Glomerulus
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney: it filters blood, reabsorbs and secretes substances, and forms urine. Each kidney has approximately one million.

n.0: The renal corpuscle (glomerulus plus capsule) is the filtering part of a nephron, not the whole unit.
n.2: A renal pyramid is a region of the medulla containing parts of many nephrons and collecting ducts.
n.3: The glomerulus is the capillary tuft where filtration happens; it is only one part of a nephron.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Blood enters each glomerulus through one arteriole and leaves through another. Which vessel delivers blood into the glomerulus?
o: Efferent arteriole
Peritubular capillary
Afferent arteriole
Renal vein
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The afferent arteriole carries blood into the glomerulus; the efferent arteriole carries it out to the peritubular capillaries. (Afferent = arrives; efferent = exits.)

n.0: The efferent arteriole carries blood out of the glomerulus, not into it.
n.1: Peritubular capillaries receive blood from the efferent arteriole after it leaves the glomerulus.
n.3: Veins drain blood away from the kidney tissue; they do not supply the glomerulus.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: The renal corpuscle is the part of the nephron where blood is first filtered. Which two structures together make up the renal corpuscle?
o: Glomerulus and proximal convoluted tubule
Glomerular capsule and nephron loop
Afferent and efferent arterioles
Glomerulus and glomerular capsule
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The renal corpuscle is the glomerulus (capillary tuft) surrounded by the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule. Filtration happens there, not in the tubule.

n.0: The proximal convoluted tubule follows the capsule; it is part of the renal tubule, not the corpuscle.
n.1: The nephron loop (loop of Henle) is part of the tubule and lies mainly in the medulla.
n.2: These arterioles supply and drain the glomerulus but are not the corpuscle itself.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: The wall of the urinary bladder must stretch a great deal as it fills with urine. Which tissue lines the bladder and allows this stretching?
o: Simple columnar epithelium
Simple squamous epithelium
Stratified squamous epithelium
Transitional epithelium
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), whose cells change shape from rounded to flattened as the bladder fills.

n.0: Simple columnar epithelium lines much of the digestive tract and is built for secretion and absorption.
n.1: Simple squamous epithelium is a thin layer built for diffusion and filtration, not for stretching.
n.2: Stratified squamous epithelium resists abrasion, as in the skin and esophagus, but does not stretch like urothelium.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A surgeon reviews the location of the kidneys before a kidney procedure. Which statement about kidney position is correct?
o: They lie behind the peritoneum, the right slightly lower
They lie inside the peritoneal cavity, the right slightly lower
They lie inside the peritoneal cavity, the left slightly lower
They lie behind the peritoneum, the left slightly lower
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The kidneys are retroperitoneal, at about T12 to L3. The liver sits above the right kidney, so it lies slightly lower than the left. The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys.

n.1: The right kidney is lower, but the kidneys are retroperitoneal, not inside the peritoneal cavity.
n.2: Both parts are wrong: the kidneys are retroperitoneal, and the right one sits lower because of the liver.
n.3: The kidneys are retroperitoneal, but the right kidney, not the left, sits lower because the liver lies above it.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Urination involves two sphincters around the urethra. Which statement correctly describes these sphincters?
o: Both are smooth muscle, and both are under involuntary control
Internal is smooth and involuntary; external is skeletal and voluntary
Both are skeletal muscle, and both are under voluntary control
Internal is skeletal and voluntary; external is smooth and involuntary
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The internal urethral sphincter is smooth muscle under involuntary control; the external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle, so it can be voluntarily controlled.

n.0: The internal sphincter is smooth and involuntary, but the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.
n.2: The external sphincter is skeletal and voluntary, but the internal sphincter is smooth muscle and involuntary.
n.3: This reverses the two: the internal sphincter is the smooth, involuntary one.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A women's health clinic leaflet notes that urinary tract infections are more common in females than in males. Which anatomical difference best explains this?
o: The female urethra is longer, so urine pools in it between voids
The female ureters are shorter, so bacteria reach the kidneys sooner
The female urethra is shorter, so bacteria reach the bladder sooner
The female urethra carries both urine and reproductive fluids
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The female urethra is about 4 cm long, compared with about 20 cm in males, so bacteria from outside have a shorter route to the bladder.

n.0: The female urethra is shorter (about 4 cm) than the male urethra (about 20 cm), not longer.
n.1: The key difference is the urethra, not the ureters; bacteria enter from outside through the urethra and reach the bladder first.
n.3: Carrying both urine and semen describes the male urethra; the female urethra carries only urine.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Several structures pass through the hilum on the medial side of each kidney. Which statement correctly describes these structures and their direction of flow?
o: The renal vein enters; the renal artery and ureter exit
The renal artery enters; the renal vein and ureter exit
The renal vein and ureter enter; the renal artery exits
The renal artery and ureter enter; the renal vein exits
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: At the hilum, the renal artery brings blood in, while the renal vein carries blood out and the ureter carries urine out to the bladder.

n.0: Arteries carry blood to an organ, so the renal artery enters and the renal vein exits.
n.2: Both directions are reversed: the renal artery brings blood in, and the renal vein and ureter carry blood and urine out.
n.3: The renal artery does enter, but the ureter carries urine away from the kidney, so it exits.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: In a healthy person, which of the following pass from the blood in the glomerulus into the glomerular capsule as part of the filtrate? Select all that apply.
o: Albumin and other large plasma proteins
Urea
Glucose
Platelets
Red blood cells
Sodium ions
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Blood pressure pushes water and small solutes, such as glucose, amino acids, ions and urea, through the glomerulus into the capsule. Blood cells and large plasma proteins stay in the blood.

n.0: Large plasma proteins are held back by the filter; protein in urine suggests glomerular damage.
n.3: Platelets are cell fragments, far too large to pass the glomerular filter.
n.4: Red blood cells are too large to be filtered; blood in urine suggests glomerular damage.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Place the structures in the order that filtrate flows through them, starting where filtrate first collects after leaving the glomerulus.
o: Proximal convoluted tubule
Nephron loop (loop of Henle)
Renal pelvis
Distal convoluted tubule
Collecting duct
Glomerular capsule
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Filtrate collects in the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule, then flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, down and up the nephron loop, through the distal convoluted tubule and into a collecting duct. Urine then drains through the minor and major calyces into the renal pelvis and on to the ureter.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Place the vessels in the order that blood flows through them as it passes through a kidney, starting with the first.
o: Renal vein
Glomerulus
Afferent arteriole
Renal artery
Peritubular capillaries
Efferent arteriole
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Blood arrives in the renal artery and its branches, enters each glomerulus through an afferent arteriole, leaves through an efferent arteriole into the peritubular capillaries around the tubule, and finally drains into the renal vein.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: About 99% of the filtrate formed each day is returned to the blood. Which part of the nephron reabsorbs the largest share of the filtered water and sodium?
o: Collecting duct
Ascending limb of the nephron loop
Proximal convoluted tubule
Distal convoluted tubule
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the most: normally all of the glucose and amino acids and about 65% of the sodium and water, plus bicarbonate.

n.0: The collecting duct fine-tunes water reabsorption under ADH, but it handles a much smaller share than the PCT.
n.1: The ascending limb pumps out sodium and chloride but is impermeable to water.
n.3: The DCT fine-tunes sodium, potassium and calcium under hormones; it is not the main site of bulk reabsorption.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A routine urinalysis shows a large amount of protein in a patient's urine, while the rest of the results are normal. Damage to which part of the nephron is most likely?
o: Distal convoluted tubule
Nephron loop
Glomerulus
Collecting duct
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Large plasma proteins are normally kept out of the filtrate by the glomerular filter. Protein in the urine therefore suggests glomerular damage.

n.0: The DCT fine-tunes ions under hormonal control; filtration happens in the renal corpuscle.
n.1: The nephron loop builds the medullary concentration gradient; it is not the protein filter.
n.3: The collecting duct adjusts water reabsorption; it does not decide whether proteins enter the filtrate.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: After several hours of yard work on a hot day without drinking water, a man's blood becomes more concentrated and his ADH level rises. Where does ADH act, and what is the effect on his urine?
o: Proximal tubule; urine becomes more dilute
Collecting duct; urine becomes more concentrated
Collecting duct; urine becomes more dilute
Proximal tubule; urine becomes more concentrated
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: ADH from the posterior pituitary inserts aquaporins in the collecting ducts, so more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.

n.0: Both parts are wrong: ADH acts on the collecting duct and makes urine more concentrated, lowering its volume.
n.2: ADH increases water reabsorption, so urine becomes more concentrated, not more dilute.
n.3: ADH acts on the collecting duct, not the PCT; the PCT reabsorbs water mainly without hormonal control.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex acts on the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. What is its effect on the handling of sodium and potassium?
o: Water is reabsorbed while sodium is unchanged
Sodium is reabsorbed and potassium is secreted
Sodium and potassium are both reabsorbed
Potassium is reabsorbed and sodium is secreted
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb sodium (water follows) and secrete potassium, raising blood volume and blood pressure.

n.0: Water reabsorption with no change in sodium describes ADH, not aldosterone.
n.2: Aldosterone increases potassium secretion into the urine, not potassium reabsorption.
n.3: This reverses aldosterone's action, a common trap: it keeps sodium and excretes potassium.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A drop in blood pressure triggers the release of renin, the first step in a chain that raises blood pressure again. Which statement about renin is correct?
o: It is an enzyme in the lungs that forms angiotensin II
It is an enzyme from juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney
It is a hormone secreted by the adrenal cortex
It is a hormone from the heart atria that lowers pressure
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Renin is an enzyme released by juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney when blood pressure or sodium is low. It converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

n.0: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), found mostly in the lungs, forms angiotensin II; renin acts earlier.
n.2: The adrenal cortex releases aldosterone later in the pathway; renin comes from the kidney.
n.3: ANP from the atria lowers blood pressure; renin is part of the system that raises it.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: After drinking several beers at a party, a woman produces a large volume of pale, dilute urine. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Alcohol inhibits ADH, so collecting ducts reclaim less water
Alcohol blocks glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Alcohol stimulates ADH, which increases urine output
Alcohol raises aldosterone, so more sodium is excreted
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Alcohol inhibits ADH release. With less ADH, fewer aquaporins sit in the collecting ducts, less water is reabsorbed, and a large volume of dilute urine results.

n.1: Blocked glucose reabsorption would put glucose in the urine; that is not how alcohol increases urine volume.
n.2: ADH reduces urine output; alcohol inhibits it rather than stimulating it.
n.3: Aldosterone causes sodium reabsorption, not sodium excretion.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A patient receives a large volume of intravenous fluid, and the increased blood volume stretches the walls of the heart's atria. Which response helps return blood volume toward normal?
o: ADH is released, adding aquaporins to collecting ducts
Renin is released, increasing angiotensin II
ANP is released, increasing sodium and water excretion
ANP is released, increasing sodium reabsorption
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Stretched atria release atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), which makes the kidneys lose more sodium and water, lowering blood volume and blood pressure: the opposite of RAAS.

n.0: ADH increases water reabsorption, which would raise blood volume further.
n.1: Renin and angiotensin II raise blood volume and pressure, which would worsen the overload.
n.3: ANP is the right hormone, but it increases sodium excretion; sodium reabsorption is aldosterone's effect.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A fasting patient's urine test is positive for glucose. In a healthy kidney, where is filtered glucose reabsorbed, and what condition does this finding most suggest?
o: Collecting duct; diabetes mellitus
Collecting duct; diabetes insipidus
Proximal tubule; diabetes insipidus
Proximal tubule; diabetes mellitus
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Step 1: the PCT normally reabsorbs all filtered glucose, so urine contains none. Step 2: glucose in the urine (glycosuria) means blood glucose is so high that the PCT is overwhelmed, which suggests diabetes mellitus.

n.0: Diabetes mellitus is the right condition, but glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT, not the collecting duct.
n.1: Glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT, and diabetes insipidus causes large volumes of dilute urine, not glucose in urine.
n.2: The PCT is the right site, but diabetes insipidus is an ADH problem causing dilute urine, not glucose in urine.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Besides forming urine, the kidneys perform several other functions. Which of the following are functions of the kidneys? Select all that apply.
o: Producing antidiuretic hormone
Secreting erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production
Converting ammonia into urea
Activating vitamin D to its active form, calcitriol
Secreting aldosterone into the blood
Secreting hydrogen ions and reabsorbing bicarbonate
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: The kidneys secrete erythropoietin, activate vitamin D (calcitriol), and help control acid-base balance by secreting H+ and reabsorbing or making bicarbonate. They also regulate blood volume, blood pressure and electrolytes.

n.0: ADH is made by the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary; it acts on the kidneys.
n.2: Urea is made in the liver from ammonia; the kidneys excrete it.
n.4: Aldosterone is secreted by the adrenal cortex; it acts on the kidneys.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: Place the steps of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in order, starting with the first event after blood pressure falls.
o: Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I
ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II
Juxtaglomerular cells release renin
Sodium and water are retained and blood pressure rises
Angiotensin II triggers aldosterone release
A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Low blood pressure makes juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Renin converts angiotensinogen (from the liver) into angiotensin I, which ACE (mostly in the lungs) converts into angiotensin II. Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction and aldosterone release; aldosterone makes the kidneys retain sodium and water, so blood pressure rises.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A healthy adult's glomerular filtration rate is 125 mL/min. At this rate, how many liters of filtrate do the kidneys form in 24 hours? Enter your answer in liters, as a whole number.

tr.3: Multiplied by 24 but forgot the 60 minutes in each hour.
tr.180000: Left the answer in milliliters instead of converting to liters.
tr.7.5: Converted to liters per hour but did not multiply by 24 hours.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: 125 mL/min x 60 min/h = 7,500 mL per hour. 7,500 mL x 24 h = 180,000 mL per day. 180,000 mL / 1,000 mL per L = 180 L of filtrate per day.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.q: A patient's kidneys form 180 L of filtrate per day, and the tubules reabsorb 99.2% of it. Ignoring the small volume added by secretion, how many liters of urine are produced per day? Enter your answer in liters, rounded to the nearest tenth.

tr.178.6: Calculated the volume reabsorbed (178.56 L) instead of the volume left as urine.
tr.14.4: Used 8% instead of 0.8% for the share not reabsorbed.

A&P: Digestive & Urinary.w: Step 1: the share not reabsorbed is 100% - 99.2% = 0.8%. Step 2: 0.8% of 180 L = 0.008 x 180 = 1.44 L, which rounds to 1.4 L of urine per day (within the normal 1 to 2 L).

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: After a large holiday dinner, Aisha relaxes on the couch as her stomach and intestines increase their activity. Which nerve carries most of the autonomic output that drives this response?
o: Vagus nerve (CN X)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Accessory nerve (CN XI)
Thoracolumbar nerves from T1 to L2
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: increased digestive activity at rest is a parasympathetic (rest and digest) effect, and most parasympathetic output to the thoracic and abdominal organs travels in the vagus nerve, cranial nerve X.

n.1: CN IX serves the head and throat; the main parasympathetic supply to the stomach and intestines is the vagus nerve (CN X).
n.2: CN XI is not the parasympathetic nerve to the abdominal organs; that role belongs to the vagus nerve (CN X).
n.3: Outflow from T1 to L2 is the sympathetic (thoracolumbar) division, which slows digestion rather than stimulating it.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A rare disorder damages the efferent fibers of the autonomic nervous system while sparing all other nerve fibers. Which function would be directly affected?
o: Changes in heart rate during exercise
Sensing stretch of a full stomach wall
Voluntary flexing of the elbow joint
Detection of pain from the skin of the hand
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Autonomic efferent (motor) fibers control cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands, so adjusting the heart rate would be lost. Sensory (afferent) fibers and somatic motor fibers are spared.

n.1: Sensing stretch is a sensory (afferent) function; the afferent fibers are spared.
n.2: Flexing the elbow uses skeletal muscle, which is controlled by somatic motor fibers that are spared.
n.3: Pain detection travels on afferent (sensory) fibers, which are spared.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Autonomic motor fibers leave the spinal cord between vertebral levels T1 and L2. Which division do these fibers belong to, and what is one effect they produce?
o: Sympathetic; they slow digestion and urination
Parasympathetic; they stimulate digestion and urination
Parasympathetic; they slow the heart rate
Sympathetic; they constrict the bronchioles
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: outflow from T1 to L2 is the thoracolumbar, or sympathetic, division. Sympathetic effects include slowing digestion and urination, as well as dilating the bronchioles and pupils and raising the heart rate.

n.1: Stimulating digestion and urination is parasympathetic, and parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral, not thoracolumbar.
n.2: Slowing the heart is a parasympathetic effect, but parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral, not T1 to L2.
n.3: The division is right, but sympathetic stimulation dilates the bronchioles; constriction is parasympathetic.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: At the target organs they control, the two autonomic divisions mainly release different neurotransmitters. Which pair lists the main parasympathetic neurotransmitter first and the main sympathetic neurotransmitter second?
o: Acetylcholine, then norepinephrine
Acetylcholine for both divisions
Acetylcholine, then epinephrine
Norepinephrine, then acetylcholine
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine at their target organs. The main sympathetic effector neurotransmitter is norepinephrine.

n.1: Acetylcholine is the parasympathetic transmitter; the sympathetic division mainly releases norepinephrine at its targets.
n.2: Epinephrine is mainly a hormone released into the blood by the adrenal medulla; sympathetic nerve endings mainly release norepinephrine.
n.3: This reverses the two divisions: acetylcholine is parasympathetic and norepinephrine is sympathetic.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A sudden loud crash in the hallway activates the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system. Which responses does this division produce? Select all that apply.
o: Constriction of the pupils
Increased salivation
Release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Dilation of the bronchioles
Contraction of the bladder wall to empty it
Glycogen breakdown that raises blood glucose
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Sympathetic (fight or flight) effects include dilating the bronchioles, raising blood glucose by breaking down glycogen and stimulating the adrenal medulla to release epinephrine, along with a faster heart rate and dilated pupils.

n.0: Sympathetic stimulation dilates the pupils; constriction is a parasympathetic effect.
n.1: Salivation is stimulated by the parasympathetic division.
n.4: Emptying the bladder is promoted by the parasympathetic division; the sympathetic division slows urination.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A hiker rounds a bend and nearly steps on a rattlesnake. Which combination of changes would his autonomic nervous system most likely produce in the next few seconds?
o: Faster heart rate, dilated pupils and increased digestion
Faster heart rate, constricted pupils and slowed digestion
Slower heart rate, dilated pupils and increased digestion
Faster heart rate, dilated pupils and slowed digestion
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: A sudden threat triggers the sympathetic (fight or flight) division, which increases the heart rate, dilates the pupils and slows digestion at the same time.

n.0: Sympathetic stimulation slows digestion; increased digestion is a parasympathetic (rest and digest) effect.
n.1: Constricted pupils are a parasympathetic effect; sympathetic stimulation dilates them.
n.2: A slower heart rate and increased digestion are parasympathetic effects; the sympathetic response speeds the heart and slows digestion.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A study guide asks where the autonomic nervous system fits in the overall organization of the nervous system. Which statement places it correctly?
o: It is the sensory division of the central nervous system
It is a branch of the somatic division that serves the internal organs
It is a branch of the central nervous system that controls skeletal muscle
It is a motor (efferent) branch of the peripheral nervous system
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The PNS has a sensory (afferent) division and a motor (efferent) division. The motor division splits into the somatic division (skeletal muscle) and the autonomic division (cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands), which in turn splits into sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

n.0: The autonomic nervous system is a motor division of the PNS, not a sensory part of the CNS.
n.1: Somatic and autonomic are sister branches of the motor division; the autonomic division is not part of the somatic division.
n.2: Skeletal muscle is controlled by the somatic division, and the autonomic division belongs to the PNS, not the CNS.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Stretch receptors in the bladder wall signal that the bladder is full. The signal travels to the spinal cord, and the reply makes the smooth muscle of the bladder wall contract. Which fibers carried the incoming and outgoing signals?
o: Afferent fibers in; somatic motor fibers out
Afferent fibers in; sympathetic fibers out
Afferent fibers in; parasympathetic fibers out
Efferent fibers in; parasympathetic fibers out
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: incoming sensory signals travel on afferent fibers, and contraction of the bladder's smooth muscle to promote urination is a parasympathetic (autonomic motor) effect.

n.0: Somatic motor fibers control skeletal muscle; the bladder wall is smooth muscle under autonomic control.
n.1: The sympathetic division slows urination; the parasympathetic division contracts the bladder wall.
n.3: Signals entering the CNS travel on afferent fibers; efferent fibers carry commands out.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: In a typical multipolar neuron, which structure receives incoming signals from other cells and conducts them toward the cell body?
o: Dendrite
Axon terminal
Axon
Axon hillock
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Dendrites receive signals from other cells and carry them toward the cell body (soma). The axon then carries impulses away from the cell body to the axon terminals.

n.1: Axon terminals release neurotransmitter at the far end of the axon; they send signals rather than receive them.
n.2: The axon carries impulses away from the cell body, not toward it.
n.3: The axon hillock is the trigger zone where an action potential starts, between the cell body and the axon.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A biopsy of the sciatic nerve, which is part of the peripheral nervous system, shows myelinated axons. Which cells produced the myelin sheath around these axons?
o: Oligodendrocytes
Schwann cells
Satellite cells
Astrocytes
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is made by Schwann cells. In the central nervous system, oligodendrocytes make it.

n.0: Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the CNS, not in peripheral nerves such as the sciatic nerve.
n.2: Satellite cells are PNS glia that surround cell bodies in ganglia; Schwann cells form PNS myelin.
n.3: Astrocytes are CNS glia that support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier; they do not make myelin.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: At rest, the inside of a typical neuron is about -70 mV relative to the outside. Which mechanism uses ATP directly to help maintain this resting membrane potential?
o: Na+/K+ pump moving 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in
Voltage-gated Na+ channels letting Na+ flow in
Ca2+ channels letting Ca2+ into the axon terminal
Na+/K+ pump moving 2 Na+ out and 3 K+ in
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out of the cell and 2 K+ in. Together with K+ leak channels, this keeps the inside of the resting neuron negative.

n.1: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open at threshold and cause depolarization; they are passive channels, not an ATP-driven pump.
n.2: Ca2+ channels at the axon terminal open during synaptic transmission; they do not maintain the resting potential.
n.3: The ratio is reversed: the pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: When a stimulus brings a neuron's membrane to threshold, the membrane rapidly depolarizes. Which ion movement is directly responsible for this depolarization?
o: Na+ being pumped out of the cell
Na+ flowing into the cell
K+ flowing out of the cell
K+ flowing into the cell
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: At threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes into the cell, making the inside less negative (depolarization).

n.0: Pumping Na+ out is the work of the Na+/K+ pump, which maintains the resting potential rather than depolarizing the membrane.
n.2: K+ flowing out of the cell causes repolarization, the phase after depolarization.
n.3: K+ does not cause depolarization by entering; Na+ entry depolarizes the membrane.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Two axons have the same diameter, but one is myelinated and the other is not. Why does an impulse travel faster along the myelinated axon?
o: Myelin carries the impulse in place of the axon membrane
The impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next
Myelin increases the size of each action potential
Myelin releases neurotransmitter along the axon's length
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Myelin insulates the axon, so the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier (gap in the myelin) to the next. This saltatory conduction is faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon.

n.0: Myelin is insulation; the action potential is still generated by the axon membrane at the nodes of Ranvier.
n.2: Action potentials are all-or-none; myelin speeds conduction but does not make each action potential larger.
n.3: Neurotransmitter is released from axon terminals at the synapse, not by myelin along the axon.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A researcher stimulates a neuron with a stimulus well above threshold and then with a stimulus twice as strong. How does the neuron's response to the stronger stimulus differ?
o: Action potentials fire more often; each is the same size
Each action potential is about twice as large
Action potentials keep the same rate, but each one lasts longer
Each action potential travels about twice as fast
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached, each one is the same size. A stronger stimulus increases how often action potentials fire, not their size.

n.1: Action potentials are all-or-none, so a stronger stimulus does not make each one larger.
n.2: Stimulus strength is coded by firing frequency; the rate rises rather than staying the same.
n.3: Conduction speed depends on the axon itself, such as whether it is myelinated, not on stimulus strength.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Place the events of a single action potential in the order they occur, starting with the first.
o: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in
K+ flows out of the cell and the membrane repolarizes
A brief hyperpolarization occurs during the refractory period
Na+ channels close and voltage-gated K+ channels open
The membrane depolarizes to threshold, about -55 mV
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: A stimulus brings the membrane to threshold (about -55 mV). Voltage-gated Na+ channels then open and Na+ rushes in (depolarization). Next the Na+ channels close and K+ channels open, so K+ flows out and the membrane repolarizes. A brief hyperpolarization follows during the refractory period.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Place the events of chemical transmission across a synapse in the order they occur, starting with the first.
o: Vesicles release neurotransmitter by exocytosis
Ca2+ enters the axon terminal
An action potential reaches the axon terminal
Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft
Neurotransmitter binds receptors on the postsynaptic cell
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The action potential reaches the axon terminal, which lets Ca2+ enter. The Ca2+ triggers vesicles to release neurotransmitter by exocytosis. The neurotransmitter crosses the synaptic cleft and binds receptors on the postsynaptic cell, so the signal travels one way.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: At the junction between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fiber, a neurotransmitter triggers contraction and is then broken down by an enzyme in the synaptic cleft. Which neurotransmitter is it?
o: Acetylcholine
Glutamate
Dopamine
Norepinephrine
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: At the neuromuscular junction, motor neurons release acetylcholine, which is broken down in the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase.

n.1: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter of the CNS, not the transmitter released onto skeletal muscle.
n.2: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter of the brain, not the one released at the neuromuscular junction.
n.3: Norepinephrine is the main sympathetic effector neurotransmitter, not the transmitter at the neuromuscular junction.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A histology student summarizes the structure of nervous tissue. Which of her statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Most sensory neurons are structurally multipolar
Interneurons are the most numerous functional type of neuron
Gray matter consists mainly of cell bodies, dendrites and unmyelinated axons
Axons carry impulses toward the cell body
Microglia act as phagocytes within the CNS
White matter consists mainly of neuron cell bodies
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Gray matter is cell bodies, dendrites and unmyelinated axons. Interneurons (association neurons in the CNS) are the most numerous functional type, and microglia are the phagocytes of the CNS.

n.0: Most sensory neurons are unipolar (pseudounipolar); multipolar neurons include most motor neurons.
n.3: Axons carry impulses away from the cell body; dendrites carry them toward it.
n.5: White matter consists mainly of myelinated axons; cell bodies are found in gray matter.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which type of glial cell is the most numerous in the central nervous system and helps form the blood-brain barrier?
o: Oligodendrocytes
Ependymal cells
Astrocytes
Microglia
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Astrocytes are the most numerous glial cells of the CNS. They support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier.

n.0: Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the CNS.
n.1: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and help make cerebrospinal fluid.
n.3: Microglia are the phagocytes of the CNS; they are not the most numerous glia and do not form the blood-brain barrier.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A toxin blocks voltage-gated K+ channels in a neuron while Na+ channels continue to work normally. Which phase of the action potential would be most directly impaired?
o: Repolarization
Depolarization
Ca2+ entry at the axon terminal
Reaching threshold
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: depolarization depends on Na+ entering through Na+ channels, while repolarization depends on K+ leaving through voltage-gated K+ channels. Blocking the K+ channels therefore impairs repolarization.

n.1: Depolarization is caused by Na+ entering through Na+ channels, which still work normally.
n.2: Ca2+ enters the axon terminal through Ca2+ channels, not K+ channels.
n.3: Threshold is reached as the stimulus opens Na+ channels; it does not depend on voltage-gated K+ channels.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: After a fall, Diego has damage confined to his cerebellum. Which problem is he most likely to show during his recovery?
o: Loss of control of breathing rhythm
Inability to understand spoken language
Loss of balance and poorly coordinated movement
Inability to regulate body temperature and thirst
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The cerebellum coordinates movement and controls balance and posture, so damage to it produces unsteady, poorly coordinated movement.

n.0: Breathing rhythm is set by the medulla oblongata, with help from the pons, not the cerebellum.
n.1: Understanding spoken language depends on Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe.
n.3: Body temperature and thirst are regulated by the hypothalamus.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A drug overdose depresses the brain region containing the vital centers that set heart rate, breathing rhythm and blood pressure. Which region is this?
o: Primary motor cortex
Hypothalamus
Cerebellum
Medulla oblongata
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The medulla oblongata of the brainstem contains the vital centers for heart rate, breathing rhythm and blood pressure, as well as reflexes such as coughing and swallowing.

n.0: The primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe controls voluntary movement, not heart rate or breathing rhythm.
n.1: The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst and water balance; the vital centers are in the medulla oblongata.
n.2: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and posture; it does not contain the vital centers.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: During surgery on the spinal cord, the surgeon separates the protective membranes one at a time. Which meningeal layer lies directly against the surface of the spinal cord?
o: Pia mater
Arachnoid mater
Dura mater
Choroid plexus
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: From outer to inner, the meninges are the dura mater, arachnoid mater and pia mater. The pia mater is the innermost layer, lying directly on the brain and spinal cord.

n.1: The arachnoid mater is the middle layer; the subarachnoid space beneath it holds cerebrospinal fluid.
n.2: The dura mater is the outermost, toughest meningeal layer.
n.3: The choroid plexus makes cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles; it is not one of the meninges.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A stroke damages Mrs. Lee's occipital lobe, while the rest of her cerebrum is unaffected. Which function is she most likely to lose?
o: Processing of sounds and speech
Planning of voluntary movement
Processing of visual information
Perception of touch and temperature
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The occipital lobe contains the visual cortex, so damage there impairs the processing of visual information.

n.0: Hearing and language comprehension are handled by the temporal lobe.
n.1: Planning and voluntary motor control are functions of the frontal lobe.
n.3: Touch and temperature are processed by the somatosensory cortex of the parietal lobe.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: After a stroke, Mr. Okafor understands questions but struggles to produce fluent speech. Damage to which area, in which lobe, best explains this?
o: Broca's area in the frontal lobe
Broca's area in the temporal lobe
Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe
Wernicke's area in the frontal lobe
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: trouble producing speech with comprehension intact points to Broca's area (speech production), and Broca's area lies in the frontal lobe, usually on the left.

n.1: Broca's area is the right area, but it lies in the frontal lobe, not the temporal lobe.
n.2: Wernicke's area handles language comprehension, which is intact here.
n.3: Wernicke's area handles comprehension and lies in the temporal lobe, so both parts are wrong.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Signals from the eyes, ears, taste buds and skin pass through one structure in the diencephalon before reaching the cerebral cortex. Which structure is this?
o: Corpus callosum
Hypothalamus
Thalamus
Pons
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The thalamus is the relay station that sends sensory information on to the cerebral cortex. Smell is the one sense not relayed through it first.

n.0: The corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres; it does not relay incoming sensory signals to the cortex.
n.1: The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and controls the pituitary gland; it is not the main sensory relay.
n.3: The pons is part of the brainstem; it relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum and helps regulate breathing.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A tumor near the base of the brain disrupts a patient's body temperature control, thirst and pituitary hormone secretion. Which single structure is most likely affected?
o: Thalamus
Pineal gland
Medulla oblongata
Hypothalamus
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst and water balance and controls the pituitary gland, so one lesion there explains all three problems.

n.0: The thalamus relays sensory information to the cortex; it does not control temperature, thirst or the pituitary.
n.1: The pineal gland secretes melatonin for the sleep-wake cycle.
n.2: The medulla oblongata controls heart rate, breathing and blood pressure, not thirst or pituitary secretion.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: An injury cuts the ventral (anterior) roots of several spinal nerves in the lower back but leaves the dorsal roots intact. Which result is expected in the areas these nerves supply?
o: Loss of sensation with muscle strength preserved
Loss of both sensation and muscle strength
Loss of pain sensation with touch preserved
Muscle weakness with sensation preserved
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: the ventral root carries motor fibers out to muscles, while the dorsal root carries sensory fibers in. Cutting only the ventral roots causes weakness but spares sensation.

n.0: This pattern fits damage to the dorsal (sensory) roots, which are intact here.
n.1: Sensation travels in the dorsal roots, which are intact, so sensation is preserved.
n.2: Both pain and touch enter through the intact dorsal roots, so neither is lost.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A finger touches a hot pan and the arm pulls away before the person feels pain. Place the parts of this reflex arc in the order the signal passes through them, starting with the first.
o: Motor neuron
Interneuron in the spinal cord
Sensory neuron
Flexor muscle of the arm
Pain receptor in the skin
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: A reflex arc runs receptor, sensory neuron, integration center, motor neuron, effector. The pain receptor in the skin detects the heat, the sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord, an interneuron integrates it, the motor neuron carries the command out and the flexor muscle (effector) pulls the arm away.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A student is reviewing a cross section of the spinal cord. Which statements about the spinal cord are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Its dorsal root ganglia hold the cell bodies of sensory neurons
Its dorsal roots carry motor commands out to skeletal muscles
In adults it ends at about the L1 to L2 vertebral level
Its outer layer is gray matter, as in the cerebral cortex
Its gray matter lies inside, surrounded by white matter
It gives rise to 12 pairs of spinal nerves
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: In the spinal cord, butterfly-shaped gray matter lies inside white matter. Dorsal root ganglia contain sensory neuron cell bodies, and in adults the cord ends at about L1 to L2, below which the cauda equina continues.

n.1: Dorsal roots are sensory; motor commands leave through the ventral roots.
n.3: The spinal cord is the reverse of the cerebrum: its gray matter is inside and its white matter outside.
n.5: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves; 12 pairs is the number of cranial nerves.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: When asked to stick out his tongue, a patient cannot move it normally, although his taste and facial expressions are intact. Which cranial nerve is most likely damaged?
o: Facial nerve (CN VII)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) controls tongue movement.

n.0: The facial nerve controls facial expression and taste on the front of the tongue, both intact here.
n.2: The trigeminal nerve carries face sensation and controls chewing, not tongue movement.
n.3: Despite its name, CN IX is not the motor nerve of the tongue; tongue movement is controlled by CN XII.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Tapping the patellar tendon makes the leg kick forward, while stepping on a tack makes the foot pull away. How does the patellar reflex differ from this withdrawal reflex?
o: It depends on conscious awareness in the cerebral cortex
It has no interneuron between the sensory and motor neurons
It uses an interneuron, while the withdrawal reflex does not
It is processed in the cerebellum before the motor response
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is monosynaptic: the sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron in the spinal cord. Withdrawal reflexes use interneurons.

n.0: Reflexes are rapid and involuntary; the spinal cord processes them before the brain is aware.
n.2: This reverses the two: withdrawal reflexes use interneurons, and the patellar reflex does not.
n.3: Both reflexes are processed in the spinal cord; the cerebellum is not part of the reflex arc.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which photoreceptors are concentrated in the fovea centralis of the retina and provide color vision and sharp detail in bright light?
o: Cones
Hair cells
Rods
Bipolar neurons
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Cones detect color and fine detail in bright light and are concentrated in the fovea centralis.

n.1: Hair cells are the sensory receptors of the cochlea and inner ear, not the retina.
n.2: Rods work in dim light, give black-and-white vision and serve peripheral vision; they are not concentrated in the fovea.
n.3: Bipolar neurons in the retina pass signals along, but they are not the photoreceptors that detect light.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: As Marisol walks from a dark theater into bright sunlight, her pupils shrink. Which structure of the eye changes the size of the pupil?
o: Lens
Ciliary muscle
Cornea
Iris
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The pupil is the opening in the iris, and the iris controls its size to regulate how much light enters the eye.

n.0: The lens focuses light on the retina; it does not change the size of the pupil.
n.1: The ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens, not the size of the pupil.
n.2: The cornea is the clear front surface that light passes through first; it cannot change size.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: During an airplane's descent, swallowing helps relieve the pressure in Keisha's ears. Which structure connects the middle ear to the pharynx and equalizes this pressure?
o: Semicircular canals
Tympanic membrane (eardrum)
Auditory (Eustachian) tube
External auditory canal (ear canal)
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The auditory (Eustachian) tube connects the middle ear to the pharynx; opening it, for example by swallowing, equalizes pressure on both sides of the eardrum.

n.0: The semicircular canals are inner ear structures for balance.
n.1: The tympanic membrane separates the outer ear from the middle ear; it is the structure the pressure acts on, not a passage to the pharynx.
n.3: The external auditory canal leads from the auricle to the eardrum; it does not connect to the pharynx.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Each eye has a small blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina at the optic disc. Why does no image form at this point?
o: It contains no photoreceptors
It contains rods but no cones
It lies in front of the lens
It is covered by the opaque sclera
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The optic disc has no photoreceptors (no rods or cones), so light falling on it cannot be detected.

n.1: A region with rods would still detect light in black and white; the optic disc has neither rods nor cones.
n.2: The optic disc is part of the retina at the back of the eye, behind the lens.
n.3: The sclera is the white outer layer of the eyeball; it does not cover the inner surface of the retina.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Place the structures in the order light passes through them on its way to the photoreceptors, starting with the first.
o: Vitreous humor
Lens
Cornea
Aqueous humor
Pupil
Retina
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Light enters through the cornea, crosses the aqueous humor, passes through the pupil (the opening in the iris), is focused by the lens, crosses the vitreous humor and reaches the photoreceptors of the retina.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Place the structures in the order sound vibrations pass through them after traveling down the external auditory canal, starting with the first.
o: Stapes
Incus
Malleus
Cochlea
Oval window
Tympanic membrane
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Sound vibrates the tympanic membrane, which moves the ossicles in order (malleus, incus, stapes). The stapes pushes on the oval window, setting up waves in the fluid of the cochlea, where hair cells in the organ of Corti generate nerve impulses.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Spinning rapidly on an office chair leaves Tomás dizzy. Which structures contain the receptors that detect the rotation of his head?
o: Auditory (Eustachian) tube
Cochlea and organ of Corti
Cerebellum
Semicircular canals
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The semicircular canals of the inner ear contain the hair-cell receptors that detect rotation of the head. Together with the vestibule they sense balance, and their signals travel on CN VIII.

n.0: The auditory tube equalizes pressure in the middle ear; it does not sense movement.
n.1: The cochlea and its organ of Corti detect sound for hearing, not head rotation.
n.2: The cerebellum uses balance signals to coordinate movement and posture, but it has no receptors; rotation is detected in the semicircular canals.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: When Priya looks up from her phone to a distant sign, the shape of her lens changes to keep the image focused on the retina. Which structures change the lens shape?
o: Fibers of the choroid layer
Muscles of the iris
Ciliary muscles
Muscles moved by the abducens nerve
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens so it can focus light from near or distant objects on the retina.

n.0: The choroid is the vascular layer of the eye; it does not change the shape of the lens.
n.1: The muscles of the iris change pupil size, not lens shape.
n.3: The abducens nerve (CN VI) moves the eyeball laterally; it does not focus the lens.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A student is comparing the two types of photoreceptors in the retina. Which statements correctly describe rods? Select all that apply.
o: They produce black-and-white vision
They are important for peripheral vision
They are concentrated in the fovea centralis
They detect color in bright light
They work best in dim light
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Rods work in dim light, give black-and-white vision and are important for peripheral vision. Cones handle color and sharp detail in bright light and are concentrated in the fovea centralis.

n.2: Cones, not rods, are concentrated in the fovea centralis.
n.3: Cones detect color in bright light; rods give black-and-white vision.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A child's ear infection leaves fluid behind the tympanic membrane, so the ossicles cannot vibrate freely. Where is the problem, and which step of hearing is impaired?
o: Outer ear; collecting sound waves into the canal
Middle ear; passing vibrations to the oval window
Middle ear; converting vibrations to nerve impulses
Inner ear; converting vibrations to nerve impulses
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: the space behind the tympanic membrane that holds the ossicles is the middle ear, and the ossicles pass vibrations from the eardrum to the oval window. Fluid there weakens that transmission.

n.0: The outer ear (auricle and canal) lies in front of the tympanic membrane, not behind it.
n.2: The location is right, but nerve impulses are generated by hair cells in the cochlea, not in the middle ear.
n.3: Converting vibrations to nerve impulses happens in the cochlea of the inner ear, but the fluid and ossicles are in the middle ear.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which cranial nerve carries visual signals away from the retina, and which lobe of the cerebrum processes these signals?
o: Oculomotor nerve (CN III); parietal lobe
Oculomotor nerve (CN III); occipital lobe
Optic nerve (CN II); occipital lobe
Optic nerve (CN II); temporal lobe
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: the optic nerve (CN II) carries visual signals from the retina, and vision is processed in the occipital lobe.

n.0: CN III is a motor nerve to the eye, and the parietal lobe processes touch and body position.
n.1: The occipital lobe is right, but CN III moves the eye and constricts the pupil; it does not carry visual signals.
n.3: The nerve is right, but the temporal lobe processes hearing, not vision.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which special sense sends its signals to the cerebral cortex without first being relayed through the thalamus?
o: Hearing (audition)
Smell (olfaction)
Balance (equilibrium)
Taste (gustation)
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Smell (olfaction) is the one sense whose signals are not relayed through the thalamus before reaching the cortex.

n.0: Hearing signals pass through the thalamus before reaching the auditory cortex.
n.2: Balance signals are also relayed through the thalamus; smell is the exception.
n.3: Taste signals are relayed through the thalamus on their way to the cortex.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: The pancreas contains both endocrine and exocrine tissue. Which feature describes its endocrine tissue but not its exocrine tissue?
o: It secretes digestive enzymes into the small intestine
It releases secretions through ducts into the duodenum
It releases hormones directly into the blood
It sends its signals to targets along nerve fibers
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Endocrine tissue is ductless and releases hormones (such as insulin and glucagon from the pancreatic islets) into the blood, where they reach target cells with matching receptors.

n.0: Digestive enzymes are the product of the exocrine pancreas, delivered through ducts.
n.1: Releasing secretions through ducts is the defining feature of exocrine tissue.
n.3: Signaling along nerve fibers is how the nervous system works; endocrine signals travel in the blood.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: ADH and oxytocin enter the bloodstream from the posterior pituitary gland. Where are these two hormones synthesized?
o: In the posterior pituitary
In the adrenal cortex
In the hypothalamus
In the anterior pituitary
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: ADH and oxytocin are made by the hypothalamus and transported to the posterior pituitary, which stores and releases them.

n.0: The posterior pituitary stores and releases ADH and oxytocin, but it does not make them.
n.1: The adrenal cortex makes aldosterone and cortisol, not ADH or oxytocin.
n.3: The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones, such as GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A night-shift nurse finds that her normal sleep-wake rhythm is disrupted. Which gland and hormone normally regulate this rhythm, with secretion rising in darkness?
o: Pineal gland; cortisol
Anterior pituitary; cortisol
Pineal gland; melatonin
Anterior pituitary; melatonin
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which rises in darkness and regulates the sleep-wake (circadian) rhythm.

n.0: The pineal gland is right, but cortisol is made by the adrenal cortex.
n.1: The anterior pituitary makes ACTH, not cortisol (adrenal cortex) or melatonin (pineal gland).
n.3: Melatonin comes from the pineal gland, not the anterior pituitary.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Seconds after a near-miss on the freeway, Andre's heart races and his hands shake. Which hormone and source produce this short-term stress response?
o: Epinephrine from the adrenal cortex
Norepinephrine from the adrenal cortex
Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Cortisol from the adrenal medulla
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The adrenal medulla (inner region) releases epinephrine and norepinephrine for the short-term, fight-or-flight stress response.

n.0: Epinephrine is made by the adrenal medulla; the adrenal cortex makes aldosterone, cortisol and small amounts of androgens.
n.1: Norepinephrine is released by the adrenal medulla, not the adrenal cortex.
n.3: Cortisol is made by the adrenal cortex and drives the long-term stress response.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which hormone is produced by the anterior pituitary gland and stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol?
o: GHRH
CRH
TSH
ACTH
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol.

n.0: GHRH is a hypothalamic releasing hormone that acts on the anterior pituitary to promote growth hormone release, not on the adrenal cortex.
n.1: CRH is a releasing hormone made by the hypothalamus; it acts on the anterior pituitary, not directly on the adrenal cortex.
n.2: TSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the thyroid, not the adrenal cortex.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A physiology student sorts hormones by chemical type. Which of these are steroid hormones that cross the cell membrane and bind receptors inside target cells? Select all that apply.
o: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
Testosterone
Insulin
Cortisol
Aldosterone
Epinephrine
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Steroid hormones are made from cholesterol, are lipid-soluble and bind intracellular receptors. Cortisol, aldosterone and testosterone are steroids.

n.0: ADH is a peptide hormone that binds a cell-membrane receptor.
n.2: Insulin is a peptide hormone that binds a cell-membrane receptor.
n.5: Epinephrine is an amine hormone that binds a cell-membrane receptor.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Glucagon is a peptide hormone, and cortisol is a steroid hormone. Which statement correctly compares where each binds its receptor on or in a target cell?
o: Glucagon binds an intracellular receptor; cortisol binds a surface receptor
Both bind surface receptors and act through second messengers such as cAMP
Glucagon binds a surface receptor; cortisol binds an intracellular receptor
Both cross the membrane and bind receptors that change gene expression
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: peptide hormones such as glucagon are water-soluble, so they bind cell-membrane receptors and act through second messengers. Steroid hormones such as cortisol are lipid-soluble, so they cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors.

n.0: This reverses the two: peptides bind surface receptors and steroids bind intracellular receptors.
n.1: This fits glucagon, but cortisol is a steroid that binds an intracellular receptor.
n.3: This fits cortisol, but glucagon is water-soluble and cannot cross the membrane; it binds a surface receptor.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Besides T3 and T4, the thyroid gland secretes a third hormone from its parafollicular (C) cells. Which hormone is it, and what does it do?
o: Calcitonin; it lowers blood calcium
Calcitonin; it raises blood calcium
Thymosin; it promotes T-cell maturation
Parathyroid hormone; it raises blood calcium
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid secrete calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium by favoring bone deposition and reducing osteoclast activity.

n.1: The hormone is right, but calcitonin lowers blood calcium; PTH raises it.
n.2: Thymosin is made by the thymus, not by the thyroid gland.
n.3: Parathyroid hormone is made by the parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid, not by thyroid C cells.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A patient has intense thirst and passes very large volumes of dilute urine, but his blood glucose is normal. A deficiency of which hormone, from which gland, best explains this?
o: Aldosterone released from the adrenal medulla
Insulin released from the pancreatic beta cells
ADH released from the anterior pituitary
ADH released from the posterior pituitary
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: large volumes of dilute urine with normal glucose is diabetes insipidus, a deficiency of ADH, and ADH is released from the posterior pituitary.

n.0: Aldosterone is made by the adrenal cortex, not the medulla, and diabetes insipidus is a lack of ADH.
n.1: Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus with high blood glucose, but this patient's glucose is normal.
n.2: The hormone is right, but ADH is released from the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A patient has lost weight without dieting, feels hot in cool rooms, has a rapid heart rate and has bulging eyes. Excess secretion of which hormones best explains these findings?
o: T3 and T4 from the thyroid gland
Calcitonin from the thyroid gland
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex
Growth hormone from the anterior pituitary
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: T3 and T4 raise metabolic rate and heat production. Excess, as in Graves' disease, causes weight loss, heat intolerance, a fast heart rate and bulging eyes (exophthalmos).

n.1: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium; it does not raise metabolic rate or heat production.
n.2: Excess cortisol causes Cushing's syndrome; heat intolerance, weight loss and bulging eyes point to excess thyroid hormone.
n.3: Excess growth hormone causes gigantism or acromegaly, not this picture of a raised metabolic rate.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Over several years, a 34-year-old woman's hands, feet and jaw gradually enlarge, long after her growth plates have closed. Which hormone is in excess, and what is the condition called?
o: Cortisol; Cushing's syndrome
Growth hormone; gigantism
Thyroxine; gigantism
Growth hormone; acromegaly
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: enlargement of hands, feet and jaw points to excess growth hormone, and excess GH after the growth plates close is acromegaly.

n.0: Cushing's syndrome is excess cortisol and does not cause enlargement of the hands, feet and jaw.
n.1: Gigantism is excess GH before the growth plates close; hers have already closed.
n.2: Gigantism is excess growth hormone before the growth plates close; excess thyroxine raises metabolic rate instead, and her growth plates have closed.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Which organ, not usually listed among the classic endocrine glands, secretes erythropoietin (EPO) to stimulate red blood cell production?
o: Heart
Kidney
Spleen
Red bone marrow
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The kidneys secrete erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates red blood cell production.

n.0: The heart's atria secrete ANP, which lowers blood volume and pressure, not EPO.
n.2: The spleen removes old red blood cells from circulation; it does not secrete EPO.
n.3: Red bone marrow makes red blood cells in response to EPO; it does not secrete the hormone.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Shortly after Jamal eats a large pasta dinner, his blood glucose rises. Which hormone does his pancreas release in response, and from which cells?
o: Glucagon, from pancreatic alpha cells
Insulin, from pancreatic beta cells
Insulin, from pancreatic alpha cells
Glucagon, from pancreatic beta cells
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: High blood glucose after a meal triggers the beta cells of the pancreatic islets to release insulin, which lowers glucose by moving it into cells and storing it as glycogen.

n.0: Glucagon raises blood glucose, so it is released when glucose is low, not after a meal.
n.2: Insulin is the right hormone, but it comes from beta cells; alpha cells make glucagon.
n.3: Glucagon raises blood glucose and is made by alpha cells, so both parts are wrong.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A lab result shows that a patient's blood calcium is below normal. Which hormone responds by stimulating osteoclasts to release calcium from bone?
o: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Calcitonin
Aldosterone
Parathyroid hormone (PTH)
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Low blood calcium triggers the parathyroid glands to release PTH, which raises calcium by stimulating osteoclasts, increasing kidney reabsorption of calcium and activating vitamin D.

n.0: TSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the thyroid to release T3 and T4; it does not regulate calcium.
n.1: Calcitonin is released when calcium is high and lowers it by reducing osteoclast activity.
n.2: Aldosterone controls Na+ and K+ handling by the kidneys, not blood calcium.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: After several hours of hiking without water, Grace becomes dehydrated and her ADH secretion rises. How does this change the urine her kidneys produce?
o: Smaller volume of more dilute urine
Smaller volume of more concentrated urine
Larger volume of urine containing more sodium
Larger volume of more dilute urine
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) makes the collecting ducts reabsorb more water, so the kidneys produce a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

n.0: Reabsorbing more water leaves the remaining urine more concentrated, not more dilute.
n.2: ADH reduces urine volume; increased sodium and water loss is the effect of ANP from the heart.
n.3: This is the effect of low ADH; ADH is anti-diuretic, so it reduces urine output.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: In the thyroid axis, rising blood levels of T3 and T4 reduce the release of TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the anterior pituitary. What type of control is this?
o: Negative feedback
Positive feedback
Direct nervous control
Antagonistic hormone control
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The end product (T3 and T4) switches off the signals that produced it, reversing the change. That is negative feedback, the way most hormone levels are controlled.

n.1: Positive feedback amplifies a change until an end event, as oxytocin does in labor; here the change is being reversed.
n.2: The signals in this loop travel as hormones in the blood, not along nerves.
n.3: Antagonistic control means two hormones with opposite effects, such as insulin and glucagon; this is one hormone suppressing its own signals.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Place the steps of the thyroid hormone axis in order, starting with the first signal from the brain and ending with the feedback step.
o: The hypothalamus releases TRH
High T3 and T4 levels inhibit TRH and TSH release
TSH stimulates the thyroid gland to release T3 and T4
Blood levels of T3 and T4 rise above the set point
TRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: The hypothalamus releases TRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release TSH. TSH stimulates the thyroid to release T3 and T4, so their blood levels rise. Once the levels are high, T3 and T4 inhibit TRH and TSH release (negative feedback), bringing thyroid output back down.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Between meals, Lena's blood glucose falls below its set point. Which hormone responds, and by which process does her liver raise blood glucose?
o: Insulin; breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis)
Glucagon; storage of glucose as glycogen (glycogenesis)
Insulin; storage of glucose as glycogen (glycogenesis)
Glucagon; breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis)
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: low blood glucose triggers the alpha cells to release glucagon, and glucagon makes the liver break down stored glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis), raising blood glucose.

n.0: Insulin lowers blood glucose and is released after meals, not when glucose is low.
n.1: Glucagon is the right hormone, but storing glucose as glycogen lowers blood glucose; that is an effect of insulin.
n.2: Both parts lower blood glucose: insulin is released after meals and promotes glycogenesis, the opposite of what low glucose requires.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: When blood pressure and blood volume fall, the adrenal cortex increases its secretion of aldosterone. Which effect of aldosterone on the kidneys helps restore blood volume?
o: Reabsorbing Na+ (water follows) and excreting K+
Reabsorbing K+ (water follows) and excreting Na+
Excreting Na+ and water to reduce the workload on the heart
Reabsorbing Ca2+ in the distal tubule to raise blood volume
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Aldosterone makes the kidneys reabsorb Na+, with water following by osmosis, and excrete K+. The retained water raises blood volume and blood pressure.

n.1: This reverses the ions: aldosterone causes Na+ retention and K+ excretion.
n.2: Excreting Na+ and water lowers blood volume; that is the action of ANP from the heart.
n.3: Increasing Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal tubule is an action of PTH and controls blood calcium, not blood volume.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: During weeks of ongoing stress before final exams, which hormone sustains Mei's long-term stress response by raising blood glucose and suppressing inflammation?
o: Cortisol from the adrenal cortex
Cortisol from the adrenal medulla
Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Cortisol, a glucocorticoid from the adrenal cortex, drives the long-term stress response: it raises blood glucose by gluconeogenesis, is anti-inflammatory and suppresses immunity.

n.1: Cortisol is the right hormone, but it comes from the adrenal cortex, not the medulla.
n.2: Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla drives the short-term, fight-or-flight response, not weeks of sustained stress.
n.3: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex controls Na+ and K+ and blood volume, not glucose or inflammation.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A routine blood test shows that a patient's calcium level has dropped below its normal range. Which responses would be expected as the body restores it? Select all that apply.
o: Increased secretion of parathyroid hormone
Increased loss of calcium from the kidneys into the urine
Increased deposition of calcium into the bone matrix
More active vitamin D, so the gut absorbs more calcium
Increased calcitonin secretion from the thyroid C cells
Increased osteoclast activity releasing calcium from bone
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Low blood calcium triggers PTH release. PTH stimulates osteoclasts to release calcium from bone, makes the kidneys keep calcium and activates vitamin D so the gut absorbs more calcium.

n.1: PTH makes the kidneys keep calcium, so urinary calcium loss would fall, not rise.
n.2: Depositing calcium into bone lowers blood calcium; that is the calcitonin response to high calcium.
n.4: Calcitonin is released when blood calcium is high and lowers it, so its secretion would fall.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: A 45-year-old patient with obesity has high blood glucose even though his pancreas still produces insulin. Which description best fits his condition?
o: Type 1 diabetes mellitus caused by beta-cell destruction
Type 2 diabetes mellitus caused by insulin resistance
Diabetes insipidus caused by a lack of ADH
Type 1 diabetes mellitus caused by insulin resistance
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is mainly insulin resistance (with a relative deficiency) and is linked to obesity and inactivity; insulin is still produced.

n.0: Beta-cell destruction leaves no insulin, but this patient still produces insulin.
n.2: Diabetes insipidus is an ADH problem causing dilute urine; it does not raise blood glucose.
n.3: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of beta cells; insulin resistance defines type 2.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: Alcohol inhibits the secretion of ADH. Compared with a well-hydrated person who has not been drinking, what would be expected in a person who has had several alcoholic drinks?
o: Less water reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so more dilute urine
Less water reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so less urine
More water reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so less urine
More Na+ reabsorbed in the collecting ducts, so more concentrated urine
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: ADH acts on the collecting ducts to increase water reabsorption, so less ADH means less water is reabsorbed there and a larger volume of more dilute urine is produced.

n.1: ADH acts on the collecting ducts, not the proximal tubule, and reabsorbing less water produces more urine, not less.
n.2: This is the effect of more ADH; alcohol lowers ADH.
n.3: Na+ reabsorption is controlled by aldosterone, and lower ADH makes urine more dilute, not more concentrated.

A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.q: An autoimmune process destroys a patient's adrenal cortex but spares the adrenal medulla. Which hormone deficiencies, and which effect, would be expected?
o: Low epinephrine and norepinephrine; a weaker fight-or-flight response
