Low cortisol and aldosterone; high blood glucose from gluconeogenesis
Low cortisol and aldosterone; low blood pressure from Na+ loss
Low cortisol and aldosterone; high blood pressure from Na+ retention
A&P: Nervous & Endocrine.w: Two steps: the adrenal cortex makes cortisol and aldosterone, so both fall (Addison's disease). Without aldosterone the kidneys lose Na+ and the water that follows it, so blood volume and blood pressure fall.

n.0: Epinephrine and norepinephrine come from the adrenal medulla, which is spared.
n.1: The deficiencies are right, but cortisol raises blood glucose by gluconeogenesis, so losing it tends to lower glucose rather than raise it.
n.3: The deficiencies are right, but aldosterone causes Na+ retention, so its loss leads to Na+ loss and lower blood pressure.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: In a classroom demonstration, a chicken bone is soaked in vinegar until its mineral salts dissolve. The bone keeps its shape but can now be bent easily. Which matrix component remains and gives this flexibility?
o: Collagen fibers
Osteocytes within lacunae
Elastin fibers
Calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite)
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Bone matrix is about one-third organic, mostly collagen (flexibility and tensile strength), and two-thirds inorganic calcium phosphate as hydroxyapatite (hardness). Acid dissolves the mineral and leaves the collagen framework, so the bone bends.

n.1: Osteocytes maintain the matrix but are cells, not the fibrous part of the matrix that resists bending forces.
n.2: Elastin gives stretch and recoil in skin and elastic cartilage; the organic fiber of bone matrix is collagen.
n.3: Hydroxyapatite gives bone its hardness and is the part the acid dissolves; once it is gone the bone loses rigidity.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A 64-year-old woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis several years after menopause. Which change in bone remodeling best accounts for her loss of bone mass?
o: Osteoblast formation outpaces osteoclast resorption
Osteoclast resorption outpaces osteoblast formation
Calcitonin rises and stimulates osteoclast resorption
Osteoblasts resorb more matrix as estrogen declines
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Bone is constantly remodeled by osteoblasts (which build) and osteoclasts (which resorb). After menopause estrogen falls, resorption exceeds formation, and bone mass is lost: osteoporosis.

n.0: If formation outpaced resorption, bone mass would increase rather than decrease.
n.2: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts; it does not stimulate bone resorption.
n.3: Osteoblasts build bone; resorbing matrix is the job of osteoclasts.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Blood calcium drops below its normal range, and the parathyroid glands respond by increasing hormone secretion. What effect does this hormone have on bone tissue?
o: Osteoblast activity rises, depositing Ca2+ into the matrix
Osteoclast activity rises, releasing Ca2+ from the matrix
Osteoclast activity falls, keeping Ca2+ stored in the matrix
Calcitonin release rises, moving Ca2+ out of the matrix
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Step 1: low blood Ca2+ triggers release of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Step 2: PTH raises blood Ca2+ by stimulating osteoclast activity, which resorbs matrix and releases Ca2+ (bone stores about 99% of the body's calcium).

n.0: Osteoblast deposition would move calcium out of the blood and into bone, the opposite of what PTH achieves.
n.2: Reducing osteoclast activity lowers blood Ca2+, which matches calcitonin, not PTH.
n.3: Calcitonin comes from the thyroid gland, not the parathyroids, and it lowers blood calcium rather than releasing it from bone.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A student is reviewing the features of spongy (cancellous) bone. Which statements about spongy bone are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Its spaces hold red marrow in flat bones
It forms the dense outer wall of the diaphysis
It fills the epiphyses of long bones
Its basic units are tightly packed osteons
It is built from a lattice of trabeculae
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Spongy bone is a lighter network of trabeculae whose spaces hold red marrow. It fills the epiphyses of long bones and the interior of flat bones and vertebrae. Compact bone, built of osteons, forms the dense outer layer, including the wall of the diaphysis.

n.1: The dense outer wall of the diaphysis is compact (cortical) bone; spongy bone is light and porous.
n.3: Osteons (Haversian systems) are the units of compact bone; spongy bone is organized as trabeculae without osteons.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A 30-year-old fractures the tibia in a fall. Place the stages of fracture repair in the order they occur, starting with the first.
o: A bony (hard) callus replaces the soft callus
A hematoma (blood clot) forms at the break
A fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus bridges the gap
Osteoclasts and osteoblasts remodel the bony callus
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Fracture repair runs hematoma, then fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus, then bony (hard) callus, then remodeling, in which osteoclasts remove excess bone and osteoblasts reshape the site toward its original form.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: During fetal development, most bones form by replacing a hyaline cartilage model. Which bone instead forms directly within a fibrous membrane by intramembranous ossification?
o: Humerus
Vertebra
Femur
Clavicle
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Intramembranous ossification builds bone directly in a fibrous membrane: the flat bones of the skull, the clavicles and some facial bones. Long bones and vertebrae form by endochondral ossification, replacing a hyaline cartilage model.

n.0: The humerus is a long bone that forms by endochondral ossification from a cartilage model.
n.1: Vertebrae are irregular bones that form by endochondral ossification from cartilage models.
n.2: The femur is a long bone that forms by endochondral ossification from a cartilage model.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A surgeon reattaches a torn tendon to the outer surface of a long bone. Which structure covers that surface, carries blood vessels and nerves, and adds bone to increase the bone's width?
o: Articular cartilage
Endosteum
Periosteum
Synovial membrane
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The periosteum is the outer membrane of a bone: it carries vessels and nerves, anchors tendons, and adds bone to the surface (appositional growth in width) and during repair.

n.0: Articular cartilage covers joint surfaces, is avascular and does not anchor tendons or add width.
n.1: The endosteum lines the internal medullary cavity, not the outer surface where tendons attach.
n.3: The synovial membrane lines a joint capsule and secretes synovial fluid; tendons do not anchor to it.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: After six months on a space station, an astronaut has lost bone density in the legs despite eating a normal diet. Which principle best explains this loss?
o: Bone remodels in response to the mechanical stress on it
Osteoclasts resorb bone when blood calcium rises above normal
Bone mass is fixed once the epiphyseal plates close
Calcitonin rises when the skeleton bears less weight
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Bone remodeling responds to mechanical stress (Wolff's law): weight-bearing load stimulates bone formation. Without load, resorption by osteoclasts exceeds formation by osteoblasts, so bone density falls.

n.1: High blood calcium triggers calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclasts; resorption is driven by low blood calcium (PTH) and, in this case, by the loss of mechanical load.
n.2: Bone is remodeled throughout life; adults gain or lose bone mass long after the growth plates close.
n.3: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts, so it would tend to preserve bone; it does not explain the loss.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A student is sorting bones into the axial and appendicular divisions of the skeleton. Which of the following bones belongs to the axial skeleton?
o: Hip bone (os coxae)
Clavicle
Hyoid
Scapula
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The axial skeleton (80 bones) is the skull, hyoid, auditory ossicles, vertebral column and rib cage. The pectoral girdle (clavicle, scapula) and the pelvic girdle (hip bones) belong to the appendicular skeleton.

n.0: The hip bones form the pelvic girdle, which is appendicular even though it joins the sacrum.
n.1: The clavicle is part of the pectoral girdle, which belongs to the appendicular skeleton.
n.3: The scapula is part of the pectoral girdle, which belongs to the appendicular skeleton.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A physical therapist moves a patient's thigh through flexion, abduction, rotation and circumduction at the hip, then bends and straightens the elbow at the humeroulnar joint. Which pairing correctly classifies these two synovial joints?
o: Hip: ball-and-socket; humeroulnar: pivot
Hip: ball-and-socket; humeroulnar: hinge
Hip: condyloid; humeroulnar: hinge
Hip: condyloid; humeroulnar: pivot
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint: the rounded femoral head sits in the cup-shaped acetabulum, allowing multiaxial movement including rotation and circumduction. The humeroulnar joint is a uniaxial hinge that allows flexion and extension; forearm rotation happens at the radioulnar joints, the proximal one being a pivot.

n.0: The humeroulnar joint is a hinge that allows only flexion and extension; the pivot joint at the elbow is the proximal radioulnar joint, which rotates the radius.
n.2: The hip is not condyloid: condyloid (ellipsoid) joints such as the wrist are biaxial and do not allow true rotation, which the hip performs.
n.3: Both are misclassified: a condyloid joint cannot rotate as the hip does, and the humeroulnar joint is a hinge, not the radioulnar pivot.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which set gives the correct number of separate vertebrae in each region of a typical adult's vertebral column, listed as cervical, thoracic, lumbar?
o: 5 cervical, 12 thoracic, 7 lumbar
12 cervical, 7 thoracic, 5 lumbar
7 cervical, 5 thoracic, 12 lumbar
7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: An adult has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic (one for each pair of ribs) and 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the fused sacrum and coccyx: 26 bones in all.

n.0: This swaps the cervical and lumbar counts; the neck has 7 cervical vertebrae.
n.1: This swaps the cervical and thoracic counts; there are 12 thoracic vertebrae to match the 12 pairs of ribs.
n.2: This swaps the thoracic and lumbar counts; there are 5 large lumbar vertebrae.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which ribs are called floating ribs because they have no anterior attachment to the sternum, either directly or through costal cartilage?
o: Ribs 8 through 12
Ribs 11 and 12
Ribs 1 through 7
Ribs 8 through 10
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs, each with its own costal cartilage to the sternum. Ribs 8 to 12 are false ribs: 8 to 10 attach through the cartilage of rib 7, and 11 and 12 are floating ribs with no anterior attachment.

n.0: Ribs 8 to 12 are the false ribs; within that group, 8 to 10 still attach indirectly, so they do not float.
n.2: Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs that attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilage.
n.3: Ribs 8 to 10 are false ribs that reach the sternum indirectly through rib 7's costal cartilage.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: In anatomical position, which pairing correctly describes where the radius lies in the forearm and where the tibia lies in the leg?
o: Radius lateral; tibia lateral
Radius lateral; tibia medial
Radius medial; tibia medial
Radius medial; tibia lateral
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: In anatomical position (palms forward) the radius is on the lateral, thumb side of the forearm and the ulna is medial. In the leg the large, weight-bearing tibia is medial and the thin fibula is lateral.

n.0: The tibia is medial; the lateral leg bone is the fibula.
n.2: The radius is lateral; the medial forearm bone is the ulna.
n.3: Both are reversed: the ulna is the medial forearm bone and the fibula is the lateral leg bone.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: How are the sutures that join the cranial bones of an adult skull classified, both by structure and by the amount of movement they allow?
o: Cartilaginous joints that are slightly movable
Cartilaginous joints that are immovable
Fibrous joints that are slightly movable
Fibrous joints that are immovable
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Sutures are fibrous joints: the bones are held together by short connective tissue fibers with no joint cavity. Functionally they are synarthroses (immovable).

n.0: Slightly movable cartilaginous joints (symphyses) include the pubic symphysis and the intervertebral discs.
n.1: Immovable cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) include the epiphyseal plate and the first rib-sternum joint, not sutures.
n.2: A slightly movable fibrous joint is a syndesmosis, such as the distal tibiofibular joint; sutures are immovable.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which type of tissue forms the intervertebral discs and the menisci of the knee, where it resists compression and absorbs shock between bones?
o: Hyaline cartilage
Dense regular connective tissue
Fibrocartilage
Elastic cartilage
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Fibrocartilage is the strongest, most shock-absorbing cartilage, with thick collagen bundles. It forms the intervertebral discs, the knee menisci and the pubic symphysis.

n.0: Hyaline cartilage covers articular surfaces and forms costal cartilage and growth plates; it is not the disc or meniscus tissue.
n.1: Dense regular connective tissue forms tendons and ligaments, not the discs or menisci.
n.3: Elastic cartilage gives flexible support in the ear auricle and epiglottis.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Starting from anatomical position, a patient turns the forearm so that the palm faces backward, with the radius crossing over the ulna. What is this movement called?
o: Circumduction
Inversion
Supination
Pronation
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Pronation turns the palm to face posteriorly (or downward) as the radius crosses over the ulna. Supination is the reverse, returning the palm to face anteriorly as in anatomical position.

n.0: Circumduction is a cone-shaped movement of a limb, as at the shoulder or hip.
n.1: Inversion turns the sole of the foot inward; it is a foot movement.
n.2: Supination turns the palm forward or upward; in anatomical position the forearm is already supinated.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which of the following joints are correctly matched with their type of synovial joint? Select all that apply.
o: Knee: hinge
Thumb carpometacarpal: saddle
Atlantoaxial (C1-C2): pivot
Wrist (radiocarpal): ball-and-socket
Elbow (humeroulnar): pivot
Hip: condyloid
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The knee is a (modified) hinge joint, the atlantoaxial joint between C1 and C2 is a pivot joint that rotates the head, and the thumb carpometacarpal joint is the classic saddle joint.

n.3: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is condyloid (ellipsoid) and biaxial; the ball-and-socket joints are the shoulder and hip.
n.4: The humeroulnar joint is a hinge; the pivot joint at the elbow is the proximal radioulnar joint.
n.5: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint; condyloid joints include the wrist and the knuckles.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Place these parts of the vertebral column in order from superior to inferior, starting with the part closest to the skull.
o: Sacrum
Coccyx
Atlas
Axis
Lumbar vertebrae
Thoracic vertebrae
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: From the skull downward: the atlas (C1) holds the skull, the axis (C2) lies just below it with the dens the atlas pivots around, then the remaining cervical vertebrae, the 12 thoracic vertebrae (articulate with the ribs), the 5 lumbar vertebrae (largest weight-bearing bodies), the sacrum (5 fused) and the coccyx (usually 4 fused) at the bottom.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Counting the carpals, metacarpals and phalanges, how many bones form the skeleton of one adult hand, from the wrist to the fingertips? Enter a whole number.

tr.26: using 7 carpals, which is the number of tarsals in the foot (7 + 5 + 14)
tr.28: giving the thumb 3 phalanges like the other fingers (8 + 5 + 15)

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: 8 carpals + 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges = 27. The thumb has 2 phalanges and each of the other four fingers has 3, so the phalanges total 2 + (4 x 3) = 14.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: In the classification of bones by shape, to which category does the patella (kneecap) belong?
o: Irregular
Flat
Sesamoid
Short
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Sesamoid bones form within tendons, and the patella is the classic example. Short bones are cube-like (carpals, tarsals), flat bones are thin (cranial bones, sternum, ribs, scapulae) and irregular bones include the vertebrae.

n.0: Irregular bones, such as the vertebrae, have complex shapes and do not develop within tendons.
n.1: Flat bones are thin and often curved, such as the cranial bones, sternum, ribs and scapulae.
n.3: Short bones are roughly cube-shaped, such as the carpals and tarsals, and do not form inside tendons.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A tissue sample shows branched, striated cells, each with one central nucleus, joined end to end by intercalated discs. From which location was the sample most likely taken?
o: Wall of the stomach
Wall of a large artery
Biceps brachii of the arm
Wall of the heart
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Branched, striated cells with usually one nucleus, joined by intercalated discs (gap junctions plus desmosomes), are cardiac muscle, found only in the heart wall.

n.0: The stomach wall is smooth muscle: spindle-shaped, nonstriated cells without intercalated discs.
n.1: Artery walls contain smooth muscle, which is nonstriated and lacks intercalated discs.
n.2: The biceps brachii is skeletal muscle: long, cylindrical, multinucleated fibers without intercalated discs.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A histology lab compares the three muscle types. Which description matches smooth muscle, such as the muscle found in the wall of the small intestine?
o: Spindle-shaped cells, one nucleus, nonstriated, involuntary
Branched cells, intercalated discs, striated, involuntary
Long cylindrical cells, many nuclei, striated, voluntary
Spindle-shaped cells, many nuclei, striated, voluntary
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped (fusiform) with one nucleus, lack striations and are under involuntary control by the autonomic nervous system and hormones. They produce slow, sustained contractions such as peristalsis.

n.1: Branched, striated, involuntary cells joined by intercalated discs describe cardiac muscle.
n.2: Long, cylindrical, multinucleated, striated, voluntary fibers describe skeletal muscle.
n.3: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, but they have one nucleus, no striations and involuntary control.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: An ankle sprain stretches or tears ligaments, while a ruptured Achilles injury involves a tendon. Which statement correctly contrasts these two connective tissue structures?
o: Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join muscle to muscle
Tendons join bone to bone; ligaments join muscle to bone
Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone
Tendons join muscle to muscle; ligaments join bone to bone
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Tendons attach muscle to bone (the calcaneal tendon anchors the gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus). Ligaments attach bone to bone and stabilize joints, which is why a sprain is a ligament injury.

n.0: Ligaments connect bone to bone across joints, not muscle to muscle.
n.1: This reverses the two: tendons attach muscle to bone and ligaments attach bone to bone.
n.3: Tendons anchor muscle to bone, not muscle to muscle.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A person lifts a grocery bag by flexing the elbow. Which muscle acts as the antagonist to the prime mover during this movement?
o: Pectoralis major
Biceps brachii
Deltoid
Triceps brachii
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: In elbow flexion the biceps brachii is the agonist (prime mover). The triceps brachii, which extends the elbow, is the antagonist: it relaxes and stretches as the biceps contracts.

n.0: The pectoralis major flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm at the shoulder; it does not oppose elbow flexion.
n.1: The biceps brachii is the prime mover (agonist) of elbow flexion, not its antagonist.
n.2: The deltoid abducts the arm at the shoulder; it does not oppose elbow flexion.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: During elbow flexion, the biceps brachii pulls the radius toward the shoulder while its attachments on the scapula stay fixed. How is the attachment on the radius classified?
o: Origin, because it is on the bone that moves
Origin, because it is farther from the trunk
Insertion, because it is on the bone that moves
Insertion, because it is on the stationary bone
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The origin is the attachment on the more stationary bone (here the scapula); the insertion is on the bone that moves (the radius). During contraction the insertion is pulled toward the origin.

n.0: The attachment on the moving bone is the insertion; the origin is on the more stationary bone.
n.1: Origin and insertion are defined by which bone moves, not by distance from the trunk; the moving radius carries the insertion.
n.3: The insertion is on the bone that moves; the stationary attachment is the origin.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Standing in a cold wind, a hiker begins to shiver. Which statement best explains how shivering helps maintain body temperature?
o: Dermal blood vessels dilate, carrying warm blood out to the skin
Cardiac muscle beats faster, and its extra contractions make the heat
Smooth muscle in vessel walls contracts rhythmically and releases heat
Skeletal muscles contract involuntarily, releasing heat as they use ATP
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Shivering is rapid, involuntary contraction of skeletal muscle triggered by the hypothalamus. Much of the energy released as the muscles use ATP is lost as heat, so heat production rises and body temperature is maintained. Constriction of dermal vessels conserves heat but does not produce it.

n.0: Dilation of dermal vessels sends warm blood to the surface and releases heat; in the cold these vessels constrict to conserve it.
n.1: A faster heartbeat is not shivering; shivering is repeated contraction of the large mass of skeletal muscle, which is the main source of the extra heat.
n.2: Shivering is contraction of skeletal muscle, not vascular smooth muscle; narrowing of dermal vessels conserves heat but is not shivering.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A patient is asked to rise up onto the toes. Which movement occurs at the ankle, and which muscles act as the prime movers?
o: Plantar flexion by the tibialis anterior
Dorsiflexion by the gastrocnemius and soleus
Dorsiflexion by the tibialis anterior
Plantar flexion by the gastrocnemius and soleus
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Step 1: rising onto the toes points the foot downward, which is plantar flexion. Step 2: the prime movers of plantar flexion are the gastrocnemius and soleus, acting through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.

n.0: The tibialis anterior produces dorsiflexion, not plantar flexion.
n.1: The gastrocnemius and soleus plantar flex the ankle; dorsiflexion is the action of the tibialis anterior.
n.2: Dorsiflexion lifts the toes toward the shin, the opposite of rising onto the toes.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A soccer player straightens the knee forcefully to kick a ball. Which muscle group is the prime mover for this knee movement?
o: Quadriceps femoris
Gastrocnemius and soleus
Gluteus maximus
Hamstring muscles
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Straightening the knee is extension, and the quadriceps femoris (including the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis) is the prime mover of knee extension.

n.1: The gastrocnemius and soleus plantar flex the ankle; they do not extend the knee.
n.2: The gluteus maximus extends the hip; it does not cross the knee to straighten it.
n.3: The hamstrings flex the knee and extend the hip; they oppose knee extension.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A nurse asks a patient to raise the arm out to the side until it is level with the shoulder. Which muscle is the prime mover for this abduction of the arm?
o: Pectoralis major
Latissimus dorsi
Trapezius
Deltoid
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The deltoid, which caps the shoulder, is the prime mover of arm abduction (moving the arm away from the midline). It is also a common intramuscular injection site.

n.0: The pectoralis major flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm.
n.1: The latissimus dorsi extends and adducts the arm, the opposite direction to abduction.
n.2: The trapezius elevates and retracts the scapula and extends the head; it does not abduct the arm at the shoulder joint.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: During quiet, restful breathing, which muscles contract to enlarge the thoracic cavity so that air flows into the lungs?
o: External intercostals and rectus abdominis
Internal intercostals and rectus abdominis
Diaphragm and external intercostals
Diaphragm and internal intercostals
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: In quiet inspiration the diaphragm (the main muscle of inspiration) contracts and flattens while the external intercostals lift the ribs. Both enlarge the thoracic cavity, pressure in the lungs falls and air flows in. Quiet expiration is mostly passive recoil; the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles act in forced expiration.

n.0: The external intercostals do help, but the rectus abdominis flexes the trunk and assists forced expiration, and the diaphragm is missing.
n.1: The internal intercostals and abdominal muscles such as the rectus abdominis are muscles of forced expiration, not inspiration.
n.3: The diaphragm is right, but the internal intercostals pull the ribs down during forced expiration; they do not act in quiet inspiration.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Cardiac muscle and skeletal muscle differ in many ways. Which features do these two muscle types share? Select all that apply.
o: Actin and myosin organized into sarcomeres
Spindle-shaped cells with one nucleus
Long cylindrical cells with many nuclei
Striated appearance under a microscope
Cells joined by intercalated discs
Voluntary control by somatic motor neurons
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Both are striated because their actin and myosin are arranged in repeating sarcomeres. Skeletal muscle is voluntary, with long multinucleated fibers; cardiac muscle is involuntary, with branched cells that usually have one nucleus and are joined by intercalated discs.

n.1: Spindle-shaped cells with one nucleus describe smooth muscle, not either of these types.
n.2: Long multinucleated cells are skeletal fibers; cardiac cells are branched and usually have one nucleus.
n.4: Intercalated discs are found in cardiac muscle and are absent from skeletal muscle.
n.5: Voluntary somatic control belongs to skeletal muscle; cardiac muscle is involuntary and autorhythmic.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which of the following structures is made of smooth muscle?
o: Myocardium
Arrector pili
Muscles of facial expression
Diaphragm
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The arrector pili are small bundles of smooth muscle attached to hair follicles; their contraction makes hairs stand up (goosebumps). Other smooth muscle sites include blood vessels, airways, the iris and hollow organs.

n.0: The myocardium is cardiac muscle: involuntary like smooth muscle, but striated, with branched cells joined by intercalated discs.
n.2: Muscles of facial expression are striated, voluntary skeletal muscles, even though many insert into the skin rather than onto bone.
n.3: The diaphragm is skeletal muscle; it contracts automatically during quiet breathing but is striated and can be controlled voluntarily.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: When a skeletal muscle fiber is stimulated, calcium ions flood the sarcoplasm. To which protein do these calcium ions bind directly to begin the process of contraction?
o: Tropomyosin
Troponin
Actin
Myosin
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Ca2+ binds troponin on the thin filament. This shifts tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin, so myosin heads can form cross-bridges.

n.0: Tropomyosin is the strand that covers actin's binding sites; it is moved by troponin, not bound by Ca2+.
n.2: Actin carries the binding sites for myosin; calcium acts on troponin, which then uncovers those sites.
n.3: Myosin heads bind actin and ATP; calcium does not bind myosin to start skeletal muscle contraction.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: In a resting skeletal muscle fiber, most of the calcium that will trigger the next contraction is stored in which structure?
o: Sarcolemma
Sarcoplasmic reticulum
Transverse (T) tubules
Mitochondria
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The sarcoplasmic reticulum, the muscle fiber's smooth ER, stores Ca2+ and releases it when an action potential arrives; during relaxation the Ca2+ is pumped back in using ATP.

n.0: The sarcolemma is the muscle cell membrane that conducts the action potential; it is not the internal calcium store.
n.2: T-tubules carry the action potential deep into the fiber; they do not store the calcium.
n.3: Mitochondria produce ATP by aerobic respiration; they are not the calcium store that triggers contraction.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A motor neuron's action potential reaches the neuromuscular junction of a skeletal muscle fiber. Which neurotransmitter is released there to stimulate the fiber?
o: Norepinephrine
Acetylcholine
Dopamine
Serotonin
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: At the neuromuscular junction the motor neuron releases acetylcholine (ACh), which binds receptors on the sarcolemma and triggers a muscle action potential. Acetylcholinesterase then breaks ACh down.

n.0: Norepinephrine is released by most sympathetic postganglionic neurons, not by motor neurons at skeletal muscle.
n.2: Dopamine acts in brain pathways that influence movement, but it is not released at the neuromuscular junction.
n.3: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter of the brain and gut; it does not stimulate skeletal muscle fibers.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Place these levels of skeletal muscle organization in order from largest to smallest, starting with the whole muscle.
o: Myofilament (actin or myosin)
Whole muscle wrapped in epimysium
Myofibril
Sarcomere
Fascicle wrapped in perimysium
Muscle fiber wrapped in endomysium
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: A muscle (epimysium) contains fascicles (perimysium), each a bundle of muscle fibers, which are single cells (endomysium). Each fiber is packed with myofibrils, which are chains of sarcomeres, the contractile units built from thin actin and thick myosin myofilaments.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: During a strong concentric contraction of the biceps brachii, which change occurs within each sarcomere of its fibers?
o: The H zone widens as the Z discs move apart
The A band shortens while the I band keeps its length
The I band and H zone shorten while the A band keeps its length
The actin and myosin filaments shorten as the Z discs move closer
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: In the sliding filament model, thin actin filaments slide toward the M line: the Z discs move closer and the I band and H zone shorten. The A band equals the length of the thick myosin filaments, so it stays the same. The filaments slide; they do not shorten.

n.0: In contraction the H zone narrows and the Z discs move closer together, not apart.
n.1: The A band is the length of the myosin filaments, which do not shorten; it is the I band that narrows.
n.3: Neither filament shortens; actin and myosin slide past each other while keeping their lengths.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A few hours after death, the skeletal muscles of the body become stiff and rigid. Which explanation of this rigor mortis is correct?
o: Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin
Excess acetylcholine keeps restimulating the fibers
Without ATP, myosin heads cannot attach to actin
Without calcium, troponin keeps tropomyosin in place
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Step 1: after death, ATP production stops. Step 2: ATP must bind a myosin head to release it from actin, so the cross-bridges stay locked and the muscles remain rigid.

n.1: Acetylcholine release requires living motor neurons and is cleared by acetylcholinesterase; the stiffness comes from the lack of ATP.
n.2: If myosin could not attach, the muscles would stay limp; the problem is that attached heads cannot let go.
n.3: Tropomyosin blocking actin would prevent cross-bridges and keep muscle relaxed, not rigid.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: The same arm muscles are used to lift a pencil and then a heavy suitcase. How does the nervous system chiefly increase the force the muscle produces for the suitcase?
o: Each fiber contracts harder in response to a single impulse
More motor units are recruited to contract at once
The myosin filaments lengthen to form more cross-bridges
More troponin is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: A single fiber follows the all-or-none principle, so whole-muscle force is graded by recruiting more motor units (one motor neuron plus all the fibers it supplies) and by raising the frequency of stimulation.

n.0: Each fiber responds all-or-none to an impulse; force is graded at the level of the whole muscle.
n.2: Myofilaments keep their length during contraction; they slide past one another.
n.3: The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca2+, not troponin; troponin is part of the thin filament.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: During a 10-second sprint, a runner quickly uses up the ATP already stored in the leg muscles. Which source then regenerates ATP most rapidly for the next several seconds?
o: Oxygen stored on myoglobin
Aerobic respiration in mitochondria
Creatine phosphate
Anaerobic glycolysis
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Muscle energy sources come into play in sequence: stored ATP (a few seconds), then creatine phosphate, which transfers its phosphate to ADP almost instantly (about 10 to 15 seconds), then anaerobic glycolysis, then aerobic respiration.

n.0: Myoglobin stores oxygen for aerobic respiration; it does not regenerate ATP directly.
n.1: Aerobic respiration yields the most ATP but is the slowest pathway, so it is not the most rapid source.
n.3: Anaerobic glycolysis is fast but follows creatine phosphate as the main source after the first several seconds.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: During an all-out 400-meter sprint, lactic acid builds up in a runner's leg muscles. Which process produces this lactic acid?
o: Breakdown of creatine phosphate
Glycolysis when oxygen supply is short
Hydrolysis of ATP by myosin heads
Aerobic respiration in the mitochondria
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: When oxygen delivery cannot meet demand, pyruvate from glycolysis is converted to lactic acid. Anaerobic glycolysis is fast but yields 2 ATP per glucose.

n.0: Creatine phosphate donates its phosphate to ADP, leaving creatine; it does not form lactic acid.
n.2: Myosin's hydrolysis of ATP yields ADP and phosphate to power the stroke; it does not form lactic acid.
n.3: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water, not lactic acid.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Skeletal muscle fibers are wide cells, yet all their myofibrils contract almost at the same moment. What do the transverse (T) tubules do that makes this possible?
o: Store calcium ions between contractions
Release acetylcholine onto the sarcolemma
Carry the impulse deep into the fiber
Anchor thin filaments at each Z disc
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: T-tubules are inward folds of the sarcolemma that carry the action potential deep into the fiber, next to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so Ca2+ is released around every myofibril at once.

n.0: Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not in the T-tubules.
n.1: Acetylcholine is released by the motor neuron's axon terminal at the neuromuscular junction.
n.3: Thin filaments are anchored at the Z discs themselves; T-tubules conduct the impulse.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A person performs one slow biceps curl: raising a dumbbell, holding it still at mid-height for five seconds, then lowering it slowly. Which statements about the biceps brachii are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Raising the dumbbell is a concentric contraction
Lowering it slowly is an isometric contraction
Holding it still is an isometric contraction
Lowering it slowly is an eccentric contraction
Holding it still is a concentric contraction
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Isotonic contractions change muscle length: concentric when the muscle shortens (lifting) and eccentric when it lengthens under load (lowering). Isometric contractions build tension with no change in length (holding still).

n.1: While lowering, the biceps lengthens under load, which is eccentric; isometric means no change in length.
n.4: While holding still, the biceps keeps the same length, which is isometric; concentric means the muscle shortens.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Place these events of skeletal muscle contraction in the order they occur, starting with the signal from the motor neuron.
o: An action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and T-tubules
ATP binds myosin, releasing the head from actin
Acetylcholine is released at the neuromuscular junction
Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Calcium binds troponin, moving tropomyosin off actin's binding sites
Myosin heads bind actin and perform the power stroke
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: ACh released at the neuromuscular junction triggers a muscle action potential that travels along the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules. The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca2+, which binds troponin so tropomyosin uncovers actin. Energized myosin heads form cross-bridges and pull actin toward the M line (power stroke), and ATP binding then releases each head so the cycle can repeat.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which layer of the epidermis is the deepest and contains the dividing stem cells that replace the cells continually shed from the skin surface?
o: Stratum spinosum
Stratum corneum
Stratum basale
Stratum granulosum
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The stratum basale (germinativum) is the deepest epidermal layer: a single row of dividing stem cells that push new keratinocytes upward. It also holds melanocytes and Merkel cells.

n.0: The stratum spinosum lies just above the basale and contains Langerhans cells; it is not the deepest layer.
n.1: The stratum corneum is the most superficial layer of dead, flattened, keratin-filled cells.
n.3: The stratum granulosum is a middle layer where keratinization advances and cells begin to die.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which epidermal cell produces a pigment that absorbs ultraviolet radiation and helps protect the DNA of nearby skin cells from damage?
o: Keratinocyte
Merkel cell
Melanocyte
Langerhans (dendritic) cell
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Melanocytes in the stratum basale make melanin, a pigment that absorbs UV radiation and shields the DNA of surrounding keratinocytes.

n.0: Keratinocytes, the most numerous epidermal cells, make keratin, a tough waterproofing protein rather than a UV-absorbing pigment.
n.1: Merkel cells in the stratum basale act as receptors for light touch.
n.3: Langerhans (dendritic) cells are immune cells in the stratum spinosum that present antigens.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A tissue sample taken just beneath the epidermis contains blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles and a dense mesh of collagen and elastin fibers. Which layer and tissue type does it show?
o: Smooth muscle tissue of the dermis
Connective tissue of the dermis
Epithelial tissue of the epidermis
Adipose tissue of the hypodermis
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The dermis lies beneath the epidermis and is connective tissue: areolar in the papillary layer and dense irregular in the reticular layer, rich in collagen (strength) and elastin (stretch), with vessels, nerves, follicles and glands.

n.0: The dermis does contain tiny arrector pili muscles, but its main tissue is connective tissue, not smooth muscle.
n.2: The epidermis is avascular stratified squamous epithelium; it has no blood vessels or collagen mesh.
n.3: The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is mostly fat with areolar tissue, not a dense collagen and elastin mesh.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which sweat glands are distributed over most of the body surface, open directly onto the skin through pores, and secrete watery sweat that cools the body?
o: Sebaceous glands
Eccrine glands
Ceruminous glands
Apocrine glands
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Eccrine (merocrine) sweat glands are the most numerous, are found almost everywhere (especially palms, soles and forehead), open onto the surface through pores and secrete watery sweat for thermoregulation.

n.0: Sebaceous glands secrete oily sebum, usually into hair follicles; they do not produce sweat.
n.2: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands in the ear canal that produce earwax.
n.3: Apocrine glands are found in the axillary and anogenital regions, open into hair follicles and become active at puberty.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A biopsy from the sole of the foot shows a clear layer of flattened dead cells between the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum. A biopsy from the upper arm lacks it. Which layer is this?
o: Papillary layer
Stratum spinosum
Stratum basale
Stratum lucidum
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The stratum lucidum is a thin, clear layer between the granulosum and corneum that is present in the thick skin of the palms and soles and absent from thin skin.

n.0: The papillary layer is the superficial part of the dermis, below the whole epidermis.
n.1: The stratum spinosum lies below the granulosum and is present in both thick and thin skin.
n.2: The stratum basale is the deepest epidermal layer and is present in all skin.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A patient who spends almost no time outdoors develops low blood calcium. Which sequence best describes the skin's normal role in calcium absorption from the intestine?
o: Melanocytes secrete vitamin D3 after UVB exposure; the kidneys then activate it
UVB converts a cholesterol derivative directly into active calcitriol in skin
Sebaceous glands secrete vitamin D3 in sebum; the liver then activates it
UVB makes vitamin D3 from a cholesterol derivative; liver and kidneys activate it
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Step 1: in the skin, UVB converts a cholesterol derivative to vitamin D3, an inactive precursor. Step 2: the liver and kidneys convert it to active calcitriol, which increases calcium absorption from the gut. Little sun means little D3 and poorer Ca2+ absorption.

n.0: Melanocytes make melanin, which absorbs UV; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative in the skin, and the liver also takes part in activation.
n.1: The skin makes only the precursor; activation to calcitriol takes place in the liver and kidneys.
n.2: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum to lubricate skin; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative, and the kidneys also take part in activation.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: While jogging on a hot afternoon, a person's body temperature starts to rise. Which pair of skin responses is mainly responsible for releasing the excess heat?
o: Dermal vessels constrict; eccrine glands secrete sweat
Dermal vessels constrict; arrector pili muscles contract
Dermal vessels dilate; eccrine glands secrete sweat
Dermal vessels dilate; apocrine glands secrete sweat
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: To lose heat, dermal blood vessels dilate so more warm blood reaches the surface, and eccrine glands secrete watery sweat that cools the skin as it evaporates.

n.0: Constriction of dermal vessels conserves heat, the opposite of what is needed here.
n.1: Vessel constriction and arrector pili contraction are heat-conserving responses to cold.
n.3: Apocrine glands in the axillae and groin respond mainly to stress and puberty; eccrine glands are the main thermoregulators.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Which glands secrete an oily substance, usually into hair follicles, that softens skin and hair, slows water loss and helps inhibit bacterial growth?
o: Sebaceous glands
Ceruminous glands
Apocrine sweat glands
Eccrine sweat glands
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Sebaceous (oil) glands secrete sebum, usually into hair follicles. Sebum lubricates and softens skin and hair, slows water loss and is antibacterial. They are absent from the palms and soles.

n.1: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands that produce earwax in the ear canal.
n.2: Apocrine glands also open into hair follicles, but they secrete a thicker sweat, not oily sebum.
n.3: Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface through pores and secrete watery sweat.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: Two healthy adults have very different natural skin tones. Which difference between their skin best explains this?
o: The amount of melanin their melanocytes produce
The number of melanocytes in their stratum corneum
The number of melanocytes in their stratum basale
The amount of keratin made by their keratinocytes
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: People have similar numbers of melanocytes; differences in natural skin color come mainly from how much melanin those melanocytes produce (with smaller contributions from carotene and hemoglobin).

n.1: Melanocytes are located in the stratum basale, not the dead stratum corneum.
n.2: Melanocyte numbers are similar between people; it is their melanin output that differs.
n.3: Keratin is a structural, waterproofing protein, not the main pigment behind skin tone.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A student is summarizing the structure of the epidermis for a study guide. Which statements about the epidermis are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Its melanocytes lie mainly in the stratum corneum
It is stratified squamous epithelium
It is avascular
Most of its cells are keratinocytes
It is built mainly of collagen and elastin
Its deepest layer is the stratum corneum
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with no blood vessels of its own (it is nourished from the dermis). Keratinocytes are its most numerous cells.

n.0: Melanocytes lie in the stratum basale, the deepest layer.
n.4: Collagen and elastin fibers are features of the dermis, which is connective tissue.
n.5: The stratum corneum is the most superficial layer; the deepest is the stratum basale.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: A splinter pierces the thick skin of the palm. Place the layers in the order the splinter passes through them, starting at the skin surface.
o: Stratum corneum
Stratum basale
Stratum lucidum
Papillary layer of the dermis
Stratum granulosum
Stratum spinosum
A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: From the surface inward: stratum corneum, stratum lucidum (present in thick skin of palms and soles), stratum granulosum, stratum spinosum and stratum basale, then the dermis, whose superficial part is the papillary layer. Mnemonic from the surface: Come, Let's Get Sun Burned.

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.q: An adult has burns covering the entire right arm and the entire front of the trunk. Using the adult rule of nines, what percentage of total body surface area is burned? Enter a whole number.

tr.18: counting the front of the trunk as 9%, like an arm (9 + 9)
tr.36: counting the arm as 18%, the value for a leg (18 + 18)
tr.45: adding the back of the trunk as well (9 + 18 + 18)

A&P: Skeletal, Muscular & Integumentary.w: Adult rule of nines: each arm is 9% and the front of the trunk is 18%. 9 + 18 = 27%.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: After a vasectomy, a man's semen contains no sperm, yet its volume is only slightly reduced. Which explanation accounts for this?
o: Most of the fluid enters past the cut, from the seminal vesicles and prostate
Most of the fluid comes from the seminiferous tubules, which keep secreting
Most of the fluid is made in the epididymis, which lies past the cut
Most of the fluid comes from the bulbourethral glands, which drain into the ductus
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Two steps. (1) A vasectomy cuts the ductus (vas) deferens, so sperm from the seminiferous tubules and epididymis cannot pass. (2) The seminal vesicles (about 60% of semen) join the tract at the ejaculatory duct, and the prostate surrounds the urethra; both lie downstream of the cut, so their fluid still makes up most of the semen.

n.1: The seminiferous tubules produce sperm and lie upstream of the cut, so nothing from them reaches the ejaculate.
n.2: The epididymis lies before the ductus deferens, upstream of the cut, and it matures and stores sperm rather than making most of the semen fluid.
n.3: The bulbourethral glands add a small amount of mucus, and they drain into the urethra, not the ductus deferens.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Place the structures in the order sperm pass through them, starting where sperm are produced and ending where they leave the body during ejaculation.
o: Epididymis
Ejaculatory duct
Spongy (penile) urethra
Prostatic urethra
Ductus (vas) deferens
Seminiferous tubules
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules, mature and are stored in the epididymis, travel through the ductus deferens (via the inguinal canal), enter the ejaculatory duct where the seminal vesicle duct joins, then pass through the prostatic urethra inside the prostate and finally the spongy urethra of the penis (the short membranous urethra lies between those two). Mnemonic: SEVEn UP.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: In a man, Sertoli cells increase their secretion of inhibin as sperm production rises. Which hormonal change follows most directly from the higher inhibin level?
o: Higher GnRH secretion by the hypothalamus
Lower testosterone secretion by the Sertoli cells
Lower FSH secretion by the anterior pituitary
Lower LH secretion by the anterior pituitary
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Inhibin from Sertoli cells is a negative-feedback signal that suppresses FSH release from the anterior pituitary, slowing spermatogenesis. Testosterone is the main feedback signal that holds LH in check.

n.0: Inhibin is an inhibitory feedback signal, so it would not raise GnRH output.
n.1: Sertoli cells do not secrete testosterone; Leydig cells do, under LH control.
n.3: LH is held in check mainly by testosterone feedback; inhibin targets FSH.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: The testes sit in the scrotum, outside the pelvic cavity, instead of inside the abdomen. Which statement best explains why this position matters for sperm production?
o: Sperm mature inside the scrotal sac before they move into the epididymis
Spermatogenesis works best about 2 to 3 degrees Celsius below core body temperature
Spermatogenesis works best about 2 to 3 degrees Celsius above core body temperature
Leydig cells stop secreting testosterone when held at core body temperature
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules works best at about 2 to 3 degrees Celsius below core body temperature, so the scrotum holds the testes outside the body cavity.

n.0: Sperm mature in the epididymis after leaving the seminiferous tubules, not in the scrotal sac before reaching it.
n.2: The scrotum keeps the testes cooler than the body core, not warmer.
n.3: The position matters for spermatogenesis in the tubules; testosterone secretion by Leydig cells is not what the cooler setting protects.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: A normal human sperm cell fertilizes a normal secondary oocyte. Which statement about the chromosomes carried by that sperm is correct?
o: It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, carrying either an X or a Y chromosome
It is diploid, carrying 46 chromosomes including one X and one Y
It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, and the egg's chromosome sets the child's sex
It is haploid with 23 chromosomes, each sperm carrying an X chromosome
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Meiosis makes sperm haploid (n = 23). Each sperm carries either an X or a Y, so the sperm determines the child's sex; the egg carries an X. Fertilization restores the diploid number (2n = 46).

n.1: Gametes are haploid; 46 chromosomes is the diploid number restored at fertilization.
n.2: The egg carries an X in every case, so it is the sperm's X or Y that sets the child's sex.
n.3: It is the egg that carries an X in every case; sperm carry either an X or a Y.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: In a sample of testicular tissue, 25 primary spermatocytes each complete both meiotic divisions normally. How many spermatids are produced in total? Enter a whole number.

tr.25: One gamete per cell, as in oogenesis.
tr.50: Counting meiosis I only (2 secondary spermatocytes per primary spermatocyte).

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Each primary spermatocyte goes through meiosis I (giving 2 secondary spermatocytes) and meiosis II (giving 4 haploid spermatids). Unlike oogenesis, which yields 1 ovum plus polar bodies, no cells are lost as polar bodies. 25 x 4 = 100 spermatids.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which statements about the hormonal control of the testes are correct? Select all that apply.
o: FSH and testosterone together stimulate spermatogenesis via Sertoli cells.
FSH from the posterior pituitary acts on the Sertoli cells.
Testosterone raises GnRH output by positive feedback on the hypothalamus.
LH stimulates interstitial (Leydig) cells to secrete testosterone.
Leydig cells line the seminiferous tubules and nourish developing sperm.
Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which suppresses FSH release.
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: LH acts on Leydig cells, which secrete testosterone. FSH, together with testosterone, acts through the Sertoli cells to drive spermatogenesis. Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which suppresses FSH.

n.1: FSH is released by the anterior pituitary, not the posterior pituitary.
n.2: Testosterone exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH and LH.
n.4: Sertoli cells, not Leydig cells, line the tubules and nourish developing sperm; Leydig cells sit between the tubules.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: A semen analysis shows sperm with normal heads and tails but abnormal midpieces. Which function would be most directly impaired in these sperm?
o: Releasing enzymes that digest the oocyte's outer layers
Supplying the ATP that powers movement of the tail
Storing the fructose that sperm use as an energy source
Delivering 23 chromosomes to the oocyte at fertilization
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: The midpiece is packed with mitochondria that make ATP to power the flagellum. A defective midpiece leaves the tail short of energy, reducing motility.

n.0: The penetrating enzymes sit in the acrosome on the head, which is normal here.
n.2: Fructose is supplied in seminal vesicle fluid; it is not stored in the sperm's midpiece.
n.3: The chromosomes are in the nucleus of the head, which is normal here.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: After ovulation, the fimbriae sweep the secondary oocyte into the uterine tube. In a typical pregnancy, where does fertilization of the oocyte take place?
o: In the ampulla of the uterine tube
In the ruptured follicle of the ovary
In the functional layer of the endometrium
In the cervical canal of the uterus
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla, the wide outer portion of the uterine tube. Cilia and peristalsis then move the developing embryo to the uterus, where it implants in the endometrium.

n.1: The oocyte leaves the ovary at ovulation; the ruptured follicle then becomes the corpus luteum.
n.2: The endometrium is where the blastocyst implants about a week later, not where fertilization occurs.
n.3: Sperm pass through the cervix on the way up; fertilization happens farther along, in the uterine tube.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: In a typical 28-day cycle, the dominant follicle releases a secondary oocyte around day 14. Which hormonal event directly causes this ovulation?
o: A sharp fall in estrogen from the follicles
A surge of FSH from the anterior pituitary
A surge of LH from the anterior pituitary
A surge of progesterone from the corpus luteum
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: High estrogen from the dominant (Graafian) follicle triggers the LH surge from the anterior pituitary, and the LH surge causes the follicle to rupture and release the secondary oocyte.

n.0: Estrogen is high, not falling, just before ovulation; high estrogen is what triggers the LH surge.
n.1: FSH stimulates follicle growth earlier in the follicular phase; the LH surge is what causes ovulation.
n.3: The corpus luteum forms from the ruptured follicle after ovulation, so its progesterone cannot trigger ovulation.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum. Which hormone does the corpus luteum mainly secrete, and what is its main effect on the uterus?
o: Progesterone, which keeps the endometrium in its secretory state
Estrogen, which rebuilds the endometrium after menstruation
FSH, which prepares the endometrium for implantation
Progesterone, which stimulates contractions of the myometrium
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: The corpus luteum secretes mainly progesterone (plus some estrogen). Progesterone maintains the thickened, secretory endometrium and relaxes the myometrium, preparing the uterus for implantation.

n.1: Rebuilding the endometrium in the proliferative phase is driven by estrogen from growing follicles before ovulation.
n.2: FSH is an anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates follicles; the corpus luteum does not secrete it.
n.3: Progesterone relaxes the myometrium; oxytocin is the hormone that stimulates uterine contractions.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: A new mother notices that milk begins flowing from her breasts within seconds after her infant starts to suckle. Which hormone, from which gland, causes this milk ejection?
o: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
Prolactin from the anterior pituitary
Oxytocin from the anterior pituitary
Prolactin from the posterior pituitary
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary causes milk ejection (let-down). Prolactin from the anterior pituitary drives milk production.

n.1: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production, not the rapid ejection of milk.
n.2: Oxytocin causes ejection, but it is released from the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary.
n.3: Prolactin is an anterior pituitary hormone, and it governs milk production rather than ejection.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: A home pregnancy test detects a hormone in urine shortly after a blastocyst implants. Which statement correctly identifies this hormone and its role in early pregnancy?
o: hCG from the mother's anterior pituitary, which keeps the corpus luteum alive
Progesterone from the corpus luteum, which keeps the endometrium intact
hCG from the embryo's trophoblast, which keeps the corpus luteum alive
LH from the mother's anterior pituitary, which triggers implantation
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Pregnancy tests detect hCG, secreted by the trophoblast of the implanted blastocyst (later the placenta). hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive so it keeps secreting progesterone, which maintains the endometrium.

n.0: hCG is made by the embryo's trophoblast, not by the mother's pituitary.
n.1: Progesterone does maintain the endometrium, but home pregnancy tests detect hCG, not progesterone.
n.3: LH triggers ovulation, not implantation, and it is not the hormone pregnancy tests detect.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Place these events of a typical 28-day ovarian and uterine cycle in order, starting with day 1 of the cycle.
o: Estrogen from growing follicles rebuilds the endometrium (proliferative phase)
The functional layer of the endometrium is shed (menstrual phase)
An LH surge causes the dominant follicle to release a secondary oocyte
The corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone levels fall
Progesterone from the corpus luteum makes the endometrium secretory
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Days 1 to 5: menstrual phase, as the functional layer is shed. Days 6 to 14: FSH-stimulated follicles secrete estrogen that rebuilds the endometrium (proliferative phase). About day 14: high estrogen triggers the LH surge and ovulation. Days 15 to 28: the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and the endometrium is secretory. Without pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates near the end of the cycle, progesterone falls, and menstruation begins again.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which statement correctly describes the cell that the ovary releases at ovulation and the stage its meiosis has reached?
o: A mature ovum that completed meiosis II before leaving the ovary
A secondary oocyte that completes meiosis II if it is fertilized
A primary oocyte that completes meiosis I in the uterine tube
A secondary oocyte that completed meiosis II at the LH surge
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Primary oocytes stay arrested in prophase I from before birth until puberty. Each cycle, one completes meiosis I just before ovulation, forming a secondary oocyte and the first polar body. The secondary oocyte is released and finishes meiosis II only if a sperm fertilizes it.

n.0: Meiosis II is not finished before ovulation; it is completed after fertilization.
n.2: Meiosis I is completed just before ovulation, so the released cell is already a secondary oocyte.
n.3: The LH surge is followed by completion of meiosis I, not meiosis II; meiosis II waits for fertilization.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Six primary oocytes and six primary spermatocytes complete meiosis normally, and each oocyte is fertilized so that meiosis II finishes. How many ova and how many sperm result in total?
o: 6 ova and 24 sperm
6 ova and 12 sperm
24 ova and 24 sperm
12 ova and 24 sperm
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Two steps. (1) Oogenesis divides the cytoplasm unequally, so each primary oocyte yields 1 ovum plus polar bodies: 6 x 1 = 6 ova. (2) Spermatogenesis yields 4 sperm per primary spermatocyte: 6 x 4 = 24 sperm.

n.1: This counts 2 sperm per spermatocyte, which stops after meiosis I; meiosis II gives 4 per spermatocyte.
n.2: This treats oogenesis like spermatogenesis; polar bodies are not functional ova, so each oocyte gives 1 ovum.
n.3: This counts the first polar body as a second ovum; polar bodies degenerate and are not ova.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: To slow preterm labor, a patient is given a drug that blocks oxytocin receptors in the uterus. The activity of which part of the uterus is this drug intended to reduce?
o: Myometrium, the smooth muscle layer
Cervix, the narrow lower neck
Endometrium, the glandular lining
Perimetrium, the outer serous layer
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Two steps. (1) Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary stimulates uterine contractions in labor. (2) Those contractions come from the myometrium, the smooth muscle layer of the uterine wall. Blocking oxytocin receptors aims to quiet the myometrium.

n.1: The cervix is the lower neck that opens into the vagina; the contractions oxytocin drives come from the myometrium of the uterine wall.
n.2: The endometrium is the lining where implantation occurs and that is shed in menstruation; it does not generate labor contractions.
n.3: The perimetrium is the thin outer covering of the uterus; it does not produce the contractions of labor.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: A 56-year-old woman has gone through menopause, and her ovaries no longer contain functioning follicles. Which pattern of hormone levels is expected in her blood?
o: High estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with low FSH and LH
Low estrogen and progesterone with high FSH and LH
Low estrogen with high progesterone and low FSH
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Two steps. (1) With the follicles exhausted, the ovaries make little estrogen and progesterone. (2) Those hormones normally exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so without them FSH and LH rise.

n.0: Without functioning follicles the ovaries cannot keep estrogen and progesterone high.
n.1: Falling ovarian hormones remove negative feedback, so FSH and LH rise rather than fall.
n.3: Progesterone comes mainly from the corpus luteum, which forms after ovulation, so it is low after menopause; FSH is high.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which events occur during the luteal phase of a 28-day cycle in which pregnancy does not occur? Select all that apply.
o: An LH surge triggers rupture of the dominant follicle.
The corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone falls.
FSH stimulates the growth of a dominant follicle.
The corpus luteum secretes progesterone.
The endometrium is in its secretory phase.
The functional layer of the endometrium is shed.
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: The luteal phase (about days 15 to 28) follows ovulation: the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, the endometrium is secretory, and with no embryo making hCG the corpus luteum degenerates late in the phase, so progesterone falls.

n.0: The LH surge and follicle rupture occur at ovulation, about day 14, which ends the follicular phase.
n.2: FSH-driven growth of the dominant follicle happens in the follicular phase, before ovulation.
n.5: Shedding of the functional layer is the menstrual phase (days 1 to 5), which follows the fall in progesterone.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: About a week after fertilization, the developing human implants in the endometrium of the uterus. Which stage implants, and how is it correctly described?
o: Blastocyst, a solid ball of cells made by cleavage
Morula, a hollow ball with a trophoblast layer
Blastocyst, a hollow ball with a trophoblast layer
Morula, a solid ball of cells made by cleavage
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Development runs zygote, cleavage, morula, blastocyst, implantation, embryo (to week 8), fetus (week 9 to birth). The blastocyst implants about 6 to 7 days after fertilization, and its trophoblast later forms part of the placenta and secretes hCG.

n.0: Blastocyst is the right stage, but it is hollow (a fluid-filled cavity ringed by trophoblast); the solid ball made by cleavage is the morula.
n.1: A hollow ball with a trophoblast layer is the blastocyst; the morula is a solid ball with no cavity or trophoblast, and it comes first.
n.3: The morula is the solid ball formed by cleavage, but it develops into a blastocyst before implantation; the morula does not implant.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: A student is sorting the body's defenses into categories for a study guide. Which of the following belongs in the first line of defense, the external barriers?
o: Complement proteins that lyse microbes
Interferons released by virus-infected cells
Lysozyme in tears and saliva
Neutrophils that engulf bacteria in the tissues
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: The first line of defense is the external barriers: intact skin, mucous membranes and mucus, cilia, stomach acid, and secretions such as tears and saliva that contain the antibacterial enzyme lysozyme.

n.0: Complement proteins circulate in the blood plasma, a second-line defense.
n.1: Interferons act inside the body after a virus has infected cells, a second-line defense.
n.3: Neutrophils are internal phagocytes, part of the second line of defense.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Within hours of bacteria entering a cut on the hand, white blood cells pour into the injured tissue. Which phagocytes typically arrive first and in the largest numbers?
o: Neutrophils
Natural killer cells
Dendritic cells
Macrophages
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Neutrophils are the first phagocytes to arrive in large numbers at a site of bacterial infection. Monocytes follow and become macrophages.

n.1: NK cells kill virus-infected and tumor cells; they are not the phagocytes that clear bacteria from a wound.
n.2: Dendritic cells are phagocytes best known for presenting antigen to T cells; they are not the first wave that floods infected tissue.
n.3: Macrophages develop from monocytes that arrive after the neutrophils.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: After a splinter pierces the skin, mast cells near the wound release histamine. Which effect of histamine directly produces the redness and swelling around the splinter?
o: Release of pyrogens that reset the hypothalamus
Vasodilation with decreased capillary permeability
Vasodilation with increased capillary permeability
Vasoconstriction with decreased capillary permeability
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Histamine dilates local blood vessels (more blood flow: redness and heat) and makes capillaries leakier (fluid moves into the tissue: swelling). These changes also help phagocytes reach the site.

n.0: Pyrogens resetting the hypothalamus cause fever, a body-wide response, not local redness and swelling.
n.1: Vasodilation explains the redness, but the swelling needs increased permeability so fluid leaks into the tissue.
n.3: Vasoconstriction would reduce blood flow and redness; histamine dilates vessels.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: A cell infected with a virus secretes proteins that diffuse to nearby cells and help those cells resist infection by the virus. Which innate defense does this describe?
o: Antibodies from plasma cells
Interferons
Histamine from mast cells
Complement proteins
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Interferons are made by virus-infected cells and protect neighboring cells, an innate second-line defense.

n.0: Antibodies come from plasma cells in the adaptive response, not from the infected cell itself.
n.2: Histamine from mast cells drives inflammation; it does not help neighboring cells resist a virus.
n.3: Complement proteins circulate in plasma, lyse microbes and enhance phagocytosis; infected cells do not secrete them to protect their neighbors.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which cell destroys virus-infected cells and tumor cells without needing prior exposure to a specific antigen, making it part of innate rather than adaptive immunity?
o: Cytotoxic (CD8) T cell
Natural killer cell
Helper (CD4) T cell
Plasma cell
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Natural killer (NK) cells are innate defenders that kill virus-infected and tumor cells without prior exposure to the antigen.

n.0: Cytotoxic T cells also kill infected cells, but they must first be activated by a specific antigen, so they are adaptive.
n.2: Helper T cells coordinate the adaptive response; they do not kill cells directly.
n.3: Plasma cells secrete antibodies in the adaptive humoral response.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: A patient with a bacterial infection develops a moderate fever. Which statement best describes how the fever arises and how it helps the body?
o: Histamine resets the hypothalamic set point, and moderate heat activates memory cells
Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic set point, and moderate heat inhibits pathogens
Pyrogens reset the pituitary set point, and moderate heat inhibits pathogens
Pyrogens reset the hypothalamic set point, giving an antigen-specific adaptive defense
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Fever is an innate, nonspecific second-line defense. Pyrogens released during infection reset the temperature set point in the hypothalamus, and a moderate rise in body temperature inhibits pathogens.

n.0: Pyrogens, not histamine, reset the set point; histamine drives local inflammation, and memory cells belong to adaptive immunity.
n.2: The body's temperature set point is in the hypothalamus, not the pituitary.
n.3: Fever is innate and nonspecific; it does not target one antigen the way adaptive immunity does.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Place these events of the inflammatory response to a contaminated skin wound in order, starting with the first.
o: Mast cells release histamine and other mediators
Phagocytes squeeze out of capillaries and move toward the site
Local blood vessels dilate and capillaries become leakier
Phagocytes engulf and destroy the bacteria
Tissue is injured and bacteria enter the wound
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Injury lets bacteria in. Mast cells (and basophils) release histamine, which causes vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, producing redness, heat, swelling and pain. Phagocytes then leave the capillaries (diapedesis) and follow chemical signals to the site (chemotaxis), where they engulf the invaders (phagocytosis).

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: After a car accident, a patient's ruptured spleen is surgically removed. Which normal function is most directly lost along with the spleen?
o: Absorbing dietary fats through lacteals in the intestine
Filtering lymph before it returns to the bloodstream
Maturing T lymphocytes before they enter circulation
Filtering blood and removing worn-out red blood cells
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: The spleen, the largest lymphoid organ, filters blood rather than lymph: it removes old or damaged red blood cells and platelets and mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens.

n.0: Lacteals in the intestinal villi absorb dietary fats; the spleen has no part in fat absorption.
n.1: Filtering lymph is the job of the lymph nodes; the spleen filters blood.
n.2: T lymphocytes mature in the thymus, not the spleen.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Lymph collected from the left arm, the abdomen and both legs must return to the bloodstream. By which route does this lymph re-enter the blood?
o: Thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein
Right lymphatic duct into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the superior vena cava
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: The thoracic duct drains most of the body, including both legs, the abdomen and the left arm, into the left subclavian vein. The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and thorax.

n.1: The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and thorax, not the left arm or the legs.
n.2: The thoracic duct joins the venous system on the left side, at the left subclavian vein.
n.3: The thoracic duct empties into the left subclavian vein, not directly into the superior vena cava.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Lymphatic vessels have no pump like the heart, yet lymph from the legs still moves steadily up toward the veins of the upper chest. Which mechanism keeps it moving one way?
o: Rhythmic pumping by the lymph nodes, with valves
Pressure from the right ventricle, with valves
Skeletal muscle and breathing movements, with valves
Suction as the spleen filters the lymph, with valves
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Lymph is moved by the squeezing of skeletal muscles and the pressure changes of breathing; valves in the lymphatic vessels keep the flow one-way toward the subclavian veins.

n.0: Lymph nodes filter lymph and house lymphocytes and macrophages; they do not contract to pump it along.
n.1: The right ventricle pumps blood out to the lungs; it gives no push to lymph, which drifts through low-pressure vessels toward the veins.
n.3: The spleen filters blood, not lymph, and it does not draw lymph through the lymphatic vessels.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Which of the following are part of the second line of defense, the internal nonspecific (innate) defenses? Select all that apply.
o: Plasma cells secreting antibodies
Complement proteins
Fever
Cytotoxic T cells
Natural killer cells
Lysozyme in saliva
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Second-line defenses act inside the body and are nonspecific: phagocytes, NK cells, inflammation, fever, complement proteins and interferons.

n.0: Antibody-secreting plasma cells belong to the third line, adaptive humoral immunity.
n.3: Cytotoxic T cells are antigen-specific lymphocytes of the third line, adaptive cell-mediated immunity.
n.5: Lysozyme in saliva and tears is a first-line, external barrier defense.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: After several axillary lymph nodes are removed during breast cancer surgery, a patient develops lasting swelling of the arm on that side. Which lymphatic function best explains the swelling?
o: Filtering blood and removing worn-out red blood cells
Returning excess interstitial fluid to the blood
Absorbing dietary fats through lacteals in the villi
Filtering lymph to trap microbes before it reaches the blood
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Lymphatic vessels collect excess interstitial fluid (lymph) and return it to the blood. Removing the axillary nodes disrupts drainage from the arm, so fluid builds up in the tissues.

n.0: Filtering blood and removing old red blood cells is a function of the spleen, not the axillary lymph nodes.
n.2: Lacteals absorb fats in the intestinal villi; they do not drain the arm.
n.3: The nodes do filter lymph, but losing that filter would raise infection risk; the swelling comes from fluid that is no longer drained.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: During a humoral immune response to a bacterial toxin, which cells secrete large amounts of antibodies that circulate in the blood and lymph?
o: Cytotoxic T cells that recognize the toxin
Plasma cells derived from activated B cells
Helper T cells that coordinate the response
Memory B cells that persist after infection
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: Activated B cells divide and differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies, and memory B cells, which wait for a later exposure.

n.0: Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly in cell-mediated immunity; they do not make antibodies.
n.2: Helper T cells release cytokines that activate B cells, but they do not secrete antibodies.
n.3: Memory B cells give a faster response on re-exposure; the antibody-secreting cells are plasma cells.

A&P: Reproductive & Immune.q: Both B and T lymphocytes arise from stem cells in red bone marrow. Where does each type of lymphocyte complete its maturation before it can respond to antigens?
o: T cells in the thymus; B cells in red bone marrow
T cells in the lymph nodes; B cells in red bone marrow
T cells in the thymus; B cells in the spleen
T cells in red bone marrow; B cells in the thymus
A&P: Reproductive & Immune.w: T cells mature in the thymus (T for thymus), and B cells mature in red bone marrow. These are the two primary lymphoid organs.

n.1: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs that house mature lymphocytes; T cells mature in the thymus.
