The i allele is recessive to both the IA and IB alleles.
Biology.w: ABO shows multiple alleles: IA and IB are codominant with each other, and both are dominant over i. Type O requires ii.

n.0: IA and IB are codominant; a person with IAIB expresses both and is type AB.
n.1: Type AB shows both A and B antigens fully, which is codominance, not a blend.
n.2: i is recessive. A person must have two copies (ii) to be type O.

Biology.q: A man with red-green color blindness, an X-linked recessive trait, has children with a woman who carries no color-blindness allele. Which outcome is expected?
o: Half of the sons are color-blind and half of the daughters are carriers.
All of the daughters are carriers and none of the sons are color-blind.
Half of the daughters are color-blind and none of the sons are affected.
All of the sons are color-blind and none of the daughters are carriers.
Biology.w: Step 1: the father passes his X (with the allele) to every daughter and his Y to every son. Step 2: daughters get a normal X from the mother, so all are carriers; sons get the mother's normal X, so none are affected.

n.0: This is the pattern for a carrier mother and a normal father, not an affected father and a noncarrier mother.
n.2: Each daughter gets a normal X from her mother, which masks the recessive allele, so she is a carrier, not affected.
n.3: Sons receive the father's Y, not his X, so they cannot inherit his X-linked allele.

Biology.q: Hemophilia A is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. Why is the disorder seen much more often in males than in females?
o: Males have one X, so one recessive allele is expressed.
Males inherit the allele from their fathers.
The allele is carried on the Y chromosome.
The allele acts as dominant in males and recessive in females.
Biology.w: Males (XY) have only one X chromosome (hemizygous), so a single recessive allele on it is expressed. Females need two copies to be affected.

n.1: Sons get their X from their mother; the father gives sons his Y.
n.2: The gene is on the X chromosome. Y-linked traits pass only from father to son.
n.3: The allele is recessive in both sexes; males show it because they have no second X to mask it.

Biology.q: Adult height in a population forms a smooth bell-shaped range rather than a few distinct categories, and it is also affected by childhood nutrition. Which explanation best fits this pattern?
o: Codominance between two alleles of one gene
Incomplete dominance at a single gene locus
Polygenic inheritance, with environmental effects
Multiple alleles of one gene, with one dominant
Biology.w: Polygenic traits are controlled by many genes whose effects add up, producing a continuous range; environment such as nutrition also affects the phenotype.

n.0: Codominance at one gene gives a few distinct phenotypes, such as types A, B and AB, not a smooth range.
n.1: Incomplete dominance at one gene gives three phenotypes (such as red, pink and white), not a continuous range.
n.3: Multiple alleles at one gene still give a few separate categories, as in the four ABO blood types.

Biology.q: In a family pedigree, two unaffected parents have a daughter who is affected by a rare genetic disorder. Which inheritance pattern and parental genotypes best fit this pedigree?
o: Autosomal dominant, with one parent a carrier
Autosomal recessive, with both parents carriers
Y-linked, passed from the father to the daughter
X-linked recessive, with the mother a carrier
Biology.w: Step 1: unaffected parents with an affected child means the trait is recessive and both parents carry it. Step 2: an affected daughter with an X-linked recessive trait would need an affected father, and this father is unaffected, so the pattern is autosomal recessive.

n.0: In autosomal dominant inheritance anyone with one copy is affected, so an affected child needs an affected parent.
n.2: Y-linked traits pass from father to son; daughters do not receive a Y chromosome.
n.3: For a daughter to have an X-linked recessive trait she needs the allele from her father too, which would make him affected.

Biology.q: A genetics handout lists inherited disorders by pattern of inheritance. Which disorders are inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern? Select all that apply.
o: Cystic fibrosis
Huntington disease
Red-green color blindness
Sickle cell disease
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Hemophilia A
Biology.w: Hemophilia A, red-green color blindness and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are X-linked recessive, which is why they are far more common in males.

n.0: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive; it affects males and females equally.
n.1: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant.
n.3: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive.

Biology.q: A woman who is a carrier of hemophilia A (XHXh) and a man without hemophilia (XHY) plan a family. What percentage of their sons are expected to have hemophilia? Enter a whole-number percent.

tr.0: assumed a son inherits X-linked alleles from the father
tr.25: gave the share of all children affected, not of sons
tr.100: assumed every son of a carrier is affected

Biology.w: Sons get the Y from the father and one X from the mother. Half of the mother's eggs carry Xh, so 1/2 = 50% of sons (XhY) are expected to have hemophilia.

Biology.q: In snapdragons, flower color shows incomplete dominance: red (RR), pink (RW) and white (WW). Two pink plants are crossed and produce 240 seedlings. How many seedlings are expected to have pink flowers? Enter a whole number.

tr.60: gave the red or the white class
tr.180: used the 3:1 ratio of complete dominance

Biology.w: RW x RW gives 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW, so 2/4 = 1/2 are pink. 240 x 1/2 = 120.

Biology.q: After a large meal, a person's liver and skeletal muscles store excess glucose as a highly branched polysaccharide. Which molecule is formed?
o: Glycogen
Starch
Cellulose
Chitin
Biology.w: Animals store glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles. Starch is the plant storage form.

n.1: Starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants, not animals.
n.2: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide in plant cell walls.
n.3: Chitin is a structural polysaccharide in fungal walls and insect exoskeletons.

Biology.q: A lab analysis shows that an unknown macromolecule from a cell contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, but no phosphorus. Which type of macromolecule is it most likely to be?
o: A nucleic acid
A protein
A carbohydrate
A phospholipid
Biology.w: Step 1: nitrogen rules out carbohydrates and simple fats. Step 2: the absence of phosphorus rules out nucleic acids and phospholipids, leaving protein (C, H, O, N, often S).

n.0: Nucleic acids contain phosphorus in their phosphate groups.
n.2: Common carbohydrates such as sugars, starch and glycogen contain only C, H and O, so nitrogen points away from them.
n.3: Phospholipids contain a phosphate group, so phosphorus would be present.

Biology.q: Butter is solid at room temperature, while olive oil is liquid. Which difference in their fatty acids best explains this?
o: Butter's fats contain more glycerol molecules per fatty acid.
Olive oil's fatty acids carry more hydrogen atoms per carbon.
Butter's fatty acids are mostly saturated and pack tightly together.
Butter's fatty acids have more C=C double bonds, which form kinks.
Biology.w: Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds, so their straight chains pack tightly and the fat is solid. Unsaturated fatty acids in oils have double bonds that kink the chains.

n.0: Every triglyceride has one glycerol and three fatty acids; the difference is saturation.
n.1: This is reversed: saturated fatty acids such as butter's carry the most hydrogen. Olive oil's C=C double bonds mean fewer hydrogens.
n.3: This is reversed: double bonds and kinks belong to unsaturated fats, which are liquid.

Biology.q: Two glucose molecules are joined to form the disaccharide maltose. Which description of this reaction is correct?
o: A water molecule is released, forming a peptide bond.
A water molecule is released, forming a glycosidic bond.
A water molecule is added, forming a peptide bond.
A water molecule is added, forming a glycosidic bond.
Biology.w: Monomers are joined by dehydration synthesis, which releases water. Bonds between sugars are glycosidic bonds.

n.0: Peptide bonds join amino acids, not sugars.
n.2: This combines both errors: adding water breaks bonds, and peptide bonds join amino acids.
n.3: Adding water is hydrolysis, which breaks polymers apart rather than joining them.

Biology.q: A patient with lactose intolerance makes too little lactase. When lactase does digest lactose, which two monosaccharides are released?
o: Glucose and galactose
Galactose and fructose
Glucose and glucose
Glucose and fructose
Biology.w: Lactose (milk sugar) = glucose + galactose. Lactase hydrolyzes it into those two monosaccharides.

n.1: Galactose + fructose is not one of the common dietary disaccharides.
n.2: Glucose + glucose make maltose.
n.3: Glucose + fructose make sucrose (table sugar).

Biology.q: The rate of a human enzyme-catalyzed reaction rises as the temperature increases from 20 °C to 37 °C, then drops sharply at 50 °C. What best explains the drop?
o: The heat raises the activation energy of the reaction.
The enzyme denatures, and its active site loses its shape.
The enzyme is used up as it converts more of the substrate.
The heat breaks the peptide bonds in the enzyme's chain.
Biology.w: Above its optimum (about 37 °C for most human enzymes) the enzyme denatures: its folding is disrupted, the active site changes shape, and the substrate no longer fits.

n.0: Enzymes work by lowering activation energy. The drop is due to loss of enzyme shape, not a change in activation energy.
n.2: Enzymes are catalysts and are not consumed by the reactions they speed up.
n.3: Denaturation disrupts folding; the peptide bonds of the primary sequence stay intact.

Biology.q: In liver cells, the enzyme catalase greatly speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. How does catalase increase the reaction rate?
o: It increases the total energy the reaction releases.
It is consumed and becomes part of the products.
It shifts the equilibrium toward more products.
It lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
Biology.w: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower activation energy, are not consumed, and do not change the overall energy released.

n.0: Enzymes do not change the overall energy change of the reaction, only the energy needed to start it.
n.1: Enzymes are not consumed; they are released unchanged and reused.
n.2: Enzymes do not change the equilibrium of a reaction; they help it reach equilibrium faster.

Biology.q: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach, where the pH is about 2. If pepsin passes into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, what will most likely happen to its activity?
o: It will fall, since pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum.
It will stay the same, since pH does not affect enzymes.
It will rise, since trypsin activates pepsin at pH 8.
It will rise, since enzymes work faster in basic solutions.
Biology.w: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin works best near pH 2, so at pH 8 its shape changes and activity falls. Trypsin, with an optimum near pH 8, works in the small intestine.

n.1: pH strongly affects enzyme shape and activity.
n.2: Trypsin is a separate protein-digesting enzyme with its own optimum; it does not boost pepsin.
n.3: Enzymes do not all work faster in basic conditions; each has its own optimum, and pepsin's is acidic.

Biology.q: A drug molecule shaped like an enzyme's substrate binds to the active site and slows the reaction. Adding much more substrate restores the normal rate. Which type of inhibition is this?
o: Noncompetitive inhibition
Competitive inhibition
Substrate saturation
Denaturation by heat
Biology.w: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and competes with the substrate, so raising substrate concentration can overcome it.

n.0: A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape; extra substrate does not overcome it.
n.2: Saturation is the plateau reached when all active sites are busy; it is not inhibition.
n.3: Denaturation is loss of enzyme shape from heat or extreme pH, not binding of an inhibitor.

Biology.q: When phospholipids are placed in water, they arrange themselves into a double layer. Which feature of phospholipid structure explains this arrangement?
o: Their tails are polar and are attracted to the surrounding water.
Their hydrophilic heads face water while hydrophobic tails face inward.
Their three fatty acid tails make them dissolve in water.
Their nonpolar heads face water while polar tails face inward.
Biology.w: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic (polar) phosphate head and two hydrophobic (nonpolar) fatty acid tails. In water the heads face outward and the tails hide inside, forming a bilayer.

n.0: The fatty acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic, so they avoid water.
n.2: Phospholipids have two fatty acid tails (triglycerides have three), and the tails repel water.
n.3: Polarity is reversed: the heads are polar and the tails are nonpolar.

Biology.q: A nutrition student is classifying carbohydrates found in foods and in the body. Which of these are polysaccharides? Select all that apply.
o: Glycogen
Starch
Lactose
Cellulose
Sucrose
Glucose
Biology.w: Starch (plant storage), glycogen (animal storage) and cellulose (plant cell walls) are polysaccharides, long chains of glucose units.

n.2: Lactose is a disaccharide (glucose + galactose).
n.4: Sucrose is a disaccharide (glucose + fructose).
n.5: Glucose is a monosaccharide, the monomer of these polysaccharides.

Biology.q: Place the levels of protein structure in order, starting with the simplest level and ending with the most complex.
o: R-group interactions fold the chain into its overall 3-D shape.
Hydrogen bonds along the backbone form helices and pleated sheets.
Amino acids are linked in a specific sequence by peptide bonds.
Two or more folded polypeptide chains join, as in hemoglobin.
Biology.w: Primary (amino acid sequence) -> secondary (alpha helix and beta pleated sheet from backbone hydrogen bonds) -> tertiary (overall 3-D shape from R-group interactions) -> quaternary (two or more chains, such as the four chains of hemoglobin).

Biology.q: A college student with a common cold caused by a rhinovirus asks a clinic nurse for an antibiotic. Which statement best explains why an antibiotic will not help?
o: Viruses are not cells and lack the targets antibiotics act on.
Viruses are prokaryotic cells whose walls block antibiotics.
Rhinoviruses multiply too fast for antibiotics to act.
Rhinoviruses are bacteria that have become drug resistant.
Biology.w: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria by acting on bacterial structures and processes. Viruses are not cells (no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of their own), so antibiotics have no effect on them.

n.1: Viruses are not cells at all, prokaryotic or otherwise, and they have no cell wall.
n.2: Speed of replication is not the problem. Antibiotics have no bacterial target to act on in a virus, however slowly it multiplies.
n.3: Rhinoviruses are viruses, not bacteria, so antibiotic resistance does not apply to them.

Biology.q: Researchers isolate a new bacterium from every sick animal in an outbreak and grow it in pure culture. According to Koch's postulates, what should they do next?
o: Treat the sick animals with an antibiotic and record recovery.
Re-isolate the bacterium from a newly infected animal.
Find the bacterium in each diseased animal in the outbreak.
Introduce the cultured bacterium into a healthy animal.
Biology.w: Koch's postulates: (1) the microbe is found in all diseased hosts, (2) it is isolated and grown in pure culture, (3) it causes the disease when introduced into a healthy host, (4) it is re-isolated from that host. Steps 1 and 2 are done, so step 3 is next.

n.0: Treating with antibiotics is not one of Koch's postulates and would not show that the microbe causes the disease.
n.1: Re-isolating the microbe is the final step (4); it can only follow infection of a healthy host.
n.2: Finding the microbe in all diseased hosts is step 1, which the researchers have already done.

Biology.q: A traveler returns from a tropical region with cycles of fever and chills and is diagnosed with malaria. Which statement correctly identifies the cause and how it spread?
o: A bacterium, spread through contaminated drinking water
A bacterium, spread by the bite of infected deer ticks
A virus, spread by the bite of Anopheles mosquitoes
A protozoan, spread by the bite of Anopheles mosquitoes
Biology.w: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium, a single-celled eukaryote. The female Anopheles mosquito is the vector that carries it, not the cause.

n.0: Malaria is vector-borne; waterborne protozoan illness is giardiasis.
n.1: Ticks spread Lyme disease, caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, not malaria.
n.2: The mosquito is the correct vector, but the pathogen is a protozoan, not a virus.

Biology.q: A high school wrestler develops a red, ring-shaped, scaly rash and is diagnosed with tinea corporis (ringworm). Which type of medication is appropriate for this infection?
o: An antiviral
An antibiotic for bacteria
An antihelminthic for worms
An antifungal
Biology.w: Despite its name, ringworm (tinea) is a fungal skin infection, so it is treated with an antifungal.

n.0: Antivirals target viruses; tinea is caused by a fungus.
n.1: Antibiotics target bacteria; tinea is caused by a fungus.
n.2: Ringworm is not caused by a worm; the name comes from the ring-shaped rash.

Biology.q: A sample of bacteria from a patient's wound is Gram stained and appears purple under the microscope. What does this result indicate about the bacteria?
o: Gram-negative, with an outer lipid membrane
Gram-negative, with a thick peptidoglycan wall
Gram-positive, with a thin wall and outer membrane
Gram-positive, with a thick peptidoglycan wall
Biology.w: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that holds the purple (violet) stain. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin wall plus an outer membrane and stain pink or red.

n.0: An outer membrane is the Gram-negative feature, and those bacteria stain pink, not purple.
n.1: Gram-negative bacteria stain pink and have a thin peptidoglycan layer, not a thick one.
n.2: A thin wall with an outer membrane is the Gram-negative structure, which does not stain purple.

Biology.q: A hospital places a patient with active tuberculosis in a negative-pressure room and staff wear fitted respirators. Which feature of tuberculosis transmission explains these precautions?
o: TB spreads mainly on objects such as bed rails and doorknobs.
TB bacteria travel in tiny particles that stay suspended in air.
TB is caused by a virus that passes through surgical masks.
TB spreads mainly in large droplets that fall within 2 meters.
Biology.w: Tuberculosis (bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis) is spread by the airborne route: tiny particles stay suspended and travel on air currents, so airflow control and respirators are needed.

n.0: Spread by contaminated objects (fomites) would call for surface cleaning, not special airflow; TB spreads through the air.
n.2: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium, not a virus.
n.3: Large droplets that fall within about 1 to 2 meters describe droplet spread, as with influenza; TB is airborne.

Biology.q: Before giving an injection, a nurse cleans the patient's skin with an alcohol-based solution to reduce the number of microbes. What is this practice called?
o: Sterilization
Antisepsis
Disinfection
Pasteurization
Biology.w: Antisepsis reduces microbes on living tissue such as skin. Disinfection is for objects and surfaces.

n.0: Sterilization kills all microbes including endospores (as in an autoclave) and is not done on skin.
n.2: Disinfection reduces pathogens on objects and surfaces, not on living tissue.
n.3: Pasteurization is gentle heating of foods such as milk, not skin preparation.

Biology.q: After a long course of a broad-spectrum antibiotic, a patient develops severe diarrhea caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile in the colon. Which explanation is most likely?
o: The antibiotic converted harmless gut bacteria into C. difficile.
The antibiotic killed normal gut bacteria that kept C. difficile in check.
The antibiotic caused the patient's own colon cells to divide rapidly.
The antibiotic weakened the colon wall, letting viruses enter.
Biology.w: Normal microbiota compete with pathogens. Killing them with an antibiotic lets an opportunistic pathogen such as C. difficile overgrow.

n.0: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria; they do not turn one bacterial species into another.
n.2: The diarrhea is caused by an overgrowing pathogen, not by the patient's own cells dividing.
n.3: C. difficile is a bacterium, and the disease here is bacterial overgrowth, not viral entry.

Biology.q: A patient stops taking a prescribed antibiotic after three days because she feels better. Why can this practice contribute to antibiotic resistance?
o: The drug makes each bacterium change to resist it.
Her body itself becomes resistant to the antibiotic.
Viruses in her body learn to resist antibiotics.
Surviving bacteria tend to be the most resistant ones.
Biology.w: An incomplete course kills the most susceptible bacteria first; the survivors are more likely to carry resistance, and they multiply. This is natural selection, and resistance genes can also spread on plasmids.

n.0: Antibiotics do not make bacteria change on purpose; they select bacteria that already carry resistance.
n.1: Resistance is a property of the bacteria, not of the patient's body.
n.2: Antibiotics do not act on viruses, so viral resistance to them is not the issue.

Biology.q: An infection-control handout groups diseases by the type of pathogen that causes them. Which of these diseases are caused by bacteria? Select all that apply.
o: Lyme disease
Malaria
Tuberculosis
Strep throat
Influenza
Athlete's foot
Biology.w: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi, spread by ticks) and strep throat (Streptococcus pyogenes) are bacterial.

n.1: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium.
n.4: Influenza is caused by a virus.
n.5: Athlete's foot is caused by a fungus.

Biology.q: Place the links in the chain of infection in order, starting with the infectious agent and ending with the person who becomes infected.
o: Mode of transmission
Susceptible host
Infectious agent
Reservoir
Portal of exit
Portal of entry
Biology.w: The pathogen (infectious agent) lives in a reservoir, leaves through a portal of exit, travels by a mode of transmission, enters a new host through a portal of entry, and infects a susceptible host. Breaking any link stops the spread.

Biology.q: Place the stages of viral replication in the order they occur when an influenza virus infects a host cell, starting with the first.
o: New virus particles are assembled.
The virus attaches to receptors on the host cell.
New virus particles are released from the cell.
The viral genome is copied and viral proteins are made.
The virus or its genome enters the host cell.
Biology.w: Viruses replicate only inside host cells: attachment -> entry -> copying of the viral genome and synthesis of viral proteins on the host's ribosomes -> assembly -> release.

Chemistry.q: An atom of iron-56 has an atomic number of 26. How many neutrons are in the nucleus of this atom? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.26: Gave the number of protons (the atomic number) instead of neutrons.
tr.56: Gave the mass number, which counts protons and neutrons together.
tr.82: Added the mass number and atomic number instead of subtracting.

Chemistry.w: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 56 - 26 = 30.

Chemistry.q: Sulfur has atomic number 16. In the body, sulfur is often found as the sulfide ion, S2-. How many electrons does one S2- ion contain? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.14: Subtracted 2, treating the anion as if it had lost electrons like a cation.
tr.16: Gave the electron count of the neutral atom and ignored the charge.

Chemistry.w: A neutral sulfur atom has 16 electrons, equal to its 16 protons. A 2- charge means the atom gained 2 electrons: 16 + 2 = 18 electrons (with 16 protons, net charge 2-).

Chemistry.q: Place these models of the atom in the order in which they were proposed, starting with the earliest.
o: Bohr's electrons orbiting in fixed energy levels
The electron cloud model with orbitals
Thomson's plum pudding model with embedded electrons
Dalton's solid, indivisible sphere
Rutherford's small, dense, positive nucleus in mostly empty space
Chemistry.w: Dalton proposed atoms as solid, indivisible spheres. Thomson then discovered the electron and pictured it embedded in a positive sphere (plum pudding). Rutherford's gold foil experiment revealed a small, dense, positive nucleus. Bohr placed electrons in fixed energy levels around that nucleus. The modern quantum mechanical (electron cloud) model describes electrons in orbitals.

Chemistry.q: In a classic experiment, most alpha particles fired at thin gold foil passed straight through, but a few bounced back almost directly toward the source. What did this result reveal about the atom?
o: It has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus
It contains neutral particles with about a proton's mass
Its electrons travel in fixed circular energy levels
It is a positive sphere with electrons spread through it
Chemistry.w: Rutherford's gold foil experiment: most particles passing through showed the atom is mostly empty space, and the few sharp rebounds showed the positive charge and nearly all the mass are packed into a tiny, dense nucleus.

n.1: Neutral particles (neutrons) were discovered by Chadwick in 1932, not by the gold foil experiment.
n.2: Fixed energy levels were Bohr's later model, based on light emitted by atoms, not on gold foil scattering.
n.3: This is Thomson's plum pudding model, which the gold foil results disproved; a spread-out positive charge could not bounce particles straight back.

Chemistry.q: A model of an atom is being built for a classroom display. Which statement correctly describes where most of an atom's mass and most of its volume are found?
o: Most mass is in the nucleus; most volume is the electron cloud
Most mass and most volume are both in the nucleus
Most mass is in the electron cloud; most volume is the nucleus
Mass is split evenly between the nucleus and the electron cloud
Chemistry.w: Protons and neutrons (each about 1 amu) are in the nucleus, so the nucleus holds nearly all the mass. Electrons are nearly massless but occupy the electron cloud, which takes up nearly all of the atom's volume.

n.1: The nucleus is tiny compared with the whole atom; the electron cloud takes up almost all the volume.
n.2: This reverses the facts. Electrons have negligible mass, and the nucleus is a tiny fraction of the volume.
n.3: Electrons have about 1/1836 the mass of a proton, so the electron cloud contributes almost no mass.

Chemistry.q: A radioactive tracer used for a hospital scan has a half-life of 6 hours. A 40-mg dose is prepared at 8:00 a.m. About how much of the tracer remains undecayed at 2:00 a.m. the next day?
o: 10 mg
5 mg
2.5 mg
Chemistry.w: From 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 a.m. is 18 hours, which is 18 / 6 = 3 half-lives. Each half-life halves the amount: 40 mg to 20 mg to 10 mg to 5 mg (1/8 of the original).

n.0: This divides 40 by 3 half-lives. Each half-life halves the amount; it does not remove an equal share.
n.1: 10 mg remains after 2 half-lives (12 hours, at 8:00 p.m.), not after the full 18 hours.
n.3: 2.5 mg would remain after 4 half-lives (24 hours), one half-life too many.

Chemistry.q: A student is reviewing the three subatomic particles before a quiz. Which statements about these particles are correct? Select all that apply.
o: The mass number equals protons plus electrons
The number of protons equals the atomic number
Electrons are found in the nucleus with the protons
Protons and neutrons have about the same mass
Electrons have about the same mass as protons
Neutrons carry no electrical charge
Chemistry.w: Protons and neutrons each have a mass of about 1 amu, neutrons are neutral (charge 0), and the atomic number is defined as the number of protons.

n.0: Mass number counts the particles in the nucleus: protons plus neutrons, not electrons.
n.2: Electrons occupy energy levels in the electron cloud around the nucleus; only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.
n.4: An electron's mass is about 1/1836 of a proton's, which is why electrons are ignored in the mass number.

Chemistry.q: A particle has 20 protons, 22 neutrons and 18 electrons. Calcium has atomic number 20 and argon has atomic number 18. Which best identifies this particle?
o: A calcium-42 cation with a charge of 2+
A calcium-38 cation with a charge of 2+
A calcium-42 anion with a charge of 2-
An argon-40 atom with no net charge
Chemistry.w: Step 1: 20 protons means the element is calcium, and the mass number is 20 + 22 = 42. Step 2: 20 positive charges and 18 negative charges give a net charge of 2+. The particle is a calcium-42 ion, Ca2+.

n.1: 38 adds protons and electrons. Mass number is protons plus neutrons: 20 + 22 = 42.
n.2: With two fewer electrons than protons, the charge is positive. A 2- ion would need 22 electrons.
n.3: The element is set by protons, not electrons. Having 18 electrons does not make it argon.

Chemistry.q: Magnesium, an element needed for muscle and nerve function, has atomic number 12. Which arrangement of electrons, listed by shell from the nucleus outward, describes a neutral magnesium atom?
Chemistry.w: Electrons fill the lowest shells first. The first shell holds 2 and the second holds 8, which accounts for 10 electrons; the remaining 2 go into the third shell: 2, 8, 2. Magnesium therefore has 2 valence electrons, matching its place in group 2.

n.0: The second shell fills to 8 before any electrons enter the third shell.
n.1: The third shell can hold more than 1 electron, so both remaining electrons go into it rather than starting a fourth shell.
n.3: The second shell holds a maximum of 8 electrons, so it cannot hold 10.

Chemistry.q: Phosphorus, found in bones and in ATP, has atomic number 15 and is located in period 3 and group 15 of the periodic table. How many valence electrons does a neutral phosphorus atom have?
Chemistry.w: Phosphorus has 15 electrons arranged 2, 8, 5, so its outer shell holds 5 valence electrons. For main-group elements in groups 13-18, the valence count is the group number minus 10 (group 15 = 5).

n.0: 15 is the atomic number and the group number, but group 15 elements have 5 valence electrons, not 15.
n.1: 10 is the number of inner (core) electrons in the first two shells, not the outer-shell electrons.
n.2: 3 is the period number (the number of occupied shells), or the number of electrons phosphorus needs to complete an octet; neither is its valence count.

Chemistry.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react with water in a similar way, producing hydrogen gas and a basic solution. What do these three elements have in common that explains their similar reactions?
o: Each has the same number of occupied shells
Each sits in the same period of the table
Each has one electron in its outer shell
Each has a full, stable outer electron shell
Chemistry.w: Lithium, sodium and potassium are all in group 1 (alkali metals). Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, here one, and valence electrons determine chemical behavior.

n.0: They have different numbers of shells (2, 3 and 4). Shell number is what a period shares, and it does not set reactivity patterns.
n.1: They are in the same group (column), not the same period (row). Elements across a period have different properties.
n.3: A full outer shell describes the unreactive noble gases. Alkali metals react readily because they have a single outer electron to lose.

Chemistry.q: A student describes an unknown element as dull, brittle in its solid form, and a poor conductor of heat and electricity. In which region of the periodic table is this element most likely found?
o: The left side, among the alkali metals
The center, among the transition metals
The staircase line, among the metalloids
The upper right, among the nonmetals
Chemistry.w: Dull luster, brittleness and poor conductivity are the properties of nonmetals, which are found in the upper right of the periodic table (plus hydrogen).

n.0: Alkali metals are shiny, soft metals that conduct heat and electricity well.
n.1: Transition metals are shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors.
n.2: Metalloids have intermediate properties and are semiconductors; they conduct better than typical nonmetals.

Chemistry.q: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. According to the octet rule, which ion does an oxygen atom most commonly form when it bonds with a metal such as magnesium?
o: O2-, an anion formed by gaining two electrons
O2+, a cation formed by gaining two electrons
O6+, a cation formed by losing six electrons
O-, an anion formed by gaining one electron
Chemistry.w: Oxygen needs 2 more electrons to reach a stable octet of 8. Gaining 2 electrons (each with a 1- charge) gives the oxide ion, O2-. Nonmetals typically gain electrons to form anions.

n.1: Gaining negatively charged electrons makes an ion more negative, so the charge would be 2-, not 2+.
n.2: Losing six electrons would take far more energy than gaining two; nonmetals such as oxygen gain electrons.
n.3: Gaining one electron would leave oxygen with 7 valence electrons, one short of an octet. A 1- charge fits halogens, which start with 7.

Chemistry.q: A lab report lists three elements measured in a patient's blood tests by their symbols: K, Na and Fe. Which names match these symbols, in the same order?
o: Krypton, sodium, iron
Potassium, nitrogen, iron
Potassium, sodium, iron
Calcium, sodium, iron
Chemistry.w: Several symbols come from Latin names: K is potassium (kalium), Na is sodium (natrium) and Fe is iron (ferrum).

n.0: Krypton's symbol is Kr. K is potassium.
n.1: Nitrogen's symbol is N. Na is sodium.
n.3: Calcium's symbol is Ca. K is potassium.

Chemistry.q: Early versions of the periodic table placed the elements in order of increasing atomic mass. In the modern periodic table, the elements are arranged in order of increasing which quantity?
o: Number of valence electrons
Atomic mass
Number of neutrons
Number of protons
Chemistry.w: The modern table (after Moseley) is arranged by increasing atomic number, which is the number of protons. Mendeleev's earlier table used atomic mass.

n.0: Valence electrons repeat in each period (1 through 8), so they set the group, not the overall order.
n.1: Atomic mass was Mendeleev's ordering; a few pairs (such as tellurium and iodine) are out of mass order in the modern table.
n.2: Neutron number varies between isotopes and does not increase steadily across the table.

Chemistry.q: Silicon, used in computer chips, is located in period 3 of the periodic table. What does the period number tell you about the structure of a silicon atom?
o: It has three valence electrons
It forms ions with a charge of 3+
It is third from the top in its group
Its electrons occupy three shells
Chemistry.w: The period (row) number equals the number of occupied electron shells. Silicon (14 electrons) is arranged 2, 8, 4: three shells, with 4 valence electrons.

n.0: The number of valence electrons comes from the group, not the period. Silicon is in group 14 and has 4 valence electrons.
n.1: The period number does not give an ion's charge, and silicon, with 4 valence electrons, does not typically form 3+ ions.
n.2: Silicon is second in group 14, below carbon. The period number refers to shells, not position within a group.

Chemistry.q: Silicon and germanium are used in computer chips. Both are shiny, gray solids, yet they shatter when struck and conduct electricity only moderately. To which category of elements do they belong?
o: Nonmetals
Transition metals
Alkaline earth metals
Metalloids
Chemistry.w: Metalloids lie along the staircase line between metals and nonmetals and mix their properties: a metallic luster with nonmetal brittleness, and conductivity between the two (semiconductors). Silicon and germanium are classic metalloids.

n.0: Solid nonmetals can be brittle, but they are typically dull and poor conductors (insulators), not shiny semiconductors.
n.1: Transition metals are shiny, but they are malleable rather than brittle and conduct electricity well.
n.2: Alkaline earth metals (group 2) are shiny metals that conduct electricity well, unlike these moderate conductors.

Chemistry.q: When a sample containing sodium is held in a flame, the flame turns a bright yellow-orange. Which process in the sodium atoms produces this colored light?
o: Electrons absorbing heat and moving to higher energy levels
Excited electrons falling back to lower energy levels
Protons leaving the nucleus as the atoms are strongly heated
Sodium atoms combining with oxygen to form a new compound
Chemistry.w: Heat excites electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back to lower levels, they emit the extra energy as light of specific colors, which is why each element has a characteristic flame color and emission spectrum.

n.0: Absorbing energy raises electrons to higher levels, but light is given off when they drop back down, not as they move up.
n.2: Protons do not leave the nucleus in a flame; flame color comes from electron transitions.
n.3: Flame color is a property of the element's electrons, not of a combustion product; sodium compounds give the same color.

Chemistry.q: A student is preparing a summary of the halogens, the elements in group 17 of the periodic table. Which properties are typical of these elements? Select all that apply.
o: They have full outer shells and rarely react
They are the most reactive group of metals
They gain one electron to form 1- ions
They lose one electron to form 1+ ions
They have seven valence electrons
They exist as diatomic molecules such as Cl2
Chemistry.w: Halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) have 7 valence electrons, gain 1 electron to form 1- ions, and exist as diatomic molecules (F2, Cl2, Br2, I2). They are the most reactive nonmetals.

n.0: Full outer shells and low reactivity describe the noble gases in group 18.
n.1: The most reactive metals are the alkali metals in group 1. Halogens are nonmetals.
n.3: Halogens gain one electron to complete an octet, giving a 1- charge. A 1+ charge belongs to the alkali metals.

Chemistry.q: Chlorine has atomic number 17. In a neutral chlorine atom, how many electrons occupy the outermost (third) electron shell? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.1: Counted the electrons chlorine needs to gain, not the electrons it has.
tr.8: Assumed the outer shell is a full octet; chlorine is one electron short of 8.
tr.17: Gave the total number of electrons, not the outer-shell count.

Chemistry.w: Fill shells from the inside: first shell 2, second shell 8, which uses 10 electrons. The remaining 17 - 2 - 8 = 7 electrons are in the third shell (arrangement 2, 8, 7), matching chlorine's place in group 17.

Chemistry.q: Lithium, sodium, potassium and rubidium are all in group 1 of the periodic table. Which of these elements has the largest atomic radius, and what is the reason?
o: Rubidium, because it has the most occupied electron shells
Lithium, because it has the fewest protons pulling inward
Rubidium, because its nucleus pulls hardest on its electrons
Rubidium, because it has the most valence electrons
Chemistry.w: Atomic radius increases down a group because each element down the column adds another occupied electron shell, placing the outer electrons farther from the nucleus. Rubidium, lowest of the four, is largest.

n.1: Lithium is the smallest of the four. Having fewer protons does not outweigh having fewer shells.
n.2: Rubidium is largest, but because of its extra shells; its outer electron is actually held less tightly than in the smaller atoms.
n.3: All group 1 elements have the same number of valence electrons (one), so valence count cannot explain the size difference.

Chemistry.q: Moving from left to right across period 3, from sodium to chlorine, how does atomic radius change, and what explains the change?
o: It increases, because each element adds more electrons
It increases, because a new electron shell is added each time
It decreases, because more protons pull the same shells closer
It holds steady, because the number of shells stays the same
Chemistry.w: Across a period, electrons are added to the same outer shell while the nuclear charge (number of protons) increases. The stronger pull draws the electron cloud inward, so atomic radius decreases from left to right.

n.0: More electrons are added, but they go into the same shell while the growing nuclear charge pulls them in, so radius shrinks.
n.1: A new shell is added when moving down a group (or starting a new period), not across a period.
n.3: The shell count is unchanged, but the rising number of protons still pulls the shells closer, so radius does change.

Chemistry.q: Electronegativity is a measure of how strongly an atom attracts the shared electrons in a chemical bond. Which of these elements has the highest electronegativity?
o: Fluorine
Iodine
Oxygen
Francium
Chemistry.w: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, so it is highest at the upper right of the table (excluding noble gases). Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

n.1: Iodine is a halogen, but it sits far down group 17; electronegativity decreases down a group.
n.2: Oxygen is highly electronegative but lies one place left of fluorine in period 2, so it is slightly lower.
n.3: Francium, at the lower left of the table, has one of the lowest electronegativities of all elements.

Chemistry.q: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom. Which movement on the periodic table generally leads to elements with higher first ionization energy?
o: Moving up a group, or left to right across a period
Moving down a group, or right to left across a period
Moving down a group, or left to right across a period
Moving up a group, or right to left across a period
Chemistry.w: Ionization energy increases left to right across a period (more protons hold the same shell tighter) and increases up a group (outer electrons are closer to the nucleus). It is highest at the upper right.

n.1: Both of these movements lower ionization energy; this describes the direction toward the most reactive metals.
n.2: Moving left to right raises ionization energy, but moving down a group lowers it, because outer electrons are farther from the nucleus.
n.3: Moving up a group raises ionization energy, but moving right to left lowers it, because nuclear charge decreases.

Chemistry.q: Lithium, sodium, potassium and cesium all react with water, but with very different vigor. Which of these metals reacts most vigorously, and why?
o: Cesium, because it has the most valence electrons to give away
Lithium, because it has the highest electronegativity of the four
Lithium, because its outer electron sits closest to the nucleus
Cesium, because its outer electron is the easiest to remove
Chemistry.w: Metal reactivity increases down a group. Cesium's single valence electron is farthest from the nucleus and most shielded, so it has the lowest ionization energy and is lost most easily.

n.0: All four are group 1 metals with one valence electron, so the number of valence electrons does not differ.
n.1: Lithium does have the highest electronegativity of the four, but that makes it hold electrons more tightly and react less vigorously.
n.2: An electron close to the nucleus is held tightly, which makes lithium the least reactive of these metals.

Chemistry.q: A chlorine atom gains one electron to become a chloride ion, Cl-, which is the main anion in blood plasma. How does the radius of Cl- compare with that of a neutral chlorine atom?
o: The ion is larger, because the extra electron adds repulsion
The ion is smaller, because the gained electron adds attraction
The ion is the same size, because its proton count is unchanged
The ion is smaller, because it has lost its outermost shell
Chemistry.w: Anions are larger than their parent atoms. The added electron increases repulsion among electrons while the number of protons pulling them in stays the same, so the electron cloud spreads out.

n.1: Electrons repel each other; adding one without adding protons expands the electron cloud.
n.2: The protons are unchanged, but the extra electron changes the balance of attraction and repulsion, so the size changes.
n.3: Losing an outer shell happens when a metal atom forms a cation, which is why cations are smaller. Chlorine gains an electron.

Chemistry.q: A chemist needs an element whose chemical properties are most similar to those of sulfur (group 16, period 3). Which element should she choose, and why?
o: Chlorine, in the same period as sulfur
Phosphorus, with the nearest atomic mass
Selenium, in the same group as sulfur
Sodium, with the same number of shells
Chemistry.w: Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so they have similar chemical properties. Selenium is directly below sulfur in group 16; both have 6 valence electrons.

n.0: Elements in the same period have different numbers of valence electrons and different properties; chlorine has 7.
n.1: Similar atomic mass does not mean similar chemistry; phosphorus has 5 valence electrons.
n.3: Sharing the number of shells (the same period) does not give similar properties; sodium is a reactive metal with 1 valence electron.

Chemistry.q: Place these elements in order of increasing atomic radius, starting with the smallest atom.
o: Carbon
Potassium
Fluorine
Lithium
Oxygen
Chemistry.w: Fluorine, oxygen, carbon and lithium are all in period 2, where atomic radius increases from right to left (fewer protons pull the same two shells less tightly): F < O < C < Li. Potassium is in period 4, below lithium's group, and has two more occupied shells, so it is the largest.

Chemistry.q: Place these elements in order of increasing electronegativity, starting with the element that has the weakest pull on shared electrons.
o: Chlorine
Sulfur
Potassium
Sodium
Magnesium
Chemistry.w: Electronegativity decreases down a group and increases across a period. Potassium is below sodium in group 1, so it is lowest. Sodium, magnesium, sulfur and chlorine are all in period 3, so electronegativity rises from left to right across them: K < Na < Mg < S < Cl.

Chemistry.q: A tutor asks a student to identify correct statements about periodic trends for the main-group elements. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Electronegativity is highest at the lower left of the table
Ionization energy increases down a group
Metallic character increases down a group
Atomic radius increases left to right across a period
Electronegativity increases left to right across a period
Atomic radius increases down a group
Chemistry.w: Down a group, atoms gain shells, so radius and metallic character increase. Across a period, nuclear charge rises, so electronegativity increases (and radius decreases).

n.0: Electronegativity is highest at the upper right (fluorine); the lower left holds the least electronegative elements.
n.1: Ionization energy decreases down a group because outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and easier to remove.
n.3: Atomic radius decreases across a period as more protons pull the same shells inward.

Chemistry.q: Neon is used in lighted signs partly because it does not react with the glass tube or the metal electrodes. What best explains neon's very low chemical reactivity?
o: Its outer shell is already full with 8 electrons
Its 8 valence electrons are easily shared in bonds
Its single valence electron is held very tightly
Its large atomic radius keeps other atoms away
Chemistry.w: Neon is a noble gas (group 18). Its outer shell is full (2, 8), so it has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, which makes it very unreactive.

n.1: A full octet is stable; neon does not share its valence electrons to form bonds.
n.2: Neon has 8 valence electrons, not 1. A single valence electron describes the very reactive alkali metals.
n.3: Size does not explain it: argon and krypton are larger noble gases and are also unreactive, because they too have a full outer shell.

Chemistry.q: Element X is in period 3, group 2, and element Y is in period 3, group 17. Based on periodic trends, which statement correctly compares X with Y?
o: X has the larger radius and the higher electronegativity
X has the larger radius and the lower ionization energy
X has the smaller radius and the lower electronegativity
X has the smaller radius and the higher ionization energy
Chemistry.w: Step 1: X and Y are in the same period, and X is to the left. Step 2: Moving left across a period, radius increases while ionization energy and electronegativity decrease. So X (magnesium) is larger and has a lower ionization energy than Y (chlorine).

n.0: X is larger, but electronegativity is lower toward the left of a period, so X's is lower.
n.2: X's electronegativity is lower, but its radius is larger, not smaller, because it has fewer protons pulling on the same shells.
n.3: This reverses the trend. Elements toward the left of a period are larger and hold electrons less tightly.

Chemistry.q: A nurse pours 30 mL of cough syrup from a tall, narrow bottle into a wide, shallow dosing cup. The syrup takes the shape of the cup but still measures 30 mL. Which description of the syrup's particles explains this behavior?
o: They are squeezed by the cup walls into the new shape
They are far apart and move freely to fill any container
They stay close together but can slide past one another
They vibrate in fixed positions that hold a set volume
Chemistry.w: Liquids have a definite volume but no definite shape. Their particles stay close together (so the volume stays 30 mL) but can slide past one another (so the syrup flows into the shape of the cup).

n.0: Liquids are nearly incompressible; the volume stays 30 mL, so the particles are not being pushed closer together.
n.1: Particles that are far apart and move freely describe a gas, which would spread to fill the whole container instead of keeping 30 mL.
n.3: Particles vibrating in fixed positions describe a solid, which keeps its own shape instead of taking the shape of the cup.

Chemistry.q: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. When a block of it sits in an open cooler, it slowly disappears as a gas and never forms a puddle of liquid. What is this phase change called?
o: Condensation
Sublimation
Evaporation
Deposition
Chemistry.w: Sublimation is the change directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state. Dry ice, iodine and mothballs all sublime. It is endothermic.

n.0: Condensation is gas becoming liquid, the opposite direction and a different pair of states.
n.2: Evaporation is a change from liquid to gas at the surface; dry ice skips the liquid state.
n.3: Deposition is the reverse change, gas directly to solid (as when frost forms).

Chemistry.q: A beaker of crushed ice at 0 °C is heated steadily on a hot plate. While the ice is melting and some solid is still present, what happens to the temperature of the ice-water mixture?
o: It stays at 0 °C, because the energy breaks attractions between molecules
It rises to 4 °C, where water is densest, before melting is complete
It rises steadily, because the heat raises the molecules' kinetic energy
It falls slightly, because melting releases heat to the surroundings
Chemistry.w: During a phase change, the temperature stays constant. The added energy (heat of fusion) goes into breaking the attractions holding molecules in the solid, not into raising their average kinetic energy. This is the flat plateau on a heating curve.

n.1: Water is densest at about 4 °C, but the mixture does not warm above 0 °C until all the ice has melted.
n.2: The temperature rises before and after melting, but not during it; the energy is used to change the state.
n.3: Melting absorbs heat (endothermic). Freezing is the change that releases heat.

Chemistry.q: Which of these everyday phase changes releases energy to its surroundings rather than absorbing energy from them?
o: Sweat evaporating from the skin during exercise
An ice cube melting in a glass of lemonade
Water vapor condensing on a cool bathroom mirror
Mothballs subliming slowly in a closed closet
Chemistry.w: Condensation (gas to liquid) is exothermic: as vapor molecules come together and form attractions, energy is released. Freezing, condensation and deposition release heat; melting, vaporization and sublimation absorb it.

n.0: Evaporation absorbs heat from the skin, which is why sweating cools the body.
n.1: Melting is endothermic; the ice absorbs heat from the lemonade, cooling the drink.
n.3: Sublimation (solid to gas) absorbs energy, like melting and vaporization.

Chemistry.q: A sealed container of nitrogen gas is warmed from 20 °C to 40 °C. Which quantity does the temperature reading of the gas directly measure?
o: The number of particle collisions in one second
The potential energy stored between particles
The average kinetic energy of the gas particles
The total heat energy stored in the whole sample
Chemistry.w: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample. Warming the gas makes its particles move faster on average.

n.0: Collision frequency rises with temperature, but it is a result of faster motion, not what temperature measures.
n.1: Potential energy between particles changes during phase changes, while temperature stays constant; temperature tracks kinetic energy.
n.3: Total heat energy depends on the amount of substance as well as the temperature; temperature measures the average energy per particle.

Chemistry.q: Pasta takes longer to cook in boiling water in Denver, Colorado (elevation about 5,280 feet) than in Miami, Florida, near sea level. What explains this difference?
o: Colder air at high altitude removes heat from the pot more quickly
Thinner air holds less oxygen, which lowers water's boiling point
Lower air pressure at high altitude lowers water's boiling point
Higher air pressure at high altitude slows the escape of molecules
Chemistry.w: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure. At high altitude, air pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature (below 100 °C). The boiling water is cooler, so food cooks more slowly.

n.0: Once water boils, its temperature is set by the boiling point, not by the outside air temperature.
n.1: The boiling point is lower at altitude, but the cause is lower air pressure; the oxygen content of the air does not set the boiling point of water.
n.3: Air pressure is lower, not higher, at high altitude. Higher pressure (as in a pressure cooker) raises the boiling point.

Chemistry.q: A sealed syringe holds 20 mL of air at a pressure of 1 atm. The plunger is pushed in until the pressure of the air doubles, with the temperature held constant. What is the new volume of the air?
o: 5 mL
10 mL
20 mL
40 mL
Chemistry.w: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related (P1V1 = P2V2). 1 atm x 20 mL = 2 atm x V2, so V2 = 20 / 2 = 10 mL. Doubling the pressure halves the volume.

n.0: 5 mL would be the volume if the pressure were quadrupled, not doubled.
n.2: Gases are compressible; the volume changes when the pressure changes.
n.3: This treats pressure and volume as directly related. They are inversely related, so the volume falls.

Chemistry.q: A flexible, sealed balloon is moved from a warm kitchen into a freezer. The pressure on the balloon stays about the same. What happens to the balloon, and which gas law describes this change?
o: It expands, as described by Charles's law
It shrinks, as described by Boyle's law
It expands, as described by Gay-Lussac's law
It shrinks, as described by Charles's law
Chemistry.w: Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its kelvin temperature. Cooling the gas slows its particles, so the balloon shrinks.

n.0: Charles's law is the right law, but volume falls when temperature falls, so the balloon shrinks.
n.1: The balloon shrinks, but Boyle's law relates pressure and volume at constant temperature; here temperature changes at constant pressure.
n.2: Gay-Lussac's law relates pressure and temperature at constant volume, and a cooled gas does not expand.

Chemistry.q: In winter, a layer of ice forms on top of a pond while liquid water remains below it. Which statement correctly explains why ice floats on liquid water?
o: Molecules in ice move faster than in liquid, so they spread farther apart
Ice has fewer hydrogen bonds than water, so it is less dense
Trapped air in the crystals lowers the density of ice below that of water
Hydrogen bonds lock ice into an open lattice that is less dense than water
Chemistry.w: When water freezes, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open, hexagonal lattice that takes up more space than the liquid. Ice is therefore less dense than liquid water and floats; water is densest at about 4 °C.

n.0: Molecules in a solid move less, not more, than in the liquid; they vibrate in fixed positions.
n.1: Ice has more hydrogen bonds, not fewer: each molecule is locked to four neighbors, and that rigid open network is what lowers its density.
n.2: Pure, clear ice with no bubbles still floats. The low density comes from the hydrogen-bonded lattice, not trapped air.

Chemistry.q: A block of ice at -20 °C is heated steadily until it becomes steam at 120 °C. Place the stages of the heating curve in the order in which they occur, starting with the first.
o: Liquid water warms from 0 °C to 100 °C
Ice melts at a constant 0 °C
Ice warms from -20 °C to 0 °C
Steam warms from 100 °C to 120 °C
Water boils at a constant 100 °C
Chemistry.w: Heating curve of water: the solid warms to its melting point, then the temperature holds at 0 °C while it melts (heat of fusion). The liquid then warms to 100 °C, holds there while it boils (heat of vaporization), and finally the gas warms above 100 °C. The plateaus are the phase changes.

Chemistry.q: A science teacher lists several phase changes for a class discussion on energy. Which of these processes absorb heat from their surroundings? Select all that apply.
o: Steam condensing on a lid
Dry ice subliming in a cooler
Sweat evaporating from skin
Ice melting on a sidewalk
Water freezing in an ice tray
Frost forming on a window
Chemistry.w: Changes that move toward a higher-energy state absorb heat (endothermic): melting (solid to liquid), sublimation (solid to gas) and evaporation (liquid to gas).

n.0: Condensation (gas to liquid) releases heat.
n.4: Freezing (liquid to solid) releases heat; it is exothermic.
n.5: Frost forms by deposition (gas to solid), which releases heat.

Chemistry.q: Oxygen gas can be squeezed into a small tank for a patient's portable supply, but liquid water barely changes volume even under great pressure. What explains this difference?
o: Gas particles move slowly, so they can be packed together
Gas particles attract one another more strongly than liquids
Gas particles are smaller than the particles of a liquid
Gas particles are far apart with much empty space between them
Chemistry.w: According to kinetic molecular theory, gas particles are far apart compared with their size, so there is a lot of empty space that can be reduced by pressure. Liquid particles are already close together.

n.0: Gas particles move fast, not slowly; they have the highest kinetic energy of the three common states.
n.1: Attractions between gas particles are weaker, not stronger, than in a liquid; a gas compresses because of the empty space between its particles.
n.2: Compressibility depends on the space between particles, not their size; water molecules are similar in size to oxygen molecules.

Chemistry.q: A homeowner notices four changes in the kitchen over one weekend. Which of these is a chemical change rather than a physical change?
o: Sugar dissolving and vanishing in a mug of hot tea
Bubbles forming throughout a pot of boiling water
A cut apple slice turning brown on the counter
Frost forming on the inside of the freezer door
Chemistry.w: A cut apple browns because compounds in the fruit react with oxygen in the air to form new, brown substances: a chemical change signaled by a color change. Dissolving, boiling and deposition change form or state but leave the same substance.

n.0: Dissolving is physical: the sugar molecules are still sugar and can be recovered by evaporating the water, even though they seem to vanish.
n.1: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapor, still H2O, so boiling is a physical change of state despite the gas.
n.3: Frost forms by deposition, water vapor turning directly into ice; a new solid appears, but it is still H2O, so the change is physical.

Chemistry.q: Ethanol is used in hand sanitizers. Which of these properties of ethanol is a chemical property rather than a physical property?
o: It has a density of 0.79 g/mL at 20 °C
It mixes with water in any proportion
It boils at 78 °C at sea-level pressure
It burns in air to form CO2 and water
Chemistry.w: A chemical property describes a substance's ability to react and form new substances. Flammability (burning to form carbon dioxide and water) is a chemical property.

n.0: Density is a physical (intensive) property measured without changing the substance.
n.1: Solubility is a physical property; ethanol mixed with water is still ethanol.
n.2: Boiling point is a physical property; boiling does not change ethanol into a new substance.

Chemistry.q: A jeweler cuts a solid gold bar into two unequal pieces. Which property of each piece is the same as that of the original, whole bar?
o: Its density
Its mass
Its volume
Its surface area
Chemistry.w: Density is an intensive property: it does not depend on the amount of material. Each piece of gold has the same mass-to-volume ratio (about 19.3 g/cm3) as the whole bar.

n.1: Mass is an extensive property; each piece has less mass than the whole bar.
n.2: Volume is extensive; cutting the bar divides its volume between the pieces.
n.3: Surface area depends on the size and shape of a piece, so it changes when the bar is cut; it is not an intensive property.

Chemistry.q: Both water and air are made of more than one element. Which statement correctly distinguishes water from air?
o: Both are mixtures, because each can be separated by boiling
Water is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen; air is a compound of gases
Both are compounds, because each contains more than one element
Water is a compound in a fixed ratio; air is a mixture that varies
Chemistry.w: Water (H2O) is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen are chemically bonded in a fixed 2:1 ratio and can be separated only by a chemical change. Air is a mixture of gases (mostly N2 and O2) whose proportions can vary and can be separated physically.

n.0: Boiling water only changes its state to vapor; it does not separate the hydrogen and oxygen, so water is not a mixture.
n.1: This reverses the categories. Water's elements are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio; air's gases are physically mixed.
n.2: Containing more than one element does not make something a compound; the elements must be chemically combined in a fixed ratio, which is not true of air.

Chemistry.q: A 54-gram metal sample is lowered into a graduated cylinder, and the water level rises from 30.0 mL to 50.0 mL. What is the density of the metal in grams per milliliter? Enter your answer rounded to the nearest tenth.

tr.1.8: Divided by the starting water level (30 mL) instead of the volume displaced.
tr.1.1: Divided by the final water level (50 mL) instead of the volume displaced.
tr.0.4: Divided volume by mass (20 / 54) instead of mass by volume.

Chemistry.w: Step 1: volume by water displacement = 50.0 mL - 30.0 mL = 20.0 mL. Step 2: density = mass / volume = 54 g / 20.0 mL = 2.7 g/mL.

Chemistry.q: A plastic bead has a mass of 12 g and a volume of 15 mL. It is dropped into a beaker of water, which has a density of 1.0 g/mL. What happens to the bead, and why?
o: It floats, because its density is 0.8 g/mL
It sinks, because its density is 1.8 g/mL
It sinks, because its density is 1.25 g/mL
It floats, because its density is 0.08 g/mL
Chemistry.w: Step 1: density = mass / volume = 12 g / 15 mL = 0.8 g/mL. Step 2: an object less dense than the fluid it is placed in floats; 0.8 g/mL is less than water's 1.0 g/mL, so the bead floats.

n.1: 1.8 g/mL comes from adding mass and volume before dividing; density is simply 12 / 15.
n.2: 1.25 g/mL comes from dividing volume by mass (15 / 12). Density is mass divided by volume.
n.3: The bead does float, but 0.08 g/mL is a decimal-place slip; 12 / 15 = 0.8.

Chemistry.q: A student mixes two clear, colorless solutions in a test tube. Within seconds, a cloudy yellow solid forms and slowly settles to the bottom. What does this observation most likely indicate?
o: A chemical change, because a precipitate has formed
A physical change, because two liquids were mixed
A physical change, because the solid can be filtered off
A chemical change, because the mixture is now uneven
Chemistry.w: The formation of a precipitate (an insoluble solid) from two solutions is a sign of a chemical change: a new substance with new properties has been produced. Other signs include unexpected gas, color change, light and temperature change.

n.1: Mixing alone can be physical, but here a new solid substance appeared, which signals a reaction.
n.2: Being able to separate the solid by filtration does not make the change physical; the solid is a newly formed substance.
n.3: The change is chemical, but the reason is the new substance; a heterogeneous mixture can also form by purely physical mixing.

Chemistry.q: When water boils, bubbles form throughout the liquid and rise to the surface. Why is boiling classified as a physical change even though gas bubbles appear?
o: The bubbles are hydrogen and oxygen that recombine on cooling
The bubbles are water vapor, so no new substance forms
The bubbles are air that was dissolved in the water before heating
Heating causes physical changes, and gas bubbles confirm this
Chemistry.w: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapor, H2O in the gas state. Changing state does not produce a new substance, so boiling is a physical change. Gas bubbles signal a chemical change only when they come from a new substance.

n.0: Boiling does not split water into hydrogen and oxygen; that would be a chemical change (decomposition, as in electrolysis).
n.2: A few early bubbles are dissolved air, but the bubbles that form throughout boiling water are water vapor.
n.3: Heat can cause chemical changes too, such as cooking an egg; heating is not what makes boiling physical.

Chemistry.q: A pharmacy technician sorts four samples on a shelf. Which of these samples is a homogeneous mixture?
o: Oil and vinegar dressing
Distilled water
Sand stirred into water
Salt dissolved in water
Chemistry.w: Salt water is a solution, a homogeneous mixture: the dissolved salt is spread evenly, so every part has the same composition, and the proportions can vary.

n.0: Oil and vinegar separate into visible layers, so the dressing is a heterogeneous mixture.
n.1: Distilled water is a pure substance, the compound H2O, not a mixture.
n.2: Sand does not dissolve and settles out, so sand in water is a heterogeneous mixture (a suspension).

Chemistry.q: A lab has a clear, uniform mixture of ethanol, which boils at 78 °C, and water, which boils at 100 °C. Which method would best separate the two liquids?
o: Filtration
Centrifugation
Distillation
Decanting
Chemistry.w: Distillation separates liquids by their different boiling points: heating the mixture vaporizes the lower-boiling ethanol first, and the vapor is condensed and collected separately.

n.0: Filtration separates an undissolved solid from a liquid; dissolved liquids pass straight through the filter.
n.1: Centrifugation separates suspended particles by density; it cannot separate a uniform solution of two liquids.
n.3: Decanting pours off a liquid layer from a solid or a separate liquid layer; ethanol and water do not form layers.

Chemistry.q: A student is sorting examples of changes in matter for a lab report. Which of these are physical changes? Select all that apply.
o: Toasting a slice of bread in a toaster
An antacid tablet fizzing in a glass of water
Dissolving table salt in water
Crushing an aspirin tablet into powder
A silver spoon tarnishing in a drawer
Freezing orange juice into ice pops
Chemistry.w: Crushing changes only the size of the particles, dissolving salt separates ions that are still sodium and chloride, and freezing changes state. In each case no new substance forms, so these are physical changes.

n.0: Toasting browns the bread through chemical reactions that form new substances.
n.1: The fizzing is carbon dioxide produced when the antacid reacts with water and acid, a chemical change.
n.4: Tarnish is silver sulfide, a new substance formed when silver reacts with sulfur compounds in the air.

Chemistry.q: Fresh milk scatters a beam of light shone through it, and its tiny dispersed particles do not settle out even after the milk stands for hours. How is milk best classified?
o: A solution
A suspension
A compound
A colloid
Chemistry.w: A colloid is a mixture whose dispersed particles are larger than in a solution but do not settle; they scatter light (the Tyndall effect). Milk, fog and gelatin are colloids.

n.0: Solution particles are too small to scatter a light beam; a true solution looks clear.
n.1: Suspension particles are large enough to settle out on standing and can be filtered.
n.2: Milk is a mixture of many substances in variable proportions, not a single compound with a fixed ratio.

Chemistry.q: Sodium, a reactive metal, combines with chlorine, a nonmetal, to form sodium chloride (NaCl), the main salt in normal saline. Which statement correctly describes the bond in NaCl?
o: Covalent, formed as the two atoms share a pair of electrons
Metallic, formed by a sea of electrons around both atoms
Ionic, formed as sodium transfers an electron to chlorine
Ionic, formed as chlorine transfers an electron to sodium
Chemistry.w: A metal and a nonmetal with a large difference in electronegativity form an ionic bond. Sodium loses its single valence electron to chlorine, producing Na+ and Cl- ions that are held together by electrostatic attraction.

n.0: Sharing electron pairs describes covalent bonds, which form mainly between nonmetals.
n.1: Metallic bonding holds atoms of a metal together; NaCl is a metal combined with a nonmetal.
n.3: The bond is ionic, but the electron moves from the metal (sodium) to the nonmetal (chlorine), not the other way.

Chemistry.q: A student is classifying four compounds by bond type. Which of these compounds is held together by covalent bonds?
o: Carbon dioxide (CO2)
Potassium bromide (KBr)
Magnesium oxide (MgO)
Calcium chloride (CaCl2)
Chemistry.w: Covalent bonds form when nonmetal atoms share electron pairs. Carbon and oxygen are both nonmetals, so CO2 is a covalent (molecular) compound.

n.1: Potassium is a metal, so potassium bromide is ionic (K+ and Br-).
n.2: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen is a nonmetal, so MgO is ionic (Mg2+ and O2-).
n.3: Calcium is a metal, so calcium chloride is ionic (Ca2+ and two Cl-).

Chemistry.q: In a water molecule, the oxygen atom pulls the shared electrons more strongly than the hydrogen atoms do. Which choice correctly describes the O-H bonds and the water molecule as a whole?
o: Polar covalent bonds in a linear, nonpolar molecule
Polar covalent bonds in a bent, polar molecule
Ionic bonds in a bent molecule with full charges
Nonpolar covalent bonds in a bent, polar molecule
Chemistry.w: Unequal sharing makes each O-H bond polar covalent: oxygen gets a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge. Because the molecule is bent, the bond polarities do not cancel, so water is a polar molecule.

n.0: Water is bent, not linear. A linear shape (as in CO2) would let the bond polarities cancel.
n.2: Electrons are shared, not fully transferred, between oxygen and hydrogen, so there are partial charges, not full ionic charges.
n.3: Nonpolar bonds involve equal sharing; oxygen's stronger pull makes the O-H bonds polar.

Chemistry.q: The two strands of a DNA double helix are held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases. Which statement about these hydrogen bonds is correct?
o: They are stronger than the covalent bonds within each strand
They form when electrons transfer from hydrogen to nitrogen
They are weaker than the covalent bonds within each strand
They form when hydrogen shares an electron pair with carbon
Chemistry.w: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on another N, O or F atom. They are much weaker than covalent bonds, which is why DNA strands can be separated for replication while each strand's backbone stays intact.

n.0: Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds; that weakness lets the strands unzip.
n.1: Hydrogen bonds involve partial charges, not a transfer of electrons, which would make ions.
n.3: A C-H bond is an ordinary covalent bond. Hydrogen bonds need hydrogen attached to N, O or F.

Chemistry.q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but the same compound conducts well when it is melted or dissolved in water. What explains this difference?
o: Its ions are locked in a lattice in the solid but free to move when liquid
Melting or dissolving breaks covalent bonds and frees their electrons
Heat and water both supply extra electrons that the solid crystal lacks
Its electrons are shared in the solid but transferred once dissolved
Chemistry.w: An electric current needs mobile charged particles. In solid NaCl the Na+ and Cl- ions are fixed in a crystal lattice; melting or dissolving lets the ions move, so the compound conducts. Ionic compounds conduct when melted or dissolved, not as solids.

n.1: NaCl contains ionic bonds, not covalent bonds, and the moving charges are ions, not freed electrons.
n.2: Neither heat nor water adds electrons; conduction comes from the existing ions becoming mobile.
n.3: NaCl is ionic in both states; its electrons were transferred when the compound formed, not when it dissolves.

Chemistry.q: A chemistry worksheet shows the expression 3 Ca(OH)2, meaning three formula units of calcium hydroxide. How many atoms in total does this expression represent? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.5: Counted one formula unit and ignored the coefficient 3.
tr.9: Did not apply the subscript 2 to both O and H inside the parentheses (3 x 3).
tr.12: Applied the subscript to hydrogen but not to oxygen (3 x 4).

Chemistry.w: One Ca(OH)2 contains 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H (the subscript 2 applies to everything inside the parentheses), which is 5 atoms. The coefficient 3 multiplies the whole unit: 3 x 5 = 15 atoms (3 Ca, 6 O, 6 H).

Chemistry.q: Copper is drawn into thin wires for electrical cables and conducts electricity very well. Which type of bonding between copper atoms explains these properties?
o: Metallic bonding, with delocalized electrons moving among cations
Hydrogen bonding, with weak attractions between copper atoms
Covalent bonding, with electron pairs shared between copper atoms
Ionic bonding, with electrons transferred between copper atoms
Chemistry.w: In metallic bonding, metal cations sit in a sea of delocalized electrons. The mobile electrons carry current, and the cations can slide past one another without breaking the bond, which makes metals ductile and malleable.

n.1: Hydrogen bonds need hydrogen bonded to N, O or F; they do not form between copper atoms.
n.2: Localized shared pairs would not let electrons flow freely or let layers slide, so covalent bonding cannot explain conduction and ductility.
n.3: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal; identical copper atoms do not transfer electrons to one another.

Chemistry.q: Place these attractive forces in order of strength, starting with the weakest.
o: London dispersion forces
Covalent bonds
Hydrogen bonds
Dipole-dipole attractions
Chemistry.w: Intermolecular forces rank London dispersion < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonds. All three are weaker than the covalent bonds that hold atoms together within a molecule.

Chemistry.q: Water (H2O) boils at 100 °C, while hydrogen sulfide (H2S), a molecule of similar shape, boils at about -60 °C. What best explains water's much higher boiling point?
o: Stronger covalent bonds within each water molecule
Hydrogen bonding between neighboring water molecules
Ionic bonds between the hydrogen and oxygen atoms
A larger molar mass than hydrogen sulfide molecules
Chemistry.w: Boiling separates molecules from each other, so it depends on intermolecular attractions. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds (H bonded to O, attracted to O on a neighbor); H2S cannot, because sulfur is not N, O or F. Extra energy is needed to overcome these attractions.

n.0: Boiling does not break the covalent bonds inside a molecule; steam is still H2O.
n.2: The O-H bonds in water are polar covalent, not ionic.
n.3: Water (18 g/mol) is lighter than H2S (34 g/mol), so molar mass would predict the opposite.

Chemistry.q: A chemistry teacher asks which pair of elements would most likely combine to form an ionic compound. Which pair should the students choose?
o: Copper and zinc
Potassium and bromine
Phosphorus and chlorine
Nitrogen and oxygen
Chemistry.w: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal with a large electronegativity difference. Potassium (an alkali metal) readily loses an electron to bromine (a halogen), forming KBr.

n.0: Copper and zinc are both metals; together they form an alloy (brass) held by metallic bonding.
n.2: Phosphorus and chlorine are both nonmetals and form covalent bonds, as in PCl3.
n.3: Nitrogen and oxygen are both nonmetals, so they share electrons in covalent bonds.

Chemistry.q: A student is identifying substances whose molecules contain polar covalent bonds, where electrons are shared unequally. Which substances contain polar covalent bonds? Select all that apply.
o: Hydrogen gas (H2)
Ammonia (NH3)
Chlorine gas (Cl2)
Oxygen gas (O2) from a medical cylinder
Hydrogen chloride (HCl)
Water (H2O)
Chemistry.w: Bonds between two different nonmetals with different electronegativities are polar covalent: O-H in water, N-H in ammonia and H-Cl in hydrogen chloride.

n.0: Both atoms in H2 are identical, so they share electrons equally: a nonpolar covalent bond.
n.2: Cl2 is made of two identical atoms, so its bond is nonpolar covalent.
n.3: O2 has two identical atoms sharing electrons equally, so its bond is nonpolar.

Chemistry.q: Magnesium (group 2) bonds with chlorine (group 17). Using the usual charges of their ions, which choice gives the formula of the compound and its type of bonding?
o: MgCl2, held together by covalent bonds
MgCl, held together by ionic bonds
MgCl2, held together by ionic bonds
Mg2Cl, held together by ionic bonds
Chemistry.w: Step 1: magnesium loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+, and chlorine gains 1 to form Cl-. Step 2: two Cl- ions balance one Mg2+, giving MgCl2. A metal combined with a nonmetal forms an ionic compound.
