n.0: The formula is right, but a metal and a nonmetal transfer electrons, forming ionic, not covalent, bonds.
n.1: One Cl- (1-) cannot balance one Mg2+ (2+); the formula would carry a net charge of 1+.
n.3: Two Mg2+ ions and one Cl- give a net charge of 3+; the ratio is reversed.

Chemistry.q: When a strip of zinc is placed in hydrochloric acid, bubbles of hydrogen gas form: Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. Which type of reaction does this equation represent?
o: Decomposition
Single replacement
Double replacement
Synthesis
Chemistry.w: In a single replacement reaction (A + BC → AC + B), one element takes the place of another in a compound. Zinc replaces hydrogen in HCl, forming ZnCl2 and releasing H2.

n.0: Decomposition (AB → A + B) starts with a single compound; this reaction has two reactants.
n.2: Double replacement (AB + CD → AD + CB) swaps partners between two compounds; here one reactant is a free element.
n.3: Synthesis (A + B → AB) combines reactants into a single product; this reaction has two products.

Chemistry.q: When solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride are mixed, a white solid forms: AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO3. How is this reaction best classified?
o: Synthesis, forming one new solid product
Decomposition, splitting into two products
Double replacement, forming a precipitate
Single replacement, forming a precipitate
Chemistry.w: The two compounds exchange partners (AB + CD → AD + CB): silver pairs with chloride and sodium pairs with nitrate. The insoluble AgCl appears as a white precipitate.

n.0: Synthesis gives a single product; this reaction gives two (AgCl and NaNO3).
n.1: Decomposition starts with one compound breaking apart; here two compounds react.
n.3: A precipitate does form, but both reactants are compounds that swap ions, so it is double, not single, replacement.

Chemistry.q: A student balances the equation H2 + O2 → H2O by rewriting the product as H2O2, so that each side has two oxygen atoms. Why is this method incorrect?
o: The product needs more hydrogen atoms rather than oxygen
Changing a subscript changes the identity of the substance
Hydrogen and oxygen must appear in a 1:1 ratio as products
The coefficients must be equal on both sides of the arrow
Chemistry.w: Equations are balanced with coefficients only. Changing a subscript changes the substance itself: H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, not water. The correct balanced equation is 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O.

n.0: The product does need more oxygen, but the fix is a coefficient (2 H2O), not changing the formula of the product.
n.2: Water has a 2:1 ratio of hydrogen to oxygen; a 1:1 ratio is exactly what turns water into hydrogen peroxide.
n.3: Coefficients do not have to match across the arrow; atom counts must. In 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O the coefficients total 3 on the left and 2 on the right.

Chemistry.q: In a sealed flask, 10.0 g of baking soda reacts completely with 20.0 g of vinegar, producing carbon dioxide gas that stays inside the flask. What is the total mass of the flask's contents after the reaction?
o: Less than 30.0 g, because a gas has very little mass
Less than 30.0 g, because some mass is converted into energy
More than 30.0 g, because a new compound has formed
Exactly 30.0 g, because atoms are rearranged, not lost
Chemistry.w: The law of conservation of mass: atoms are rearranged in a reaction, not created or destroyed, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants (10.0 g + 20.0 g = 30.0 g) in a closed system.

n.0: Gas does have mass; in a sealed flask the carbon dioxide is still counted. Mass would seem to drop only if the gas escaped from an open container.
n.1: In ordinary chemical reactions the mass change from energy release is far too small to measure; mass is conserved.
n.2: Forming a new compound rearranges the same atoms, so the total mass does not increase.

Chemistry.q: Propane burns according to the unbalanced equation C3H8 + O2 → CO2 + H2O. When the equation is balanced using the smallest whole-number coefficients, what is the coefficient of O2? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.4: Copied the coefficient of H2O instead of counting the oxygen atoms needed.
tr.10: Gave the number of oxygen atoms instead of the number of O2 molecules.

Chemistry.w: Balance C first: 3 C gives 3 CO2. Balance H next: 8 H gives 4 H2O. Count O on the right: 3 x 2 + 4 x 1 = 10 O atoms, which needs 10 / 2 = 5 O2. Balanced: C3H8 + 5 O2 → 3 CO2 + 4 H2O.

Chemistry.q: A student checks four chemical equations for a lab report. Which of these equations is correctly balanced?
o: N2 + 3 H2 → NH3
2 Na + Cl2 → NaCl
CH4 + O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O
Chemistry.w: In 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O, each side has 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms, so the equation is balanced.

n.1: The left side has 2 N and 6 H, the right has 1 N and 3 H; the balanced form is N2 + 3 H2 → 2 NH3.
n.2: The left side has 2 Na and 2 Cl, the right has 1 of each; the balanced form is 2 Na + Cl2 → 2 NaCl.
n.3: The left side has 2 O atoms and the right has 4 (2 in CO2 and 2 in 2 H2O); the balanced form is CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O.

Chemistry.q: In the reaction 2 Na + Cl2 → 2 NaCl, each neutral sodium atom becomes a sodium ion, Na+. Which statement correctly describes what happens to sodium?
o: Sodium is reduced, because its charge increases
Sodium is reduced, because it loses an electron
Sodium is oxidized, because it loses an electron
Sodium is oxidized, because it gains an electron
Chemistry.w: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG). Sodium loses one electron to become Na+, so it is oxidized; chlorine gains the electron and is reduced.

n.0: A rising (more positive) charge means electrons were lost, which is oxidation; reduction lowers the charge.
n.1: Losing electrons is oxidation, not reduction. Reduction is the gain of electrons.
n.3: Gaining an electron would give sodium a negative charge; forming Na+ requires losing one.

Chemistry.q: Burning natural gas on a stove and photosynthesis in a plant leaf are both chemical reactions. Which statement correctly classifies their energy changes?
o: Burning is exothermic; photosynthesis is endothermic
Both are endothermic, because both need energy to start
Both are exothermic, because both involve oxygen gas
Burning is endothermic; photosynthesis is exothermic
Chemistry.w: Combustion releases heat and light to the surroundings (exothermic). Photosynthesis absorbs energy from sunlight and stores it in glucose (endothermic).

n.1: Needing a spark to start describes activation energy; a reaction that starts this way can still release more energy than it absorbs overall.
n.2: Involving oxygen does not decide the energy change; photosynthesis absorbs energy even though it releases oxygen.
n.3: This reverses the two. Burning warms the surroundings, while photosynthesis takes in light energy.

Chemistry.q: Glucose reacts completely with oxygen in a combustion-type reaction: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → ? Which products correctly complete the balanced equation?
o: 6 CH2O + 6 O2
6 CO2 + 6 H2O
6 CO + 6 H2O + 3 O2
Chemistry.w: Complete combustion of a compound containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water. Balancing: 6 C gives 6 CO2, 12 H gives 6 H2O, and 6 x 2 + 6 = 18 O atoms on the right match 6 + 12 = 18 on the left. The same overall equation describes cellular respiration.

n.0: This is balanced, but it leaves the oxygen unreacted; the products of complete combustion are CO2 and H2O.
n.2: This is balanced, but complete combustion forms CO2, not carbon monoxide, and O2 is consumed, not produced.
n.3: This is balanced, but hydrogen ends up as water, not H2 gas, and oxygen gas is a reactant here, not a product.

Chemistry.q: Hydrogen peroxide stored in a clear bottle slowly breaks down when exposed to light, according to the equation 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2. Which type of reaction is this?
o: Decomposition
Single replacement
Combustion
Synthesis
Chemistry.w: A decomposition reaction (AB → A + B) breaks one compound into two or more simpler substances. Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen.

n.1: Single replacement needs a free element replacing another in a compound; there is only one reactant here.
n.2: Combustion is a fuel reacting with O2 to produce CO2 and H2O; here O2 is produced, not consumed.
n.3: Synthesis is the reverse pattern: two or more reactants combine into one product.

Chemistry.q: Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen according to 2 H2 + O2 → 2 H2O, releasing heat and light. Which classifications correctly apply to this reaction? Select all that apply.
o: Synthesis
Oxidation-reduction
Double replacement
Exothermic
Endothermic
Decomposition
Chemistry.w: Two reactants combine into one product (synthesis, A + B → AB). The reaction releases heat and light (exothermic). Hydrogen loses electrons to oxygen, so hydrogen is oxidized and oxygen is reduced (redox), as in all combustion.

n.2: Double replacement needs two compounds swapping partners; both reactants here are elements.
n.4: The reaction releases heat and light, so it is exothermic, not endothermic.
n.5: Decomposition breaks one compound apart; here two elements combine into one compound.

Chemistry.q: Place the steps for balancing a chemical equation in the order a student should perform them, starting with the first.
o: Recount the atoms to confirm every element is balanced
Count the atoms of each element on both sides of the arrow
Write the correct formulas for all reactants and products
Add coefficients to balance one element at a time
Chemistry.w: First write correct formulas, which are never changed afterward. Then count the atoms of each element on each side, adjust coefficients one element at a time, and finally recount to check that every element balances (using the smallest whole-number coefficients).

Chemistry.q: A glowing wooden splint smolders slowly in air, but when it is placed in a jar of pure oxygen, it bursts into flame. Which factor best explains the faster reaction in pure oxygen?
o: A higher concentration of one of the reactants
A larger surface area of the wood exposed in the jar
A lower activation energy for oxygen in a closed jar
A catalyst present in pure oxygen but missing in air
Chemistry.w: Air is only about 21% oxygen. In pure oxygen, there are many more O2 molecules per unit volume, so they collide with the wood far more often. Raising the concentration of a reactant increases the reaction rate.

n.1: The splint is the same piece of wood in both cases, so its surface area has not changed.
n.2: Activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway; it changes when a catalyst is added, not when oxygen is concentrated.
n.3: Oxygen is a reactant in combustion, not a catalyst, and the rate rises because there is more of it.

Chemistry.q: A patient is told to chew an antacid tablet thoroughly rather than swallow it whole so it neutralizes stomach acid faster. Which factor explains the faster reaction?
o: Greater surface area of the tablet exposed to acid
Higher concentration of the antacid in each particle
Lower activation energy for each antacid particle
Higher temperature produced by the act of chewing
Chemistry.w: Breaking a solid into small pieces exposes more of its particles to the other reactant, increasing the number of collisions per second. Greater surface area increases the reaction rate.

n.1: Chewing breaks the tablet into smaller pieces but does not change the concentration of antacid within each piece.
n.2: Chewing does not change the reaction pathway, so the activation energy stays the same; only a catalyst lowers it.
n.3: Chewing does not noticeably warm the tablet; the effect comes from the increased surface area.

Chemistry.q: Most chemical reactions speed up when the temperature rises, and many roughly double in rate for every 10 °C increase. What is the main reason raising the temperature increases a reaction rate?
o: Particles move faster, which lowers the activation energy needed
Particles grow larger, so they collide with one another more often
Particles gain mass, so each collision transfers more energy
Particles move faster, so more collisions have the activation energy
Chemistry.w: At a higher temperature particles move faster, which slightly increases collision frequency but, more importantly, greatly increases the fraction of collisions that have at least the activation energy. More effective collisions mean a faster reaction.

n.0: Temperature changes the particles' energy, not the activation energy of the reaction; a catalyst is what lowers activation energy.
n.1: Heating does not change the size of particles; it increases how fast they move.
n.2: Particle mass is unchanged by heating; the extra energy is kinetic energy from faster motion.

Chemistry.q: A reversible reaction in a sealed container is allowed to run until it reaches dynamic equilibrium. Which statement is true once equilibrium is reached?
o: Forward and reverse rates are equal; amounts hold steady
Reactant and product concentrations have become equal
The forward rate is faster, so products keep building up
Both reactions have stopped, so the amounts stay constant
Chemistry.w: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant, though usually not equal to each other.

n.1: Concentrations become constant, not necessarily equal; an equilibrium mixture can be mostly products or mostly reactants.
n.2: If the forward rate were faster, the system would not yet be at equilibrium.
n.3: Amounts are constant, but both reactions keep running; equilibrium is dynamic, not stopped.

Chemistry.q: Ammonia is made by the reaction N2 + 3 H2 ⇌ 2 NH3. While the mixture is at equilibrium, more N2 gas is pumped into the container. How does the system respond?
o: It shifts right, forming more NH3
It stays put, because the rates were equal
It shifts left, forming more N2
It shifts left, forming more H2
Chemistry.w: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to counteract a stress. Adding a reactant (N2) is relieved by using some of it up, so the equilibrium shifts right, toward the product, forming more NH3.

n.1: Adding N2 speeds the forward reaction, so the rates are no longer equal until the system shifts and reaches a new equilibrium.
n.2: The system responds by consuming some of the added N2, not by making more of it.
n.3: Shifting left would produce more reactants and increase the stress; adding a reactant drives the reaction toward products.

Chemistry.q: Consider the gas-phase reaction 2 SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2 SO3 at equilibrium. If the volume of the container is decreased, raising the pressure, which way will the equilibrium shift?
o: Toward SO2 and O2, the side with more moles of gas
Toward SO3, the side with fewer moles of gas
Toward SO2 and O2, because pressure favors reactants
No shift, because pressure changes rates, not position
Chemistry.w: Increasing pressure shifts an equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas, which reduces the pressure. The left side has 2 + 1 = 3 moles of gas and the right side has 2, so the shift is toward SO3.

n.0: Shifting toward more gas molecules would raise the pressure further; the system shifts to reduce the stress.
n.2: Pressure does not favor reactants as a rule; it favors whichever side has fewer moles of gas.
n.3: Changing pressure by changing volume does shift an equilibrium when the two sides have different numbers of gas moles.

Chemistry.q: The reaction 2 NO2 ⇌ N2O4 releases heat in the forward direction (it is exothermic). If this equilibrium mixture is heated, how will the equilibrium respond?
o: It shifts right, because heating speeds the forward rate
It shifts right, toward N2O4, the exothermic direction
It does not shift, because heat affects rate, not equilibrium
It shifts left, toward NO2, the endothermic direction
Chemistry.w: For an exothermic reaction, heat acts like a product. Adding heat is a stress that the system relieves by shifting in the endothermic direction, which is to the left, producing more NO2.

n.0: Heating speeds both directions, but it speeds the endothermic (reverse) reaction more, so the net shift is left.
n.1: Shifting in the exothermic direction would release even more heat; raising temperature favors the endothermic direction.
n.2: Temperature changes do shift equilibrium; it is a catalyst that leaves the equilibrium position unchanged.

Chemistry.q: A chemist adds a catalyst to a reaction mixture that has already reached equilibrium. What happens to the equilibrium amounts of reactants and products?
o: They stay the same, because both rates rise equally
They shift toward more products, as the forward rate rises
They shift toward more reactants, as the reverse rate rises
They change as the catalyst is gradually used up
Chemistry.w: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and reverse reactions equally, so both rates increase by the same factor. Equilibrium is reached faster, but the equilibrium amounts do not change, and the catalyst is not consumed.

n.1: The forward rate does rise, but the reverse rate rises equally, so there is no net shift toward products.
n.2: The reverse rate rises, but by the same factor as the forward rate, so there is no shift toward reactants.
n.3: A catalyst is not consumed by the reaction; it is recovered unchanged at the end.

Chemistry.q: In the blood, CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3-. A patient who is breathing very slowly retains extra CO2. How does this affect the equilibrium and the blood pH?
o: It shifts left, raising H+ and lowering pH
It shifts left, lowering H+ and raising pH
It shifts right, raising H+ and raising pH
It shifts right, raising H+ and lowering pH
Chemistry.w: Step 1: adding CO2 (a reactant) shifts the equilibrium to the right, producing more H2CO3 and therefore more H+. Step 2: more H+ means a lower pH, so retained CO2 tends to cause acidosis. Breathing faster blows off CO2 and shifts the equilibrium left.

n.0: A left shift would use up H+, not raise it; the direction and the H+ change contradict each other.
n.1: Adding a reactant shifts an equilibrium right, not left. A left shift happens when CO2 is blown off.
n.2: The shift and the rise in H+ are right, but more H+ lowers pH; pH and H+ concentration move in opposite directions.

Chemistry.q: On an energy diagram for a reaction, the curve rises from the reactants to a peak and then falls to the products. What does the height from the reactants up to the peak represent?
o: The activation energy needed to start the reaction
The change in energy between reactants and products
The total energy released by the reaction
The energy stored in the bonds of the products
Chemistry.w: The 'hill' between the reactants and the peak is the activation energy, the minimum energy colliding particles need to react. A catalyst lowers this peak.

n.1: The overall energy change (delta H) is the difference between the reactant and product levels, which does not include the peak.
n.2: The energy released is the drop from the reactants down to the products, not the rise to the peak.
n.3: The energy of the products is the level of the curve after the peak, not the height of the climb.

Chemistry.q: Equal masses of zinc react with equal volumes of hydrochloric acid under five sets of conditions. Place the setups in order of reaction rate, starting with the slowest.
o: Zinc powder in 2 M acid at 20 °C
Zinc granules in 1 M acid at 20 °C
Zinc powder in 1 M acid at 20 °C
Zinc powder in 2 M acid at 40 °C
One zinc lump in 1 M acid at 20 °C
Chemistry.w: Each step changes one factor that speeds the reaction. Breaking the zinc from a lump into granules and then powder increases its surface area; doubling the acid concentration increases collisions; raising the temperature increases the share of collisions with enough energy. The warm, concentrated acid with powdered zinc is fastest.

Chemistry.q: Enzymes in the body and platinum in a car's catalytic converter both act as catalysts. Which statements about catalysts are correct? Select all that apply.
o: They are recovered chemically unchanged after the reaction
They increase the rate of both forward and reverse reactions
They shift the equilibrium toward the products
They are used up as the reaction proceeds
They provide a reaction pathway with lower activation energy
They raise the activation energy so collisions carry more energy
Chemistry.w: A catalyst speeds a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy. It speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster without being shifted, and it is not consumed. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

n.2: A catalyst speeds both directions equally, so it does not change the position of equilibrium.
n.3: A catalyst is not consumed; it is regenerated and can be used again.
n.5: Catalysts lower, not raise, the activation energy.

Chemistry.q: A pharmacist prepares an iodine tincture by dissolving a small amount of solid iodine in a much larger volume of ethanol, with no water added. Which choice correctly identifies the parts of this solution?
o: Iodine is the solute; ethanol is the solvent
Ethanol is the solute; iodine is the solvent
Both are solutes, because no water is present to dissolve them
Iodine is the solute; the tincture is the solvent
Chemistry.w: The solute is the substance being dissolved (usually the smaller amount), and the solvent is the substance doing the dissolving (usually the larger amount). Water is the most common solvent, but in a tincture the solvent is alcohol: iodine is the solute and ethanol is the solvent.

n.1: This reverses the roles: the iodine is the substance being dissolved, and the ethanol, present in the larger amount, does the dissolving.
n.2: Water is the most common solvent, but not a requirement; here ethanol, the larger amount, does the dissolving, so it is the solvent.
n.3: The tincture is the whole solution, not one of its parts; the solvent is the ethanol that dissolves the iodine.

Chemistry.q: A cook notices that olive oil forms a separate layer on water but dissolves easily in hexane, a liquid made of nonpolar molecules. Which statement explains this behavior?
o: Hexane is denser than water, so it holds more dissolved oil
Nonpolar oil dissolves in nonpolar hexane but not in polar water
Oil is an ionic compound that dissolves best in hexane
Polar oil dissolves in polar hexane but not in nonpolar water
Chemistry.w: 'Like dissolves like': nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents, and polar or ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents. Oil is nonpolar, so it mixes with hexane but not with polar water.

n.0: Density decides which layer floats, not whether a substance dissolves; hexane is actually less dense than water.
n.2: Ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents such as water, not in nonpolar hexane; oil is nonpolar and molecular.
n.3: The rule is applied correctly, but the labels are reversed: oil and hexane are nonpolar, and water is polar.

Chemistry.q: An opened bottle of soda goes flat much faster when it is left on a hot porch than when it is kept in a refrigerator. Which statement best explains this?
o: Gases are more soluble in warmer liquids
Warming raises the gas pressure above the soda
Heat breaks the dissolved CO2 into C and O2
Gases are less soluble in warmer liquids
Chemistry.w: Unlike most solids, gases become less soluble as temperature rises. Warm soda can hold less dissolved carbon dioxide, so the gas escapes faster and the drink goes flat.

n.0: This reverses the rule for gases; more soluble gas would keep the soda fizzy longer when warm.
n.1: Higher gas pressure above a liquid would force more gas into solution, not less (Henry's law).
n.2: Warming a drink does not decompose carbon dioxide; the CO2 simply comes out of solution as a gas.

Chemistry.q: A student tests four liquids with a simple conductivity tester that lights a bulb when current flows. Which liquid will light the bulb?
o: Table sugar (sucrose) dissolved in water
Pure distilled water
Ethanol mixed with an equal volume of water
Potassium chloride dissolved in water
Chemistry.w: Ionic compounds such as KCl dissociate into ions (K+ and Cl-) in water. Mobile ions carry current, so the solution is an electrolyte and conducts electricity.

n.0: Sucrose dissolves as whole molecules, not ions, so its solution is a nonelectrolyte.
n.1: Pure water contains too few ions to conduct noticeably; dissolved ions are what make tap and salt water conduct.
n.2: Ethanol dissolves as neutral molecules, so the mixture does not conduct.

Chemistry.q: A solution is made by dissolving 0.25 mole of glucose in enough water to make 500 mL of solution. What is the molarity of the solution? Enter your answer in moles per liter (M), rounded to the nearest tenth.

tr.2: Divided liters by moles (0.5 / 0.25) instead of moles by liters.

Chemistry.w: Molarity = moles of solute / liters of solution. Convert 500 mL to 0.500 L, then 0.25 mol / 0.500 L = 0.5 M.

Chemistry.q: Normal saline used for IV fluids is 0.9% (w/v) sodium chloride. How many grams of sodium chloride are dissolved in 1 liter of normal saline?
o: 9 g
Chemistry.w: Step 1: % (w/v) means grams of solute per 100 mL of solution, so 0.9% is 0.9 g per 100 mL. Step 2: 1 liter is 1,000 mL, or 10 x 100 mL, so the bag holds 0.9 x 10 = 9 g of NaCl.

n.0: 0.9 g is the amount in 100 mL, not in a full liter.
n.1: 0.09 g misplaces the decimal point; it is ten times too small even for 100 mL, let alone a liter.
n.3: 90 g would be a 9% solution; this moves the decimal point one place too far.

Chemistry.q: A pharmacist must prepare 200 mL of a 2 M solution by diluting a 10 M stock solution with water. What volume of the stock solution is needed? Enter your answer in milliliters as a whole number.

tr.160: Gave the volume of water to add, not the volume of stock needed.

Chemistry.w: Use C1V1 = C2V2 (the moles of solute do not change on dilution). 10 M x V1 = 2 M x 200 mL, so V1 = 400 / 10 = 40 mL of stock, made up to 200 mL with 160 mL of water.

Chemistry.q: A student adds sugar to water at 25 °C and stirs for several minutes, but some sugar crystals remain undissolved on the bottom of the glass. How should the liquid in the glass be classified?
o: Saturated, so it cannot dissolve any other solute
Unsaturated, because the stirring is not yet complete
Saturated, holding the most sugar it can at 25 °C
Supersaturated, holding more sugar than its maximum
Chemistry.w: A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve at that temperature; any extra stays undissolved. The leftover crystals show the sugar solution has reached its limit at 25 °C.

n.0: It is saturated, but a solution saturated with sugar can still dissolve other solutes, such as salt.
n.1: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more solute; undissolved crystals after thorough stirring show it cannot.
n.3: A supersaturated solution holds more than the normal maximum with no undissolved solid; it is unstable and made by careful cooling.

Chemistry.q: Stirring a cup of iced tea makes the added sugar dissolve faster. Which statement correctly describes what stirring changes?
o: The temperature of the tea, which raises the solubility
The solubility of sugar, so more sugar can dissolve in total
The speed of dissolving, but not the solubility of sugar
Both the solubility of sugar and the speed of dissolving
Chemistry.w: Stirring brings fresh solvent into contact with the solute, increasing the rate of dissolving. Solubility, the maximum amount that can dissolve, depends on temperature (and pressure for gases), not on stirring.

n.0: Stirring does not noticeably change the temperature of the tea, so it does not change solubility.
n.1: Stirring affects how fast sugar dissolves, not the total amount that can dissolve.
n.3: Stirring changes the rate only; solubility at a given temperature is fixed.

Chemistry.q: Red blood cells are placed in a salt solution that has a higher solute concentration than the fluid inside the cells. What happens to the cells?
o: Salt moves into the cells until they burst
Water moves out of the cells, and they shrink
Water moves both ways equally, and size holds
Water moves into the cells, and they swell
Chemistry.w: In osmosis, water moves across a semipermeable membrane toward the higher solute concentration. The outside solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the cells and they shrink (crenate).

n.0: Osmosis is the movement of water, not salt; the cells lose water and shrink.
n.2: Equal movement both ways describes an isotonic solution, such as 0.9% saline.
n.3: Swelling happens in a hypotonic solution, where the outside solute concentration is lower.

Chemistry.q: Place pure water and three aqueous solutions, each made with 1 mole of solute per kilogram of water, in order of freezing point, starting with the highest freezing point.
o: Calcium chloride (CaCl2) solution
Sodium chloride (NaCl) solution
Glucose solution
Pure water
Chemistry.w: Freezing point depression is a colligative property: the more dissolved particles, the lower the freezing point. Pure water has no solute particles (freezes at 0 °C). Glucose dissolves as 1 particle per unit, NaCl gives 2 ions, and CaCl2 gives 3 ions, so the CaCl2 solution has the lowest freezing point.

Chemistry.q: A fish tank owner wants the water to hold as much dissolved oxygen as possible. Which changes would increase the amount of oxygen gas that can dissolve in the water? Select all that apply.
o: Heating the water
Cooling the water
Lowering the air pressure above the water's surface
Raising the pressure of oxygen above the water
Stirring the water faster
Chemistry.w: Gases are more soluble in colder liquids, and, by Henry's law, more gas dissolves when the pressure of that gas above the liquid is higher.

n.0: Heating lowers the solubility of gases; warm water holds less oxygen.
n.2: Lowering the pressure above the water lets dissolved gas escape, as when a soda is opened.
n.4: Stirring changes how quickly gas dissolves or escapes, not the maximum amount that can dissolve.

Chemistry.q: Solution A has a pH of 3 and solution B has a pH of 6. How does the hydrogen ion concentration of solution A compare with that of solution B?
o: 30 times greater
1,000 times greater
3 times greater
1,000 times smaller
Chemistry.w: The pH scale is logarithmic: each 1-unit drop in pH is a 10-fold increase in [H+]. From pH 6 to pH 3 is 3 units, so A has 10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000 times the hydrogen ion concentration of B.

n.0: This multiplies the 3-unit difference by 10 instead of raising 10 to the third power.
n.2: This treats the pH scale as linear (6 - 3 = 3). Each pH unit is a tenfold change.
n.3: The size of the difference is right, but the lower pH (A) has the higher [H+], so A is more acidic, not less.

Chemistry.q: A student dips strips of red and blue litmus paper into a household cleaner. The red strip turns blue, and the blue strip stays blue. What does this result show about the cleaner?
o: It is a base, with a pH below 7
It is an acid, with a pH below 7
It is a base, with a pH above 7
It is neutral, with a pH of 7
Chemistry.w: Bases turn red litmus blue; acids turn blue litmus red. A red strip turning blue identifies a base, and bases have a pH above 7.

n.0: It is a base, but a pH below 7 describes an acid; bases have a pH above 7.
n.1: An acid would turn the blue strip red and leave the red strip unchanged, which is the opposite of what was seen.
n.3: A neutral solution would not change the color of either litmus strip.

Chemistry.q: Ammonia reacts with water according to NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH-. Which substance acts as a Bronsted-Lowry base in the forward reaction, and why?
o: NH3, because it accepts a proton from water
NH3, because it donates a proton to water
NH3, because it contains a hydroxide ion
H2O, because it accepts a proton from NH3
Chemistry.w: A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton (H+) acceptor. NH3 takes an H+ from water and becomes NH4+, so NH3 is the base and water acts as the acid (proton donor).

n.1: Donating a proton is what an acid does. NH3 gains a proton to become NH4+.
n.2: NH3 contains no hydroxide ion; it is a base because it accepts a proton, which is the point of the Bronsted-Lowry definition.
n.3: Water loses a proton here (becoming OH-), so water is the acid, not the base.

Chemistry.q: A lab reports that a patient's arterial blood has a pH of 7.32. How should this value be classified?
o: Alkalosis, because it is above the neutral pH of 7
Acidosis, because it is below the normal range of 7.35-7.45
Normal, because blood is slightly acidic at about 7.3
Normal, because it is within 0.5 of the neutral pH of 7
Chemistry.w: Normal blood pH is 7.35-7.45, which is slightly basic. A pH below 7.35 is acidosis and a pH above 7.45 is alkalosis, so 7.32 is acidosis even though it is above 7.

n.0: Blood is judged against its normal range, not against neutral 7; 7.32 is below that range, which is acidosis.
n.2: Normal blood is slightly basic (7.35-7.45), not slightly acidic, and 7.32 falls below the normal range.
n.3: The healthy range is narrow (7.35-7.45); being near 7 is not the standard for blood.

Chemistry.q: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is described as a strong acid, while the acetic acid in vinegar is a weak acid. What does the term 'strong' refer to?
o: How completely the acid ionizes in water
How many hydrogen atoms each molecule holds
How concentrated the acid solution is
How much base is needed to neutralize it
Chemistry.w: Acid strength refers to the degree of ionization: a strong acid such as HCl ionizes completely in water, while a weak acid such as acetic acid ionizes only partially.

n.1: The number of hydrogen atoms does not set strength; acetic acid (CH3COOH) has four hydrogens but is weak.
n.2: Concentration is how much acid is dissolved in a volume; a strong acid can be dilute and a weak acid concentrated.
n.3: The amount of base needed depends on the moles of acid present, not on whether the acid is strong or weak.

Chemistry.q: An antacid containing magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, is taken to neutralize excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach. What are the products of this neutralization reaction?
o: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas
Magnesium chloride and carbon dioxide
Magnesium chloride and water
Magnesium oxide and chlorine gas
Chemistry.w: Acid + base → salt + water. Mg(OH)2 + 2 HCl → MgCl2 + 2 H2O: the salt is magnesium chloride, and H+ from the acid joins OH- from the base to form water.

n.0: Hydrogen gas forms when an acid reacts with an active metal, not with a hydroxide base.
n.1: Carbon dioxide forms when an acid reacts with a carbonate antacid (such as CaCO3); magnesium hydroxide contains no carbon.
n.3: Neutralization swaps ions to give a salt and water; it does not produce chlorine gas or an oxide.

Chemistry.q: The carbonic acid-bicarbonate system helps keep blood pH within its normal range. Which statement best describes how a buffer such as this one works?
o: It pairs a strong acid with a strong base in equal amounts
It makes blood neutral, holding its pH close to 7.0
It resists pH change when a little acid or base is added
It sends added acid to the kidneys for removal within seconds
Chemistry.w: A buffer, usually a weak acid and its conjugate base, resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added: the base part absorbs added H+, and the acid part neutralizes added OH-. Its capacity is limited.

n.0: Buffers are made from a weak acid and its conjugate base (H2CO3 and HCO3-); a strong acid and strong base would simply neutralize each other.
n.1: Blood is kept slightly basic, at 7.35-7.45, not neutral; the buffer limits pH change around that value rather than moving it to 7.0.
n.3: The kidneys adjust H+ and HCO3- over hours to days; the buffer itself acts chemically and at once, binding added H+ with bicarbonate.

Chemistry.q: A cleaning solution has a pOH of 3 at 25 °C. What is the pH of the solution? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.3: Copied the pOH as the pH.

Chemistry.w: At 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, so pH = 14 - 3 = 11. The solution is basic (pH above 7).

Chemistry.q: A few drops of phenolphthalein indicator are added to a clear, colorless solution, and the solution turns pink. Which of these could the solution be?
o: Distilled water
Dilute sodium hydroxide
Carbonated water
Dilute acetic acid (vinegar)
Chemistry.w: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic and neutral solutions and turns pink in basic solutions. Sodium hydroxide is a strong base.

n.0: Pure water is neutral (pH 7), so phenolphthalein stays colorless.
n.2: Carbonated water contains carbonic acid, so it is acidic and the indicator stays colorless.
n.3: Vinegar is acidic, so phenolphthalein stays colorless.

Chemistry.q: Place these substances in order of pH, starting with the most acidic and ending with the most basic.
o: Household ammonia
Stomach acid
Black coffee
Human blood
Pure water
Chemistry.w: Approximate pH values: stomach acid 1.5-3.5, black coffee about 5, pure water 7 (neutral), blood 7.35-7.45 (slightly basic) and household ammonia about 11. Lower pH means more acidic.

Chemistry.q: A student is listing the typical properties of acids for a study guide. Which properties are characteristic of acids? Select all that apply.
o: They react with zinc to release hydrogen gas
They turn blue litmus paper red
They taste sour
They turn phenolphthalein pink
They accept protons from water molecules
They feel slippery to the touch
Chemistry.w: Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red, and react with active metals such as zinc to release hydrogen gas (H2). They donate protons (H+).

n.3: Phenolphthalein turns pink in bases; it stays colorless in acids.
n.4: Accepting protons defines a Bronsted-Lowry base; acids donate protons.
n.5: A slippery, soapy feel is a property of bases.

Chemistry.q: A 0.001 M solution of hydrochloric acid (HCl) is compared with a 1 M solution of acetic acid. Which statement correctly compares the two acids?
o: HCl is the stronger acid, because its solution is more concentrated
Acetic acid is the stronger acid, because its solution is more concentrated
HCl is the stronger acid, even though its solution is more dilute
The two are equally strong, because both release hydrogen ions
Chemistry.w: Strength and concentration are different ideas. HCl is a strong acid because it ionizes completely; acetic acid is weak because it ionizes only partly. Here the strong acid happens to be in the more dilute solution.

n.0: HCl is stronger, but its solution is the more dilute one (0.001 M vs 1 M).
n.1: A more concentrated solution does not make an acid stronger; acetic acid is weak at any concentration.
n.3: Both release H+, but HCl ionizes completely and acetic acid only partly, so they differ in strength.

Scientific Reasoning.q: In a biology lab, a student is asked to find the weight of a bag of potting soil in newtons rather than its mass in grams. Which instrument reads this quantity directly?
o: A two-pan balance with standard masses
A spring scale
A triple-beam balance
An electronic analytical balance
Scientific Reasoning.w: Weight is a force, measured in newtons. A spring scale reads force directly from how far its spring stretches. Balances compare an object against known masses and report mass in grams.

n.0: A two-pan balance compares the object with standard masses, so it measures mass, not weight.
n.2: A triple-beam balance measures mass in grams by balancing riders on beams, not force in newtons.
n.3: An analytical balance reports mass in grams to high precision; it is not used to report weight in newtons.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A graduated cylinder holds 42.0 mL of water. A student lowers a small stone into it, and the level rises to 57.5 mL. A balance shows the stone's mass is 31.0 g. What is the density of the stone?
o: 2.0 g/mL
Scientific Reasoning.w: Step 1: volume by water displacement = final level - initial level = 57.5 mL - 42.0 mL = 15.5 mL. Step 2: density = mass / volume = 31.0 g / 15.5 mL = 2.0 g/mL.

n.0: This divides volume by mass (15.5 / 31.0); density is mass divided by volume.
n.1: This divides the mass by the final water level (31.0 / 57.5) instead of by the displaced volume.
n.2: This divides the mass by the starting water level (31.0 / 42.0) instead of by the change in level.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student has a stained cheek-cell slide in focus under the low-power objective of a compound light microscope and then rotates to the high-power objective. Which next step is correct technique?
o: Lower the stage fully and refocus with the coarse knob
Raise the stage with the coarse knob until it nears the slide
Sharpen the image with the coarse adjustment knob
Sharpen the image with the fine adjustment knob
Scientific Reasoning.w: Focus is found first on low power with the coarse knob. Once on high power, the objective sits very close to the slide, so the image is sharpened with the fine adjustment knob.

n.0: Starting over with the coarse knob is unnecessary; a microscope that was in focus on low power needs a fine adjustment on high power.
n.1: Moving the stage up with the coarse knob on high power risks the objective striking the slide.
n.2: The coarse knob moves the stage in large steps; on high power it can drive the objective into the slide and break it.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A cell-culture protocol calls for 0.075 L of buffer solution. The graduated cylinder on the bench is marked in milliliters. Enter the volume to measure, in milliliters, as a whole number.

tr.750: Moved the decimal point four places.
tr.7.5: Moved the decimal point only two places (multiplied by 100, the centi factor).
tr.0.000075: Divided by 1,000 instead of multiplying when going from a larger to a smaller unit.

Scientific Reasoning.w: 1 L = 1,000 mL. Converting from a larger unit (liters) to a smaller unit (milliliters) means multiplying: 0.075 x 1,000 = 75 mL. Move the decimal point three places to the right.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A research protocol lists a vitamin supplement dose as 3 mg, but the lab's analysis software accepts doses in micrograms (mcg). Which value should be entered?
o: 300 mcg
Scientific Reasoning.w: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg (milli is 10⁻³ and micro is 10⁻⁶, a factor of 1,000 apart). Going from a larger unit to a smaller one, multiply: 3 x 1,000 = 3,000 mcg.

n.0: This is the number of micrograms in 3 g, not 3 mg (a factor of 1,000,000 is grams to micrograms).
n.1: This uses a factor of 100, as between meters and centimeters; milli and micro are a factor of 1,000 apart.
n.3: This divides by 1,000. Converting to a smaller unit gives a larger number, so multiply.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student sorting metric rulers and measuring tools by scale is asked to rank five lengths. Place the lengths in order from largest to smallest, starting with the largest.
o: 1 micrometer
1 centimeter
1 dekameter
1 kilometer
1 decimeter
Scientific Reasoning.w: 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 dam = 10 m; 1 dm = 0.1 m; 1 cm = 0.01 m; 1 micrometer = 0.000001 m (10⁻⁶ m). Deka (10) and deci (0.1) sound alike but sit on opposite sides of the base unit: King Henry Died By Drinking Chocolate Milk (kilo, hecto, deka, base, deci, centi, milli), with micro three steps below milli.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A chemistry student needs to dispense small liquid volumes with high precision during a titration lab. Which items are designed for precise volume measurement? Select all that apply.
o: Erlenmeyer flask
Pipette
Burette
Test tube
Volumetric flask
Beaker
Scientific Reasoning.w: Burettes (used in titration), pipettes and volumetric flasks are calibrated for precise volumes. A volumetric flask holds one exact volume; a pipette and burette deliver small precise volumes.

n.0: An Erlenmeyer flask is a container for swirling and mixing; its markings are approximate.
n.3: A test tube is a container for small samples and reactions, not a measuring tool.
n.5: A beaker is for holding, mixing and heating; its markings give a rough volume.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student views a blood smear through a compound light microscope with a 10x eyepiece (ocular lens) and a 40x objective lens. Enter the total magnification as a whole number.

tr.4: Divided the objective by the eyepiece.
tr.40: Used the objective lens alone and left out the eyepiece.
tr.50: Added the two lenses (10 + 40) instead of multiplying them.

Scientific Reasoning.w: Total magnification = ocular magnification x objective magnification = 10 x 40 = 400 (400x).

Scientific Reasoning.q: A lab thermometer is checked in a water bath held at exactly 50.0 °C. Readings: Trial 1, 47.1 °C; Trial 2, 47.0 °C; Trial 3, 47.2 °C. Which statement best describes the thermometer?
o: It is neither accurate nor precise.
It is accurate but not precise.
It is precise but not accurate.
It is both accurate and precise.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Precision is how close repeated readings are to each other; these agree within 0.2 °C, so they are precise. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; all three are about 3 °C low, so the thermometer is not accurate (a systematic error, such as poor calibration).

n.0: The readings agree within 0.2 °C of each other, so they are precise.
n.1: This swaps the terms: the readings agree closely with each other (precise) but sit far from 50.0 °C (not accurate).
n.3: Readings 3 °C below the known temperature are not accurate, however tightly they cluster.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student records the mass of a tiny crystal as 0.004050 g on an analytical balance. How many significant figures does this measurement contain?
Scientific Reasoning.w: Leading zeros (0.00) are placeholders and never count. The 4 and 5 count, the zero between them counts, and the trailing zero after the decimal point counts: 4, 0, 5, 0 = 4 significant figures.

n.0: This counts the zeros after the decimal point that come before the 4; leading zeros are not significant.
n.1: This drops the final zero; a trailing zero to the right of a decimal point is significant.
n.3: This counts every digit written, including all the leading zeros.

Scientific Reasoning.q: An electronic balance shows 0.20 g with nothing on the pan, but a student does not zero it. Each of five samples is then recorded 0.20 g heavier than its true mass. Which best describes this error?
o: Systematic error, which reduces accuracy
Systematic error, which reduces precision
Random error, which reduces precision
Random error, which reduces accuracy
Scientific Reasoning.w: An error that shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction is systematic. It moves the results away from the true values, so it reduces accuracy; the readings can still agree with each other.

n.1: A constant offset does not spread the readings out, so precision is unaffected; accuracy is what suffers.
n.2: Random error varies unpredictably from reading to reading; a constant 0.20 g offset is not random.
n.3: The error is identical every time, so it is systematic, not random.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Students timing how long a solution takes to change color get times that scatter a few seconds above and below each other with no pattern. Which change best reduces the effect of this error on their result?
o: Keep the trial closest to the predicted time
Let a different student time each trial
Run more trials and average the times
Recalibrate the stopwatch against a reference clock
Scientific Reasoning.w: Unpatterned scatter is random error. Repeating trials and averaging lets random highs and lows cancel, which reduces its effect on the result.

n.0: Choosing the trial that matches the prediction biases the data toward the expected answer.
n.1: Changing timers adds another source of variation between trials rather than reducing it.
n.3: Recalibration corrects a systematic error (a consistent offset), not random scatter.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student measures the density of an aluminum block as 2.43 g/cm³. The accepted value is 2.70 g/cm³. Enter the percent error as a whole number.

tr.11: Divided by the measured value (0.27 / 2.43) instead of the accepted value.
tr.27: Used the difference (0.27) times 100 without dividing by the accepted value.
tr.90: Divided the measured value by the accepted value (2.43 / 2.70) without finding the difference.

Scientific Reasoning.w: Percent error = |measured - accepted| / accepted x 100% = |2.43 - 2.70| / 2.70 x 100% = 0.27 / 2.70 x 100% = 10%.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A ruler is marked in millimeters (every 0.1 cm). The tip of a leaf lies about halfway between the 6.3 cm and 6.4 cm marks. Which recording follows the standard rule for reporting a measurement?
o: 6.4 cm
6.3 cm
Scientific Reasoning.w: A measurement is reported to one estimated digit beyond the smallest marking. The smallest marking is 0.1 cm, so the student reports to 0.01 cm: 6.35 cm.

n.1: Two digits beyond the smallest marking claims more precision than a millimeter ruler can give.
n.2: Rounding up to the next mark throws away the estimated digit and misstates the length.
n.3: This stops at the smallest marking and drops the estimated digit the scale allows.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A rectangular area on a microscope slide is measured as 2.5 cm by 3.42 cm. A student multiplies to find the area. How should the area be reported with the correct number of significant figures?
o: 8.6 cm²
9 cm²
8.55 cm²
Scientific Reasoning.w: 2.5 x 3.42 = 8.55. In multiplication, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures of the inputs: 2.5 has 2 and 3.42 has 3, so report 2 significant figures: 8.6 cm².

n.1: This rounds to 1 significant figure; the least precise input (2.5) has 2.
n.2: Adding a trailing zero claims 4 significant figures, more than either measurement supports.
n.3: This keeps 3 significant figures, but 2.5 cm limits the answer to 2.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student adds three reagents to a beaker and records their masses as 12.11 g, 0.3 g and 1.456 g. How should the total mass be reported?
Scientific Reasoning.w: Step 1: add, 12.11 + 0.3 + 1.456 = 13.866 g. Step 2: in addition, the answer keeps the fewest decimal places of the inputs; 0.3 g has one decimal place, so report 13.9 g.

n.1: This reports every digit from the calculator, implying more precision than 0.3 g allows.
n.2: This rounds to the ones place; the least precise value (0.3 g) supports one decimal place.
n.3: This keeps two decimal places, matching 12.11 g, but 0.3 g has only one.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Four lab groups each weigh a certified 10.00 g mass three times. Group A: 9.71, 10.32, 9.95 g. Group B: 10.41, 10.42, 10.40 g. Group C: 10.01, 9.99, 10.00 g. Group D: 9.62, 10.45, 10.21 g. Which group's results are both accurate and precise?
o: Group D
Group B
Group C
Group A
Scientific Reasoning.w: Group C's readings agree within 0.02 g of each other (precise) and center on 10.00 g (accurate).

n.0: Group D's readings spread over more than 0.8 g and average above 10.00 g.
n.1: Group B is precise (within 0.02 g) but about 0.4 g too high, so it is not accurate.
n.3: Group A averages close to 10.00 g, but its readings spread over 0.6 g, so it is not precise.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A new digital thermometer is compared with a reference reading of 37.0 °C. Its four readings are 36.4, 37.6, 36.9 and 37.1 °C, which average 37.0 °C. Which description fits these results?
o: Accurate on average but not precise
Both precise and accurate overall
Shifted high by a systematic error
Precise but off from the reference
Scientific Reasoning.w: The mean equals the reference value, so the readings are accurate on average. They spread over 1.2 °C, so they are not precise, like darts scattered around the bullseye.

n.1: Readings that differ by up to 1.2 °C from one another are not precise.
n.2: A systematic error shifts readings one way; these fall on both sides of 37.0 °C and average to it.
n.3: The readings spread over 1.2 °C, so they are not precise, and their mean matches the reference.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Throughout a lab, a student reads the water level in each graduated cylinder while standing and looking down at the meniscus. Which statement describes the effect on the volume data?
o: The error spreads out the readings but leaves their mean accurate.
The readings become more precise because the angle is the same each time.
Readings shift the same way each time, so averaging will not remove the error.
Readings scatter in both directions, so averaging trials removes the error.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Reading from above (parallax) shifts every reading in the same direction, which is systematic error. It reduces accuracy, and averaging repeated trials cannot cancel an error that always points the same way.

n.0: Parallax from a fixed angle moves the mean away from the true value, so the mean is not accurate.
n.1: Readings can agree with one another and still be wrong; the consistent angle produces a bias, not improved quality.
n.3: This describes random error; a consistent viewing angle produces a consistent shift, not scatter.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student is reviewing a data table and must flag every value that contains exactly three significant figures. Which values should be flagged? Select all that apply.
Scientific Reasoning.w: 0.00250 has 3 (leading zeros do not count; the trailing zero after the decimal does). 2.50 has 3 (trailing zero after a decimal point counts). 205 has 3 (a zero between nonzero digits counts).

n.0: 0.025 has 2 significant figures; the leading zeros are placeholders.
n.2: 0.002500 g has 4 significant figures: the 2, the 5 and both trailing zeros after the decimal point.
n.4: With no decimal point, the trailing zero in 250 is not counted as significant, giving 2 significant figures.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Under a microscope, a student estimates that a rod-shaped bacterium is 0.0000032 m long. How is this length written in scientific notation?
Scientific Reasoning.w: Move the decimal point right until one nonzero digit is in front of it: 0.0000032 becomes 3.2 after 6 moves. A number less than 1 takes a negative exponent, so the length is 3.2 × 10⁻⁶ m.

n.1: This counts 5 decimal moves instead of 6; 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ equals 0.000032.
n.2: A positive exponent describes a number greater than 1 (3,200,000), not a tiny length.
n.3: The value is equal, but the coefficient 32 is not between 1 and 10, so it is not proper scientific notation.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A clinic thermometer shows a patient's temperature as 102.2 °F. The student nurse charting it needs the value in degrees Celsius. Which value is correct?

n.0: This multiplies by 9/5, the factor for converting Celsius to Fahrenheit.
n.1: This multiplies by 5/9 first and subtracts 32 afterward; subtract 32 before multiplying.
n.2: This subtracts 32 but never multiplies by 5/9.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A chemistry teacher writes the freezing point of pure water at sea level on three different temperature scales. Which set shows the same temperature on all three scales?
Scientific Reasoning.w: Water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F = 273 K (K = °C + 273).

n.0: 373 K is the boiling point of water (100 °C), not the freezing point.
n.1: 0 K is absolute zero, about -273 °C, far below the freezing point of water.
n.2: 0 °F is about -18 °C; water freezes at 32 °F.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A bacterial culture contains 3.0 × 10⁴ cells per milliliter. A technician has 2.0 × 10³ mL of the culture. How many cells are in the full volume?
o: 6.0 × 10¹² cells
6.0 × 10¹ cells
5.0 × 10⁷ cells
6.0 × 10⁷ cells
Scientific Reasoning.w: To multiply in scientific notation, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents: (3.0 x 2.0) × 10⁽⁴⁺³⁾ = 6.0 × 10⁷ cells.

n.0: This multiplies the exponents (4 x 3 = 12); exponents are added when multiplying.
n.1: This subtracts the exponents (4 - 3), the rule for division, not multiplication.
n.2: This adds the coefficients (3.0 + 2.0); coefficients are multiplied.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A parent reports that a child's temperature was 104 °F at home. Convert this temperature to degrees Celsius. Enter your answer in degrees Celsius as a whole number.

tr.26: Multiplied by 5/9 first and then subtracted 32 (104 x 5/9 = 57.8; 57.8 - 32 = 25.8).
tr.72: Subtracted 32 but did not multiply by 5/9.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A cell-culture incubator's display reads 98.6 °F. A data logger in the same lab records temperature in kelvins. Enter the incubator temperature in kelvins, rounded to the nearest whole number.

tr.37: Converted to Celsius (37 °C) but stopped before adding 273.
tr.236: Converted to Celsius and then subtracted it from 273 instead of adding.
tr.372: Added 273 directly to the Fahrenheit reading (98.6 + 273 = 371.6) without converting to Celsius first.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A lab has 4.8 × 10⁹ bacteria to spread evenly across 1.2 × 10³ agar plates. How many bacteria go on each plate?
Scientific Reasoning.w: To divide in scientific notation, divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents: (4.8 / 1.2) × 10⁽⁹⁻³⁾ = 4.0 × 10⁶ bacteria per plate.

n.0: This subtracts the coefficients (4.8 - 1.2) instead of dividing them.
n.2: This adds the exponents (9 + 3), the rule for multiplication; division subtracts them.
n.3: This divides the exponents (9 / 3) instead of subtracting them.

Scientific Reasoning.q: An enzyme lab protocol written in Celsius says to keep samples at 30 °C, but the water bath in the lab displays only degrees Fahrenheit. Which setting matches the protocol?

n.0: This multiplies by 9/5 but leaves out adding 32.
n.1: This adds 32 but leaves out multiplying by 9/5.
n.3: This adds 32 first and then multiplies by 5/9, mixing up the two conversion formulas.

Scientific Reasoning.q: During a hard workout, a runner's core body temperature rises by 2 °C. By how much does the temperature rise on the Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales?
o: 3.6 °F and 2 K
2 °F and 2 K
3.6 °F and 275 K
Scientific Reasoning.w: This is a change, not a temperature reading. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K and a change of 1.8 °F, so 2 °C = 2 x 1.8 = 3.6 °F and 2 K. The +32 and +273 offsets apply to readings, not to differences.

n.0: This converts 2 °C as if it were a thermometer reading, adding the offsets 32 and 273 to a temperature change.
n.2: Kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size, but a Fahrenheit degree is smaller, so the change is 1.8 times larger in °F.
n.3: The Fahrenheit change is right, but adding 273 to a change is wrong; a 2 °C change is a 2 K change.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A lab report lists a healthy adult's red blood cell count as 5.2 × 10⁶ cells per microliter of blood. How is this count written in standard form?
o: 520,000 cells
Scientific Reasoning.w: A positive exponent of 6 moves the decimal point 6 places to the right: 5.2 becomes 5,200,000.

n.0: This moves the decimal point 5 places (5.2 × 10⁵).
n.1: This moves the decimal point 7 places (5.2 × 10⁷).
n.2: This treats the exponent as negative and moves the decimal point to the left.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A storage log lists five temperatures recorded on different scales. Place the temperatures in order from coldest to hottest, starting with the coldest.
A student checks a worksheet in which every value should be written in correct scientific notation. Which values are written correctly? Select all that apply.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Scientific notation is a × 10ⁿ with 1 <= a < 10. The coefficients 4.07, 1.0 and 9.99 all fall in that range; a negative exponent is allowed.

n.0: The coefficient 12.5 is 10 or greater; written correctly it is 1.25 × 10⁵.
n.1: A coefficient of 10 is not less than 10; written correctly it is 1 × 10³.
n.4: The coefficient 0.75 is less than 1; written correctly it is 7.5 × 10⁻⁴.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Maria notices that bread in her kitchen grows mold faster in summer than in winter. She asks whether temperature affects mold growth and reads several articles on fungi. What is her next step in the scientific method?
o: Report to classmates that temperature affects mold growth
Place bread slices at three temperatures and record mold daily
Predict that bread kept warmer will grow mold more quickly
Conclude that warm air causes faster mold growth on bread
Scientific Reasoning.w: After observing, asking a question and doing background research, the next step is to form a hypothesis: a testable prediction such as "bread kept warmer will grow mold more quickly." The experiment is designed to test it.

n.0: Communicating results is the last step; there are no results yet to report.
n.1: This is the experiment, which comes after the hypothesis it is designed to test.
n.3: A conclusion is drawn after data are collected and analyzed, not before any testing.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A biology class is planning an investigation on pea plants and light. Which statement is written as a testable scientific hypothesis?
o: Pea plants should be given as many hours of light as a grower can provide.
Pea plants grown under bright light are more attractive than shaded ones.
Do pea plants grow taller when they receive more hours of light each day?
If pea plants get 8 hours of light daily instead of 4, they will grow taller.
Scientific Reasoning.w: A hypothesis is a testable, tentative prediction, often in "If ... then ..." form. Plant height can be measured under two light conditions, so this statement can be supported or refuted by data.

n.0: This is a recommendation about what growers should do, not a prediction that can be tested.
n.1: "More attractive" is an opinion that cannot be measured objectively, so it is not testable.
n.2: This is the research question; a hypothesis is a statement that predicts an answer.

Scientific Reasoning.q: In a class discussion about how science works, a student asks how a scientific law differs from a scientific theory. Which statement gives the correct distinction?
o: A law explains why an event happens; a theory describes the pattern.
A theory becomes a law once enough experiments have proven it correct.
A theory is an educated guess that scientists have not yet tested.
A law describes what consistently happens; a theory explains why.
Scientific Reasoning.w: A law describes a consistent pattern, often mathematically (conservation of mass), without explaining it. A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation of many observations (cell theory). They do different jobs, so theories do not turn into laws.

n.0: This swaps the roles: laws describe, and theories explain.
n.1: Theories do not graduate into laws; a well-supported theory stays a theory because it explains rather than describes.
n.2: That describes a hypothesis; a theory is supported by extensive, repeated testing.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student's carefully controlled experiment produces data that do not support her hypothesis. According to the scientific method, what is the most appropriate response?
o: Report the results and revise the hypothesis for further testing
Reword the hypothesis to fit the data and report it as confirmed
Discard the results because the experiment did not work
Repeat the same trial until one result supports the hypothesis
Scientific Reasoning.w: Results that fail to support a hypothesis are still valid findings. The scientist reports them, revises the hypothesis and tests again; science is iterative.

n.1: A hypothesis rewritten after seeing the data has not been tested by those data, so it cannot be called confirmed.
n.2: A controlled experiment that rejects a hypothesis has worked; negative results are informative.
n.3: Repeating until a favorable result appears is cherry-picking, which biases the conclusion.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Tyler wonders why the houseplants near his window lean toward the glass. Place the steps of the scientific method in the order he should follow them, starting with the first.
o: Conduct an experiment
Draw a conclusion
Ask a question
Analyze the data
Make an observation
Form a hypothesis
Scientific Reasoning.w: The scientific method runs: observation (plants lean toward the window), question (why?), hypothesis (a testable prediction), experiment (test it), data analysis, then a conclusion that supports or rejects the hypothesis. Results are then communicated, and the cycle repeats if the hypothesis is rejected.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A nursing student investigates whether two hand sanitizers differ in how well they reduce bacteria on skin. Place her actions in the order they occur in the scientific method, starting with the first.
o: Reads published studies on alcohol-based sanitizers
Swabs hands after each sanitizer and incubates the plates
Concludes whether the data support her prediction
Counts colonies on each plate and compares the means
Predicts that the 70% alcohol gel will leave fewer bacteria
Presents her method and results to classmates for review
Scientific Reasoning.w: Background research comes first, then the hypothesis (her prediction), then the experiment (swabbing and incubating), then data analysis (counting and comparing), then the conclusion, and finally communicating results for review.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A science teacher lists four well-established statements on the board. Which statement is best classified as a scientific theory rather than a scientific law?
o: At constant temperature, a gas's pressure varies inversely with its volume.
In a closed system, total mass is the same before and after a reaction.
Two masses attract with a force that depends on their masses and distance.
All living things are made of cells, and new cells come from existing cells.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Cell theory is a broad explanation of how living things are organized and reproduce, supported by many observations. The other statements describe consistent, often mathematical, patterns without explaining why, which is what laws do.

n.0: This is Boyle's law, a mathematical description of a pattern in gases.
n.1: This is the law of conservation of mass: a description of what always happens in reactions.
n.2: This is the law of gravitation, a mathematical description of the attraction between masses.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Three trials of a student's experiment all show that bean seeds soaked overnight sprout faster than dry bean seeds, as her hypothesis predicted. Which conclusion is worded correctly?
o: The data support the hypothesis, which is now a scientific theory.
The data prove the hypothesis for the bean seeds tested.
The data support the hypothesis for seeds of all plant species.
The data support the hypothesis for the bean seeds tested.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Data support or fail to support a hypothesis; they do not prove it. A sound conclusion also stays within what was tested (bean seeds), and one small experiment does not create a theory.

n.0: A theory is a broad explanation tested many times by many scientists; one student's three trials do not turn a hypothesis into a theory.
n.1: Data support a hypothesis but never prove it; a later replicated result could still contradict it, even for bean seeds.
n.2: Only bean seeds were tested, so extending the result to every plant species generalizes beyond the population studied.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Research journals require scientists to describe their methods in enough detail for other researchers to follow. What is the main scientific purpose of this requirement?
o: It lets readers apply the results to any population.
It lets editors judge the authors' expertise and reputation.
It lets reviewers confirm that the hypothesis has been proven.
It lets other scientists repeat the work and check the results.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Scientific explanations must be reproducible. Detailed methods let independent scientists replicate the study, and peer review and replication check whether the conclusions hold.

n.0: Detailed methods show exactly who and what was studied, which limits the conclusions to that population rather than extending them.
n.1: Judging a claim by the authors' authority is not evidence; methods are described so the work itself can be checked.
n.2: Evidence supports a hypothesis but never proves it; methods are shared so the work can be checked, and possibly refuted.

Scientific Reasoning.q: After four weeks, a researcher calculates the mean height of the plants in each fertilizer group and plots the means on a bar graph. She has not yet decided what the results mean. Which step is she performing?
o: Drawing a conclusion
Analyzing the data
Conducting the experiment
Forming a hypothesis
Scientific Reasoning.w: Calculating means and graphing them is data analysis. Deciding whether the results support the hypothesis, the conclusion, comes next.

n.0: The conclusion is the decision about whether the data support the hypothesis, which she has not made yet.
n.2: Conducting the experiment was the four weeks of growing and measuring; summarizing those numbers is analysis.
n.3: The hypothesis was formed before the plants were grown.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A teacher builds a device from a jar, two balloons and a stretched rubber sheet. Pulling the sheet down inflates the balloons, showing how the diaphragm moves air into the lungs. Which description of this device is most accurate?
o: A theory that explains breathing through repeated observations
A model that simplifies the chest to explain how breathing works
A controlled experiment that tests how the diaphragm moves air
A replica that reproduces every process that occurs in the lungs
Scientific Reasoning.w: A model is a simplified physical, mathematical or conceptual representation used to explain and predict. The jar stands in for the chest cavity, the balloons for the lungs and the sheet for the diaphragm; like every model, it leaves out details such as gas exchange.

n.0: A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation stated in words or equations, not a physical device built to demonstrate a process.
n.2: A controlled experiment compares groups that differ in one variable to test a hypothesis; this device demonstrates a known process with no comparison group.
n.3: Models are simplified: the balloons inflate but do not exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide as real alveoli do.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student is writing a study guide entry on scientific theories, such as cell theory and germ theory. Which statements about a scientific theory are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It becomes a law once it has been proven.
It is well supported by repeated testing.
It explains a broad range of observations.
It can be revised when new evidence appears.
It describes a pattern but does not explain it.
It is a tentative guess that is not yet tested.
Scientific Reasoning.w: A theory is a broad, well-supported explanation of many observations that has been tested repeatedly, and like all scientific knowledge it can be revised when new evidence appears.

n.0: Theories do not graduate into laws; laws describe patterns and theories explain them.
n.4: Describing a pattern without explaining it is what a law does.
n.5: A tentative, untested explanation is a hypothesis; a theory is extensively tested.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student grows bean plants with 0, 5, 10 or 15 g of fertilizer per pot, using the same soil, pot size and daily water. After three weeks she measures each plant's height. What is the dependent variable?
o: Plant height after three weeks
Type of soil used in each pot
Mass of fertilizer in each pot
Volume of water given each day
Scientific Reasoning.w: The dependent variable is what is measured in response to the change; here, plant height. The fertilizer mass is what she deliberately changes (independent variable).

n.1: Soil type is kept the same in every pot, so it is a controlled variable.
n.2: Fertilizer mass is the independent variable: the factor the student deliberately changes.
n.3: Daily water is held constant, so it is a controlled variable.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Researchers test a new mouthwash. Group A rinses with 10 mL of it, Group B rinses with 20 mL, and Group C rinses with 10 mL of an identical-looking liquid with no active ingredient. Which is the control group?
o: Group A, which receives the standard dose
Group B, which receives the largest dose
All three groups, since rinse time is the same
Group C, which receives the inactive liquid
Scientific Reasoning.w: The control group does not receive the treatment and serves as the baseline. Group C receives a placebo, an inactive look-alike, so differences in the other groups can be credited to the active ingredient.

n.0: Group A receives the active treatment, so it is an experimental group.
n.1: The group with the most treatment is still an experimental group, not the control.
n.2: Keeping rinse time the same makes it a controlled variable; controlled variables are not the control group.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student tests whether water temperature affects how long a sugar cube takes to dissolve, using water at 20 °C, 40 °C and 60 °C. Which factors should she hold constant in every trial? Select all that apply.
o: Time for the cube to dissolve
Rate of stirring
Temperature of the water
Mass of the sugar cube
Volume of water used
Scientific Reasoning.w: Controlled variables are everything except the independent variable that could affect the dependent variable: sugar mass, water volume and stirring rate. Keeping them the same makes temperature the only possible cause of differences.

n.0: Dissolving time is the dependent variable that she measures, so it is expected to change.
n.2: Water temperature is the independent variable; it must change between trials.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student measures resting heart rate in three classmates once before and once after each drinks a caffeinated soda. Which change would most improve the reliability of her results?
o: Report the classmate whose heart rate changed the most
Also vary how much each classmate exercises beforehand
Give the same three classmates a larger caffeine dose
Test many more volunteers and repeat each measurement
Scientific Reasoning.w: Reliability is consistency of results. A larger sample and repeated trials reduce the effect of chance and outliers, so the results are more likely to be the same if the study is repeated.

n.0: Reporting the most extreme case picks an outlier and biases the result.
n.1: Adding a second variable confounds the study; changes in heart rate could no longer be credited to caffeine.
n.2: A larger dose changes the treatment; with three people tested once, the results are still easily skewed by chance.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student compares two tomato plants. Plant A gets fertilizer and sits in a sunny window; Plant B gets no fertilizer and sits in a shaded hallway. Plant A grows taller. What is the main flaw in this design?
o: Two variables differ, so the cause is unclear.
Plant height should be plotted on the x-axis.
The dependent variable should be fertilizer.
There is no control group to compare against.
Scientific Reasoning.w: A fair test changes one variable at a time. Fertilizer and light both differ, so the extra growth cannot be credited to fertilizer; light could explain it.

n.1: Height is the dependent variable, which belongs on the y-axis.
n.2: Fertilizer is what the student changes, so it is the independent variable, not the dependent variable.
n.3: Plant B, with no fertilizer, is meant as the comparison; the problem is that it also differs in light.

Scientific Reasoning.q: In a trial of a blood-pressure drug, neither the patients nor the nurses who take the readings know which patients receive the drug and which receive a placebo. Which term describes this design feature?
o: Observational study
Double-blind
Random sampling
Single-blind
Scientific Reasoning.w: In a double-blind study, neither the subjects nor the researchers who measure outcomes know group assignments, which reduces bias from both expectations.

n.0: An observational study assigns no treatment; this trial gives a drug or placebo.
n.2: Random sampling is how participants are chosen so the sample represents the population; it does not hide group assignments.
n.3: Single-blind means the subjects do not know their group, but the researchers do.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A bathroom scale shows 62.0 kg each of five times a person steps on it. A calibrated clinic scale shows the person's true mass is 60.0 kg. How is the bathroom scale best described?
o: Valid but not reliable
Reliable but not valid
Both reliable and valid
Neither reliable nor valid
Scientific Reasoning.w: Reliability is consistency: the scale gives the same reading every time. Validity is measuring what it claims to measure: it is consistently 2 kg off the true mass, so it is not valid.

n.0: This swaps the terms: identical repeated readings mean the scale is reliable.
n.2: A consistent 2 kg error means the readings do not reflect the true mass, so the scale is not valid.
n.3: The five identical readings show the scale is reliable.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A nurse records a patient's body temperature every 2 hours for 24 hours and wants to show the class how it changed across the day. Which type of graph is the best choice?
o: Histogram
Circle graph
Line graph
Bar graph
Scientific Reasoning.w: A line graph shows how a continuous variable (temperature) changes over time, with time on the x-axis.

n.0: A histogram shows how often values fall in each interval, which loses the order of the readings in time.
n.1: A circle (pie) graph shows parts of a whole that add to 100%, not change over time.
n.3: A bar graph compares separate categories; it hides the continuous trend between readings.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A class measures how fast an enzyme breaks down hydrogen peroxide at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C. How should the axes of their graph be labeled?
o: Enzyme activity on the x-axis; temperature on the y-axis
Time on the x-axis; temperature on the y-axis
Time on the x-axis; enzyme activity on the y-axis
Temperature on the x-axis; enzyme activity on the y-axis
Scientific Reasoning.w: The independent variable (temperature, which the class sets) goes on the x-axis, and the dependent variable (enzyme activity, which is measured) goes on the y-axis.

n.0: This places the dependent variable on the x-axis; it belongs on the y-axis.
n.1: This leaves the dependent variable, enzyme activity, off the graph.
n.2: Time is not the variable the class changed; temperature is the independent variable here.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Researchers review the health records of 5,000 adults and compare those who already walk daily with those who do not. They assign no activity to anyone. What type of study is this?
o: Double-blind trial
Observational study
Controlled experiment
Case study
Scientific Reasoning.w: In an observational (correlational) study, researchers record existing behavior without assigning a treatment. It can show an association but cannot by itself show cause and effect.

n.0: A double-blind trial assigns treatments and hides group membership; nothing is assigned here.
n.2: A controlled experiment requires the researcher to manipulate the independent variable, such as assigning walking.
n.3: A case study examines one person or a small group in depth, not records from 5,000 adults.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Researchers randomly select 200 adults from a city patient registry, then let each person decide whether to use a new sleep app. After a month they compare hours of sleep between users and nonusers. What is the main weakness of this design?
o: There is no comparison group for the app users.
The 200 participants were not randomly sampled.
Hours of sleep should be the independent variable.
The participants were not randomly assigned to groups.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Random assignment reduces bias.
