When participants choose their own group, the groups may differ in other ways (people who choose a sleep app may already care more about sleep), which confounds the result. Random sampling, which this study did use, only makes the sample representative of the registry.

n.0: The nonusers form a comparison group; the problem is that people chose which group to join.
n.1: The 200 adults were drawn at random from the registry, so the sample is random; the problem is how they were sorted into groups.
n.2: Hours of sleep is what the researchers measure, so it is the dependent variable; app use is the independent variable.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Students test caffeine's effect on bean germination. Group 1: 0 mg caffeine, 25 °C, 90% germinated. Group 2: 50 mg, 25 °C, 70% germinated. Group 3: 100 mg, kept on a cooler shelf at 15 °C, 30% germinated. Which conclusion is justified?
o: Temperature, not caffeine, caused Group 3's low germination.
Caffeine at 100 mg caused Group 3's low germination.
Group 3's result may reflect caffeine, temperature or both.
Caffeine may lower germination at 100 mg but not at 50 mg.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Groups 1 and 2 differ in caffeine at the same temperature, so they suggest caffeine lowers germination. Group 3 differs in both caffeine and temperature, a confounding variable, so its drop cannot be credited to either factor alone.

n.0: The design cannot single out temperature either; caffeine also differed for Group 3.
n.1: Temperature also changed for Group 3, so its result cannot be credited to caffeine alone.
n.3: Group 2, kept at the same 25 °C as Group 1, germinated 20 points less, so 50 mg also appears to lower germination.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student examines a wilting houseplant on a windowsill and writes four statements in her lab notebook. Which statement is an observation rather than an inference?
o: The plant is not getting enough nitrogen.
The roots have probably started to rot.
The plant was overwatered sometime last week.
The lower leaves are yellow with brown edges.
Scientific Reasoning.w: An observation is what is directly seen or measured: leaf color can be seen. The other statements interpret the observations to explain a cause, which makes them inferences.

n.0: A nitrogen shortage is an explanation inferred from the yellow leaves; it was not directly observed.
n.1: Root rot is a guess about a hidden part of the plant, so it is an inference.
n.2: Past overwatering is a possible cause the student is inferring, not something she saw.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Over several years, a pharmacist notices that each patient she sees taking a certain allergy drug reports drowsiness. She concludes that the drug causes drowsiness in people who take it. Which describes her reasoning?
o: Inductive, moving from specific cases to a general conclusion
Inductive, moving from a general rule to a specific case
Deductive, moving from specific cases to a general conclusion
Deductive, moving from a general rule to a specific case
Scientific Reasoning.w: Inductive reasoning builds a general conclusion from specific observations. Its conclusions are probable, not certain: one patient who does not become drowsy could overturn the generalization.

n.1: This pairs inductive with the deductive direction; she reasoned from cases to a rule.
n.2: Specific-to-general is inductive; this pairs the right direction with the wrong name.
n.3: Deductive reasoning does go from a general rule to a specific case, but she started from individual patients.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student writes: "All enzymes are proteins. Amylase is an enzyme. Therefore, amylase is a protein." Which statement correctly describes this reasoning?
o: Deductive; the conclusion must be true if the premises are true.
Inductive; the conclusion is probable but could be overturned.
Inductive; the conclusion follows from a general premise.
Deductive; the conclusion is a likely pattern drawn from cases.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Deductive reasoning moves from a general premise to a specific conclusion. If the premises are true, the conclusion is certain.

n.1: Probable conclusions that can be overturned describe inductive reasoning from cases; this argument starts from a general rule.
n.2: Reasoning from a general premise to a specific case is deductive, not inductive.
n.3: Drawing a pattern from cases is inductive; this argument applies a general rule to one case.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A city health report shows that in months when ice-cream sales are high, clinics also treat more sunburns. Which explanation is most scientifically sound?
o: Eating ice cream may make the skin more prone to burning.
Hot, sunny weather likely drives both of the increases.
The pattern shows one of the two causes the other.
Sunburn pain may lead people to buy more ice cream.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Correlation does not prove causation. A third (confounding) variable, hot sunny weather, plausibly raises both ice-cream sales and sun exposure.

n.0: This assumes causation from a correlation with no controlled evidence.
n.2: Two variables rising together can share a third cause, so the pattern does not show that either causes the other.
n.3: This reverses the direction of cause, which a correlation alone cannot establish either.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A hypothesis states that every strain of a bacterium is killed by a certain antibiotic. Forty lab tests support it. Then a replicated study by another lab finds a strain that survives the antibiotic. What is the correct conclusion?
o: The hypothesis is refuted and must be revised.
The new strain should be dropped as an outlier.
The hypothesis stands, since 40 tests outweigh one.
The hypothesis is proven for the strains tested.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Supporting evidence never proves a general claim, but one well-replicated contradicting result can refute it. The claim about every strain must be revised.

n.1: A replicated result is not an outlier; discarding inconvenient data biases the conclusion.
n.2: Science does not decide by vote; one replicated counterexample defeats a claim about every strain.
n.3: Data support hypotheses but do not prove them, and the claim was about all strains, not some.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A study of 400 healthy men aged 20 to 30 finds that a daily supplement lowered their resting heart rate. Which conclusion is best supported by this study?
o: The supplement lowers resting heart rate in adults of any age.
The supplement lowers resting heart rate in women aged 60 to 70.
The supplement will lower heart rate in patients with heart disease.
The supplement lowered heart rate in the healthy young men studied.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Sound conclusions stay within the population and conditions tested. The study included only healthy men aged 20 to 30.

n.0: Adults of other ages and sexes were not tested; the result cannot be extended to them.
n.1: Older women were not studied, so this generalizes beyond the tested population.
n.2: Only healthy men took part, so the effect in heart patients is unknown.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A website claims that an herbal tea shortens colds. It cites a celebrity endorsement and reviews from 12 happy customers. Which additional evidence would most strengthen the claim?
o: A randomized trial comparing the tea with a look-alike placebo tea
A survey finding that tea buyers report shorter colds than nonbuyers
A trial in which 300 people with colds all drank the tea and got better
A statement from a physician who recommends the tea to her patients
Scientific Reasoning.w: Only a controlled experiment can establish cause and effect. Randomly assigning people with colds to the tea or a look-alike placebo makes the groups alike except for the tea, so a difference in cold length can be credited to it.

n.1: A survey is observational: buyers chose the tea themselves and self-report their colds, so it shows an association at best, not cause.
n.2: With no comparison group, there is no way to tell whether the colds would have ended just as fast without the tea.
n.3: An authority's recommendation is not evidence; the claim still has to be tested against a control.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A nursing student documents a healing wound on day 3. Which of her notes records quantitative data?
o: The wound measures 2.4 cm in length.
The patient describes the pain as sharp.
The dressing has a faint sour odor.
The wound edges look pink and dry.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Quantitative data are numbers with units, such as a length of 2.4 cm. Descriptions of color, odor or pain quality are qualitative.

n.1: A word describing pain quality is qualitative; a 0 to 10 pain score would be quantitative.
n.2: An odor description is qualitative.
n.3: Color and texture are descriptions, which makes them qualitative data.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A science club is choosing a question for its next investigation. Which claim can be investigated scientifically?
o: Schools should require students to sleep 8 hours a night.
Dreams carry hidden messages that no measurement can detect.
Students ought to value sleep more than late-night study.
Students who sleep 8 hours score higher on memory tests.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Scientific claims must be testable and falsifiable with empirical evidence. Sleep hours and memory scores can both be measured and compared.

n.0: This is a policy recommendation about what ought to happen; data can inform it, but no observation can test an 'ought'.
n.1: A claim defined as undetectable by any measurement cannot be falsified, so it cannot be investigated scientifically.
n.2: This is a value judgment about what students should care about, which cannot be measured objectively.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A survey of 2,000 nursing students finds that those who drink more energy drinks also report higher anxiety levels. Which conclusion is justified by this survey?
o: Cutting out energy drinks will lower students' anxiety.
Energy drinks cause anxiety in nursing students.
Anxiety causes students to drink more energy drinks.
Energy-drink use and anxiety are linked in this group.
Scientific Reasoning.w: A survey is observational: it shows an association (correlation) but cannot show which variable causes which, or whether a third factor, such as exam stress, drives both.

n.0: This predicts the effect of an intervention, which requires evidence of causation.
n.1: Concluding causation from a correlation is the classic error; only a controlled experiment can show it.
n.2: Reversing the direction is still a causal claim the survey cannot support.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A study reporting that a sports drink improves endurance was paid for by the company that makes the drink. Eight cyclists were randomly assigned to the drink or a look-alike placebo, and the testers did not know who drank which. Which concerns are most relevant when evaluating this study?
o: Conflict of interest and no placebo group
No blinding and a conflict of interest
Conflict of interest and a small sample
No random assignment and a small sample
Scientific Reasoning.w: When evaluating a claim, ask whether the source is unbiased and the sample is large enough. Funding from the drink's maker is a conflict of interest, and 8 participants is easily skewed by chance. The design itself used random assignment, a placebo and blinding.

n.0: The other cyclists drank a look-alike placebo, so the study did have a placebo control.
n.1: The testers did not know who drank which, so the measurements were blinded; only the conflict of interest applies.
n.3: The cyclists were randomly assigned to groups, so assignment bias is not the concern; only the small sample is.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student is preparing a summary of what separates a scientific explanation from other kinds of claims. Which features make an explanation scientific? Select all that apply.
o: It is accepted because experts hold it.
It can be reproduced by other scientists.
It is testable and could be falsified.
It rests on many personal stories.
It is based on empirical evidence.
It is proven and closed to revision.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Scientific explanations rest on empirical evidence (observation and measurement), are testable and falsifiable, and are reproducible by others. They stay open to revision when new evidence appears.

n.0: Authority is not evidence; experts' claims must still be backed by data.
n.3: Personal stories are anecdotal evidence, which lacks controls and cannot establish cause.
n.5: Scientific explanations stay open to revision; evidence supports them but does not prove them.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A sealed syringe of air is kept at constant temperature while a student changes the pressure. Data: 100 kPa, 60 mL; 200 kPa, 30 mL; 300 kPa, 20 mL. Which relationship do the data show?
o: Direct: volume falls as pressure rises
No relationship: the values vary randomly
Direct: volume rises as pressure rises
Inverse: volume falls as pressure rises
Scientific Reasoning.w: When one variable increases as the other decreases, the relationship is inverse. Doubling the pressure halves the volume (100 kPa x 60 mL = 200 kPa x 30 mL = 300 kPa x 20 mL), the pattern of gas pressure and volume at constant temperature.

n.0: The trend is described correctly, but one variable falling as the other rises is an inverse relationship, not a direct one.
n.1: The values change in a steady, predictable pattern (pressure x volume stays constant), not randomly.
n.2: The volume does not rise; it drops from 60 mL to 20 mL as pressure increases.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A class measures an enzyme's activity at three temperatures. Data: 20 °C, 12 units; 30 °C, 24 units; 40 °C, 36 units. Which estimate of the activity at 35 °C is best supported by the data?
o: About 36 units
About 48 units
About 30 units
About 24 units
Scientific Reasoning.w: Activity rises 12 units for every 10 °C across the tested range, so halfway between 30 °C and 40 °C it should be about halfway between 24 and 36: about 30 units. Estimating between measured points (interpolation) is reliable.

n.0: 36 units is the measured value at 40 °C; 35 °C is only halfway there.
n.1: 48 units would follow the trend to 50 °C, beyond the range tested, not 35 °C.
n.3: 24 units is the measured value at 30 °C; the trend predicts a higher value at 35 °C.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A hiker drinks no water during a long, hot climb and becomes dehydrated, so the osmolality of his blood plasma rises. Which response should be predicted?
o: ADH secretion rises, and urine output rises and turns paler.
ADH secretion falls, and urine output falls and turns darker.
ADH secretion falls, and urine output rises and turns paler.
ADH secretion rises, and urine output falls and turns darker.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Dehydration raises plasma osmolality, which increases ADH (antidiuretic hormone) release. ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb more water, so the body produces less urine that is more concentrated and darker.

n.0: Rising ADH conserves water, so urine output falls rather than rises.
n.1: Less, darker urine is the right outcome, but it is caused by more ADH, not less.
n.2: ADH falls and urine becomes dilute when a person is overhydrated, the opposite situation.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A nursing student moves from a coastal city to a mountain town about 2,500 m above sea level. What should she predict about the boiling point of water when she cooks pasta there?
o: Higher, because the air pressure is higher
Higher, because the air pressure is lower
Lower, because the air pressure is lower
Lower, because the air pressure is higher
Scientific Reasoning.w: Air pressure falls as altitude rises (an inverse relationship). Water boils when its vapor pressure matches the air pressure, so lower air pressure means water boils at a lower temperature.

n.0: Air pressure is lower, not higher, at altitude, and higher pressure would raise the boiling point.
n.1: Lower air pressure lowers the boiling point; the direction of the effect is reversed.
n.3: The boiling point is lower, but because air pressure decreases with altitude, not increases.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A culture starts with one bacterial cell. It divides by binary fission every 20 minutes, and every new cell keeps dividing at that rate. Enter the number of cells after 2 hours as a whole number.

tr.7: Counted 1 cell plus 1 new cell per generation (1 + 6).
tr.12: Added 2 cells per generation (6 x 2), a linear doubling instead of exponential growth.

Scientific Reasoning.w: Step 1: 2 hours = 120 minutes, and 120 / 20 = 6 generations. Step 2: each generation doubles the population (exponential growth), so the count after n generations is 2^n = 2^6 = 64 cells (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64).

Scientific Reasoning.q: In a drug trial, doses of 10, 20 and 30 mg lowered systolic blood pressure by 5, 10 and 15 mmHg. A student predicts that a 90 mg dose would lower it by 45 mmHg. How should this prediction be evaluated?
o: It extends the trend far past the doses tested, so it is unreliable.
It is reliable, because it lies within the range of the data collected.
It is reliable, because the three data points form a straight line.
It is too low, because drug effects grow exponentially with the dose.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Predicting beyond the range tested (extrapolation) is unreliable: the trend may level off or reverse at higher doses. The data cover only 10 to 30 mg, so 90 mg is far outside them.

n.1: 90 mg is far outside the tested range of 10 to 30 mg, so the prediction is an extrapolation.
n.2: A straight line within the tested range does not show the trend continues three times beyond it.
n.3: The data rise by a steady 5 mmHg per 10 mg; nothing in them suggests exponential growth.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Activity of a human enzyme at five temperatures: 20 °C, 15 units; 30 °C, 30 units; 37 °C, 42 units; 45 °C, 20 units; 55 °C, 3 units. What is the best prediction for activity at 65 °C?
o: Lower than at 55 °C, since activity falls past the optimum
About 42 units, since the enzyme has hit its maximum
Higher than at 55 °C, since the activity cycles up and down
Higher than at 37 °C, since heat speeds up reactions
Scientific Reasoning.w: Enzyme activity rises to an optimum (37 °C here) and then falls as heat denatures the enzyme. Activity is already only 3 units at 55 °C, so at 65 °C it should be even lower, close to zero.

n.1: The maximum of 42 units occurred at 37 °C; activity has fallen steeply since then.
n.2: The data show a rise-then-fall pattern, not a repeating cycle.
n.3: Heat speeds reactions only up to the optimum; above it the enzyme denatures and activity drops, as the data show.

Scientific Reasoning.q: Reaction rate at five substrate concentrations, with enzyme amount held constant: 1 mM, 10; 2 mM, 18; 4 mM, 28; 8 mM, 33; 16 mM, 34 (rate in units per minute). What is the best prediction for the rate at 32 mM?
o: About 34, since the rate has nearly leveled off
About 44, since the rate keeps rising by a steady amount
About 68, since doubling substrate doubles the rate
About 20, since the rate falls once past an optimum
Scientific Reasoning.w: The rate rises quickly and then plateaus: from 8 to 16 mM it gains only 1 unit because the enzyme molecules are nearly saturated. Doubling the substrate again should leave the rate close to 34.

n.1: The increases shrink (8, 10, 5, 1), so the rate is leveling off, not rising steadily.
n.2: Doubling 16 mM to 32 mM does not double the rate; going from 8 to 16 mM added only 1 unit.
n.3: A rise-then-fall curve fits enzyme activity against temperature or pH, not against substrate concentration.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student runs a reaction twice with the same reactant amounts and temperature, adding a catalyst the second time. Which outcome should the student predict for the second run?
o: A faster reaction that forms the same products
A faster reaction that forms different products
A faster reaction that uses up the catalyst
A slower reaction that forms different products
Scientific Reasoning.w: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the reaction goes faster. It is not consumed and does not change which products form.

n.1: The rate rises, but the products are unchanged; a catalyst does not alter the reaction's outcome.
n.2: A catalyst is regenerated at the end of the reaction; it is not used up as a reactant.
n.3: A catalyst speeds a reaction, and the products stay the same.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A patient loses a large volume of blood in a car accident, and his blood pressure begins to fall. Which immediate compensating changes should be predicted?
o: Heart rate falls, and blood vessels dilate.
Heart rate rises, and blood vessels constrict.
Heart rate falls, and blood vessels constrict.
Heart rate rises, and blood vessels dilate.
Scientific Reasoning.w: Falling blood pressure triggers a faster heart rate and vasoconstriction, which together push blood pressure back up toward normal (negative feedback).

n.0: Both changes would lower blood pressure, worsening the problem.
n.2: Vasoconstriction is right, but a slower heart would lower blood pressure further.
n.3: A faster heart rate is right, but dilated vessels would lower blood pressure further.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A runner moves from sea level to train at high altitude for two months. Place the events in the order they occur as her body adjusts, starting with the first.
o: The kidneys detect a low blood oxygen level
The blood's oxygen-carrying capacity rises over weeks
The kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO)
Red bone marrow increases red blood cell production
Less oxygen reaches the blood from the thinner air
Scientific Reasoning.w: High altitude means less oxygen enters the blood. The kidneys sense the low oxygen and release EPO, a hormone that signals red bone marrow to make more red blood cells. Over weeks, the extra red blood cells raise the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.

Scientific Reasoning.q: A student is sorting pairs of variables for a study guide on relationships. Which pairs show an inverse relationship? Select all that apply.
o: Altitude and the boiling point of water
Gas volume and kelvin temperature at constant pressure
Altitude and air pressure
Generations of binary fission and bacterial count
Gas pressure and volume at constant temperature
Enzyme activity and temperature below the optimum
Scientific Reasoning.w: In an inverse relationship, one variable rises as the other falls: gas pressure rises as volume falls; air pressure falls as altitude rises; and the boiling point falls as altitude rises.

n.1: Gas volume rises with kelvin temperature at constant pressure, a direct relationship.
n.3: Bacterial count rises with each generation (exponential growth), so both increase together.
n.5: Below the optimum, enzyme activity rises with temperature, a direct relationship.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student is reviewing the doubling rule, in which stress placement decides whether the final consonant doubles. Which word is spelled correctly?
o: occurence
referrence
openning
referred
Conventions of Standard English.w: Re-FER is stressed on the last syllable, so the r doubles before -ed: "referred". Doubling depends on where the stress falls in the new word.

n.0: Oc-CUR is stressed on the last syllable, so the r doubles: "occurrence".
n.1: In REF-er-ence the stress moves to the first syllable, so the r does not double: "reference".
n.2: O-pen is stressed on the first syllable, so the n does not double: "opening".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A hospital volunteer is writing an announcement about a parade route. Which of the following words, all ending in a "seed" sound, is spelled correctly?
o: superceed
preceed
proceed
excede
Conventions of Standard English.w: Only three common words end in -ceed: exceed, proceed and succeed. Only supersede ends in -sede. All others end in -cede.

n.0: Supersede is the one common word ending in -sede; "superceed" wrongly gives it the -ceed ending.
n.1: Precede takes the regular -cede ending; -ceed is reserved for exceed, proceed and succeed.
n.3: Exceed is one of the three -ceed words, so "excede" is wrong.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student writing a lab report adds prefixes to base words. Which word correctly keeps every letter of both the prefix and the root?
o: disatisfied
imature
unnecessary
mispell
Conventions of Standard English.w: Adding a prefix does not change the spelling of the root: un + necessary = "unnecessary", with both n's kept.

n.0: Dis + satisfied keeps both s's: "dissatisfied".
n.1: Im + mature keeps both m's: "immature".
n.3: Mis + spell keeps both s's: "misspell".

Conventions of Standard English.q: An editor is checking adverbs formed by adding -ly in a discharge leaflet for patients. Which adverb is spelled correctly?
o: finaly
gentlely
carefuly
publicly
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Publicly" is formed by adding -ly straight to public; it is the standard exception to the -ically pattern.

n.0: Final + ly keeps both l's: "finally".
n.1: Adjectives ending in -le replace the e with y: gentle becomes "gently".
n.2: Careful + ly keeps both l's: "carefully".

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence from a hospital newsletter: "The physician noted that the patient's hemorrage had stopped before the anesthesia wore off." Which word in the sentence is misspelled?
o: physician
anesthesia
patient's
hemorrage
Conventions of Standard English.w: The correct spelling is "hemorrhage", with r-r-h; the rh comes from the Greek word part -rrhage (bursting forth).

n.0: "Physician" is spelled correctly.
n.1: "Anesthesia" is the correct US spelling (UK: anaesthesia).
n.2: "Patient's" is the correct singular possessive of patient.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nursing applicant is studying a list of commonly misspelled words before the TEAS. Which words are spelled correctly? Select all that apply.
o: embarass
occurrence
seperate
definately
privilege
accommodate
Conventions of Standard English.w: Accommodate (double c, double m), occurrence (double c, double r) and privilege (i-l-e-g-e) are correct.

n.0: The correct spelling is "embarrass", with double r and double s.
n.2: The correct spelling is "separate", with a after the p.
n.3: The correct spelling is "definitely", from the root finite.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A charge nurse is proofreading a sentence for a unit memo. Which version of the sentence is spelled correctly?
o: She was carrying the foreign samples to the lab.
She was carriing the foreign samples to the lab.
She was carrying the foriegn samples to the lab.
She was carriing the foriegn samples to the lab.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two rules apply. Before -ing, a final y is kept (carry + ing = carrying). "Foreign" is an exception to i before e and is spelled e-i.

n.1: "Carriing" wrongly changes y to i before -ing; the y is kept: "carrying".
n.2: "Foreign" is an exception spelled e-i, not i-e.
n.3: Both words are wrong: the y must stay before -ing, and "foreign" is spelled e-i.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A US health department is editing a brochure for American readers. Which sentence follows standard American spelling throughout?
o: The center will analyze each patient's behaviour.
The center will analyze each patient's behavior.
The center will analyse each patient's behavior.
The centre will analyze each patient's behavior.
Conventions of Standard English.w: American English uses -er (center), -yze (analyze) and -or (behavior). Each other version slips in one British spelling.

n.0: "Behaviour" is the British spelling; American English drops the u: "behavior".
n.2: "Analyse" is the British spelling; American English uses "analyze".
n.3: "Centre" is the British spelling; American English uses "center".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nurse is writing an incident note about several patients who share a room on a pediatric unit. Which sentence uses plural and possessive forms correctly?
o: The patients' in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
The patients in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
The patients in Room 4 asked about the childrens' toys.
The patient's in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Patients" is a plain plural subject, so it takes no apostrophe. "Children" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive adds 's: "children's".

n.0: The patients do not own anything here, so "patients'" (plural possessive) is wrong; the plain plural is needed.
n.2: "Children" already is plural; an irregular plural not ending in s takes 's, so "childrens'" is wrong.
n.3: "Patient's" uses an apostrophe to make a plain plural; plurals that show no ownership take no apostrophe.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A hospital kitchen supervisor is writing a short inventory note. Which sentence uses the correct plural form of every noun?
o: The chefs stored the knives on the shelfs.
The chefs stored the knifes on the shelves.
The cheves stored the knives on the shelves.
The chefs stored the knives on the shelves.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Many nouns ending in f or fe change to -ves (knife to knives, shelf to shelves), but some simply add s, including chef (chefs).

n.0: Shelf changes f to ves: "shelves".
n.1: Knife changes fe to ves: "knives".
n.2: Chef is an exception to the f-to-ves rule; its plural is "chefs".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A physician's note must use standard plural forms. Which sentence uses the correct plural of every noun?
o: Both diagnosis were confirmed after the two analyses.
Both diagnoses were confirmed after the two analyses.
Both diagnosises were confirmed after the two analyses.
Both diagnoses were confirmed after the two analysises.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Greek-origin nouns ending in -is form the plural by replacing -is with -es: diagnosis becomes "diagnoses" and analysis becomes "analyses" (like crisis, crises).

n.0: "Diagnosis" is the singular form, but "both" and "were" require the plural "diagnoses".
n.2: The -is ending is replaced, not kept: the plural of diagnosis is "diagnoses", not "diagnosises".
n.3: The -is ending is replaced, not kept: the plural of analysis is "analyses", not "analysises".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A clinic's front-desk sign is being revised. Which sentence uses possessive pronouns correctly?
o: The clinic updated it's hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its' hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is your's.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is yours.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, hers, ours, theirs, whose) never take an apostrophe.

n.0: "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; the possessive is "its".
n.1: "Its'" is not a word; the possessive pronoun is "its".
n.2: "Yours" is a possessive pronoun and takes no apostrophe.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A newspaper is writing about a local nurse honored for bravery. Which sentence uses the correct plural form of each noun?
o: The article included photos of the local heroes.
The article included photos of the local heros.
The article included photoes of the local heroes.
The article included photoes of the local heros.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two rules apply. Many nouns ending in consonant + o add -es (hero to heroes), but some, including photo, simply add s (photos).

n.1: Hero is a consonant + o noun that adds -es: "heroes".
n.2: Photo is an exception that adds only s: "photos".
n.3: Both are wrong: photo adds s, and hero adds -es.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Maria and Lee own one clinic together. Which sentence correctly shows their shared ownership of the clinic?
o: Maria and Lees' clinic opens at eight.
Maria's and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
Marias and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
Maria and Lee's clinic opens at eight.
Conventions of Standard English.w: For joint ownership, only the last name takes the possessive: "Maria and Lee's clinic". Separate possessives (Maria's and Lee's) signal separate ownership.

n.0: Lee is one person, so the singular possessive is "Lee's", not "Lees'".
n.1: Making both names possessive signals individual ownership, which does not fit one shared clinic.
n.2: "Marias" is a plural with no apostrophe; Maria is one person and needs no s here.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A staff newsletter describes a nurse's family. Which sentence uses the correct plural of the compound noun?
o: Both of her sisters-in-law work as nurses.
Both of her sister-in-laws work as nurses.
Both of her sister's-in-law work as nurses.
Both of her sisters-in-laws work as nurses.
Conventions of Standard English.w: In a hyphenated compound noun, the main word takes the plural: sister becomes sisters, giving "sisters-in-law".

n.1: The s goes on the main word (sister), not the end of the compound.
n.2: An apostrophe shows possession, not plurality; nothing is owned here.
n.3: The compound is pluralized once, on the main word; adding a second s is wrong.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Jada has one sister-in-law, who owns a car. Which sentence correctly shows that the car belongs to that one sister-in-law?
o: My sisters-in-law's car is in the shop.
My sister's-in-law car is in the shop.
My sister-in-law's car is in the shop.
My sister-in-laws car is in the shop.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A compound noun forms its possessive on the last word: "sister-in-law's". The singular form is used because there is one owner.

n.0: "Sisters-in-law's" is the plural possessive, but Jada has only one sister-in-law.
n.1: The possessive ending goes on the last word of the compound, not the first.
n.3: "Sister-in-laws" has no apostrophe, so it is not a possessive.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A human resources assistant is writing a bonus notice for staff. Which sentence uses possessive forms of time expressions correctly?
o: The bonus equals one week's pay for two weeks' work.
The bonus equals one weeks' pay for two weeks' work.
The bonus equals one week's pay for two week's work.
The bonus equals one weeks pay for two weeks' work.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two steps: one week is singular, so add 's (one week's pay); two weeks is a plural ending in s, so add only an apostrophe (two weeks' work).

n.1: "One week" is singular, so its possessive is "week's", not "weeks'".
n.2: "Two weeks" is plural, so the apostrophe goes after the s: "weeks'".
n.3: "One weeks pay" uses a plural with "one" and leaves out the apostrophe.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A hospital historian is writing about staff hired decades ago. Which sentence uses plurals and apostrophes correctly?
o: Several RNs' on the unit were hired in the 1990s.
Several RNs on the unit were hired in the 1990s'.
Several RNs on the unit were hired in the 1990s.
Several RN's on the unit were hired in the 1990s.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Plurals of abbreviations and numbers add s with no apostrophe: RNs, 1990s. Nothing in the sentence is possessive.

n.0: "RNs'" is a plural possessive, but the RNs do not own anything here.
n.1: A decade written in numerals takes s with no apostrophe: "1990s".
n.3: An apostrophe is not used to form the plural of an abbreviation such as RN.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student is checking a list of plural nouns for a biology report. Which plurals are formed correctly? Select all that apply.
o: beliefs
attorneys
passerbys
crises
wolfs
stimuluses
Conventions of Standard English.w: Crisis becomes crises (-is to -es); attorney adds s because it ends in vowel + y; belief is an f noun that simply adds s.

n.2: In a compound noun the main word is pluralized: "passersby".
n.4: Wolf changes f to ves: "wolves".
n.5: Stimulus is a Latin noun whose plural is "stimuli".

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence from a facilities report: "The mens' locker room and the women's lounge were repainted despite the residents' objections." Which word contains an error?
o: mens'
objections
residents'
women's
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Men" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive adds 's: "men's".

n.1: "Objections" is a plain plural that owns nothing, so no apostrophe is needed.
n.2: "Residents'" is correct: a regular plural ending in s adds only an apostrophe.
n.3: "Women's" is correct: an irregular plural not ending in s adds 's.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A volunteer coordinator is writing a note about visitors in the hospital lobby. Which sentence uses "their," "there," and "they're" correctly?
o: Their leaving their coats over there by the door.
They're leaving there coats over there by the door.
They're leaving their coats over their by the door.
They're leaving their coats over there by the door.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "They're" is the contraction of "they are", "their" shows possession (their coats), and "there" names a place (over there).

n.0: The sentence needs "they are leaving", so the contraction "they're" is required, not the possessive "their".
n.1: The coats belong to them, so the possessive "their" is required, not the place word "there".
n.2: "Over ___" names a place, so "there" is required, not the possessive "their".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nurse is documenting how long a procedure took. Which sentence uses "than" and "then" correctly?
o: The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and than left.
The test took longer then expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
The test took longer than expected, so we ate lunch and then left.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Than" makes a comparison (longer than expected); "then" shows time or sequence (and then left).

n.0: "And ___ left" shows sequence, so it needs "then".
n.1: Both are reversed: the comparison needs "than" and the sequence needs "then".
n.2: "Longer ___ expected" is a comparison, so it needs "than".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A unit manager is writing a staffing note at the end of a long shift. Which sentence uses "to," "too," and "two" correctly?
o: The two aides were too tired to finish the charts.
The too aides were too tired to finish the charts.
The two aides were too tired too finish the charts.
The two aides were to tired to finish the charts.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Two" is the number, "too" means excessively (too tired), and "to" begins the infinitive (to finish).

n.1: The number of aides requires "two".
n.2: An infinitive is formed with "to": "to finish".
n.3: "___ tired" means excessively tired, which requires "too".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A receptionist is asking about a missing medical record. Which sentence uses "who's" and "whose" correctly?
o: Who's the patient who's chart is missing?
Whose the patient who's chart is missing?
Whose the patient whose chart is missing?
Who's the patient whose chart is missing?
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Who's" is the contraction of "who is" (Who is the patient?); "whose" shows possession (whose chart).

n.0: The chart belongs to the patient, so the possessive "whose" is needed, not "who is".
n.1: Both are reversed: the opening needs "who's" and the possessive needs "whose".
n.2: The sentence opens with "Who is the patient", so it needs the contraction "who's".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A patient education sheet describes a medication's results. Which sentence uses "affect" and "effect" correctly?
o: The new medication did not affect her sleep, but it had an affect on her appetite.
The new medication did not effect her sleep, but it had an effect on her appetite.
The new medication did not effect her sleep, but it had an affect on her appetite.
The new medication did not affect her sleep, but it had an effect on her appetite.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Affect" is usually a verb meaning "to influence" (did not affect her sleep); "effect" is usually a noun meaning "result" (an effect on her appetite).

n.0: After the article "an", the noun meaning "result" is needed: "effect".
n.1: "Did not ___ her sleep" needs the verb meaning "influence", which is "affect"; "effect" as a verb means "bring about".
n.2: Both are reversed: the verb should be "affect" and the noun should be "effect".

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The school's ____ explained that honesty is a basic ____ of the honor code."
o: principal; principal
principal; principle
principle; principle
principle; principal
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Principal" names the head of a school (or means "main"); "principle" is a rule or belief, as in a principle of the honor code.

n.0: A basic rule of a code is a "principle", not a "principal".
n.2: The head of a school is the "principal", not a "principle".
n.3: Both words are reversed: the school's head is the principal, and a rule is a principle.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A physical therapist is writing a home exercise plan. Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The new exercise bike is ____, so it will ____ the walking program."
o: stationery; compliment
stationery; complement
stationary; compliment
stationary; complement
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Stationary" means not moving; "complement" means to complete or go well with. A bike that stays in place goes well with a walking program.

n.0: Both are wrong: the bike is stationary (not moving), and it complements (goes well with) the program.
n.1: "Stationery" is writing paper; a bike that does not move is "stationary".
n.2: "Compliment" means to praise; going well with something is "complement".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A charge nurse is writing a reminder about patient safety bands. Which sentence uses commonly confused words correctly?
o: All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Except" means excluding (all except Mr. Ito); "lose" means to misplace (not to lose their wristbands). "Loose" means not tight.

n.0: "Loose" is an adjective meaning not tight; misplacing something is "lose".
n.1: Both are wrong: excluding someone is "except", and misplacing something is "lose".
n.2: "Accept" means to receive; excluding someone requires "except".

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the instruction? "The respiratory therapist will ____ you to take a deep ____ before you exhale slowly."
o: advise; breathe
advice; breathe
advice; breath
advise; breath
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Advise" is the verb (will advise you); "breath" is the noun (a deep breath). "Advice" and "breathe" are the noun and verb forms of the other pair.

n.0: After "a deep" a noun is needed: "breath". "Breathe" is a verb.
n.1: Both are reversed: the verb is "advise" and the noun is "breath".
n.2: After "will" a verb is needed: "advise". "Advice" is a noun.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence from a hospital memo: "The council decided that the new policy would ensure that personnel were not allowed to leave there stations early." Which word is used incorrectly?
o: personnel
ensure
there
council
Conventions of Standard English.w: The stations belong to the personnel, so the possessive "their" is required: "leave their stations".

n.0: "Personnel" (staff) is correct; "personal" means private.
n.1: "Ensure" (make certain) is correct; "insure" means to buy insurance.
n.3: "Council" (a group that makes decisions) is correct; "counsel" means advice.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A tutor gives a student six sentences to check for commonly confused words. In which sentences is every word used correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The storm is imminent, so stay indoors.
Her new shoes are to tight to wear.
The elicit drugs were seized at the border.
He gave me some good advise yesterday.
She is conscious of the risks involved.
Please cite your sources in the report.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Imminent" means about to happen, "conscious" means aware, and "cite" means to quote or name a source.

n.1: "Excessively tight" requires "too": "too tight to wear".
n.2: Illegal drugs are "illicit"; "elicit" means to draw out.
n.3: After "some good" a noun is needed: "advice". "Advise" is a verb.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "By the time the team was ____ to begin, the patient had ____ been discharged."
o: all ready; already
all ready; all ready
already; all ready
already; already
Conventions of Standard English.w: "All ready" means completely prepared (the team was all ready to begin); "already" means by this time (had already been discharged).

n.1: "Had all ready been discharged" needs the time word "already".
n.2: Both are reversed: being prepared is "all ready", and "by this time" is "already".
n.3: Being completely prepared is "all ready"; "was already to begin" does not make sense.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nursing student is editing a shift report that joins two complete thoughts with a coordinating conjunction. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The nurse checked the patient's chart, and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart, and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse, checked the patient's chart and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
Conventions of Standard English.w: When a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) joins two independent clauses, a comma goes before the conjunction: "chart, and the doctor".

n.1: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; only the comma before "and" is needed.
n.2: The comma belongs before the conjunction, not after it.
n.3: A comma must not separate a subject (The nurse) from its verb (checked), and the comma before "and" is missing.

Conventions of Standard English.q: An aide's charting note has one subject doing two actions. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The aide measured the patient's, blood pressure and recorded it in the chart.
The aide measured the patient's blood pressure and recorded it in the chart.
The aide, measured the patient's blood pressure and recorded it in the chart.
The aide measured the patient's blood pressure, and recorded it in the chart.
Conventions of Standard English.w: This is one subject (The aide) with a compound predicate (measured ... and recorded). With no second subject, there is no second independent clause, so no comma goes before "and".

n.0: A comma must not split a possessive from the noun it modifies.
n.2: A comma must not separate the subject from its verb.
n.3: A comma before "and" is used when it joins two independent clauses; here "recorded it" has no subject of its own.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A lab supervisor is writing a note that begins with an introductory dependent clause. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon the samples were stored until Monday.
Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon, the samples, were stored until Monday.
Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon, the samples were stored until Monday.
Because, the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon, the samples were stored until Monday.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A long introductory dependent clause (Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon) is followed by a comma before the main clause.

n.0: The comma after the long introductory dependent clause is missing, so the reader runs "afternoon the samples" together.
n.1: A comma must not separate the subject (the samples) from its verb (were stored).
n.3: No comma follows the subordinating conjunction "Because".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A hospital bulletin introduces the doctor on call. Which sentence punctuates the nonessential appositive correctly?
o: Dr. Patel, the surgeon on call tonight, will review the scans.
Dr. Patel, the surgeon on call tonight will review the scans.
Dr. Patel the surgeon on call tonight, will review the scans.
Dr. Patel, the surgeon on call tonight, will review, the scans.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A nonessential appositive that renames a proper noun is set off by a pair of commas, one before it and one after it.

n.1: The closing comma after "tonight" is missing; a nonessential element needs commas on both sides.
n.2: The opening comma after "Dr. Patel" is missing.
n.3: A comma must not separate the verb (will review) from its object (the scans).

Conventions of Standard English.q: A unit has twelve patients, and only one of them fell yesterday. Which sentence correctly identifies that particular patient?
o: The patient who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two steps: with twelve patients, "who fell yesterday" is essential (restrictive) because it identifies which patient. Essential clauses take no commas.

n.1: A comma must not separate the subject from its verb (needs).
n.2: A single comma after "patient" opens an aside that is never closed.
n.3: Commas would mark the clause as nonessential, as if there were only one patient; here it is needed to identify the patient.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A community health newsletter describes a local clinic. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A proper noun is already identified, so the clause "which opened in 2020" is nonessential and needs a pair of commas.

n.1: The closing comma after "2020" is missing.
n.2: The opening comma after "Riverside Clinic" is missing.
n.3: A nonessential clause after a proper noun must be set off with commas.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nurse is writing a reflective journal entry. Which sentence punctuates the adjectives correctly?
o: It was a long, tiring shift in the busy, emergency room.
It was a long, tiring, shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Long" and "tiring" are coordinate adjectives (they could be joined by "and"), so a comma separates them. "Emergency room" is a compound noun, so "busy" takes no comma.

n.0: "Emergency" is part of the noun "emergency room", so no comma follows "busy".
n.1: No comma goes between the last adjective and the noun it modifies.
n.2: Coordinate adjectives that each describe the noun separately are separated by a comma: "long, tiring".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A press release announces a new hospital wing. Which sentence uses commas correctly with the date and the place?
o: On July 4, 2026 the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened a new wing.
On July, 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened a new wing.
On July 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas opened a new wing.
On July 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened a new wing.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two rules apply. In a full date, commas follow the day and the year when the sentence continues. In a city-state pair, commas follow the city and the state.

n.0: The comma after the year "2026" is missing.
n.1: No comma goes between the month and the day.
n.2: The comma after the state "Texas" is missing.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nurse is confirming paperwork with a patient. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Ms. Chen, you finished, the intake form didn't you?
Ms. Chen you finished the intake form, didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form, didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form didn't you?
Conventions of Standard English.w: A name in direct address is set off by a comma, and a tag question (didn't you?) is also set off by a comma.

n.0: A comma must not separate the verb (finished) from its object, and the comma before the tag question is missing.
n.1: The comma after the name in direct address is missing.
n.3: The comma before the tag question "didn't you" is missing.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A medical secretary is proofreading a memo that uses the word "however" in several positions. Which sentence contains a comma error?
o: The results were not available, however until Tuesday.
However, the results were not available until Tuesday.
The results, however, were not available until Tuesday.
The results were not available until Tuesday, however.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "However" used as an interrupter in the middle of a clause must be set off by commas on both sides: "available, however, until Tuesday". One comma is missing.

n.1: Correct: an introductory "However" is followed by a comma.
n.2: Correct: the interrupter is enclosed by a pair of commas.
n.3: Correct: a closing "however" is preceded by a comma.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A writing tutor gives a student six sentences from patient handouts. Which sentences are punctuated correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The new nurse on the night shift, works weekends.
I stayed late, but, the charts were still unfinished.
The new nurse on the night shift works weekends.
She needs rest, not more medication.
The forms, that you signed, are in the file.
Mr. Ruiz, your lab results are ready.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A long subject takes no comma before its verb; a contrasting element (not more medication) is set off by a comma; a name in direct address (Mr. Ruiz) is set off by a comma.

n.0: A comma must not separate the subject (The new nurse on the night shift) from its verb.
n.1: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; only the comma before "but" is needed.
n.4: A "that" clause is essential (restrictive), so it takes no commas.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the paragraph. (1) When flu season began, the clinic extended its hours. (2) Patients could visit on weekday evenings or on Saturday mornings. (3) The clinic hired two nurses and the staff shared the extra shifts. (4) By March, waiting times had dropped. Which sentence needs a comma added?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Conventions of Standard English.w: Sentence 3 joins two independent clauses (The clinic hired two nurses / the staff shared the extra shifts) with "and", so a comma is needed before "and". Without it, a reader first takes "two nurses and the staff" as one object.

n.0: Sentence 1 already has the comma after its introductory clause.
n.1: Sentence 2 has one clause; "or" joins two phrases, so no comma is needed.
n.3: Sentence 4 already has its comma after the introductory phrase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A lab technician is writing an update that joins two closely related complete thoughts. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The lab closed early the samples will be tested tomorrow.
Because the lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early, the samples will be tested tomorrow.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.

n.0: Two independent clauses with no punctuation between them form a run-on (fused) sentence.
n.1: "Because the lab closed early" is a dependent clause; a semicolon must join two independent clauses, so a comma belongs here.
n.3: Joining two independent clauses with only a comma creates a comma splice.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nurse is charting a change in a patient's plan, using "however" to link two independent clauses. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The patient felt better, however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better; however the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better; however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better however, the doctor ordered one more test.
Conventions of Standard English.w: When a conjunctive adverb such as "however" joins two independent clauses, use a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

n.0: Commas on both sides of "however" leave two independent clauses joined by commas, a comma splice.
n.1: The comma after "however" is missing.
n.3: With no punctuation before "however", the two independent clauses run together.

Conventions of Standard English.q: An exam-day reminder lists what test takers must bring. Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
o: Bring three items to the exam; your ID, your login, and a pen.
The items to bring are: your ID, your login, and a pen.
Bring three items to the exam: your ID, your login, and a pen.
Bring to the exam: your ID, your login, and a pen.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A colon introduces a list only after a complete independent clause: "Bring three items to the exam" can stand alone.

n.0: A semicolon does not introduce a list; it joins independent clauses or separates complex series items.
n.1: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "are".
n.3: "Bring to the exam" is incomplete (the verb has no object), so it cannot introduce a list with a colon.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A travel nurse lists the cities on her contract schedule. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The tour stops in Boise; Idaho, Reno; Nevada, and Provo; Utah.
The tour stops in: Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
The tour stops in Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
The tour stops in Boise, Idaho, Reno, Nevada, and Provo, Utah.
Conventions of Standard English.w: When series items already contain commas (city, state), semicolons separate the items so each pair stays together.

n.0: The semicolons are placed inside each pair instead of between the pairs.
n.1: A colon must not follow a preposition such as "in".
n.3: With commas only, the reader cannot tell where one city-state pair ends and the next begins.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence from a discharge checklist: "The discharge packet includes: a medication list, a follow-up card, and a diet sheet." Which revision corrects the punctuation error?
o: Move the colon to follow "packet"
Replace the colon with a comma
Delete the colon after "includes"
Replace the colon with a semicolon
Conventions of Standard English.w: A colon must not separate a verb (includes) from its objects. Deleting it lets the list follow the verb directly.

n.0: A colon after "packet" would split the subject from its verb, which is also an error.
n.1: A comma must not separate a verb from its objects.
n.3: A semicolon cannot introduce a list or separate a verb from its objects.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A wellness coordinator is writing a poster about rest. Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
o: One factor: mattered most to the team, getting enough sleep.
One factor mattered most to the team: getting enough sleep.
One factor mattered most to the team; getting enough sleep.
The factor that mattered most was: getting enough sleep.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A colon after a complete independent clause can introduce an explanation or example: "getting enough sleep" explains the factor.

n.0: A colon must not separate a subject (One factor) from its verb (mattered).
n.2: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; "getting enough sleep" is a phrase.
n.3: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "was".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A writer wants to set off an interrupting phrase that already contains commas and to give it more emphasis than parentheses would. Which punctuation should enclose the phrase?
o: A pair of colons
A pair of dashes
A pair of semicolons
A pair of brackets
Conventions of Standard English.w: A pair of dashes works like a pair of commas or parentheses but gives more emphasis, and it can enclose an element that has its own internal commas.

n.0: A colon introduces a list, explanation or quotation after an independent clause; colons are not used in pairs.
n.2: Semicolons join independent clauses or separate complex series items; they do not enclose interrupters.
n.3: Brackets mark the writer's own insertions inside a quotation.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A patient letter ends by pointing readers to an enclosed report. Which sentence uses parentheses correctly?
o: The results were normal (see the attached report.)
The results were normal. (see the attached report)
The results were normal (see the attached report).
The results were normal, (see the attached report).
Conventions of Standard English.w: When a parenthetical element ends a sentence but is not a full sentence of its own, the sentence's period goes outside the closing parenthesis.

n.0: The period belongs to the main sentence, so it goes outside the parenthesis.
n.1: A parenthetical that stands as its own sentence must begin with a capital letter and end with its own period inside the parenthesis.
n.3: No comma goes before an opening parenthesis.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student quotes a nurse who said, "He refused the medication twice." The student wants to show that "He" means Mr. Diaz. Which version of the quotation is punctuated correctly?
o: "He (Mr. Diaz) refused the medication twice."
"He [Mr. Diaz] refused the medication twice."
"He, Mr. Diaz, refused the medication twice."
"He refused the medication twice [sic]."
Conventions of Standard English.w: Brackets mark words the writer inserts into someone else's quotation to clarify it.

n.0: Parentheses inside a quotation signal the speaker's own words, not the writer's insertion.
n.2: Commas would present "Mr. Diaz" as part of what the nurse said, changing the quotation.
n.3: [sic] marks an error in the original quotation; this quotation has no error and the name is still not added.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A staff newsletter reports on a wellness program. Which sentence uses hyphens correctly?
o: Twenty-one nurses joined the self care workshop this year.
Twenty one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the selfcare workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine are hyphenated, and the prefix self- always takes a hyphen (self-care).

n.0: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, and the compound modifies the noun "workshop".
n.1: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine take a hyphen.
n.2: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, not closed up.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A hospital recruiting ad describes a surgeon. Which sentence uses hyphens correctly?
o: The highly-trained surgeon works a full-time schedule.
The highly trained surgeon works a full-time schedule.
The highly trained surgeon works a full time schedule.
The highly-trained surgeon works a full time schedule.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two rules apply. A compound adjective before a noun is hyphenated (a full-time schedule), but no hyphen follows an adverb ending in -ly (highly trained).

n.0: An -ly adverb such as "highly" is not hyphenated to the word it modifies.
n.2: "Full-time" is a compound adjective before the noun "schedule", so it needs a hyphen.
n.3: Both are wrong: "highly trained" takes no hyphen, and "full-time" before a noun needs one.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A writing center handout gives six sentences. Which sentences use semicolons and colons correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The tour visits Dayton, Ohio; Erie, Pennsylvania; and Gary, Indiana.
The forms are: the consent, the history, and the release.
The vote was postponed; because the meeting ran late.
Although the meeting ran late; the vote was held.
The kit has one gap: no sterile gloves.
The meeting ran late; therefore, the vote was postponed.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A semicolon with a conjunctive adverb joins independent clauses; a colon after a complete clause introduces an explanation; semicolons separate series items that contain commas.

n.1: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "are".
n.2: "Because the meeting ran late" is a dependent clause; a semicolon must join two independent clauses.
n.3: "Although the meeting ran late" is a dependent clause, so a comma, not a semicolon, should follow it.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A patient is writing about a clinic visit for a hospital blog that follows US conventions. Which sentence punctuates the quotation correctly?
o: The nurse said, "Take this with food," and handed me the cup.
The nurse said, "take this with food," and handed me the cup.
The nurse said, "Take this with food", and handed me the cup.
The nurse said "Take this with food," and handed me the cup.
Conventions of Standard English.w: In US style, a comma separates the dialogue tag from the quotation, the quoted sentence begins with a capital letter, and the comma after the quotation goes inside the closing quotation mark.

n.1: A quoted full sentence begins with a capital letter: "Take".
n.2: US style places commas inside the closing quotation mark, not outside.
n.3: A comma is needed after "said" to introduce the quotation.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nursing student is writing about a short poem in a class essay that follows US conventions. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Her favorite poem is "Night Shift at Mercy."
Her favorite poem is Night Shift at Mercy.
Her favorite poem is 'Night Shift at Mercy.'
Her favorite poem is "Night Shift at Mercy".
Conventions of Standard English.w: The title of a short work such as a poem goes in quotation marks, and in US style the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.

n.1: The title of a short work such as a poem must be enclosed in quotation marks.
n.2: US style uses double quotation marks; single marks are for a quotation within a quotation.
n.3: Placing the period outside the closing quotation mark is British style, not US style.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A family member is repeating a doctor's instruction and asking a question about it. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Did the doctor really say "no visitors."
Did the doctor really say "no visitors?"
Did the doctor really say "no visitors"?
Did the doctor really say "no visitors".
Conventions of Standard English.w: The whole sentence is a question, but the quoted words are not. A question mark that belongs to the whole sentence goes outside the closing quotation mark.

n.0: The sentence is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark.
n.1: The quoted words "no visitors" are not a question, so the question mark does not belong inside the quotation marks.
n.3: The sentence is a direct question, so it must end with a question mark, not a period.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A unit secretary is writing a note about a lost staff badge. Which sentence uses apostrophes correctly?
o: The nurses dont know whose badge was left in the lounge.
The nurses don't know whose badge was left in the lounge.
The nurse's don't know whose badge was left in the lounge.
The nurses don't know who's badge was left in the lounge.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Nurses" is a plain plural (no apostrophe), "don't" is a contraction of "do not" (apostrophe where the o is missing), and "whose" is a possessive pronoun (no apostrophe).

n.0: The contraction of "do not" needs an apostrophe: "don't".
n.2: "Nurses" is a plain plural subject, so it takes no apostrophe.
n.3: "Who's" means "who is"; the possessive needed here is "whose".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A receptionist is recording a phone call. Which sentence uses end punctuation correctly?
o: The patient asked, "Whether the clinic would be open on Monday?"
The patient asked whether the clinic would be open on Monday.
The patient asked whether the clinic would be open on Monday?
The patient asked, whether the clinic would be open on Monday.
Conventions of Standard English.w: This is an indirect question: it reports what was asked without quoting the exact words, so it ends with a period and takes no comma or quotation marks.

n.0: These are not the patient's exact words, so quotation marks are wrong.
n.2: An indirect question is a statement, so it ends with a period, not a question mark.
n.3: No comma separates the verb "asked" from the clause that is its object.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nurse is documenting what a worried parent asked at the bedside. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?".
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished?"
Mrs. Diaz asked "is my son's surgery finished?"
Mrs. Diaz asked, "Is my son's surgery finished"?
Conventions of Standard English.w: The quoted words are a question, so the question mark belongs inside the closing quotation mark, and it also ends the sentence; no second end mark is added.

n.0: The question mark already ends the sentence; adding a period doubles the end punctuation.
n.2: A comma should introduce the quotation, and the quoted sentence should begin with a capital letter.
n.3: The question mark belongs to the quotation, so it goes inside the closing quotation mark.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A board member's comment is quoted in a hospital newsletter. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: She called the plan "a good start;" the board disagreed.
She called the plan, "a good start"; the board disagreed.
She called the plan "a good start," the board disagreed.
She called the plan "a good start"; the board disagreed.
Conventions of Standard English.w: In US style, semicolons and colons go outside the closing quotation mark (only periods and commas go inside).

n.0: A semicolon goes outside the closing quotation mark.
n.1: The quoted words are part of the sentence's structure (the plan is called something), so no comma should introduce them.
n.2: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student cites a chapter titled Heart Sounds from a textbook titled Clinical Basics. Following US conventions, how should the two titles be formatted?
o: Chapter in italics; textbook in quotation marks
Both titles in quotation marks
Both titles in italics
Chapter in quotation marks; textbook in italics
Conventions of Standard English.w: Titles of short works and parts of works (chapters, articles, poems, songs) go in quotation marks; titles of long works (books, journals, films) are italicized.

n.0: This reverses the rule: the part (chapter) takes quotation marks and the whole book is italicized.
n.1: A book is a long work, so its title is italicized, not placed in quotation marks.
n.2: A chapter is a short part of a work, so its title goes in quotation marks.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student is writing about an instructor who asked the class to label a word. Which sentence is punctuated correctly in US style?
o: The instructor said, "Write 'aseptic' on the first line."
The instructor said, 'Write "aseptic" on the first line.'
The instructor said, "Write 'aseptic' on the first line".
The instructor said, "Write "aseptic" on the first line."
Conventions of Standard English.w: In US style, the outer quotation uses double quotation marks, a quotation inside it uses single marks, and the period goes inside the closing marks.

n.1: This reverses US style, which puts double marks outside and single marks inside.
n.2: In US style the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.
n.3: A quotation within a quotation takes single marks so the reader can tell where each ends.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the paragraph. (1) The nurse asked, "Have you eaten today?" (2) The patient said that he wasn't hungry. (3) She wondered why he had skipped breakfast? (4) Later, she wrote "poor appetite" in his chart. Which sentence contains an end-punctuation error?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Conventions of Standard English.w: Sentence 3 is an indirect question (she wondered why ...), which is a statement and ends with a period, not a question mark.

n.0: Sentence 1 correctly places the question mark inside the quotation, because the quoted words are a question.
n.1: Sentence 2 is an indirect quotation, correctly ending with a period.
n.3: Sentence 4 is a statement ending with a period after the quoted phrase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: An editor is checking apostrophes in a community health newsletter. Which sentences use apostrophes correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The clinic changed it's phone number.
The children's clinic closes at five.
The Garcia's are moving to Denver.
Those coats are their's, not ours.
The Garcias' house is on Elm Street.
We'll review the patients' charts today.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Children's (irregular plural + 's), Garcias' (plural family name ending in s + apostrophe), and we'll and patients' (contraction and plural possessive) are all correct.

n.0: The possessive pronoun is "its"; "it's" means "it is" or "it has".
n.2: The family name is a plain plural here (the Garcias are moving), so it takes no apostrophe.
n.3: Possessive pronouns such as "theirs" take no apostrophe.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nurse's comment is split by a dialogue tag in a staff story. Which version is punctuated and capitalized correctly?
o: "I can't stay," Leah said. "because my shift starts at noon."
"I can't stay", Leah said, "because my shift starts at noon."
"I can't stay," Leah said, "because my shift starts at noon."
"I can't stay," Leah said, "Because my shift starts at noon."
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two steps: the quotation is one sentence interrupted by the tag, so a comma follows the tag and the second part continues in lowercase. In US style the comma after "stay" goes inside the quotation mark.

n.0: A period after "said" would start a new sentence, which would need a capital; but "because ..." continues the first sentence, so a comma is needed.
n.1: In US style the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
n.3: The second part continues the same sentence, so "because" is not capitalized.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A public health department is posting its vaccination schedule. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: We hold the flu clinic every fall, starting the Monday after Labor Day.
We hold the flu clinic every fall, starting the Monday after labor day.
We hold the flu clinic every Fall, starting the Monday after Labor Day.
We hold the flu clinic every fall, starting the monday after Labor Day.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Days of the week and holidays are proper nouns (Monday, Labor Day), but seasons are not capitalized unless they are part of a name.

n.1: The name of a holiday is a proper noun, so "Labor Day" is capitalized.
n.2: Seasons such as fall are common nouns and are not capitalized.
n.3: Days of the week are proper nouns, so "Monday" is capitalized.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nursing school newsletter describes a faculty meeting. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: The Doctor spoke with professor Kim about the new course.
The doctor spoke with professor Kim about the new course.
The doctor spoke with Professor Kim about the new course.
The Doctor spoke with Professor Kim about the new course.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A title is capitalized when it comes directly before a name (Professor Kim) but not when it is used as a general noun (the doctor).

n.0: Both are reversed: the general noun is lowercase, and the title before a name is capitalized.
n.1: A title used directly before a name is capitalized: "Professor Kim".
n.3: "Doctor" is used as a general noun after "the", not as a title before a name, so it is lowercase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A new graduate is writing a cover letter about relocating for a nursing job. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: After moving to the Midwest, she drove south to visit her family.
After moving to the midwest, she drove south to visit her family.
After moving to the midwest, she drove South to visit her family.
After moving to the Midwest, she drove South to visit her family.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A compass word is capitalized when it names a region (the Midwest) but not when it gives a direction (drove south).

n.1: "The Midwest" names a region of the country, so it is capitalized.
n.2: Both are reversed: the region is capitalized and the direction is lowercase.
n.3: "Drove south" gives a direction, not a region, so it is lowercase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A patient is filling out a family contact form. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: My mom said that Aunt Rosa would call Dad tonight.
My Mom said that Aunt Rosa would call Dad tonight.
My mom said that aunt Rosa would call Dad tonight.
My mom said that Aunt Rosa would call dad tonight.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A family word is lowercase after a possessive (my mom), capitalized as a title before a name (Aunt Rosa), and capitalized when used in place of a name (Dad).

n.1: After the possessive "my", "mom" is a common noun and is lowercase.
n.2: "Aunt" is a title before the name Rosa, so it is capitalized.
n.3: "Dad" is used as a name here, with no possessive before it, so it is capitalized.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A prenursing student is describing her grades in an application essay. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: She passed Biology 101, but her English and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed biology 101, but her English and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed Biology 101, but her english and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed Biology 101, but her English and Chemistry grades were lower.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A specific numbered course is a proper noun (Biology 101). General school subjects are lowercase (chemistry), except languages, which are always capitalized (English).

n.1: A specific course name with a number is capitalized: "Biology 101".
n.2: Languages are proper nouns, so "English" is capitalized even as a subject.
n.3: "Chemistry" is a general subject here, not a course title, so it is lowercase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A disaster relief report describes a shelter. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: The American Red Cross opened a shelter near Lake Michigan last Winter.
The American red cross opened a shelter near Lake Michigan last winter.
The American Red Cross opened a shelter near Lake Michigan last winter.
The American Red Cross opened a shelter near lake Michigan last winter.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Every main word of an organization's name (American Red Cross) and a specific place (Lake Michigan) is capitalized; seasons are lowercase.

n.0: Seasons such as winter are common nouns and are lowercase.
n.1: All main words in the organization's name are capitalized: "Red Cross".
n.3: "Lake" is part of the proper name "Lake Michigan", so it is capitalized.
