Conventions of Standard English.q: A nurse educator is titling a patient handout and must use standard title case. Which title is capitalized correctly?
o: A guide to caring for patients in the home
A Guide to Caring for Patients in the Home
A Guide To Caring For Patients In The Home
a Guide to Caring for Patients in the Home
Conventions of Standard English.w: In title case, capitalize the first and last words and all major words (nouns, verbs, adjectives); lowercase articles and short prepositions in the middle (to, for, in, the).

n.0: This is sentence case; title case capitalizes the major words such as Guide, Caring, Patients and Home.
n.2: Short prepositions (to, for, in) and articles (the) in the middle of a title are lowercase in title case.
n.3: The first word of a title is always capitalized, even when it is an article.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A clinic's welcome script quotes a nurse whose sentence is interrupted by a tag. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: "when you arrive," the nurse said, "check in at the front desk."
"When you arrive," the nurse said, "check in at the front desk."
"When you arrive," the nurse said, "Check in at the front desk."
"When you arrive," The nurse said, "check in at the front desk."
Conventions of Standard English.w: The quotation is one sentence split by a tag, so it begins with a capital letter (When) and the second part continues in lowercase (check).

n.0: A quoted sentence begins with a capital letter: "When".
n.2: The second part continues the same quoted sentence, so "check" is lowercase.
n.3: The tag continues the sentence after a comma, so "the" is lowercase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student is writing a history paper about nursing. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: During the Civil War, many irish immigrants served as nurses.
During the civil war, many Irish immigrants served as nurses.
During the Civil War, many Irish Immigrants served as nurses.
During the Civil War, many Irish immigrants served as nurses.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Named historical events (the Civil War) and nationalities (Irish) are proper nouns; general nouns such as immigrants are lowercase.

n.0: Nationalities are proper adjectives, so "Irish" is capitalized.
n.1: The name of a specific historical event is capitalized: "Civil War".
n.2: "Immigrants" is a common noun and is lowercase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the paragraph. (1) Last summer, Jamal volunteered at Mercy Hospital in Ohio. (2) He worked with a nurse named Carla Diaz. (3) Every Friday, he helped the Hospital's chaplain plan services. (4) In September, he started classes at Lakeview Community College. Which sentence contains a capitalization error?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Conventions of Standard English.w: In sentence 3, "hospital" is a general noun (the hospital's chaplain), not part of a name, so it should be lowercase.

n.0: "Mercy Hospital" is a proper name and "Ohio" is a state; "summer" is correctly lowercase.
n.1: "Carla Diaz" is a name, and "nurse" is correctly lowercase.
n.3: "September" is a month and "Lakeview Community College" is a proper name.

Conventions of Standard English.q: An editor is checking capitalization in a hospital newsletter. Which sentences are capitalized correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The President of the club called the meeting to order.
The senator met with Governor Ellis on Tuesday.
My sister speaks Spanish and studies psychology.
She was born in the Spring of 2004 in Texas.
Ask your Doctor about the new vaccine.
We drove east on Main Street to the hospital.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A title before a name is capitalized (Governor Ellis) but not a general title (the senator); a direction is lowercase (east); a named street, a language and a day are capitalized; a general subject (psychology) is lowercase.

n.0: A title that is not directly before a name (the president of the club) is lowercase.
n.3: Seasons are common nouns, so "spring" is lowercase.
n.4: "Doctor" after a possessive (your doctor) is a general noun and is lowercase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A reporter is writing about a city official's school visit. Which version of the sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: Last Winter, the mayor visited Northside High School on Oak Avenue.
Last winter, the Mayor visited Northside High School on Oak Avenue.
Last winter, the mayor visited Northside High School on Oak Avenue.
Last winter, the mayor visited Northside high school on Oak avenue.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two rules apply. Proper names of a school and a street are capitalized in full (Northside High School, Oak Avenue), but a season and a title used without a name (the mayor) are lowercase.

n.0: Seasons are common nouns, so "winter" is lowercase.
n.1: "Mayor" is not followed by a name, so it is lowercase.
n.3: "High School" and "Avenue" are parts of proper names, so they are capitalized.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student is classifying sentences from a hospital orientation booklet by structure. Which of the following is a compound sentence?
o: The nurse and the aide checked and recorded the vital signs.
The clinic opened early, but the lab stayed closed until nine.
Because the lab was closed, the samples waited until morning.
When the storm hit, the power failed, and the generator started.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A compound sentence has two or more independent clauses and no dependent clause. "The clinic opened early" and "the lab stayed closed until nine" are joined by a comma and "but".

n.0: This is a simple sentence: one independent clause with a compound subject (nurse and aide) and a compound verb (checked and recorded).
n.2: This is complex: "Because the lab was closed" is a dependent clause attached to one independent clause.
n.3: This is compound-complex: two independent clauses plus the dependent clause "When the storm hit".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nursing student is reviewing sentence structure before the TEAS. Which of the following is a complex sentence?
o: Although she studied all week, Rosa felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week and felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week, yet she felt nervous before the exam.
Rosa studied all week; she still felt nervous before the exam.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. "Although she studied all week" is dependent (it begins with a subordinating conjunction); "Rosa felt nervous before the exam" is independent.

n.1: One subject with two verbs (studied and felt) is a simple sentence with a compound predicate.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by a comma and "yet" make a compound sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses joined by a semicolon make a compound sentence.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A pharmacy newsletter describes the work of a pharmacist and her intern. Which of the following is a simple sentence?
o: The pharmacist counted the pills while her intern labeled them.
The pharmacist and her intern counted, sorted, and labeled the pills.
The pharmacist counted the pills, and her intern labeled them.
After the pharmacist counted the pills, the intern labeled them, and they left.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A simple sentence has exactly one independent clause. A compound subject (pharmacist and intern) and a series of verbs (counted, sorted, and labeled) still form one clause.

n.0: "While her intern labeled them" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by ", and" make a compound sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses plus the dependent clause "After the pharmacist counted the pills" make it compound-complex.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence from a shift report: "When the shift ended, Maya charted her notes, and Luis restocked the supply cart." Which statement correctly describes the structure of this sentence?
o: It is compound-complex because it has two independent clauses and a dependent clause.
It is complex because it opens with the dependent clause "When the shift ended."
It is compound because two independent clauses are joined by a comma and "and."
It is simple because it has one subject performing a series of related actions.
Conventions of Standard English.w: The sentence has two independent clauses (Maya charted her notes; Luis restocked the supply cart) and one dependent clause (When the shift ended), so it is compound-complex.

n.1: A complex sentence has only one independent clause; this one has two.
n.2: A compound sentence has no dependent clause; this one also has "When the shift ended".
n.3: There are two subjects (Maya, Luis) with their own verbs, so there are two independent clauses, not one.

Conventions of Standard English.q: An infection-control poster uses sentences with different purposes. Which sentence is imperative?
o: You washed your hands before you entered the patient's room.
Did you wash your hands before you entered the patient's room?
Please wash your hands before you enter the patient's room.
What a relief it was to wash my hands after that long shift!
Conventions of Standard English.w: An imperative sentence gives a command or makes a request, with the subject "you" understood: "[You] Please wash your hands."

n.0: This makes a statement, so it is declarative.
n.1: This asks a question, so it is interrogative.
n.3: This expresses strong feeling, so it is exclamatory.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "The patient's fever broke overnight; therefore, the doctor canceled the blood culture." How is this sentence classified by structure?
o: Compound
Simple
Complex
Compound-complex
Conventions of Standard English.w: Both parts are independent clauses. "Therefore" is a conjunctive adverb, not a subordinating conjunction, so it does not create a dependent clause; a semicolon joins the two clauses, making the sentence compound.

n.1: There are two independent clauses, not one.
n.2: "Therefore" does not make the second clause dependent, so there is no dependent clause.
n.3: Compound-complex needs a dependent clause, and this sentence has none.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nursing instructor asks students to identify a compound-complex sentence in a set of examples. Which sentence is compound-complex?
o: Ana and Ben missed the bus and arrived late to the lecture.
Because Ana missed the bus, she arrived late to the lecture.
Ana arrived on time, but Ben, who missed the bus, was late.
Ana missed the bus, so she arrived late to the lecture.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two independent clauses (Ana arrived on time; Ben was late) plus a dependent relative clause (who missed the bus) make a compound-complex sentence.

n.0: One independent clause with a compound subject and compound verb is a simple sentence.
n.1: One dependent clause and one independent clause make a complex sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses with no dependent clause make a compound sentence.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the two sentences: "The clinic ran out of flu vaccine. Staff placed a new order." Which option combines them into a complex sentence?
o: The clinic ran out of flu vaccine; staff placed a new order.
When the clinic ran out of flu vaccine, staff placed a new order.
The clinic ran out of flu vaccine, so staff placed a new order.
The clinic ran out of flu vaccine and then placed a new order.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Adding the subordinating conjunction "When" turns the first clause into a dependent clause, so the result has one dependent and one independent clause: a complex sentence.

n.0: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, making a compound sentence.
n.2: A comma and "so" join two independent clauses, making a compound sentence.
n.3: This has one subject with two verbs, so it is a simple sentence (and it changes who placed the order).

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student is checking whether sentences about a retired nurse contain a dependent clause. Which sentence is complex?
o: The nurse trained me, and she retired last spring.
The nurse who trained me retired last spring.
The nurse trained me and retired last spring.
Trained by experts, the nurse retired last spring.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two steps: "who trained me" has its own subject (who) and verb (trained), so it is a dependent relative clause; with the independent clause "The nurse retired last spring", the sentence is complex.

n.0: Two independent clauses with no dependent clause make a compound sentence.
n.2: One subject with two verbs is a simple sentence with a compound predicate.
n.3: "Trained by experts" is a participial phrase (no subject-verb pair), so the sentence is simple.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the paragraph. (1) Kayla works nights at a nursing home. (2) She checks on residents and updates their charts. (3) When a resident cannot sleep, she brings warm milk. (4) Her job is tiring, but she loves it. Which sentence is complex?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Conventions of Standard English.w: Sentence 3 has a dependent clause (When a resident cannot sleep) and an independent clause (she brings warm milk), so it is complex.

n.0: Sentence 1 is simple: one independent clause.
n.1: Sentence 2 is simple: one subject with a compound verb (checks and updates).
n.3: Sentence 4 is compound: two independent clauses joined by ", but".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A tutor gives a student six sentences from a patient handout. Which sentences are simple sentences? Select all that apply.
o: The staff stayed calm because the night was quiet.
If the form is signed, the nurse will file it.
The aide lifted the patient, and the nurse adjusted the bed.
The aide lifted the patient carefully and adjusted the bed.
Both the doctor and the nurse signed the form.
During the long night shift, the staff stayed calm.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Each simple sentence has one independent clause: a compound subject, an introductory prepositional phrase or a compound verb does not add a clause.

n.0: "Because the night was quiet" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.
n.1: "If the form is signed" is a dependent clause, so the sentence is complex.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by ", and" make a compound sentence.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A writer wants to turn "The doctor reviewed the X-ray, and she ordered a CT scan" into a simple sentence without changing its meaning. Which revision does this correctly?
o: After the doctor reviewed the X-ray, she ordered a CT scan.
The doctor, who reviewed the X-ray, ordered a CT scan.
The doctor reviewed the X-ray; she ordered a CT scan.
The doctor reviewed the X-ray and ordered a CT scan.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Removing the second subject (she) leaves one subject with a compound predicate (reviewed ... and ordered): one independent clause, a simple sentence.

n.0: "After the doctor reviewed the X-ray" is a dependent clause, so the result is complex.
n.1: "Who reviewed the X-ray" is a dependent relative clause, so the result is complex.
n.2: A semicolon joining two independent clauses still makes a compound sentence.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student is labeling word groups taken from a patient education leaflet. Which group of words is a dependent clause?
o: during the long night shift
the nurse finished her charting
running down the hospital hallway
because the pharmacy was closed
Conventions of Standard English.w: A dependent clause has a subject and a verb (the pharmacy was) but begins with a subordinating conjunction (because), so it cannot stand alone.

n.0: This is a prepositional phrase: it has no subject-verb pair.
n.1: This has a subject and verb and expresses a complete thought, so it is an independent clause.
n.2: This is a participial phrase: "running" is a verbal with no subject.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "After the meeting, the staff ate lunch in the break room." What is the word group "After the meeting"?
o: An appositive phrase
An independent clause
A prepositional phrase
A dependent clause
Conventions of Standard English.w: "After" works here as a preposition with the object "the meeting". There is no verb, so the group is a phrase, not a clause.

n.0: An appositive renames a nearby noun; "After the meeting" tells when, it does not rename anything.
n.1: An independent clause needs a subject and verb and must express a complete thought.
n.3: A dependent clause needs a subject and a verb (for example, "After the meeting ended"); this group has no verb.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A clinic's front-desk assistant is writing a schedule note. Which sentence uses the articles "a" and "an" correctly?
o: The aide waited an hour before ordering a uniform.
The aide waited a hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited an hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited a hour before ordering a uniform.
Conventions of Standard English.w: The choice depends on the first sound, not the first letter: "an hour" (silent h, vowel sound) and "a uniform" (begins with a "you" consonant sound).

n.1: Both are reversed: "an hour" and "a uniform".
n.2: "Uniform" begins with a consonant "y" sound, so it takes "a".
n.3: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so it takes "an".

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "The nurse carefully explained the very complex procedure." Which word is an adverb that modifies an adjective?
o: complex
explained
very
carefully
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Very" is an adverb that modifies the adjective "complex", telling how complex the procedure is.

n.0: "Complex" is the adjective being modified; it describes the noun "procedure".
n.1: "Explained" is the verb of the sentence.
n.3: "Carefully" is an adverb, but it modifies the verb "explained", not an adjective.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "Whenever the alarm sounds, the staff report to the lobby." Which part of the sentence is the independent clause?
o: Whenever the alarm sounds, the staff
the staff report to the lobby
Whenever the alarm sounds
to the lobby
Conventions of Standard English.w: "The staff report to the lobby" has a subject (staff) and a verb (report) and can stand alone as a sentence.

n.0: This joins the dependent clause to the subject but leaves out the verb, so it is not a clause.
n.2: "Whenever" is a subordinating conjunction, so this clause is dependent.
n.3: "To the lobby" is a prepositional phrase with no subject or verb.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "Walking every day lowers blood pressure." How does the phrase "Walking every day" function?
o: As an infinitive phrase acting as an adverb
As the main verb of the sentence
As a gerund phrase acting as a noun
As a participial phrase acting as an adjective
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Walking every day" is the subject of the verb "lowers". An -ing verbal used as a noun is a gerund, so this is a gerund phrase acting as a noun.

n.0: An infinitive phrase begins with "to" (to walk).
n.1: The main verb is "lowers"; an -ing word without a helping verb cannot be the main verb.
n.3: A participial phrase modifies a noun; this phrase is itself the subject.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "Smiling at the child, the nurse gave the injection." What is "Smiling at the child"?
o: A participial phrase modifying "nurse"
A gerund phrase acting as the subject
A dependent clause modifying "gave"
An infinitive phrase showing purpose
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Smiling at the child" is an -ing verbal phrase that describes the nurse, so it is a participial phrase acting as an adjective.

n.1: The subject of the sentence is "the nurse"; the phrase describes the subject rather than acting as it.
n.2: A clause needs a subject and a verb; this phrase has no subject.
n.3: An infinitive phrase begins with "to".

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student is studying verbal phrases for an English quiz. Which sentence contains an infinitive phrase?
o: The patient went to the cafeteria after lunch.
The patient wanted to rest after lunch.
The patient resting after lunch felt better.
Resting after lunch helped the patient.
Conventions of Standard English.w: An infinitive is "to" + the base form of a verb: "to rest" (to rest after lunch) is an infinitive phrase.

n.0: "To the cafeteria" is "to" + a noun, which is a prepositional phrase, not an infinitive.
n.2: "Resting after lunch" is a participial phrase describing "patient".
n.3: "Resting after lunch" is a gerund phrase acting as the subject.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A staff memo describes a charge nurse in several ways. Which sentence contains an appositive phrase?
o: Ms. Lee, the charge nurse, approved the schedule.
Ms. Lee, approving the schedule, thanked the charge nurse.
Ms. Lee approved the schedule for the charge nurse.
Ms. Lee, who is the charge nurse, approved the schedule.
Conventions of Standard English.w: An appositive phrase is a noun phrase that renames the noun beside it: "the charge nurse" renames Ms. Lee.

n.1: "Approving the schedule" is a participial phrase.
n.2: "For the charge nurse" is a prepositional phrase.
n.3: "Who is the charge nurse" has a subject and a verb, so it is a relative (dependent) clause, not a phrase.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "The aide remained on the unit because it was busy, so she skipped lunch until three." Which word is a subordinating conjunction?
o: remained
until
so
because
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Because" introduces the dependent clause "because it was busy", so it is a subordinating conjunction.

n.0: "Remained" is the main verb of the independent clause, not a conjunction.
n.1: "Until" is followed only by "three" (no subject or verb), so here it is a preposition.
n.2: "So" joins two independent clauses here, so it is a coordinating conjunction.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "The patient seemed anxious before surgery." What part of speech is "anxious" in this sentence?
o: Adjective modifying "patient"
Noun acting as a subject complement
Adverb modifying "seemed"
Verb completing "seemed"
Conventions of Standard English.w: "Seemed" is a linking verb, so the word after it describes the subject: "anxious" is a predicate adjective describing "patient".

n.1: "Anxious" describes the patient rather than naming something; a noun complement would rename the subject (for example, "seemed a calm patient").
n.2: After a linking verb the describing word modifies the subject (a noun), so it is an adjective; the adverb form would be "anxiously".
n.3: The whole verb is "seemed"; "anxious" is not a verb form, so it cannot complete the verb.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "The nurse who works nights trained the student whom we hired." How many dependent clauses does it contain?
o: Three
Zero
Two
One
Conventions of Standard English.w: There are two relative clauses, each with its own subject and verb: "who works nights" and "whom we hired". The independent clause is "The nurse trained the student".

n.0: "The nurse trained the student" is the independent clause, so it is not counted.
n.1: Clauses beginning with relative pronouns (who, whom) are dependent clauses.
n.3: Both "who works nights" and "whom we hired" are dependent clauses, not just one.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A charge nurse is reviewing statements in a staff training packet. Which of the following is a complete sentence?
o: The nurse who works nights trained the new aide.
Because the nurse who works nights trained the aide.
Running to the clinic before the nurse's night shift.
The nurse who works nights and trains the new aides.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "The nurse ... trained the new aide" has a subject (nurse), a main verb (trained) and a complete thought; "who works nights" is a relative clause inside it.

n.1: "Because" makes the whole word group a dependent clause, which cannot stand alone.
n.2: This is a participial phrase with no subject and no main verb.
n.3: The verbs "works" and "trains" both belong to the relative clause beginning with "who", so "The nurse" has no main verb: a fragment.

Conventions of Standard English.q: An editor is checking a clinic newsletter for sentence errors. Which of the following is a comma splice?
o: The bus was late; we missed the appointment.
The bus was late, so we missed the appointment.
The bus was late, we missed the appointment.
Because the bus was late, we missed the appointment.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma. "The bus was late" and "we missed the appointment" can each stand alone.

n.0: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
n.1: A comma plus the coordinating conjunction "so" correctly joins two independent clauses.
n.3: The first clause is dependent (Because ...), so a comma after it is correct.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the run-on sentence from an incident report: "The power went out the generator started within seconds." Which revision corrects it?
o: The power went out, however the generator started within seconds.
The power went out, the generator started within seconds.
The power went out and, the generator started within seconds.
The power went out, and the generator started within seconds.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A comma followed by a coordinating conjunction (and) correctly joins two independent clauses.

n.0: "However" is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma before it still leaves a comma splice.
n.1: Adding only a comma turns the run-on into a comma splice.
n.2: The comma must come before the conjunction, not after it.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the paragraph from a clinic flyer. (1) The clinic offers free flu shots. (2) Every Saturday from nine to noon. (3) Patients should bring their insurance cards. (4) Walk-ins are welcome. Which sentence is a fragment?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Conventions of Standard English.w: Sentence 2 has no subject and no verb; it is a group of prepositional phrases telling when. It could be joined to sentence 1.

n.0: Sentence 1 has a subject (clinic) and a verb (offers) and is complete.
n.2: Sentence 3 has a subject (Patients) and a verb (should bring) and is complete.
n.3: Sentence 4 has a subject (Walk-ins) and a verb (are) and is complete.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence from a nursing note: "The patient felt dizzy, however, she refused to sit down." Which revision corrects the comma splice?
o: The patient felt dizzy, she, however, refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy, however she refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy; however, she refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy however, she refused to sit down.
Conventions of Standard English.w: When a conjunctive adverb such as "however" joins two independent clauses, a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it.

n.0: Moving "however" inside the second clause still leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma.
n.1: A comma before "however" still joins two independent clauses with only a comma: a comma splice.
n.3: With no punctuation before "however", the two independent clauses run together.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the word groups from a medication note: "Because the patient was allergic to penicillin. The doctor prescribed a different antibiotic." Which revision correctly fixes the fragment?
o: Because the patient was allergic to penicillin, the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
Because the patient was allergic to penicillin; the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
Because the patient was allergic to penicillin the doctor, prescribed a different antibiotic.
The patient was allergic to penicillin, the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
Conventions of Standard English.w: The dependent clause (Because ... penicillin) is attached to the independent clause with a comma, giving a correct complex sentence.

n.1: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; the first part is a dependent clause.
n.2: The comma is misplaced: it separates the subject (the doctor) from its verb, and the comma after the introductory clause is missing.
n.3: Removing "Because" leaves two independent clauses joined by only a comma: a comma splice.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A unit manager is editing a weekly staffing update. Which of the following sentences is structured correctly?
o: The clinic was short-staffed on Friday. Because several walk-ins arrived before nine.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
Although the clinic was short-staffed, the nurses kept every visit on schedule.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday, several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
Conventions of Standard English.w: A dependent clause (Although the clinic was short-staffed) followed by a comma and an independent clause is a correct complex sentence.

n.0: The second word group begins with "Because" and has no independent clause, so it is a fragment.
n.1: Two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction form a run-on (fused) sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma form a comma splice.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A student is checking notes from a clinical rotation. Which of the following is a fragment?
o: Hoping to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
She hoped to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
Finish your charting before the end of the shift.
Hoping to finish, she charted before the end of the shift.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two steps: "Hoping" is a participle, not a main verb, and the word group has no subject, so it cannot stand alone.

n.1: This has a subject (She) and a main verb (hoped), so it is complete.
n.2: This is an imperative sentence; its subject "you" is understood, so it is complete.
n.3: The participial phrase is attached to the independent clause "she charted ...", so it is complete.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the paragraph from a hand-hygiene poster. (1) Hand hygiene prevents infection. (2) Staff should wash for at least twenty seconds they should also dry their hands fully. (3) Sanitizer works when hands are not visibly soiled. (4) Gloves do not replace washing. Which sentence is a run-on?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Conventions of Standard English.w: Sentence 2 runs two independent clauses (Staff should wash ...; they should also dry ...) together with no punctuation or conjunction.

n.0: Sentence 1 is a single independent clause.
n.2: Sentence 3 is a complex sentence: an independent clause plus the dependent clause "when hands are not visibly soiled".
n.3: Sentence 4 is a single independent clause.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the comma splice: "The roads were icy, the clinic opened late." Which revision corrects the error and shows that the icy roads caused the late opening?
o: Although the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
Because the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
The roads were icy, the clinic, therefore, opened late.
The roads were icy, but the clinic opened late.
Conventions of Standard English.w: Two steps: subordinating one clause fixes the splice, and "Because" signals cause and effect.

n.0: "Although" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.
n.2: The two independent clauses are still joined by only a comma, so the splice remains.
n.3: "But" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.

Conventions of Standard English.q: A nurse is writing patient instructions and wants every line to be a complete sentence. Which of the following is a complete sentence?
o: Please sign the consent form before the procedure.
The consent form that was signed before the procedure.
Since the consent form was signed before the procedure.
Signing the consent form before the procedure.
Conventions of Standard English.w: An imperative sentence is complete even though its subject (you) is not stated: "[You] Please sign the consent form."

n.1: "That was signed ..." is a relative clause describing the form; the subject "The consent form" has no main verb.
n.2: "Since" makes this a dependent clause, which cannot stand alone.
n.3: This is a gerund phrase with no main verb.

Conventions of Standard English.q: Read the sentence: "The reason the test was delayed is because the machine broke." Which revision corrects the faulty sentence structure?
o: The reason the test was delayed, is that the machine broke.
The reason the test was delayed is because of the machine broke.
The reason the test was delayed is that the machine broke.
The reason the test was delayed is when the machine broke.
Conventions of Standard English.w: "The reason ... is" must be completed by a noun clause (that the machine broke), not an adverb clause beginning with "because". This repairs the faulty predication.

n.0: A comma must not separate the subject (The reason the test was delayed) from its verb (is).
n.1: "Because of" must be followed by a noun phrase, not a clause with a verb (broke).
n.3: "Is when" is also faulty predication: a reason is not a time.

Knowledge of Language.q: A front-desk sign is being revised before it is posted. Which sentence uses correct subject-verb agreement in inverted word order?
o: There is two forms that every new patient must sign at check-in.
On the counter sit two charts that still need a provider's signature.
Here is the signed consent forms for the two new patients.
There was several reasons that the appointment had to be moved.
Knowledge of Language.w: When a sentence is inverted, find the subject after the verb. "Charts" is the subject of "sit," and both are plural, so "On the counter sit two charts" is correct.

n.0: In a "there" sentence the subject follows the verb. The subject is "forms" (plural), so it must be "There are."
n.2: The subject that follows the verb is "forms" (plural), so it must be "Here are the signed consent forms."
n.3: The subject is "reasons" (plural), which comes after the verb, so it must be "There were."

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is editing a short article about a nursing school's admissions trends. Which sentence from the article uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Twenty dollars are the fee that each applicant pays to submit a form.
The news about the new admission deadlines was posted on Monday.
A number of applicants has asked whether the essay is required.
The number of applicants to the program have doubled since 2020.
Knowledge of Language.w: "News" ends in -s but is singular, so it takes "was." Remember: "the number of" is singular, "a number of" is plural, and a sum of money is singular.

n.0: An amount of money treated as one sum is singular: "Twenty dollars is the fee."
n.2: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb: "A number of applicants have asked."
n.3: "The number of" is singular (it names one figure), so the verb must be "has doubled."

Knowledge of Language.q: A preceptor is writing an incident note about an equipment check. Which sentence uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: The nurse, along with two students, are checking the crash cart.
Neither the students nor the nurse are checking the crash cart today.
The nurse and two students, with the instructor, is checking the cart.
The nurse, as well as two students, is checking the crash cart.
Knowledge of Language.w: Phrases such as "as well as," "along with" and "together with" do not make a subject plural. The subject is "nurse," so the verb is "is."

n.0: "Along with two students" is an intervening phrase, not part of the subject. The subject "nurse" is singular, so the verb must be "is."
n.1: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "nurse," which is singular, so it must be "is."
n.2: "The nurse and two students" is a compound subject joined by "and," which is plural, so the verb must be "are."

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a radiology department update: "The quality of the images from the older scanners have improved since the software update." Which revision corrects the agreement error?
o: Change "scanners" to "scanner."
Change "images" to "image."
Change "have improved" to "were improved."
Change "have improved" to "has improved."
Knowledge of Language.w: The subject is "quality" (singular). "Of the images from the older scanners" is an intervening phrase, so the verb must be singular: "has improved."

n.0: "Scanners" is inside a prepositional phrase and is not the subject; the plural verb "have" would still disagree with "quality."
n.1: "Images" is also inside a prepositional phrase; the true subject "quality" still needs "has," so the error remains.
n.2: "Were" is still plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject "quality," and it changes the meaning to passive.

Knowledge of Language.q: A supply clerk writes four notes for the end-of-day inventory report. Which note uses correct subject-verb agreement with an indefinite pronoun such as some, all, most or none?
o: Some of the patients in the waiting room is asking about the delay.
Most of the hand sanitizer in the supply room has been used this week.
All of the lab samples from this morning has been labeled and stored.
None of the water in the pitchers were changed during the night shift.
Knowledge of Language.w: Some, any, none, all, most and more are singular or plural depending on the noun they refer to. "Sanitizer" is uncountable, so "most of the hand sanitizer has" is correct.

n.0: "Some" refers to "patients" (plural) here, so the verb must be "are asking."
n.2: "All" takes its number from the noun after "of." "Samples" is plural, so the verb must be "have been labeled."
n.3: "None" refers to "water," an uncountable noun, so it takes a singular verb: "was changed."

Knowledge of Language.q: A charge nurse is reviewing sentences for a unit handbook. Which sentences use correct subject-verb agreement? Select all that apply.
o: Each of the new monitors come with a three-year warranty.
Everybody in both classes wants the exam moved to Friday.
The supply of masks in the storage rooms is running low.
The doctor's notes on the patient's progress was hard to read.
Either the pharmacist or the technicians are available after 6 p.m.
Knowledge of Language.w: With "either...or," the verb agrees with the nearer subject ("technicians are"). "Everybody" is singular ("wants"). "Supply" is the subject of "is," not "masks" or "rooms."

n.0: "Each" is always singular, so it must be "Each of the new monitors comes"; "monitors" is inside the phrase "of the new monitors."
n.3: The subject is "notes" (plural); "on the patient's progress" is an intervening phrase, so the verb must be "were."

Knowledge of Language.q: A volunteer coordinator drafts four sentences for a hospital welcome packet. Which sentence contains an error in subject-verb agreement?
o: The bag of IV fluid hanging by the bed is due to be replaced.
Neither of the two applicants has submitted a transcript yet.
There are a clipboard and two pens at the front desk for visitors.
Each of the patients on the third floor have a call button.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Each" is always singular, so the verb must be "has": "Each of the patients on the third floor has a call button." The plural "patients" sits inside a prepositional phrase.

n.0: This sentence is correct: the subject "bag" is singular and takes "is"; "of IV fluid hanging by the bed" does not change it.
n.1: This sentence is correct: "neither" used as a pronoun is singular, so "has submitted" agrees.
n.2: This sentence is correct: the subject after the verb is compound ("a clipboard and two pens"), so the plural "are" agrees.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph from a clinic notice. (1) The clinic's new hours begin next week. (2) Patients who arrive after 5 p.m. will be seen by the on-call provider. (3) A list of the providers' schedules are posted at the front desk. (4) Questions about the change go to the office manager. Which sentence contains a subject-verb agreement error?
o: Sentence 4
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Knowledge of Language.w: In sentence 3 the subject is "list" (singular), so the verb must be "is posted." "Of the providers' schedules" is an intervening phrase.

n.0: The subject "questions" is plural and "go" is plural; "about the change" does not affect agreement.
n.1: "Patients" is plural, and "will be seen" works for any subject; the clause "who arrive" agrees with "patients."
n.3: "Hours" is plural and "begin" is a plural verb, so sentence 1 agrees.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is editing a reflection paper about a clinical skills lab. Which sentence from the paper uses pronoun case correctly?
o: Him and his sister both applied to the nursing program this year.
Between you and me, the new skills schedule is an improvement.
The instructor asked Maria and I to demonstrate the bed transfer.
The award went to Devon and myself for the hand-hygiene project.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Between" is a preposition, and the object of a preposition takes the objective case: "between you and me."

n.0: "Him and his sister" is the subject, so the subjective case is needed: "He and his sister."
n.2: "Maria and I" is the object of "asked," so the objective case is needed: "asked Maria and me." Drop "Maria and" to test: "asked me."
n.3: "Myself" is reflexive and has no antecedent in the sentence; the object of "to" needs "me": "to Devon and me."

Knowledge of Language.q: A clinic receptionist is writing questions for a new front-desk guide. Which sentence uses who or whom correctly?
o: The student whom earned the top score will speak at graduation.
Whom do you think will be named the new charge nurse?
To whom should I send the completed insurance forms?
Whom is responsible for the night count of controlled drugs?
Knowledge of Language.w: "Whom" is the objective form. In "To whom should I send," the pronoun is the object of the preposition "to" (send them to him), so "whom" is correct.

n.0: The pronoun is the subject of "earned" (she earned), so it must be "who."
n.1: Ignore "do you think": the pronoun is the subject of "will be named" (he will be named), so it must be "Who."
n.3: The pronoun is the subject of "is responsible" (he is responsible), so it must be "Who."

Knowledge of Language.q: A nursing club is printing a flyer about clinical placements. Which sentence on the flyer uses the pronouns "we" and "us" correctly?
o: Us students were asked to arrive by 6:30 a.m. for clinicals.
The new policy was explained to we volunteers on Monday.
The instructor gave us students extra time on the dosage exam.
Several of we applicants had questions about the essay prompt.
Knowledge of Language.w: Drop the noun to test: "The instructor gave us extra time" is correct, so "gave us students" is correct. "Us" is the indirect object of "gave."

n.0: Drop "students": "Us were asked" is wrong. The phrase is the subject, so it must be "We students."
n.1: Drop "volunteers": "explained to we" is wrong. The object of "to" needs "us volunteers."
n.3: "Of" is a preposition, so its object needs the objective case: "several of us applicants."

Knowledge of Language.q: A lab manager is reviewing safety notes before they are posted. Which sentence has a pronoun that agrees with its antecedent in number and person?
o: The lab and the pharmacy will extend its hours in December.
If a student wants to pass, you have to practice every day.
All of the incubators must have its filters changed every month.
Each of the vials must be inspected for cracks before it is used.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Each" is singular, and a vial is a thing, so the singular pronoun "it" agrees in number and person.

n.0: Two antecedents joined by "and" are plural, so the pronoun must be "their hours."
n.1: The sentence shifts from third person ("a student") to second person ("you"); keep the same person throughout.
n.2: "All" refers to "incubators" (plural) here, so the pronoun must be plural: "their filters."

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a patient's visit summary: "When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, he explained the test results." Which revision removes the unclear pronoun reference?
o: When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, they explained the new test results.
Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, and he explained all of the new test results.
When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, he carefully explained the test results.
When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, the doctor explained the test results.
Knowledge of Language.w: A pronoun must point to one clear antecedent. Replacing "he" with "the doctor" shows that Dr. Okafor explained the results.

n.0: "They" is still unclear (both men? someone else?) and does not identify who explained the results.
n.1: Joining the clauses with "and" keeps the same ambiguous "he" with two possible antecedents.
n.2: Adding "carefully" does not fix the problem: "he" could still mean either man.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is citing a hospital handbook in a short report. Which sentence avoids a vague pronoun reference?
o: In the employee handbook, they state that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
They say in the employee handbook that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
The handbook and the shift schedule both list breaks, and it says they last thirty minutes.
The employee handbook states that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
Knowledge of Language.w: Every pronoun needs a clear antecedent. Making "the employee handbook" the subject removes the vague "they" or "it."

n.0: "They" is vague: the handbook is a thing, and no people have been named.
n.1: "They" has no antecedent; the sentence never names who "they" are.
n.2: "It" could mean the handbook or the shift schedule, so the reference is unclear even though both nouns are named.

Knowledge of Language.q: A nurse is writing a short thank-you note to a colleague. Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun correctly?
o: My lab partner and myself presented the case study on Monday.
Please return the signed form to Ms. Park or myself by Friday.
The residents organized the whole fundraiser theirselves this year.
Kendra reminded herself to recheck the dosage before charting it.
Knowledge of Language.w: A reflexive pronoun is correct when its antecedent is in the same clause. "Herself" refers back to "Kendra," who did the reminding.

n.0: "Myself" cannot be part of a subject; the subjective case is needed: "My lab partner and I."
n.1: "Myself" has no antecedent in this sentence; the object of "to" needs "me": "to Ms. Park or me."
n.2: "Theirselves" is nonstandard; the reflexive form is "themselves."

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a shift report: "The charge nurse divided the six patients between Tomas and I so that each of us had three." Which revision corrects the pronoun error?
o: Change "had" to "have."
Change "I" to "me."
Change "us" to "we."
Change "I" to "myself."
Knowledge of Language.w: "Between" is a preposition, so both of its objects take the objective case: "between Tomas and me."

n.0: "Each" is singular, so "had" (or "has") is right; "have" adds a tense shift and does not fix "between Tomas and I."
n.2: "Us" is correct as the object of the preposition "of"; "each of we" would create a new error.
n.3: "Myself" needs an antecedent in the sentence that refers to the same person; the object of "between" needs "me."

Knowledge of Language.q: A pharmacy intern is drafting a patient handout. Which sentence contains an inappropriate shift in pronoun person?
o: We volunteers should bring our badges to every shift this month.
Applicants should check their email often, since the school sends updates there.
If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember it.
When one reads a drug label, you should check the expiration date first.
Knowledge of Language.w: "One" is third person, but "you" is second person. Keep one point of view: "When you read a drug label, you should..."

n.0: This sentence stays in first person plural: "we" and "our."
n.1: This sentence is consistent: "applicants" and "their" are both third person plural.
n.2: This sentence stays in second person throughout ("you" and the implied "you" of "take").

Knowledge of Language.q: An instructor is grading sentences on a grammar quiz for first-year nursing students. Which sentences use pronouns correctly? Select all that apply.
o: Whom should the front desk call if the results are late?
The tutor helped Grace and myself with dosage problems.
The award was shared by Mei and her.
Dev and me will cover the weekend shifts in March.
Each of the clinics posted its holiday hours online.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Each" is singular, so "its" agrees. "By Mei and her" uses the objective case after the preposition "by." "Whom" is the object of "call" (the desk should call him).

n.1: "Myself" has no antecedent in the sentence; the object of "helped" needs "me": "Grace and me."
n.3: "Dev and me" is the subject, so it needs the subjective case: "Dev and I will cover."

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a staff memo: "The pharmacist told the technician that her shift had been changed." Which revision makes the pronoun reference clear?
o: The pharmacist told the technician that her shift had now been changed.
The pharmacist and the technician were told that her shift changed.
The pharmacist told the technician that her own shift had been changed.
The pharmacist told the technician, "Your shift has been changed."
Knowledge of Language.w: Turning the report into a direct quotation makes "your" refer clearly to the technician, the person being spoken to.

n.0: Adding "now" leaves "her" ambiguous; it could still mean the pharmacist's shift or the technician's.
n.1: "Her" now has two possible antecedents in the subject, so the reference is still unclear.
n.2: Adding "own" does not help: "her own" could still mean the pharmacist's shift or the technician's.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph from a clinic newsletter. (1) The Riverside Clinic opened a second location this spring. (2) Its new site offers evening hours for working families. (3) Patients may book appointments at either location online. (4) Dr. Liu and myself will divide our time between the two offices. Which sentence contains a pronoun error?
o: Sentence 4
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Knowledge of Language.w: In sentence 4, "myself" is part of the subject and has no antecedent; the subjective case is needed: "Dr. Liu and I will divide our time."

n.1: Sentence 3 has no pronoun error; "either location" is singular and correctly used.
n.2: Sentence 1 contains no pronoun error; it has no pronoun at all.
n.3: "Its" is the correct possessive for the clinic (one organization), with no apostrophe.

Knowledge of Language.q: A nursing student is proofreading her clinical journal. Which sentence from the journal uses the correct form of an irregular verb?
o: She has wrote three care plans for the pediatric rotation.
By the time I arrived, my preceptor had went to the meeting.
The new aide has already taken the medication safety course.
I seen the updated schedule posted near the break room.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Take" is irregular: take, took, taken. A helping verb ("has") takes the past participle "taken."

n.0: "Has" needs the past participle "written"; "wrote" is the simple past.
n.1: "Had" needs the past participle "gone"; "went" is the simple past and cannot follow a helping verb.
n.3: "Seen" is a past participle and needs a helping verb ("have seen"); otherwise use the simple past "saw."

Knowledge of Language.q: A home health aide is writing up visit notes. Which sentence uses "lie" or "lay" correctly?
o: After the procedure, the patient laid on his side for an hour.
Please lie the clean linens on the bottom shelf of the cart.
Yesterday, Ana lay down for a nap after her long night shift.
The dog has laid by the front door all afternoon long.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Lie" (to recline, no object) is lie, lay, lain. "Yesterday ... lay down" is the past tense of "lie," so it is correct.

n.0: The patient is reclining (no object), so the verb is "lie"; its past tense is "lay," not "laid."
n.1: Putting linens down takes an object, so the verb is "lay": "Please lay the clean linens."
n.3: The dog is reclining, so the verb is "lie"; its past participle is "lain": "has lain."

Knowledge of Language.q: A certified nursing assistant is charting a routine check. Which sentence keeps verb tense consistent?
o: The aide checked the patient's temperature and recorded it in the chart.
The aide checked the patient's temperature and records it in the chart.
The aide checks the patient's temperature and recorded it in the chart.
The aide checks the patient's temperature and had recorded it in the chart.
Knowledge of Language.w: Both actions happened in the same past visit, so both verbs stay in the simple past: "checked ... recorded."

n.1: The sentence shifts from past ("checked") to present ("records") for two actions in the same visit.
n.2: The sentence shifts from present ("checks") to past ("recorded") with no reason for the change.
n.3: The past perfect "had recorded" places the recording before the checking, which is illogical, and it shifts tense.

Knowledge of Language.q: A surgical unit's family liaison is writing an update. Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly to show which action happened first?
o: The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrives.
The surgeon finishes the procedure by the time the family had arrived.
The surgeon has finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
Knowledge of Language.w: The past perfect (had + past participle) marks the earlier of two past actions. The procedure ended first, then the family arrived.

n.1: "Arrives" is present tense, which clashes with "had finished"; both events are in the past.
n.2: The tenses are reversed: the earlier action (finishing) needs the past perfect, and the later one the simple past.
n.3: The present perfect "has finished" does not fit a completed past time frame set by "arrived"; use "had finished."

Knowledge of Language.q: A physical therapy assistant is writing notes after a session. Which sentence uses "rise" or "raise" correctly?
o: Prices for the required nursing textbooks have raised every semester.
The therapist asked the patient to rise his arm above his head.
The patient's temperature rose overnight, so we called the doctor.
The aide raised from her chair when the surgeon entered the room.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Rise" (rise, rose, risen) has no object; "raise" (raise, raised, raised) takes one. A temperature goes up by itself, so "rose" is correct.

n.0: Prices go up on their own (no object), so the verb must be "risen": "have risen."
n.1: Lifting an arm takes an object ("his arm"), so the verb must be "raise."
n.3: Getting up has no object, so the verb must be "rose" (past of "rise").

Knowledge of Language.q: A clinic receptionist is writing instructions for the waiting area. Which sentence uses "sit" and "set" correctly?
o: He set the tray on the table and sat beside his mother.
Please set in the chair by the window until your name is called.
The patient has set in the waiting room for over two hours.
She sat the specimen cup on the counter next to the sink.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Set" (set, set, set) means to place something and takes an object (the tray). "Sit" (sit, sat, sat) has no object (he sat).

n.1: A person resting in a chair needs "sit" (no object); "set" means to place something.
n.2: The patient is seated (no object), so the verb must be "sat": "has sat."
n.3: Placing a cup takes an object, so the verb must be "set": "She set the specimen cup."

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a pharmacy incident report: "If the order had been clearer, the pharmacy could of filled it on time." Which revision corrects the verb error?
o: Change "could of filled" to "could have filled" and "had been" to "would have been."
Change "could of filled" to "could have filled."
Change "had been" to "was."
Change "could of filled" to "could had filled."
Knowledge of Language.w: "Could of" is a mishearing of "could've." The correct form is "could have" + past participle: "could have filled."

n.0: This fixes "could of" but adds a new error: the if-clause of a past unreal condition takes "had been," not "would have been."
n.2: "Had been" is correct for a past condition that did not happen, and the "could of" error would remain.
n.3: "Could" is a helping verb and must be followed by the base form "have"; "could had filled" is ungrammatical.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is writing a persuasive paragraph for a nursing program application and must use formal written English. Which sentence uses the subjunctive mood correctly?
o: If I was the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I were the instructor, I will allow one retake per exam.
If I would be the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I were the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
Knowledge of Language.w: For an unreal or hypothetical condition, formal English uses "were" for all subjects and "would" in the main clause.

n.0: A condition contrary to fact takes the subjunctive "were" in formal writing, not "was."
n.1: An unreal "if I were" condition pairs with "would," not the future "will."
n.2: "Would" belongs in the result clause, not the if-clause; use "If I were."

Knowledge of Language.q: A writing tutor reviews sentences from nursing students' reflection papers. Which sentences use irregular verbs correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The pipes in the old wing had froze before the heat came back on.
The intern has chose a specialty in pediatric nursing.
Ms. Reyes has led the infection control team since 2021.
The patient has already swum two laps in the therapy pool.
The phone rung three times before anyone at the desk answered.
By noon, the volunteers had drunk all of the bottled water.
Knowledge of Language.w: Drink, drank, drunk; lead, led, led; swim, swam, swum. Each helping verb (had, has) is paired with the correct past participle.

n.0: After "had," use the past participle "frozen": "had frozen."
n.1: After "has," use the past participle "chosen": "has chosen."
n.4: The simple past of "ring" is "rang"; "rung" is the past participle and needs a helping verb.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph from a scholarship essay. (1) Last spring, Keisha volunteered at a free clinic in her town. (2) She checks in patients and took their blood pressure. (3) The experience showed her how much she enjoyed patient care. (4) By June, she had decided to apply to nursing school. Which sentence contains an unnecessary shift in verb tense?
o: Sentence 4
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Knowledge of Language.w: Sentence 2 shifts from present ("checks") to past ("took") while describing the same past events; it should read "She checked in patients and took..."

n.0: "Had decided" is past perfect, correctly marking a decision completed by a past point ("By June").
n.1: "Showed" and "enjoyed" are both simple past, consistent with the rest of the paragraph.
n.2: "Volunteered" is simple past, which matches "last spring."

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a quality report: "Since the new reminder policy started, the clinic has saw fewer missed appointments." Which revision corrects the verb error?
o: Change "has saw" to "seen."
Change "has saw" to "have seen."
Change "has saw" to "has seen."
Change "has saw" to "had saw."
Knowledge of Language.w: Two steps: "since" calls for the present perfect, and a singular subject ("clinic") takes "has" + the past participle "seen."

n.0: A past participle cannot stand alone as the main verb; it needs "has."
n.1: "Seen" is right, but "clinic" is singular, so the helping verb must stay "has."
n.3: "Saw" is the simple past and cannot follow any helping verb; the participle is "seen."

Knowledge of Language.q: A hospital's staff profile page is being edited. Which sentence uses verb tense correctly with the phrase "since 2019"?
o: Dr. Patel has worked at the hospital in 2019.
Dr. Patel works at the hospital since 2019.
Dr. Patel is working at the hospital since 2019.
Dr. Patel has worked at the hospital since 2019.
Knowledge of Language.w: The present perfect (has/have + past participle) shows an action that began in the past and continues now: "has worked ... since 2019."

n.0: The present perfect does not pair with a finished, specific past time such as "in 2019"; use "worked in 2019."
n.1: "Since" marks an action that began in the past and continues, which needs the present perfect "has worked."
n.2: The present progressive does not fit an ongoing span that began at a past point; use "has worked" or "has been working."

Knowledge of Language.q: A nursing student is revising the opening of a clinical narrative. Which sentence is written correctly, with no dangling modifier?
o: Walking into the clinic, it was clear that the lobby was full.
Walking into the clinic, the crowd in the lobby surprised her.
Walking into the clinic, the lobby looked crowded to Rosa.
Walking into the clinic, Rosa saw that the lobby was crowded.
Knowledge of Language.w: An introductory participial phrase must be followed by the person or thing doing the action. Rosa was walking into the clinic, so "Rosa" must come right after the comma.

n.0: "It" cannot do the walking; the person who walked in never appears as the subject.
n.1: The subject after the phrase is "the crowd," so the sentence says the crowd was walking into the clinic.
n.2: The phrase "Walking into the clinic" is followed by "the lobby," so the sentence says the lobby was walking.

Knowledge of Language.q: A clinic manager wants to say that no more than two nurses are scheduled on weekends. Which sentence places the limiting word so that it states this meaning most clearly?
o: The clinic only schedules two nurses on weekends.
Only the clinic schedules two nurses on weekends.
The clinic schedules only two nurses on weekends.
The clinic schedules two nurses only on weekends.
Knowledge of Language.w: A limiting word such as only, just, nearly or almost goes directly before the word it limits. To limit the number, "only" goes before "two nurses."

n.0: Placed before the verb, "only" limits "schedules" (it schedules and does nothing else), not the number two.
n.1: Placed before "the clinic," "only" means no other place schedules two nurses, which is a different meaning.
n.3: Placed before "on weekends," "only" means nurses are scheduled on weekends and not on weekdays.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is editing a peer's care-plan summary. Which sentence uses adjectives and adverbs correctly?
o: After a night of rest, Jordan felt well enough to go to class.
The new graduate handled the emergency calm and careful.
The cafeteria soup tasted differently after the new cook started.
The team did real good on the state safety inspection this year.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Well" can be an adjective meaning "in good health," so "felt well" is correct after the linking verb "felt."

n.1: "Calm" and "careful" describe how she handled it, so they modify a verb and must be adverbs: "calmly and carefully."
n.2: "Tasted" is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective that describes the soup: "tasted different."
n.3: "Did" is an action verb, so it needs the adverb "well"; "real" should also be the adverb "really."

Knowledge of Language.q: A pharmacy student is comparing products in a study guide. Which sentence uses a comparative or superlative form correctly?
o: The night shift is more busier than the day shift on most weekends.
Of the three dressings, the foam one is the least painful to remove.
Of the two inhalers, the blue one is the most effective for her asthma.
Of the three textbooks, this one is the better choice for anatomy.
Knowledge of Language.w: With three or more items, use the superlative (-est, most, least). Three dressings are compared, so "least painful" is correct.

n.0: "More busier" is a double comparative; use "busier" alone.
n.2: Comparing exactly two items calls for the comparative: "the more effective."
n.3: Comparing three or more items calls for the superlative: "the best choice."

Knowledge of Language.q: A quality-improvement report summarizes changes in a clinic. Which sentence uses "fewer" or "less" correctly?
o: There were fewer complaints after the new check-in system began.
The new menu offers less calories per serving than the old one did.
The weekend shift now runs with less staff members than before.
The clinic saw less patients this month than it did last month.
Knowledge of Language.w: Use "fewer" with countable plural nouns (complaints, patients, calories, staff members) and "less" with uncountable nouns (water, sodium, time).

n.1: "Calories" can be counted, so the sentence needs "fewer calories."
n.2: "Staff members" is a countable plural, so it needs "fewer staff members" ("less staff" alone would be fine).
n.3: "Patients" can be counted, so the sentence needs "fewer patients."

Knowledge of Language.q: A community health volunteer is writing a short event summary. Which sentence places the modifier "with large print" correctly?
o: The volunteer handed out flyers to the families with large print.
The volunteer with large print handed out flyers to the families.
The volunteer handed out flyers with large print to the families.
With large print, the volunteer handed out flyers to the families.
Knowledge of Language.w: A modifier belongs next to the word it describes. The large print is on the flyers, so the phrase must follow "flyers."

n.0: Placed after "families," the phrase seems to describe the families, not the flyers.
n.1: Placed after "volunteer," the phrase describes the volunteer instead of the flyers.
n.3: Placed at the start, the phrase seems to describe the volunteer, who is not printed.

Knowledge of Language.q: A home care agency is revising a client letter. Which sentence is written in standard English with no double negative?
o: The aide hadn't scarcely finished charting when the call light came on.
The patient can't hardly sit up in bed without help from staff.
The pharmacy didn't have any of the brand-name tablets in stock.
There isn't no reason for the patient to skip the follow-up visit.
Knowledge of Language.w: One negative is enough. "Didn't" is negative and "any" is neutral, so the sentence is correct.

n.0: "Scarcely" is negative in meaning, so "hadn't scarcely" is a double negative; use "had scarcely."
n.1: "Hardly" is already negative, so "can't hardly" is a double negative; use "can hardly."
n.3: "Isn't" and "no" are two negatives; use "There is no reason" or "There isn't any reason."

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a discharge summary: "After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered." Which revision corrects the dangling modifier?
o: After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's decision was to order a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's order called for a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered by the doctor.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor ordered a new medication.
Knowledge of Language.w: The person who reviewed the results (the doctor) must be the subject right after the introductory phrase.

n.0: The subject after the comma is "decision," and a decision cannot review lab results; "doctor's" is only a possessive.
n.1: The subject after the comma is "order," so the sentence says the order reviewed the results; the doctor must be the subject.
n.2: The subject after the comma is still "a new medication," so the sentence still says the medication reviewed the results.

Knowledge of Language.q: A patient satisfaction survey summary is being edited. Which sentence uses an adjective correctly after a linking verb?
o: The coffee in the staff break room tastes bitter today.
The infant is breathing good now that the fever has broken.
Their new manager seems nicely, and the staff likes her a lot.
The cafeteria food tastes differently since the new cook started.
Knowledge of Language.w: Linking verbs (taste, seem, feel, look, smell) connect the subject to an adjective that describes it: the coffee tastes bitter.

n.1: "Breathing" is an action, so it needs the adverb "well," not the adjective "good."
n.2: "Seems" is a linking verb, so it takes the adjective "nice," not the adverb "nicely."
n.3: "Tastes" links the food to a description, so it needs the adjective "different," not the adverb.

Knowledge of Language.q: An instructor is checking sentences from student case studies. Which sentences use modifiers correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The pharmacist spoke so quietly that the patient asked her to repeat herself.
To pass the licensing exam, careful studying is needed.
Nearly all of the students passed the skills check on the first try.
Of the two job offers, Darnell accepted the best one.
Having finished her charting, Mia clocked out and drove home.
Knowledge of Language.w: Mia is the one who finished charting; "quietly" is an adverb modifying "spoke"; "nearly" sits right before "all," the word it limits.

n.1: The infinitive phrase dangles: "studying" cannot pass an exam. A person must be the subject: "To pass the exam, you need to study carefully."
n.3: Two offers call for the comparative "the better one," not the superlative "best."

Knowledge of Language.q: A clinic's annual report is being proofread. Which sentence chooses correctly between "number" and "amount" or between "among" and "between"?
o: The large amount of patients in the lobby slowed down check-in.
The profits were split evenly among the two clinic owners.
A large number of applicants missed the deadline this year.
The amount of volunteers at the blood drive doubled this year.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Number" goes with countable nouns (applicants), "amount" with uncountable ones (water). "Between" is for two; "among" for three or more.

n.0: "Patients" can be counted, so the sentence needs "number," not "amount."
n.1: "Among" is for three or more; with two owners use "between."
n.3: "Volunteers" are countable, so the sentence needs "number of volunteers."

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph from a patient success story. (1) Hoping to lower her blood pressure, Mrs. Diaz began walking every morning. (2) She walked more slowly than her neighbor but went farther. (3) After three weeks, her readings were lower than before. (4) Encouraged by the results, the walks became longer. Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
Knowledge of Language.w: In sentence 4, "Encouraged by the results" is followed by "the walks," so the walks seem encouraged. Fix: "Encouraged by the results, Mrs. Diaz made her walks longer."

n.0: "Lower" correctly compares two things (readings now and before); there is no introductory modifier to dangle.
n.1: "Hoping to lower her blood pressure" is followed by "Mrs. Diaz," the person who was hoping, so the modifier is correct.
n.3: "More slowly" correctly compares two people with an adverb, and "farther" correctly refers to physical distance.

Knowledge of Language.q: A long-term care facility is updating its training description for new aides. Which sentence uses parallel structure?
o: New aides learn to take vital signs, to record intake, and how to reposition patients.
New aides learn to take vital signs, record intake, and reposition patients.
New aides learn to take vital signs, recording intake, and to reposition patients.
New aides learn taking vital signs, to record intake, and repositioning patients.
Knowledge of Language.w: Items in a series must share one grammatical form. After "learn to," the three base verbs (take, record, reposition) are parallel.

n.0: The third item switches from an infinitive ("to record") to a "how to" phrase, so the list is not parallel.
n.2: "Recording" is a gerund placed between two infinitives, which breaks the parallel pattern.
n.3: The list mixes gerunds ("taking," "repositioning") with an infinitive ("to record").

Knowledge of Language.q: A community college brochure describes a nursing pathway program. Which sentence uses "not only...but also" correctly?
o: The program not only trains nurses but also it places them in local clinics.
The program trains not only nurses but also places them in local clinics.
The program not only trains nurses but also places them in local clinics.
Not only does the program train nurses but also places them in local clinics.
Knowledge of Language.w: Correlative pairs must be followed by matching elements. Here each part is followed by a verb phrase: "not only trains ... but also places."

n.0: "But also" is followed by a full clause ("it places"), while "not only" is followed by a verb; the two parts do not match.
n.1: "Not only" precedes a noun ("nurses") but "but also" precedes a verb ("places"); each part needs the same form.
n.3: "Not only" introduces an inverted clause, but "but also" introduces a bare verb phrase, so the pair is not parallel.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a transportation notice: "Due to the fact that the main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic." Which revision is most concise while keeping the full meaning?
o: Due to the main road closure, the shuttle arrived late.
Because the main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic.
The main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic.
Since the main road was closed off, the shuttle was late in arriving to the clinic.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Due to the fact that" is a wordy way to say "because." Replacing it keeps every detail and the correct structure.

n.0: This version drops "to the clinic," so it loses part of the original meaning.
n.2: This version is shorter but joins two independent clauses with only a comma, creating a comma splice.
n.3: This version is wordier than the original idea needs ("closed off," "was late in arriving").

Knowledge of Language.q: A hospital volunteer guide is being edited for wordiness. Which sentence is written without a redundant phrase?
o: The two outpatient clinics are located in close proximity to each other.
Please repeat the instructions again for the new patients in the lobby.
Every visitor must sign in at the front desk before going upstairs.
The clinic offers a free gift to every new patient who enrolls this month.
Knowledge of Language.w: Concise writing removes words that repeat meaning. The correct sentence has no redundant pair such as "repeat again," "free gift" or "close proximity."

n.0: "Proximity" already means "closeness," so "close proximity" is redundant; "close to each other" is enough.
n.1: "Repeat" already means "say again," so "repeat ... again" is redundant.
n.3: A gift is free by definition, so "free gift" is redundant.

Knowledge of Language.q: A health blog compares two urgent care centers. Which sentence makes a logical, parallel comparison?
o: Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than those at Eastside Clinic.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than the staff at Eastside Clinic.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than at Eastside Clinic's.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than Eastside Clinic is.
Knowledge of Language.w: A comparison must set like things side by side: wait times at one clinic versus wait times ("those") at the other.

n.1: This compares wait times to the staff, two unlike things; the comparison needs "those at Eastside Clinic."
n.2: The possessive "Eastside Clinic's" leaves the noun it owns unstated, so the comparison is garbled.
n.3: This still compares wait times (plural) with a clinic (singular), which is illogical.

Knowledge of Language.q: A clinic's patient portal page explains check-in options. Which sentence uses "either...or" with parallel elements?
o: Patients can either check in on the website or at the front desk.
Either patients can check in on the website or at the front desk.
Patients either can check in on the website or the front desk.
Patients can check in either on the website or at the front desk.
Knowledge of Language.w: Place "either" and "or" directly before matching elements. Here both introduce a prepositional phrase: "on the website" and "at the front desk."

n.0: "Either" comes before a verb ("check in") but "or" comes before a prepositional phrase, so the pair is not parallel.
n.1: "Either" comes before a full clause but "or" comes before a phrase, so the two parts do not match.
n.2: "Either" precedes a verb phrase while "or" precedes a noun ("the front desk"), which is not parallel.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a hospital policy summary: "The new policy is meant to reduce wait times, improving patient satisfaction, and to lower costs." Which revision corrects the faulty parallelism?
o: Change "to lower" to "lowering."
Change "to reduce" to "reducing."
Change "improving" to "to improve."
Delete the word "and" before "to lower."
Knowledge of Language.w: Two of the three items are infinitives (to reduce, to lower). Changing "improving" to "to improve" makes all three match.

n.0: This leaves "to reduce" as an infinitive while the other two items are gerunds, so the list is still mixed.
n.1: This leaves "to lower" as an infinitive while the other two items are gerunds, so the list is still mixed.
n.3: Removing "and" does not change the forms of the items and also leaves the series without its conjunction.

Knowledge of Language.q: A state board newsletter is being edited for concise wording. Which sentence is the most concise version that keeps the full meaning?
o: To renew a license, it is required that nurses in this state complete 24 hours of continuing education.
To renew, nurses must complete 24 hours.
In order to renew a license, nurses in this state must complete 24 hours of continuing education.
To renew a license, nurses in this state must complete 24 hours of continuing education.
Knowledge of Language.w: Concise does not mean shortest. The best version removes padding ("in order to," "it is required that") and keeps every detail.

n.0: "It is required that" is a wordy construction; "must" says the same thing more directly.
n.1: This version drops what is renewed, the state, and the type of hours, so it loses meaning.
n.2: "In order to" adds words without adding meaning; "to" alone is enough.

Knowledge of Language.q: A nursing school's simulation lab description is being proofread. Which sentence uses "both...and" with parallel elements?
o: The simulation lab is both useful for students and inexpensive to run.
The simulation lab is useful both for students and inexpensive to run.
The simulation lab is both useful for students and costs little to run.
The simulation lab both is useful for students and inexpensive to run.
Knowledge of Language.w: "Both" and "and" are each followed by an adjective phrase: "useful for students" and "inexpensive to run."

n.1: "Both" now precedes a prepositional phrase ("for students") but "and" precedes an adjective.
n.2: "Both" is followed by an adjective ("useful") but "and" by a verb ("costs"), so the pair is not parallel.
n.3: "Both" is placed before the verb "is," but "and" is followed by an adjective; the two parts do not match.
