Knowledge of Language.q: A clinical instructor is reviewing four sentences from a student handbook draft. Which sentence is written with parallel structure?
o: The applicant was praised for her punctuality, her empathy, and for being skilled.
The checklist asks staff to wash hands, wear gloves, and dispose of sharps safely.
Volunteers may greet visitors, deliver flowers, or they can read to patients.
The course teaches students how to splint a fracture and controlling bleeding.
Knowledge of Language.w: All three items after "to" are base verbs (wash, wear, dispose), so the series is parallel.

n.0: Two nouns ("her punctuality," "her empathy") are followed by a gerund phrase with a repeated "for"; it should be "and her clinical skill."
n.2: The first two items are verb phrases, but the third is a full clause ("they can read"); it should be "or read to patients."
n.3: "How to splint" is paired with the gerund "controlling"; it should be "how to splint a fracture and control bleeding."

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a research summary: "The two surgeons collaborated together on a new protocol that cut postoperative infections by 30 percent." Which word should be deleted to remove a redundancy?
o: together
new
postoperative
two
Knowledge of Language.w: "Collaborate" means "work together," so "collaborated together" repeats the idea. Deleting "together" removes the redundancy.

n.1: "New" tells the reader the protocol was recently created; it is not implied by any other word.
n.2: "Postoperative" names which infections were cut; deleting it would make the claim broader than the study.
n.3: "Collaborate" implies at least two people, but "two" states exactly how many surgeons, so it adds information.

Knowledge of Language.q: A grant proposal for a nursing assistant program states its goals. Which version is both parallel and concise?
o: The goals of the program are training aides, to place them in jobs, and supporting them after they are hired.
The goals of the program are to train aides, to place them in jobs, and to support them after hiring.
The goals of the program are to train aides, to place them in jobs, and to support and help them after hiring.
The goals of the program are to train aides, placing them in jobs, and to support them after hiring.
Knowledge of Language.w: Two checks: the three goals share one form (to train, to place, to support), and no words repeat the same meaning.

n.0: The series mixes gerunds ("training," "supporting") with an infinitive ("to place").
n.2: The list is parallel, but "support and help" repeats one idea, so the sentence is not concise.
n.3: "Placing" is a gerund between two infinitives, so the series is not parallel.

Knowledge of Language.q: A nursing student is emailing her pharmacology professor to ask for a meeting about a failed exam. Which sentence is most appropriate for this audience and purpose?
o: I hereby request an audience at your earliest convenience regarding my examination.
I will stop by your office at noon tomorrow to go over my exam.
I would like to schedule a meeting to discuss my recent exam results.
I was hoping we might talk soon about a few things from class.
Knowledge of Language.w: An email to a professor calls for formal, polite language that states the purpose clearly: a meeting about exam results.

n.0: "I hereby request an audience" is inflated, stiff wording; a clear, polite request suits an email to a professor.
n.1: The writer announces a visit instead of asking for one, which is presumptuous toward the professor.
n.3: The request is vague ("a few things from class"); it never says the meeting is about the exam.

Knowledge of Language.q: A clinic is writing a handout for patients who have no medical training. Which sentence is best suited to these readers?
o: Pt should obtain BP readings BID and document all of the findings.
Check your blood pressure at the same time each morning and evening.
Check your systolic and diastolic pressure each morning and evening.
Patients with hypertension should monitor their BP readings diurnally.
Knowledge of Language.w: Plain language for a lay audience uses everyday words, short sentences and clear actions, without jargon or slang.

n.0: Clinical abbreviations (Pt, BP, BID) are jargon meant for health professionals, not patients.
n.2: The action is clear, but "systolic" and "diastolic" are medical terms a lay reader may not know.
n.3: "Hypertension," "BP" and "diurnally" are technical terms a lay reader may not understand.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is writing a formal research paper on sleep and academic performance. Which sentence is most appropriate for this paper?
o: Students who sleep fewer than six hours tend to earn lower grades.
Research shows that students who skimp on sleep see their grades tank.
Students who don't get enough sleep tend to earn lower grades.
You'd be surprised how much your sleep affects your final grades.
Knowledge of Language.w: Formal academic writing uses third person, precise wording, no contractions and no slang, and states claims objectively.

n.1: Slang ("skimp on," "tank") does not suit academic writing, even when a source is mentioned.
n.2: The contraction "don't" and the vague "enough" are informal and imprecise for a formal research paper.
n.3: Second person ("you") and a contraction ("You'd") are too conversational for a formal paper.

Knowledge of Language.q: Jasmine is sending a quick text message to a close friend to confirm their lunch plans for today. Which message best fits this audience and purpose?
o: Please be advised that I will attend our scheduled lunch at noon.
Sounds good! See you at noon at the taco place.
Maybe lunch sometime this week? Let me know what works for you.
I am writing to confirm that I will meet you for lunch at noon today.
Knowledge of Language.w: Register should match the audience. A text to a close friend is informal: short, friendly and conversational.

n.0: "Please be advised" is a formal business phrase that sounds cold in a message to a friend.
n.2: The casual tone fits, but the message fails the purpose: it does not confirm today's lunch plans.
n.3: "I am writing to confirm" is formal letter language, too stiff for a quick text to a close friend.

Knowledge of Language.q: Andre is writing a cover letter to the human resources department of a regional hospital. Which sentence is most appropriate for this letter?
o: I am eager to bring my CNA experience to your medical-surgical unit.
I'm really excited about this job, and I know I'd be a great fit.
I am, without question, the most qualified applicant you will receive.
I need a full-time job with good benefits, and your hospital offers both.
Knowledge of Language.w: A cover letter calls for a formal, confident and respectful tone that links the applicant's experience to the employer's needs.

n.1: The contractions and the vague "great fit" are too casual and give the employer no specific reason to hire.
n.2: The boastful claim sounds arrogant and cannot be supported, which suits no professional application.
n.3: The sentence focuses on what the writer wants rather than what the writer offers the hospital.

Knowledge of Language.q: A nurse manager is writing a formal report to a hospital's board of directors: "The pilot program cut readmissions by 12 percent, which is a pretty big deal for a unit of our size." Which phrase should be revised?
o: the pilot program
a pretty big deal
cut readmissions
by 12 percent
Knowledge of Language.w: "A pretty big deal" is slang. A formal report needs precise wording such as "a significant improvement for a unit of our size."

n.0: "The pilot program" is a precise, standard name for a trial program.
n.2: "Cut readmissions" is clear and accurate; "cut" is a standard verb for a reduction.
n.3: "By 12 percent" is a specific, formal way to report the result.

Knowledge of Language.q: A school nurse is making a sign to hang above the sink in a second-grade classroom. Which sentence is most appropriate for these readers?
o: Wash your hands with soap before you eat.
Wash your hands with soap prior to consuming food.
Perform hand hygiene before you eat.
Hand washing reduces the spread of germs.
Knowledge of Language.w: Young readers need short sentences, simple everyday words and a clear action to take.

n.1: "Prior to consuming food" is formal wording that young children may not know.
n.2: "Perform hand hygiene" is health-care jargon that seven-year-old readers may not understand.
n.3: This states a general fact but does not tell the children what to do at the sink.

Knowledge of Language.q: A patient is writing to a hospital billing office to dispute a charge. Which sentence best meets the purpose and the audience?
o: Please remove the $85 charge for the March 4 visit, which my insurer paid.
I am writing to you about some issues I have had lately with things on my bill.
Your careless office billed me $85 for March 4, though my insurer paid it.
Hey, quick thing: that $85 charge from March 4 should go, since insurance paid.
Knowledge of Language.w: A dispute letter should be courteous and specific: name the charge, the date and the requested action.

n.1: The sentence is polite but vague; it never says which charge is wrong or what should happen.
n.2: The facts are specific, but calling the office "careless" is accusing and likely to make the reader defensive.
n.3: The facts are specific, but "Hey, quick thing" is too casual for a letter to a billing office.

Knowledge of Language.q: Lucia is writing a personal statement for a nursing program's admissions committee. Which sentences are appropriate for this audience and purpose? Select all that apply.
o: My long-term goal is to work as a pediatric nurse in a rural clinic.
Nursing has been my dream for years, and I am super excited to start!
Without a doubt, I will be the strongest student your program has admitted.
Caring for my grandmother after her stroke showed me what skilled nursing looks like.
Volunteering at a hospice taught me to listen before I act.
Knowledge of Language.w: A personal statement may use first person, but it must stay formal and purposeful. The correct sentences give specific experiences and goals in standard language.

n.1: The intensifier "super" and the exclamation point are too casual for an admissions committee, and the sentence gives no specific experience.
n.2: The boastful, unsupported claim is arrogant and does not suit a formal personal statement.

Knowledge of Language.q: A clinic is updating a flyer for the general public: "Individuals experiencing dyspnea or diaphoresis should seek emergent evaluation." Which revision best suits this audience while keeping the meaning?
o: Persons with respiratory distress or diaphoresis require emergent care.
If you have trouble breathing or heavy sweating, get emergency care now.
If you feel a little bit off, you might think about seeing a doctor.
If you have dyspnea or heavy sweating, get emergency care now.
Knowledge of Language.w: Two checks: the revision must use plain words a lay reader knows (trouble breathing, heavy sweating) and keep the message's urgency.

n.0: "Respiratory distress," "diaphoresis" and "emergent" are still medical jargon for lay readers.
n.2: This version loses the specific symptoms and the urgency, so it changes the meaning.
n.3: The urgency is kept, but "dyspnea" is still a medical term that lay readers may not know.

Knowledge of Language.q: A nurse is ending an email to her unit manager that requests a change to next month's schedule. Which closing sentence is most appropriate?
o: Let me know ASAP, since I already told my family I'd be off that weekend.
Thanks in advance for approving this change to my schedule.
Thank you for considering my request; I am glad to discuss it at any time.
I trust you will approve this request, as I have certainly earned it by now.
Knowledge of Language.w: A professional email closes courteously, thanks the reader and offers to follow up.

n.0: "ASAP" and the assumption that the request is already approved are too informal and presumptuous.
n.1: Thanking the manager in advance "for approving" assumes the answer and pressures the reader.
n.3: The demanding tone pressures the manager and is not respectful.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph from a student's research summary. (1) A recent study examined how evening screen time affects sleep in adolescents. (2) Teens who used their phones after 9 p.m. got a lot less sleep. (3) On average, they slept 48 minutes less than peers who did not use phones at night. (4) These findings suggest that limiting evening screen use may improve rest. Which sentence does not match the formal register of the paragraph?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
Knowledge of Language.w: Sentence 2 uses informal wording ("teens," "got," "a lot less"). A formal version: "Adolescents who used their phones after 9 p.m. slept less."

n.0: Sentence 1 is formal: precise terms ("adolescents," "evening screen time") and an objective tone.
n.1: Sentence 3 is formal: it reports a specific figure in standard language.
n.2: Sentence 4 is formal: "suggest" and "may" state the conclusion with appropriate caution.

Knowledge of Language.q: A hospital's community newsletter is announcing a new screening service. Which sentence uses respectful, person-first language?
o: The clinic now offers free foot exams for people with diabetes.
The clinic now offers free foot exams for diabetics in the area.
The clinic now offers free foot exams for diabetes victims.
The clinic now offers free foot exams for diabetes sufferers.
Knowledge of Language.w: Person-first language names the person before the condition: "people with diabetes."

n.1: "Diabetics" labels people by their condition; person-first language puts the person first.
n.2: "Victims" frames people as helpless and defines them by their condition.
n.3: "Sufferers" assumes how people experience the condition and defines them by it.

Knowledge of Language.q: A city health department is writing a press release about a safety event. Which sentence uses inclusive, gender-neutral job titles?
o: The firefighters and policemen met with the council chair.
The firefighters and police officers met with the council chair.
The firefighters and police officers met with the council chairman.
The firemen and police officers met with the council chair.
Knowledge of Language.w: Bias-free writing uses titles that fit any gender: firefighter, police officer, chair or chairperson.

n.0: "Policemen" is a gendered title; the neutral term is "police officers."
n.2: "Chairman" is a gendered title; the neutral term is "chair" or "chairperson."
n.3: "Firemen" is a gendered title; the neutral term is "firefighters."

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is writing up a chemistry lab for a formal report. Which sentence uses the most precise wording?
o: The sample was heated for 10 minutes until it reached 80 degrees Celsius.
The sample was heated briefly until it reached a high temperature.
The sample was heated for several minutes until it reached 80 degrees Celsius.
The sample was heated for 10 minutes until it became very hot.
Knowledge of Language.w: Precise word choice gives exact, specific information. A lab report should state measured values, not vague impressions.

n.1: "Briefly" and "a high temperature" sound formal but give no measurable information.
n.2: The temperature is exact, but "several minutes" is vague; a lab report needs the measured time.
n.3: The time is exact, but "very hot" is vague; a lab report needs the measured temperature.

Knowledge of Language.q: Mr. Brooks is writing a letter to a hospital about a long wait in its emergency department. Which sentence has the most appropriate tone for his purpose?
o: Thanks a lot for the lovely four-hour wait; I really enjoyed it.
I waited four hours with a broken wrist and would like to know why.
I am sure the department was busy, so please disregard my concerns.
Your staff obviously could not care less about patients like me.
Knowledge of Language.w: A complaint letter should be firm, specific and courteous: state what happened and what you want.

n.0: Sarcasm is unprofessional and can be misread, so it weakens the complaint.
n.2: This polite sentence cancels the complaint, so it fails the writer's purpose.
n.3: The angry, accusing tone is likely to make the reader defensive rather than helpful.

Knowledge of Language.q: Malik is writing an essay for a nursing scholarship. Which sentence avoids clichés and is most appropriate for this essay?
o: Working as a medical scribe taught me to document care accurately.
Working as a medical scribe taught me to think outside the box every day.
At the end of the day, I know deep down that nursing is my true calling.
After my scribe job, I expect nursing school to be a walk in the park.
Knowledge of Language.w: Clichés are overused phrases. Specific, concrete statements make a stronger impression on a scholarship committee.

n.1: "Think outside the box" is a cliché; it does not say what the writer actually learned.
n.2: "At the end of the day" and "true calling" are clichés that add little specific meaning.
n.3: "A walk in the park" is a cliché, and it suggests the writer underestimates the program.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a staff policy: "Staff should utilize the aforementioned procedure in order to facilitate patient egress." Which revision replaces the inflated wording with plain language and keeps the meaning?
o: Staff should use the procedure described above as needed.
Staff should use this procedure to help patients leave.
Staff should employ the stated procedure to facilitate patient egress.
Staff should use the aforementioned procedure to help patients leave.
Knowledge of Language.w: Plain language replaces inflated words: utilize = use, facilitate = help, egress = leaving, in order to = to.

n.0: This version drops the purpose (helping patients leave), so it loses meaning.
n.2: "Employ," "facilitate" and "egress" are still inflated words for "use," "help" and "leave."
n.3: "Aforementioned" is still an inflated word; plain language would say "this procedure."

Knowledge of Language.q: A nurse is writing a reference letter for a former nursing aide: "Ms. Alvarez was ___ about following every infection-control step." Which word completes the sentence with the most positive connotation?
o: persnickety
obsessive
meticulous
nitpicky
Knowledge of Language.w: All four words describe close attention to detail, but only "meticulous" has a positive, professional connotation.

n.0: "Persnickety" is informal and suggests fussing over trivial details, a negative connotation.
n.1: "Obsessive" suggests an unhealthy fixation, a negative connotation in a reference letter.
n.3: "Nitpicky" is informal and suggests petty fault-finding, a negative connotation.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the sentence from a county health report: "The new program did a lot of good things for people in the area." Which revision replaces the vague words with specific ones?
o: The new program provided free flu shots to 2,300 county residents.
The new program did many helpful things for many people in the county.
The new program helped a large number of local people in several ways.
The new program was very beneficial in a number of important ways.
Knowledge of Language.w: Precise writing replaces vague words (things, stuff, a lot) with specific facts: what was provided, to whom and how many.

n.1: "Many helpful things" is still vague; it does not say what the program did.
n.2: "A large number" and "several ways" are still vague; the sentence never says what was done or for how many.
n.3: "Beneficial in a number of important ways" sounds formal but gives no specific detail.

Knowledge of Language.q: A nursing journal editor is checking sentences in a research article. Which sentences use bias-free language? Select all that apply.
o: The study enrolled 50 adults confined to wheelchairs.
The study included 40 people with epilepsy.
The study enrolled 50 adults who use wheelchairs.
The new nurse manager, a woman in her 30s, was surprisingly organized.
Each server at the hospital cafe received a holiday bonus.
Knowledge of Language.w: Bias-free language puts the person first ("adults who use wheelchairs," "people with epilepsy") and uses gender-neutral titles ("server").

n.0: "Confined to wheelchairs" treats the wheelchair as a limit rather than a tool; use "who use wheelchairs."
n.3: Mentioning gender and age is unnecessary here, and "surprisingly" implies a stereotype.

Knowledge of Language.q: A charge nurse must tell a coworker that a medication dose was charted at the wrong time. Which sentence has the most appropriate tone?
o: How could you possibly mess up something as basic as charting a dose?
Not to be picky, but charting is kind of a big deal, you know what I mean?
Someone on this shift, and I won't say who, charted a dose at the wrong time.
I noticed the 9 a.m. dose was charted at 11 a.m.; can we fix it together?
Knowledge of Language.w: Professional feedback is specific, respectful and focused on solving the problem.

n.0: The scolding question is condescending and likely to make the coworker defensive.
n.1: The passive-aggressive, casual phrasing is vague and unprofessional.
n.2: Hinting instead of speaking directly is indirect and can feel like public blame.

Knowledge of Language.q: A company memo is announcing job cuts at a medical billing office. Which sentence states the information most clearly and directly?
o: The company will eliminate 40 positions on March 1.
The company will reduce the size of its workforce in the coming months.
The company is exploring workforce optimization opportunities.
The company is rightsizing its human capital going forward.
Knowledge of Language.w: Clear professional writing states facts directly. Euphemisms and jargon blur important information.

n.1: This is less evasive, but it gives no number of positions and no date, so it is not the clearest statement.
n.2: "Workforce optimization" is vague jargon; it does not say what will happen or when.
n.3: "Rightsizing its human capital" is a euphemism that hides the fact that jobs are being cut.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is summarizing a small pilot study in a formal paper: "The results ___ that patients who walked daily recovered faster." Which word is most accurate and appropriate?
o: confirm
prove
suggest
establish
Knowledge of Language.w: Two checks: the word must be formal, and it must match the strength of the evidence. A small pilot study "suggests" a result.

n.0: "Confirm" presents the finding as verified, which one small pilot study cannot do.
n.1: One small pilot study cannot prove a conclusion; "prove" overstates the evidence.
n.3: "Establish" claims the finding is settled, which overstates what a small study shows.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student has drafted these supporting details for a paragraph: walking lowers blood pressure; it improves mood; it requires no special equipment. Which sentence would make the best topic sentence?
o: Most people already own a good pair of shoes for walking outside.
Walking is a simple habit that offers several health benefits.
Walking can lower blood pressure in many adults who do it daily.
Running burns more calories per mile than walking at a slow pace.
Knowledge of Language.w: A topic sentence states the main idea that all of the supporting details develop. Each detail is a benefit of walking, so the topic sentence names those benefits in general.

n.0: This sentence is a minor detail about shoes; it does not cover blood pressure, mood or equipment.
n.2: This sentence states only one of the three details, so it is too narrow to be the topic sentence.
n.3: This sentence shifts to running, which none of the supporting details discuss.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph from an infection-control newsletter. (1) Hand washing is one of the most effective ways to prevent infections in hospitals. (2) Washing for at least 20 seconds removes most germs from the skin. (3) Alcohol-based sanitizers work well when hands are not visibly dirty. (4) Many nurses say they prefer unscented soaps to scented ones. (5) Staff who clean their hands between patients protect everyone on the unit. Which sentence should be removed to improve the paragraph's unity?
o: Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 5
Sentence 4
Knowledge of Language.w: Every sentence should support the topic sentence: hand hygiene prevents infections. Sentence 4 mentions soap, but a preference for unscented soap says nothing about preventing infection, so it breaks unity.

n.0: Sentence 2 explains how long to wash, which directly supports the topic of preventing infection.
n.1: Sentence 3 adds a second hand-hygiene method, so it supports the topic.
n.2: Sentence 5 explains who benefits from hand hygiene, so it supports the topic.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph: "Community gardens offer more than fresh vegetables. Neighbors who garden together get to know one another and share skills. Gardeners also get regular outdoor exercise, and families eat more produce when they help grow it." Which sentence best concludes the paragraph?
o: Some gardeners prefer raised beds because they are easier on the back and knees.
In short, a community garden builds both good health and neighborly ties.
Vegetables such as tomatoes and peppers need at least six hours of sun each day.
However, many cities now charge a yearly fee for each garden plot in the spring.
Knowledge of Language.w: A concluding sentence sums up the main idea without adding new information. This one ties together the social, exercise and nutrition benefits.

n.0: This sentence adds a new, minor detail instead of wrapping up the main point.
n.2: This sentence adds a new gardening fact unrelated to the benefits the paragraph lists.
n.3: This sentence introduces a new idea (fees) that the paragraph has not developed.

Knowledge of Language.q: Topic sentence: "Getting enough sleep helps nursing students perform better in class." Which sentence best supports this topic sentence?
o: In one survey, students who slept seven hours outscored those who slept five on exams.
Many nursing students work part-time jobs at hospitals while they are enrolled in school.
Coffee is one of the most popular drinks among college students across the country.
Some campus dormitories set quiet hours that begin at 10 p.m. on most weeknights.
Knowledge of Language.w: Supporting sentences give evidence for the topic sentence. The survey links more sleep to higher exam scores, a direct measure of class performance.

n.1: This sentence is about student jobs; it does not show that sleep affects class performance.
n.2: This sentence about coffee does not support a claim about sleep and performance.
n.3: Quiet hours relate to sleep, but this sentence gives no evidence about performance in class.

Knowledge of Language.q: A volunteer is writing a short guide for first-time blood donors. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: After the donation, rest for about 15 minutes and have a snack.
First, drink plenty of water the day before your appointment.
Next, eat a meal rich in iron a few hours before you arrive.
Following these steps can help you feel well during and after your visit.
Before you donate blood, a few simple steps can help you prepare.
Knowledge of Language.w: The topic sentence introduces the steps. "First" and "Next" give the steps before donating, "After the donation" follows them in time, and the concluding sentence sums up the benefit of the steps.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph. (1) Telehealth visits have grown quickly over the past decade. (2) These video appointments can save patients long drives and time off work. (3) However, telehealth does not suit every patient. (4) People without reliable internet may struggle to connect. Where should this sentence be placed? "For example, a farmer who lives an hour from town can see a provider without leaving work."
o: After sentence 1
After sentence 3
After sentence 4
After sentence 2
Knowledge of Language.w: An example belongs right after the claim it illustrates. The farmer shows how video visits save long drives and time off work (sentence 2).

n.0: The example is about saving travel and work time, not about how quickly telehealth has grown.
n.1: Placed here, the example would contradict the claim that telehealth does not suit every patient.
n.2: Placed here, a success story would contradict the point about people who struggle to connect.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph from a county health report. (1) In 2015, the county had one free clinic. (2) By 2020, it had three, plus a mobile health van. (3) Last year, two more clinics opened in rural towns. (4) Access to free health care in the county has grown steadily over the past decade. Which sentence is the topic sentence?
o: Sentence 2
Sentence 1
Sentence 4
Sentence 3
Knowledge of Language.w: This paragraph moves from specific to general: the details come first, and sentence 4 states the main idea they support.

n.0: Sentence 2 is another specific detail about the number of clinics in 2020.
n.1: Sentence 1 is a specific detail (one clinic in 2015); being first does not make it the main idea.
n.3: Sentence 3 is a specific detail about last year's openings.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student's paragraph argues that hospitals should serve healthier food in their cafeterias. Which sentence would best conclude the paragraph?
o: Some hospitals currently serve meals from national fast-food chains in their lobbies.
First, cafeterias should add more fresh vegetables and whole grains to each meal.
Hospital parking fees are another issue that deserves attention from administrators.
Healthier menus would let hospitals model the habits they urge patients to adopt.
Knowledge of Language.w: A strong concluding sentence restates or extends the paragraph's main point without adding a new topic.

n.0: This sentence is a supporting detail, not a conclusion that wraps up the argument.
n.1: "First" signals the start of a list of supporting points, which belongs in the body of the paragraph.
n.2: This sentence introduces a new topic (parking) instead of closing the argument about food.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is writing a short narrative paragraph for a nursing school application. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: Last summer, Elena decided to earn her nursing assistant certificate.
Two weeks later, she started her first job at a nursing home.
When the course ended, she passed the state skills exam on her first try.
During the course, she practiced skills such as bed baths and safe transfers.
She enrolled in a six-week evening course at the community college.
Knowledge of Language.w: The paragraph is in chronological order: the decision, enrolling, practicing during the course, passing the exam when it ended, and starting a job two weeks later.

Knowledge of Language.q: Topic sentence: "Volunteering at a hospital can help students decide whether nursing is right for them." Which sentence would best develop this paragraph?
o: Nursing school tuition varies widely from one state to another across the country.
Volunteers see how nurses spend a shift, from charting to comforting families.
Hospital volunteers often wear colored vests or jackets so that visitors spot them.
Many hospitals ask volunteers to be at least 16 years old before they can apply.
Knowledge of Language.w: Development means adding relevant support. Seeing a nurse's real workday is exactly what helps a student decide whether nursing fits.

n.0: Tuition is a different topic; the sentence does not develop the idea of testing out the career.
n.2: This detail about uniforms does not support the claim about choosing a career.
n.3: This fact is about volunteer rules, not about how volunteering helps a student decide on nursing.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph from a nutrition handout. (1) Dietary fiber offers several benefits for digestion. (2) It adds bulk to stool, which helps prevent constipation. (3) Many breakfast cereals come in colorful boxes designed to appeal to children. (4) Fiber also feeds helpful bacteria in the large intestine. (5) White bread usually costs less than whole-wheat bread at the store. (6) Foods such as beans, oats and berries are good sources of fiber. Which sentences should be removed to improve the paragraph's unity? Select all that apply.
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 5
Sentence 2
Sentence 6
Sentence 4
Knowledge of Language.w: Sentence 3 (cereal box design) and sentence 5 (bread prices) mention foods but say nothing about fiber's digestive benefits or sources, so both break unity.

n.2: Sentence 2 gives a digestive benefit of fiber, which directly supports the topic sentence.
n.3: Sentence 6 tells readers where to find fiber, which supports the paragraph's purpose.
n.4: Sentence 4 gives a second digestive benefit of fiber, so it belongs.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is writing a paragraph organized from the least to the most important point. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: One benefit is simple: the rent and utility bills are split in half.
A roommate in the same program can also quiz you before major exams.
Most important, a roommate who knows long clinical days offers support when the work feels overwhelming.
Sharing an apartment with a classmate during nursing school has real advantages.
Knowledge of Language.w: The topic sentence comes first. "One benefit" opens the list, "also" adds a second point, and "Most important" signals the final, strongest point in order-of-importance organization.

Knowledge of Language.q: A unit manager's report reads: "The new scheduling app was supposed to reduce overtime. ___, overtime hours rose by 15 percent in its first month." Which transition best completes the passage?
o: Therefore
For example
However
Furthermore
Knowledge of Language.w: The second sentence contrasts with the first: overtime was expected to fall but rose. "However" signals contrast.

n.0: "Therefore" signals a result, but rising overtime is not a result of the plan to reduce it.
n.1: "For example" introduces an illustration, but the second sentence reports an unexpected outcome.
n.3: "Furthermore" adds a similar point, but the second sentence contradicts the expectation in the first.

Knowledge of Language.q: A clinic notice reads: "The clinic's only X-ray machine broke down on Monday morning. ___, patients who needed imaging were sent to the hospital across town." Which transition best completes the notice?
o: As a result
Similarly
In contrast
For instance
Knowledge of Language.w: The broken machine caused patients to be sent elsewhere, a cause-and-effect relationship. "As a result" signals an effect.

n.1: "Similarly" signals a comparison, but the second sentence describes a consequence.
n.2: "In contrast" signals a difference, but sending patients elsewhere follows from the broken machine.
n.3: "For instance" introduces an example, but sending patients away is an effect, not an example.

Knowledge of Language.q: A nutrition handout reads: "Some common foods are high in hidden sodium. ___, a single serving of some canned soups contains more than a third of the recommended daily limit." Which transition best completes the handout?
o: Nevertheless
For example
In conclusion
Likewise
Knowledge of Language.w: Canned soup is a specific case of a food with hidden sodium, so the second sentence illustrates the first. "For example" introduces an illustration.

n.0: "Nevertheless" signals contrast, but the second sentence supports the first rather than opposing it.
n.2: "In conclusion" signals a summary, but the second sentence is a specific detail.
n.3: "Likewise" compares two similar ideas, but the soup is an instance of the first claim, not a parallel claim.

Knowledge of Language.q: A wellness flyer reads: "Regular exercise strengthens the heart and lungs. ___, it can improve the quality of a person's sleep." Which transition best completes the flyer?
o: In other words
Conversely
Specifically
In addition
Knowledge of Language.w: The second sentence adds another benefit of exercise. "In addition" signals addition.

n.0: "In other words" restates the same idea, but better sleep is a new point, not a restatement.
n.1: "Conversely" signals an opposite idea, but better sleep is another benefit, not an opposite.
n.2: "Specifically" narrows the previous idea, but sleep quality is not a detail of heart and lung strength.

Knowledge of Language.q: A patient leaflet about a vaccine reads: "___ the vaccine can cause a sore arm, most patients find this side effect mild and brief." Which word or phrase best completes the sentence?
o: Because
Whenever
Unless
Although
Knowledge of Language.w: The sentence concedes a drawback (a sore arm) and then plays it down. "Although" signals concession.

n.0: "Because" signals cause, but a sore arm does not cause the side effect to be mild.
n.1: "Whenever" signals time, which does not fit a possible side effect weighed against its mildness.
n.2: "Unless" signals a condition, which makes the sentence illogical.

Knowledge of Language.q: A pharmacy newsletter is printing a short problem-and-solution paragraph. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: Many patients forget to take their evening medications.
Another option is a phone alarm set for the same time each night.
Together, these tools can help patients stay on schedule.
One simple solution is a weekly pill organizer with a labeled slot for each day.
Knowledge of Language.w: The paragraph states the problem first, then gives solutions: "One simple solution" introduces the first, "Another option" adds the second, and "Together" sums up both tools. "These tools" must follow the sentences that name them.

Knowledge of Language.q: A student is writing a paragraph for a health-policy class. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: As a result of these changes, falls at one hospital dropped by a third in a year.
Even with that drop, falls remain one of the most common injuries in hospitals.
In addition, nurses now check on high-risk patients every hour.
First, many have installed bed alarms that alert staff when a patient stands up.
Hospitals have tried several ways to reduce patient falls.
Knowledge of Language.w: The topic sentence comes first. "First" and "In addition" present two methods, "As a result of these changes" reports their effect, and "Even with that drop" must follow the sentence that reports the drop.

Knowledge of Language.q: A patient education sheet reads: "Your test shows that you have bradycardia. ___, your heart beats more slowly than normal." Which transition best completes the sheet?
o: In other words
As a result
On the other hand
For instance
Knowledge of Language.w: The second sentence restates the medical term in plain words. "In other words" signals clarification.

n.1: A slow heartbeat is what bradycardia means, not a result of having it.
n.2: "On the other hand" signals contrast, but the second sentence agrees with the first.
n.3: The second sentence defines the term rather than giving one example of it.

Knowledge of Language.q: Read the paragraph from a study-skills guide. (1) Many students believe that cramming the night before an exam is effective. (2) Therefore, research shows that spacing study sessions over several days leads to better recall. (3) For example, students who reviewed material on four separate days remembered more a week later. (4) Overall, spaced practice is a better use of study time than cramming. Which sentence uses an illogical transition?
o: Sentence 2
Sentence 4
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Knowledge of Language.w: Sentence 2 contradicts the belief in sentence 1, so it needs a contrast transition such as "However," not the cause-and-effect "Therefore."

n.1: "Overall" correctly signals a summary of the paragraph's point.
n.2: "For example" correctly introduces a specific study that illustrates sentence 2.
n.3: Sentence 1 has no transition; it introduces the belief the paragraph will challenge.

Knowledge of Language.q: A school nurse is writing a newsletter paragraph about dehydration. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: When the body loses more fluid than it takes in, blood volume drops.
Dehydration can develop quickly during a summer heat wave.
For this reason, health officials urge people to drink water before they feel thirsty.
Over time, a person may feel dizzy, tired or confused.
As a result, the heart must work harder to supply the organs.
Knowledge of Language.w: The topic sentence comes first, then a chain of causes and effects: fluid loss lowers blood volume, "As a result" the heart works harder, "Over time" symptoms appear, and "For this reason" gives the advice that follows.

Knowledge of Language.q: A pediatric clinic newsletter reads: "Children need regular checkups to track their growth. ___, older adults benefit from yearly visits that screen for age-related conditions." Which transition best completes the passage?
o: Similarly
Consequently
In conclusion
For example
Knowledge of Language.w: Both sentences describe a group that benefits from regular checkups, so the relationship is comparison. "Similarly" signals comparison.

n.1: Older adults' checkups are not caused by children's checkups, so a result transition is illogical.
n.2: The second sentence adds a new comparison rather than summing up the passage.
n.3: Older adults are not an example of children; the sentence makes a parallel point.

Knowledge of Language.q: A research summary reads: "The trial drug lowered blood pressure in most participants. ___, several participants reported dizziness and headaches." Which transitions could correctly fill the blank? Select all that apply.
o: For instance
Therefore
Similarly
However
On the other hand
Knowledge of Language.w: The second sentence presents a drawback that contrasts with the benefit in the first. "However" and "On the other hand" both signal contrast.

n.0: "For instance" introduces an example of the first sentence, but side effects are not an example of lower blood pressure.
n.1: "Therefore" signals a result, but the side effects are not a consequence of the blood pressure falling in this passage.
n.2: "Similarly" signals a matching point, but a drawback does not match a benefit.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Devon is preparing the final copy of a report on campus flu shots. Which of the following tasks belongs to the editing stage rather than the revising stage?
o: Adding a statistic to support the second main point
Fixing a pronoun that disagrees with its antecedent
Reordering paragraphs so the strongest point is last
Removing a sentence that is off topic for its paragraph
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Editing deals with sentence-level correctness: grammar, usage, punctuation, spelling and consistency. A pronoun-antecedent agreement error is a grammar problem, so fixing it is editing.

n.0: Adding support changes the content of the report, which is revising (add).
n.2: Reordering paragraphs changes the organization, which is revising (rearrange).
n.3: Cutting an off-topic sentence improves unity and content, which is revising (remove).

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: To plan an essay, Andre writes "sleep loss" in a circle in the center of a page, draws lines out to circles labeled "memory," "mood," and "driving," and then adds smaller circles branching from each. Which prewriting strategy is he using?
o: Clustering
Freewriting
Outlining
Listing
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Clustering (also called mind mapping or webbing) puts the central topic in the middle of the page and branches related ideas out from it in linked circles.

n.1: Freewriting is writing continuous sentences for a set time; Andre is drawing linked circles, not writing prose.
n.2: Outlining arranges ideas in a labeled hierarchy (I., A., 1., a.) in lines of text, not in a web of circles around a center.
n.3: Listing jots ideas down in a vertical list; it does not connect ideas visually to a central topic.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Kiara is writing a research paper on teen vaping for her health class. Which of her activities belong to the prewriting stage? Select all that apply.
o: Formatting the final copy for submission
Building an outline of main points and support
Rewriting her conclusion so it restates the thesis
Narrowing her broad topic to a manageable focus
Correcting comma splices in her second paragraph
Gathering research on the topic before writing
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Prewriting is planning: identifying purpose and audience, choosing and narrowing the topic, generating ideas, researching and outlining. Narrowing the topic, researching and outlining all happen before any drafting.

n.0: Preparing and submitting the final copy is publishing, the last stage.
n.2: Rewriting a conclusion to restate the thesis improves the content of an existing draft, which is revising.
n.4: Fixing comma splices is a sentence-level correction, which is editing.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: A student is writing a report on handwashing habits in a school cafeteria. Place the steps in the order the student should complete them, starting with the first.
o: Submit the final copy
Revise the draft's content and organization
Edit the draft for grammar and punctuation
Organize the ideas into an outline
Write a first draft from the outline
Brainstorm a list of ideas about the topic
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Brainstorming and then outlining are both prewriting (generate ideas, then organize them). Drafting turns the outline into paragraphs. Revising fixes the big picture, editing then fixes sentence-level errors, and publishing (submitting the final copy) comes last.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Kayla's first draft of a research paper on nutrition labels is complete. Place the remaining tasks in the order she should complete them, starting with the first.
o: Reorganize paragraphs and strengthen weak support
Do a final read for typos and missing words
Correct subject-verb agreement and punctuation errors
Submit the final copy to the instructor
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: After drafting, the writer revises (reorganizes and strengthens content), then edits (grammar and punctuation), then proofreads (a final check for typos and missing words), and finally publishes (submits the paper). Big-picture changes come first so that later polishing is not wasted on text that gets cut.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: While revising her report on sports injuries, Hana realizes her second section lacks evidence, so she goes back to the library to find two more studies before rewriting that section. What does this show about the writing process?
o: Adding new studies is editing, so she has moved past revising
The process is recursive, so a writer may return to an earlier stage
Research is part of drafting, so she has returned to the drafting stage
The process is linear, so research must end before revising starts
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: The writing process is recursive: writers move back and forth between stages as needed. Hana returns to a prewriting activity (research) during revising and then continues revising, which is normal.

n.0: Editing fixes sentence-level errors such as grammar, punctuation and spelling; finding sources is a prewriting task and adding evidence changes content.
n.2: She has gone back to an earlier stage, but research is a prewriting activity, not drafting; drafting turns the plan into sentences and paragraphs.
n.3: The writing process is recursive, not linear: writers often go back to research or planning while revising, exactly as Hana does.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: As Owen drafts an essay on hospital volunteering, a classmate tells him to stop and look up the spelling of each unfamiliar word as soon as he types it. Based on the writing process, what is the best advice for Owen?
o: Keep drafting, and check the spelling later during editing
Keep drafting, and check the spelling later during revising
Keep drafting, and leave the spelling for the publishing stage
Stop drafting, since spelling must be fixed before revising
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Drafting focuses on getting ideas down in sentences and paragraphs, not on perfection. Spelling is a sentence-level correction handled during editing (and the final proofread), which comes after revising and before publishing.

n.1: Revising deals with content and organization (adding, moving and cutting material); spelling is a sentence-level fix that belongs to editing.
n.2: Publishing is submitting or sharing the final copy; spelling must already be corrected by then, during editing and the final proofread.
n.3: Spelling is checked during editing, which comes after revising, not before it; stopping to fix each word while drafting interrupts the flow of ideas.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: To find ideas for an article on teen vaping, Rosa writes six headings at the top of her page: Who? What? When? Where? Why? How? She then jots answers under each one. Which stage and technique is she using?
o: Drafting, using freewriting
Prewriting, using outlining
Prewriting, using questioning
Revising, using peer feedback
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Rosa is still generating ideas before writing, so she is prewriting. Asking who, what, when, where, why and how is the questioning technique (the reporter's questions).

n.0: Freewriting is nonstop writing for a set time, and Rosa is not drafting paragraphs; she is answering six set questions.
n.1: Outlining organizes ideas into a hierarchy of main points and subpoints; Rosa is producing ideas, not ranking them.
n.3: Revising improves an existing draft; Rosa has no draft yet, and she is not responding to a reviewer.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Luis is writing an argumentative essay about school start times. Which sentence would work best as his thesis statement?
o: In this essay, I will discuss the start times of high schools across the country.
Many high schools in the United States begin classes before 8:30 in the morning.
High schools should start after 8:30 a.m. to improve teens' sleep and grades.
Should high schools start later in the morning so that teenagers get more sleep?
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: An effective thesis makes one specific, arguable claim and can preview the main points. This sentence takes a clear position (start after 8:30 a.m.) and names the reasons the essay will develop (sleep and grades).

n.0: This is an announcement of the topic ("In this essay, I will"); it states no position for the essay to argue.
n.1: This is a statement of fact that no one would dispute, so there is nothing to argue.
n.3: A question is not a thesis; the thesis should answer the question with a claim.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Brianna is organizing a standard five-paragraph essay for her English composition class. In which part of the essay does the thesis statement usually appear?
o: In the first sentence of the introduction
At the start of the first body paragraph
In the final sentence of the conclusion
At the end of the introduction
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: The introduction usually moves from a hook to background and ends with the thesis, which then leads into the body paragraphs.

n.0: The first sentence of the introduction is usually the hook that captures the reader's interest, with the thesis coming after the background.
n.1: The first body paragraph opens with a topic sentence that develops one point of the thesis; the thesis itself comes before the body.
n.2: The conclusion restates the thesis in new words; the thesis is first stated in the introduction.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Tyler is reviewing his draft of a report on campus recycling. Which change to the draft is an example of revising rather than editing?
o: Correcting the misspelled word "enviroment" in the title
Adding a missing comma after an introductory clause
Changing "their" to "there" in the second paragraph
Replacing a vague example with a specific statistic
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Revising changes content and organization. Swapping a vague example for specific evidence strengthens the support, which is a content change (replace).

n.0: Correcting a misspelling is a spelling correction, which is editing (or proofreading).
n.1: Adding a comma is a punctuation correction, which is editing.
n.2: Fixing a homophone error is a word-level correction, which is editing.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Ellen's working thesis is "Technology has changed health care." Her instructor says the thesis is too broad for a four-page paper. Which revision best fixes this problem?
o: Telehealth has made follow-up care easier for rural patients in Montana.
This paper will explain the ways technology has changed health care.
Has technology changed health care for the better or for the worse?
Technology has changed health care in many important ways over time.
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A thesis should be narrow enough to cover in the space available. Narrowing "technology" to telehealth, "health care" to follow-up care, and the population to rural patients in one state gives a focused, arguable claim.

n.1: This is an announcement of the topic, and the topic is still as broad as the original.
n.2: Turning the thesis into a question removes the claim instead of narrowing it.
n.3: Adding "in many important ways" keeps the claim just as broad and vague.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: In Carmen's formal outline, a main point is labeled I. and its first supporting idea is labeled A. How should she label a specific detail that supports idea A?
o: II.
B.
a.
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A formal outline moves from broad to specific as I., A., 1., a. A detail supporting a capital-letter point therefore takes an Arabic numeral: 1.

n.0: II. marks the next main point at the highest level of the outline.
n.1: B. would mark a second supporting idea at the same level as A., not a detail beneath A.
n.3: Lowercase a. is the next level down, used for a detail under a numbered point such as 1.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: A student is building a formal outline for a paper on nurse burnout. Place the outline labels in order from the broadest level to the most specific, starting with the broadest.
o: I.
a.
A.
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A formal outline uses Roman numerals (I.) for main points, capital letters (A.) for supporting ideas, Arabic numerals (1.) for details under those ideas, and lowercase letters (a.) for the most specific subpoints.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Jordan is drafting the thesis for an argumentative essay on hospital visiting hours. Which qualities would make his thesis statement effective? Select all that apply.
o: It makes a specific claim that a reader could dispute
It is narrow enough to support in the essay's length
It previews the main points the essay will develop
It states a fact that most readers already accept
It poses a question for the essay to explore
It opens with "In this essay, I will discuss"
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: An effective thesis is one sentence that states a specific, focused, arguable claim and often previews the main points. It must also be narrow enough to develop fully in the space available.

n.3: A widely accepted fact gives the essay nothing to argue.
n.4: A question is not a thesis; the thesis answers the question with a position.
n.5: An announcement names the topic but takes no position, so it is not a thesis.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Imani is planning the overall structure of an essay on community health fairs. Place the parts of the essay in the order they usually appear, starting with the first.
o: A conclusion that restates the thesis in new words
Body paragraphs that each develop one main point
Background on the topic
A hook that captures the reader's interest
The thesis statement
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: The introduction opens with a hook, gives background, and ends with the thesis. The body paragraphs follow, each with a topic sentence linked to the thesis. The conclusion restates the thesis in new words and sums up, with no new evidence.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: While revising, Malik notices that his conclusion introduces a new statistic about hospital costs that appears nowhere else in his essay. What is the best revision?
o: Move the statistic to a body paragraph and restate the thesis instead
Add two more statistics so the conclusion fully develops the point
Keep the statistic so the essay ends with its strongest new evidence
Change the statistic into a question to leave readers thinking
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A conclusion restates the thesis in new words and sums up; it should not introduce new evidence. Evidence belongs in a body paragraph that supports the related point.

n.1: Adding more new evidence makes the problem worse by turning the conclusion into another body paragraph.
n.2: New evidence in the conclusion is undeveloped and breaks the conclusion's job of wrapping up.
n.3: Rewording the statistic as a question still introduces new material in the conclusion and leaves the evidence unsupported.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Rachel's thesis states that community gardens improve neighborhood health by increasing access to fresh produce, encouraging exercise, and building social ties. Which topic sentence best fits her second body paragraph?
o: Friendships formed in community gardens can last for years.
Many cities have started community gardens in empty lots.
Community gardens make fresh produce easier for families to get.
Community gardens also give residents a reason to stay active.
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Body paragraphs usually follow the order of the points previewed in the thesis. The second point is exercise, so the second body paragraph's topic sentence should introduce physical activity.

n.0: Social ties are the thesis's third point, so this belongs to the third body paragraph.
n.1: This is general background that does not develop any of the thesis's three points.
n.2: Access to produce is the thesis's first point, so it belongs to the first body paragraph.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which working thesis needs revision because it states a fact rather than an arguable claim?
o: Bike lanes are the most cost-effective way for cities to cut traffic injuries.
Twelve-hour nursing shifts do more harm than good for patient safety.
Requiring a CPR course for graduation would make high schools safer places.
The CDC recommends that adults get at least seven hours of sleep each night.
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A thesis must take a position that a reader could dispute. What the CDC recommends can be checked in a single source, so this sentence reports a fact and leaves the essay nothing to argue. The other three make judgments (more harm than good, most cost-effective, would make schools safer) that a writer would have to support.

n.0: Calling bike lanes "the most cost-effective" option is an evaluation that others could challenge with other measures, so it is arguable.
n.1: Whether long shifts do "more harm than good" is a judgment that readers could dispute, so it is an arguable claim.
n.2: Whether a CPR requirement "would make" schools safer is a debatable prediction about a policy, so it is arguable.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Ana's peer reviewer leaves two comments: (1) "Your second paragraph doesn't connect to your thesis," and (2) "You wrote 'effect' where you mean 'affect.'" Which statement correctly classifies the work these comments call for?
o: Both comments call for revising, since both change the draft.
Comment 1 calls for revising, and comment 2 calls for editing.
Comment 1 calls for editing, and comment 2 calls for revising.
Both comments call for proofreading, since both point out errors.
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Step 1: a paragraph that does not support the thesis is a content and organization problem, so fixing it is revising. Step 2: choosing affect instead of effect is a word-usage correction at the sentence level, so fixing it is editing.

n.0: Any fix changes the draft, but a usage error like affect/effect is corrected in editing, not revising.
n.2: This swaps the two stages: connecting a paragraph to the thesis is revising, and fixing a word error is editing.
n.3: Proofreading is the last check for typos; reworking a paragraph so it supports the thesis is revising.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: For a paper on sleep and memory, Gabriela restates one paragraph from a journal article in her own words and her own sentence structure, keeping it about the same length as the original. What has she written, and does it need a citation?
o: A paraphrase, and it needs no citation
A summary, and it needs a citation
A direct quotation, and it needs a citation
A paraphrase, and it needs a citation
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A paraphrase restates a specific passage in the writer's own words and sentence structure at about the same length. Because the ideas still belong to the source, a paraphrase must be cited.

n.0: Changing the words does not make the ideas hers; a paraphrase without a citation is plagiarism.
n.1: A summary condenses the main ideas and is much shorter than the original; Gabriela kept the passage about the same length.
n.2: A direct quotation uses the source's exact words in quotation marks; Gabriela used her own words.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which statement could a student include in a health science paper without a citation because it counts as common knowledge?
o: Researcher Dana Kim's finding that 38% of new nurses leave within two years
A hospital report's estimate of the average cost of each patient fall
Dr. Omar Hale's argument that nurses need longer breaks during shifts
The fact that the heart pumps blood through the body's blood vessels
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Common knowledge is widely known, undisputed information that readers could find in many general sources, such as the heart pumping blood. It does not need a citation.

n.0: A specific statistic from one researcher's study is that researcher's finding and must be cited.
n.1: A cost estimate from a particular report is specific data from a source and must be cited.
n.2: An argument made by a named expert is that person's idea, so using it requires a citation even if it is paraphrased.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Ms. Ortiz is grading research papers for a nursing prerequisite course. Which situation in a student's paper is an example of plagiarism?
o: Quoting a sentence word for word with quotation marks and a citation
Using another writer's idea in her own words without naming the source
Summarizing an article's main points in her own words with a citation
Stating that the skeleton supports the body without giving a citation
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Plagiarism is presenting another person's words or ideas as your own. Rewording an idea does not make it yours, so a borrowed idea without credit to its source is plagiarism.

n.0: Exact words in quotation marks with a citation give full credit, which is correct use of a source.
n.2: A summary in the writer's own words with a citation credits the source properly.
n.3: That the skeleton supports the body is common knowledge, which needs no citation.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Jamal is paraphrasing a point from page 47 of a 2022 journal article by Maria Rivera in Nursing Today. His instructor requires APA style. Which in-text citation is formatted correctly?
o: (Rivera 47)
(Rivera, p. 47)
(Nursing Today, 2022, p. 47)
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: APA is an author-date style: the author's last name, a comma and the year, with the page (p. 47) added when the citation points to a specific part of the source: (Rivera, 2022, p. 47).

n.1: Author and page number with no year and no comma is MLA's author-page format, used mainly in the humanities.
n.2: APA is an author-date style, so the year must follow the author's name; a citation with only the author and page is incomplete.
n.3: APA in-text citations name the author, not the journal; a title stands in only when a source has no author, and this article has one.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Original sentence: "Frequent handwashing is the single most effective way to stop the spread of infection in hospitals." Which version, with a citation added, is an acceptable paraphrase?
o: Frequent handwashing is the most effective way to stop infection from spreading in hospitals.
In hospitals, the best way to keep infections from spreading is for staff to wash their hands often.
Frequent hand cleaning is the single most useful way to halt the spread of infection in hospitals.
Hospitals should place handwashing stations in every patient room to cut infection rates.
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: An acceptable paraphrase keeps the original meaning but uses the writer's own words and sentence structure. This version reorders the sentence (starting with the setting) and rewords it while keeping the same idea.

n.0: This keeps almost all of the original wording and structure, which is patchwriting, a form of plagiarism even with a citation.
n.2: Swapping a few synonyms into the original sentence structure is still patchwriting.
n.3: This adds a new recommendation the original never made, so it does not restate the source's idea.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Kenji reduces a six-page article on diabetes prevention to three sentences, in his own words, that state the article's main ideas, and he cites the article. What has Kenji written?
o: A direct quotation
A summary
A paraphrase
A reference entry
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A summary gives only the main ideas of a source, in the writer's own words, and is much shorter than the original. Like a paraphrase, it must be cited.

n.0: A direct quotation reproduces the source's exact words in quotation marks; Kenji used his own words.
n.2: A paraphrase restates one specific passage at about the same length; Kenji condensed a whole article to three sentences.
n.3: A reference entry lists a source's publication details at the end of the paper; it does not restate ideas.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Which actions by a student writing a research paper count as plagiarism? Select all that apply.
o: Summarizing a study's findings in her own words with a citation
Stating without a citation that water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit
Submitting a paper written for another course without permission
Paraphrasing an expert's argument without citing the expert
Quoting a nurse's exact words in quotation marks with a citation
Copying a sentence from a website with a citation but no quotation marks
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Plagiarism includes copying exact words without quotation marks (a citation alone does not show the words are copied), using someone's ideas without credit, and reusing your own earlier work without permission.

n.0: A summary in her own words with a citation is correct use of a source.
n.1: The freezing point of water is common knowledge, which needs no citation.
n.4: Exact words in quotation marks with a citation are properly credited.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Place the steps for writing a paraphrase of a source passage in order, starting with the first.
o: Compare your version with the original to find copied wording
Write the idea from memory in your own words and structure
Read the passage until you understand its full meaning
Set the original aside so its wording is out of sight
Rewrite any phrases that still match the original
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: First understand the passage, then put it away so its wording does not creep in, then write the idea from memory in your own words and structure. Next compare your version with the original to find borrowed phrasing, and only then can you rewrite the phrases that still match. The finished paraphrase must still be cited.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Lucia wants to use one sentence, word for word, from a nursing journal in her APA-style paper. Which combination of elements must she include?
o: Quotation marks plus a reference-list entry, with no in-text citation
Quotation marks plus an in-text citation and a reference-list entry
Quotation marks plus an in-text citation, with no reference-list entry
An in-text citation and a reference-list entry, without quotation marks
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Exact words need quotation marks to show they are copied. APA then requires both an in-text citation in the body and a full entry in the reference list at the end of the paper.

n.0: Without an in-text citation, the reader cannot tell which source the quotation comes from at the point it is used.
n.2: Every source cited in the text must also appear in the reference list.
n.3: Copied words without quotation marks are presented as her own wording, which is plagiarism even with citations.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Destiny is writing a report on patient privacy laws and is deciding how to present material from her sources. In which situation is a direct quotation a better choice than a paraphrase?
o: When the writer needs to shorten a long passage
When the source's wording is especially precise
When the idea needs to be put in simpler terms
When the passage states common knowledge
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Direct quotations should be used sparingly, for wording that is powerful or so precise that rewording would lose meaning (for example, a legal definition or a memorable phrase).

n.0: Shortening a long passage to its main ideas is the job of a summary, not a quotation.
n.2: Restating an idea in simpler, clearer terms is what a paraphrase does; a quotation keeps the source's original wording.
n.3: Common knowledge needs neither quotation marks nor a citation; it can be stated in the writer's own words.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Noah is writing a report on flu vaccine safety for his health class. Which source would be the most credible for his report?
o: A CDC web page on vaccine safety updated this year
A federal fact sheet on flu vaccines published in 2009
A health magazine article quoting two family doctors
A vaccine maker's web page summarizing its own trials
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: A credible source is current, written by experts, and free of a conflict of interest. The CDC page meets all three tests; the 2009 fact sheet is outdated, the maker's page is biased, and the magazine article is a secondhand report for general readers.

n.1: It comes from an expert agency, but a 2009 fact sheet is out of date for a report on flu vaccines, which are reformulated every season.
n.2: A popular magazine article is a secondhand account written for general readers; the agency that monitors vaccine safety is a more authoritative source.
n.3: The manufacturer profits from the vaccine, so its summary of its own trials has a conflict of interest.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Original: "Patients who walk within 24 hours after surgery tend to recover faster." A student writes, "Getting patients walking within a day of surgery tends to speed their recovery," with no citation. Which statement is correct?
o: It is plagiarism, since the borrowed idea is not credited
It is patchwriting, since it keeps the original's exact wording
It is acceptable, since the claim counts as common knowledge
It is acceptable, since paraphrased ideas need no citation
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Step 1: the student changed the wording and structure, so this is a paraphrase, not copied text. Step 2: a paraphrase still uses someone else's idea, so it must be cited; without a citation it is plagiarism.

n.1: The wording and sentence structure have been changed, so this is not patchwriting; the problem is the missing citation.
n.2: A specific research finding about recovery after surgery is not common knowledge, so it needs a citation.
n.3: Paraphrases must be cited, because the idea still comes from the source.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: During morning rounds, the nurse recorded a patient's pulse of 48 beats per minute and described it in the chart as bradycardia. Based on its prefix, what does bradycardia mean?
o: A painful heartbeat
An irregular heart rate
A slow heart rate
A fast heart rate
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: brady- means slow and cardi/o means heart, so bradycardia is a slow heart rate (a pulse of 48 fits).

n.0: Pain would come from a suffix such as -algia or -dynia; brady- describes speed, not pain.
n.1: Neither brady- nor cardia refers to rhythm; an irregular rhythm is an arrhythmia.
n.3: A fast heart rate is tachycardia; tachy- means fast, the opposite of brady-.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Before lunch, a patient with diabetes felt shaky and sweaty, and a finger-stick test confirmed hypoglycemia. Based on its word parts, what does hypoglycemia mean?
o: Low blood pressure
Low blood sugar
Sugar in the urine
High blood sugar
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: hypo- means below or deficient, glyc/o means sugar, and -emia means a blood condition, so hypoglycemia is low blood sugar.

n.0: The root glyc/o means sugar, not pressure; low blood pressure is hypotension.
n.2: Sugar in the urine would use -uria (urine condition), not -emia (blood condition).
n.3: High blood sugar is hyperglycemia; hyper- (excessive) is the opposite of hypo-.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: At the pharmacy, the technician explained that the tetanus vaccine is given as an intramuscular injection in the upper arm. Based on its prefix, where is the vaccine placed?
o: Between two muscles
Beneath the skin
Within a muscle
Around a muscle
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: intra- means within, so an intramuscular injection is placed within the muscle tissue.

n.0: Between is the meaning of inter-, the look-alike prefix; intra- means within.
n.1: Beneath the skin is subcutaneous (sub- = under, cutane/o = skin).
n.3: Around is the meaning of peri- or circum-, not intra-.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: A community clinic posts a flyer for free antenatal classes on Tuesday evenings. Based on the prefix, during what period of time are the classes meant to help parents?
o: After the baby is born
During labor and delivery
In the baby's first month
Before the baby is born
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: ante- means before and natal refers to birth, so antenatal classes are for the period before the baby is born (the same meaning as prenatal).

n.0: After birth would be postnatal; post- means after.
n.1: ante- means before, not during; during would use intra-.
n.2: The newborn period is neonatal (neo- = new), not antenatal.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: The cardiologist examined the pericardium for signs of infection after the patient's chest surgery. Based on its prefix, where is the pericardium located?
o: Around the heart
Beside the heart
Within the heart
Below the heart
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: peri- means around and cardi/o means heart, so the pericardium is the sac that surrounds the heart.

n.1: Beside is a meaning of para-, the look-alike prefix; peri- means around.
n.2: Within would use endo- or intra- (the endocardium lines the inside of the heart).
n.3: Below would use sub- or hypo-, not peri-.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: After running a race on a 95-degree afternoon, a runner collapsed and was treated in the medical tent for hyperthermia. Based on its word parts, what does hyperthermia mean?
o: Abnormally high body heat
Absence of body heat
Excessive loss of body water
Abnormally low body heat
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: hyper- means above or excessive and therm means heat, so hyperthermia is an abnormally high body temperature.

n.1: Absence would use a- or an- (without); hyper- means excessive.
n.2: Loss of body water is dehydration (hydr = water); the root here is therm (heat).
n.3: Abnormally low body heat is hypothermia; hypo- means below.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: A nursing student is sorting vocabulary words by prefix. Which words contain a prefix that means "not" or "without"? Select all that apply.
o: noninvasive
dysfunction
illegible
inhale
asymptomatic
antibiotic
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: a- means without (asymptomatic = without symptoms), non- means not (noninvasive = not entering the body), and il- means not (illegible = not readable).

n.1: dys- means bad, difficult or painful (dysfunction = abnormal function), not "not".
n.3: In inhale, in- means into (breathe in), not "not".
n.5: anti- means against (antibiotic = against life, here bacteria), not "not".

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: The patient learned to give herself insulin with a pen that delivers a subcutaneous injection into the abdomen. Based on the prefix, where is the insulin placed?
o: Upon the skin
Into a vein
Across the skin
Beneath the skin
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: sub- means under or below and cutane/o means skin, so a subcutaneous injection goes beneath the skin.

n.0: Upon or over is epi- (as in epidermis), not sub-.
n.1: Into a vein is intravenous; the root here is cutane/o (skin), not ven/o (vein).
n.2: Across or through the skin is trans- (as in transdermal).

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: Before discharge, the nurse reviewed the postoperative care instructions with the patient's family. Based on the prefix, when are these instructions meant to be followed?
o: Before the surgery
Between two surgeries
During the surgery
After the surgery
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: post- means after, so postoperative care is the care given after an operation.

n.0: Before surgery is preoperative; pre- means before.
n.1: Between is the meaning of inter-, not post-.
n.2: During surgery is intraoperative; intra- means within.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: A lab report described the patient's red blood cells as macrocytic. Using both the prefix and the root, what does macrocytic describe?
o: Cells that are smaller than normal
More cells than normal
Cells that are larger than normal
Fewer cells than normal
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: Step 1: macro- means large. Step 2: cyt/o means cell. Macrocytic therefore describes cells that are larger than normal.

n.0: Smaller than normal would be microcytic; micro- means small, the opposite of macro-.
n.1: macro- refers to size, not number; many is multi- or poly-.
n.3: A shortage of cells would use the suffix -penia (deficiency), not macro-.

Vocabulary & the Writing Process.q: A patient was diagnosed with hemiplegia and began a rehabilitation program with a physical therapist three times a week. Based on its word parts, what does hemiplegia mean?
o: Paralysis on one side of the body
Paralysis caused by a brain bleed
Paralysis affecting both of the legs
Paralysis of all four of the limbs
Vocabulary & the Writing Process.w: hemi- means half and -plegia means paralysis, so hemiplegia is paralysis of one half (one side) of the body.
